papers.title: A frontier machine intelligence for human neuroimaging
papers.abstract: Medical imaging is essential for diagnosing disease, guiding treatment and monitoring patients over time. Although artificial intelligence has advanced image interpretation, existing medical models often address restricted tasks, while general-purpose proprietary models lack access to private clinical imaging required to achieve medical expertise. Developing models that can interpret complex examinations and communicate their findings in the context of clinical decisions remains a major challenge. Here, we show that Neuro-VL, a vision-language model trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care, can interpret complete imaging examinations and engage in natural language conversations about their findings. Across internal and international datasets, Neuro-VL outperformed frontier general-purpose and specialized medical models in diagnosing, localizing, and describing abnormalities, as well as generating comprehensive radiology reports. The model also compared serial examinations to assess disease progression and more reliably resisted misleading clinical assumptions than leading frontier models from OpenAI and Google. These results extend health system learning beyond individual predictions to interactive image interpretation and longitudinal disease monitoring. They demonstrate how the collective clinical experience of health systems can be used to develop medical AI with specialized expertise and broad clinical capabilities.

papers.title: Fear of Memorizing Objects: End-to-End Zero-Shot Model-Based Object Detection
papers.abstract: This paper presents FOMO (Fear of Memorizing Objects), an end-to-end trainable transformer-based architecture for zero-shot model-based object detection. Existing approaches typically follow a proposal-and-match pipeline: target-agnostic mask proposals are generated and then matched to template features in a set of loosely coupled stages, making them susceptible to fragmented proposals in clutter and degraded matching under occlusions. FOMO elegantly replaces this paradigm by injecting object template information early in the detection pipeline: Bidirectional attention between learnable latent tokens, multi-view CAD templates, and query image features produces object-aware image features and conditioned queries which are subsequently decoded into bounding-box and confidence predictions. We train FOMO on Clutter6D, a novel large-scale synthetic dataset with over 500k images featuring more than 10k diverse object models rendered in highly cluttered scenes with multiple instances and varying occlusion levels, which addresses the limited object diversity and lack of realistic dense clutter in existing datasets for training zero-shot multi-instance algorithms. In true zero-shot fashion, FOMO achieves 54.2 mAP on BOP-Classic-Core at 0.23 s per image, ranking second overall with 3.8 pp difference to the top method while being more than 7x faster. Throughout comprehensive ablation studies we investigate and verify architectural design choices.

Accurate object detection is a fundamental computer vision task. It promotes subsequent tasks such as 6D pose estimation and tracking [42, 5, 50], and downstream robotic applications such as object grasping and manipulation [47, 37].

Accurate object detection is a fundamental computer vision task. It promotes subsequent tasks such as 6D pose estimation and tracking [42, 5, 50], and downstream robotic applications such as object grasping and manipulation [47, 37].

In literature, two contrastive paradigms exist: On the one end is conventional object detection, where algorithms are trained on annotated data with pre-defined target objects required during training (e.g., [43, 5, 42, 61]). On the other end of the spectrum are class-agnostic methods that learn a generic definition of objects (e.g., [14, 56]). An integrative link between the two opposing concepts can be described as prompt-able conditioned detection: One stream of literature investigates text-based prompts, also referred to as open vocabulary detection (e.g., [40, 17, 36, 33, 57]). Yet, text is inherently ambiguous for semantically similar objects (e.g., the prompt “shoe” describes an object category and not a specific instance — i.e., it does not distinguish between a blue and a red shoe), and many manufactured objects lack canonical names, motivating visual prompts. Instead, in this work we focus on model-based zero-shot object detection, where the CAD model of a target object is only required during inference to generate object-specific features which condition the detection estimation. The creation of these object descriptors is usually referred to as onboarding, where pre-defined viewpoints of the 3D model are rendered to produce object-specific 2D templates. State-of-the-art approaches (e.g., [38, 7, 35, 15]) further introduce three subsequent stages – proposal generation, embedding, and matching: First, candidate proposals are generated from a query image, often with Grounding DINO [33] or SAM [30]. Then, the proposals and the object templates are encoded, usually by a vision foundation model. Finally, features are matched using a similarity metric to produce predictions for all target objects.

Second, the discrete proposal–encoding–matching cascade prevents end-to-end learning, and errors introduced early propagate downstream. Furthermore, similarity thresholds are subject to careful tuning and brittle under sim-to-real shifts. Last but not least, mask-based proposals implicitly restrict bounding boxes to a modal format (i.e., reduced to visible object parts).

To overcome these drawbacks we introduce FOMO (Fear of Memorizing Objects), to the best of our knowledge the first single-stage, end-to-end trainable detector for model-based zero-shot object detection conditioned on rendered templates. FOMO elegantly redefines proposal matching with a unified architecture that injects template information into the image representation before decoding boxes, alleviating the aforementioned restrictions (Fig. 1(a)). papers.title: Cumulant dynamics of the ferromagnetic dipolar XY model
papers.abstract: We study the second-order truncated cumulant dynamics for the preparation of dynamical states in the dipolar ferromagnetic XY model on the square lattice for system sizes up to linear size L = 60. The observations lead to a transparent picture in which a coherent region of finite extent and finite magnetization forms, which is possible even for diabatic but sufficiently slow ramps. These two scales are functions of the ramp constant, the initial entropy of the system, and time. Our findings put strong requirements on future experiments addressing dipolar XY equilibrium physics in bigger system sizes.

The Mermin–Wagner theorem forbids the spontaneous breaking of a continuous symmetry such as U⁡(1)U(1) at finite temperature in two dimensions for sufficiently short-ranged interactions. For couplings decaying as a power law 1/rα1/r^{\alpha}, the theorem does not apply for α<4\alpha<4 [7]. Addressing the issue of off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO) with dipolar interactions (α=3\alpha=3) has only recently become possible experimentally: Chen et al. [5] hold arrays of Rydberg atoms in optical tweezers [3] whose resonant dipolar exchange between two Rydberg levels implements a two-dimensional X​YXY model. Arrays consisting of up to N=100N=100 atoms were prepared in a Néel-like product state in a strong staggered magnetic field, which was ramped down consequently in a near-adiabatic fashion. Chen et al. measured the site-resolved in-plane correlator Cx​x​(d)C^{xx}\!\left(d\right), which was seen to flatten out to the largest accessible separations on a time scale of t∼1−2​μt\sim 1-2\,\mus. The system was however unable to maintain this plateau at later times, leading to a profile which decays approximately linearly at t>5​μt>5\,\mus. The elementary excitations have been characterized separately by quench spectroscopy [6].

The equilibrium properties of the ferromagnetic dipolar X​YXY model are under very good theoretical control. Linear spin wave theory (LSWT) gives a quantitatively accurate description at low enough temeperatures [13]. Sbierski et al. [15] used quantum Monte Carlo simulations to obtain the thermodynamic phase diagram and its critical properties. They also simulated the experimental system, and found that a plateau of the experimentally observed magnitude cannot occur in equilibrium at the initial entropy and size of the experiment. Linear spin wave theory (LSWT) gives a quantitatively accurate description at low enough temeperatures [13]. Sbierski et al. [15] used quantum Monte Carlo simulations to obtain the thermodynamic phase diagram and its critical properties. They also simulated the experimental system, and found that a plateau of the experimentally observed magnitude cannot occur in equilibrium at the initial entropy and size of the experiment. The linearly decaying curve at later times, by contrast, was found to be compatible with quantum Monte Carlo simulations and its unusual shape is explained by the open boundary conditions that matter strongly for the linear system size, L=10L=10.

In this work we investigate the dynamics of the preparation protocol and go to larger system sizes (L∼60L\sim 60), which are becoming experimentally available. Because it is not possible to obtain exact dynamics for a large quantum system at long times, approximations are inevitable: We use a second-order cumulant truncation for the spin dynamics [8, 1, 14, 10], which propagates the one- and two-point functions and discards the connected three-point function. This has an 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{2}\right) memory cost and an 𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{3}\right) operation cost scaling, bringing lattices of size L∼60L\sim 60 within reach. We will establish which conservation laws survive the truncation, though the full dynamics at large times is quantitatively questionable. Qualitative features are however robust, from which we can deduce a transparent model and which predicts that there is a certain length scale over which the system is coherent and has a finite spontaneous magnetization (see Fig. 1). Outside this region the correlations are paramagnetic and decay therefore in dipolar fashion. The coherence length and the spontaneous magnetization are set by the initial entropy, the ramp constant, and the time. Our findings imply that equilibrium physics can only be studied if the duration of experiment can be extended significantly.

The paper is organized as follows. Section II defines the model and discusses its phase diagram. Section III discusses the initial state preparation. Section IV derives the second-order cumulant equations. Section V shows the results and interprets their physical meaning. Section VI records the conservation laws and positivity violations of the cumulant dynamics. Section VII addresses the issue of the spectrum obtained through dynamically prepared states, and, finally, we conclude in Sec. VIII.

papers.title: Development of millikelvin scintillation photodetectors with CUPID
papers.abstract: CUPID is a next-generation tonne-scale cryogenic experiment that will search for the neutrinoless double beta decay $(0\nu\beta\beta)$ of $^{100}$Mo. It will be located at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory (Italy) and will employ the cryogenic calorimetric technique to reconstruct the energy deposited in Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ crystals, in which the isotope of interest is embedded. Preliminary measurements have been performed with the CUPID VSTT (Vertical Slice Test Tower), a prototype tower designed to test the detectors' response and the apparatus' mechanical and thermal stability. In addition, a key objective was to demonstrate the improved performance of germanium-based cryogenic light detectors. In CUPID, light detection is used for both particle identification and pile-up rejection. Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ is a scintillating crystal, enabling particle identification by exploiting the dependence of light yield on particle type. This requires collecting the Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ scintillation light, peaking at $\sim$600 nm, with a $\sim$300 $\mu$m-thick high-purity germanium wafer placed next to the crystal. The wafer is also equipped with concentric Al electrodes biased at a few tens of volts. This bias improves the signal-to-noise ratio by an order of magnitude thanks to the Neganov-Trofimov-Luke effect. This work presents preliminary results on the performance of the VSTT light detectors and of its Optical Injection System.

papers.title: Spin Structure Factor of the classical Ising Model on the Centered Pyrochlore Lattice
papers.abstract: We present the spin structure factor of the Ising model on the centered pyrochlore lattice. Generalizing Henley's method [Phys. Rev. B 71, 014424] to the case of inequivalent center and vertex spins, we obtain spin correlation functions that are in excellent agreement with Monte Carlo results and can capture sharp and broadened pinch points, also at finite temperature. Our approach can be extended to other centered lattice structures in classical frustrated magnetism.

Geometrical frustration can prevent magnetic ordering giving rise to extensively degenerate ground-states governed by local constraints. A prominent example is spin ice, realized in several rare-earth pyrochlore oxides, and implemented in its simplest form at the classical level by taking Ising spins on the pyrochlore lattice [8, 23]. Its two-in–two-out constraint admits a description in terms of an emergent Coulomb phase with a divergence-free field showing algebraic correlations and featuring characteristic pinch points in the structure factor. Violations of this constraint carry emergent gauge charge in the form of magnetic monopoles [3, 4].

A prominent example is spin ice, realized in several rare-earth pyrochlore oxides, and implemented in its simplest form at the classical level by taking Ising spins on the pyrochlore lattice [8, 23]. Its two-in–two-out constraint admits a description in terms of an emergent Coulomb phase with a divergence-free field showing algebraic correlations and featuring characteristic pinch points in the structure factor. Violations of this constraint carry emergent gauge charge in the form of magnetic monopoles [3, 4].

The centered pyrochlore lattice extends this framework by placing an additional spin at the center of every tetrahedron, increasing the number of sublattices from four to six. This geometry occurs in the metal-organic framework Mn(ta)2, where (ta) denotes the 1,2,3-triazolate ligand [6, 17]. As opposed to traditional spin-ice physics, competition between center–vertex and vertex–vertex exchange interactions allows charged tetrahedral configurations to enter the ground-state manifold. For the Ising model, the ground-state phase diagram contains a monopole fluid [17], in which the vertex spins on the pyrochlore lattice sites obey the 3−13-1 rule, and the center spin aligns with the minority spin.

This raises a concrete question: how do the local constraints and the additional center-spin fluctuations determine the spin structure factor? In this work, we provide a unified framework, valid for spin-ice as well as for the monopole fluid, to calculate vertex–vertex, center–vertex, and center–center correlations at zero and finite temperature using exact conditional identities together with a self-consistent Gaussian approximation building on Henley’s projector method [9]. In fact, the spin correlation function in the monopole fluid is known exactly. Comparisons with Monte Carlo simulations test the quantitative accuracy of this description near γ=1\gamma=1. For smaller coupling ratios, we extend the construction to a three-level description which improves agreement with Monte Carlo results over the two-level approximation to higher temperatures.

papers.title: Open Vision Banana: A Fully Open Recipe for Generative Visual Perception
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that pretrained image generators encode real-world understanding beyond image synthesis. Vision Banana exploits this by framing vision tasks as conditional image editing. However, its data, weights, code, and implementation details are not public. We present Open Vision Banana (OVB), a fully open and reproducible recipe for converting pretrained generators into unified multi-task perception systems. Our analyses identify the design choices that matter most for generalization, including color encoding, prompt design, parameter adaptation, and task balancing. These choices interact, so individually helpful choices can hurt when combined with others. Starting from 4B and 9B parameter open-weight base models and using 2.1M-3.8M training pairs from public datasets, OVB surpasses Vision Banana's reported Cityscapes zero-shot performance (73.9 vs. 69.9 mIoU) and rivals state-of-the-art affine-invariant depth estimators. Its non-zero-shot variants come within five points of Vision Banana on referring and reasoning segmentation but remain further behind on instance segmentation. All models largely retain the base model's image-editing abilities. With legend ensembling, we introduce a test-time scaling method for generator-based perception. It segments an image under several class-color legends and fuses the results by majority vote, correcting unstable color-class bindings and improving mIoU by up to 8.7 points on Cityscapes and 15.0 points on COCO-Object without retraining. We release the dataset construction and processing pipeline, the training and evaluation code, as well as the final, intermediate, and ablation checkpoints. Project website: https://openvisionbanana.github.io

Image generation models have become increasingly capable of producing realistic and coherent visual content [44, 102]. A growing line of work argues that this capability reflects general visual understanding that can be utilized for perception tasks [40, 39, 124, 35].

To derive this recipe, we systematically study the design choices that turn an image generator into a perception model. As shown in Fig. 1, the analysis spans the type and composition of training data, target representations and prompt design, the choice of parameters to adapt, and inference-time readout (decoding generated RGB raw output to task specific final format).

Our experiments show that these choices have large effects and can depend on one another. A model may locate the right region yet score poorly because it paints the wrong color or breaks an output convention. In particular, low-level decisions such as the palette and prompt wording strongly affect accuracy. papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). NISP spectroscopy of gravitational arcs and multiple images
papers.abstract: Applications of strong gravitational lensing in astrophysics and cosmology critically depend on building reliable strong lensing models, which require accurate measurements of on-sky positions of multiple images and of the redshifts of the background sources from which they originate. In this context, Euclid is a unique facility, as it simultaneously provides high-resolution multi-band photometric imaging and slitless spectroscopy for an unprecedentedly large sample of gravitational lenses, most of which are newly discovered. In this work, we exploit Euclid slitless spectroscopic data to determine the redshifts of four spatially extended lensed sources, and to reconstruct emission-line images. Specifically, two of the target sources are lensed into giant arcs by the massive galaxy clusters SPT-CLJ0411$-$4819 ($z_\mathrm{d}=0.424$, where "d" denotes the lensing deflector) and Abell 2280 ($z_\mathrm{d}=0.326$). The third system is a quadruply imaged active galactic nucleus (AGN) candidate strongly lensed by a massive galaxy at $z_\mathrm{d}=0.68$, while the fourth is a galaxy-scale Einstein ring produced by a lens galaxy at $z_\mathrm{d}=0.235$. This work represents a proof of concept for the exploitation of Euclid slitless spectroscopic data in the study of strong gravitational lensing, providing one of the first determinations of spectroscopic redshifts for strongly lensed features from NISP spectra. These results demonstrate the feasibility of applying the same methodology to the very large sample of gravitational lenses that Euclid has started to discover and is expected to identify over the course of the mission.

Strong gravitational lensing is one of the most powerful techniques for probing the inner total mass distribution of galaxies and galaxy clusters (Lagattuta et al. 2026; Rihtaršič et al. 2026; Beauchesne et al. 2026; Cerny et al. 2026; Acebron et al. 2025; Vegetti et al. 2024; Patel et al. 2024; Bergamini et al. 2023; Diego et al. 2023; Caminha et al. 2023; Mahler et al. 2023; Allingham et al. 2023; Jauzac et al. 2021; Meneghetti et al. 2020; Zitrin et al. 2020; Richard et al. 2015, e.g.,), as well as for studying the physical properties of magnified (up to several orders of magnitude) high-redshift galaxies (Newman et al. 2026; Vanzella et al. 2026; Messa et al. 2026; Meštrić et al. 2022; Bradač et al. 2025; Adamo et al. 2024; Castellano et al. 2023, e.g.,). Moreover, strong lensing can provide competitive estimates of cosmological parameter values (e.g., H0H_{0}, Ωm\Omega_{\rm m}, ΩΛ\Omega_{\Lambda}) by exploiting the ratio of the angular diameter distances of multiply-lensed sources at different redshifts (Caminha et al. 2022; Magaña et al. 2018; Acebron et al. 2017; Jullo et al. 2010) and the measured time delays between multiple images of time-variable background sources (Suyu et al. 2026; Grillo et al. 2024).

The robustness of strong lensing models critically depends on precise measurements of the positions of the largest possible sample of multiple images associated with distinct background sources, which provide the primary constraints on the lens mass distribution, as well as on accurate spectroscopic determinations of the lens and source redshifts, from which the relevant cosmological distances can be inferred. In this context, the spectro-photometric data provided by the Euclid space telescope represent an unprecedented dataset for strong lensing studies (Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. 2026b; Euclid Collaboration: Walmsley et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Bergamini et al. 2026, e.g.).

papers.title: U(1)-Symmetric Spin SYK Models: Ordering, Chaos, and Transport
papers.abstract: The Sachdev--Ye--Kitaev (SYK) model provides an analytically controlled setting for strongly interacting quantum dynamics and holography, but its fermionic formulation leads to nonlocal encoding overheads on qubit-based quantum processors. We study a U(1)-symmetric spin analogue of the complex SYK model, constructed from random charge-conserving $q$-spin interactions that are native to a qubit Hilbert space. In the large-$N$, large-$q$ limit, the model reproduces the leading saddle-point structure of complex fermionic SYK under the identification of chemical potential with magnetic field and charge density with magnetization. We investigate the finite-$N$, finite-$q$ regime using exact diagonalization. A U(1)-invariant ordering susceptibility increases with system size for $q = 2, 4$ but decreases for $q = 6$, while bulk-spectrum level statistics are consistent with the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble at half filling and the Gaussian unitary ensemble in the adjacent magnetization sector. We further construct coupled-cluster chains and obtain domain-wall dynamics consistent with diffusive magnetization transport in a small-cluster regime accessible to matrix-product-state simulations. These results establish analytical benchmarks and finite-size signatures of ordering, quantum chaos, and magnetization transport in U(1)-symmetric spin-SYK models, and they motivate quantum simulation of the low-temperature, large-system regime, which remains difficult for classical methods.

papers.intro:
The Sachdev–Ye–Kitaev (SYK) model provides a paradigmatic setting in which strongly interacting quantum dynamics, many-body quantum chaos, and aspects of holography can be studied analytically [1, 2, 3]. In its complex-fermion formulation, the model consists of NN fermionic degrees of freedom with all-to-all random qq-body interactions. At large NN, its correlation functions and thermodynamics are governed by self-consistent saddle-point equations, while at large qq these equations simplify further [2, 4]. Closely related complex-SYK models display a conserved U⁡(1)U(1) charge, nontrivial thermoelectric transport, and thermodynamic structures with direct analogues in charged black-hole systems [5, 4, 6, 7]. The Schwarzian mode, a low-energy collective mode associated with approximate time-reparametrization symmetry, and the maximal-chaos bound provide the standard bridge to nearly-AdS2 quantum gravity [8, 9, 10].

At large NN, its correlation functions and thermodynamics are governed by self-consistent saddle-point equations, while at large qq these equations simplify further [2, 4]. Closely related complex-SYK models display a conserved U⁡(1)U(1) charge, nontrivial thermoelectric transport, and thermodynamic structures with direct analogues in charged black-hole systems [5, 4, 6, 7]. The Schwarzian mode, a low-energy collective mode associated with approximate time-reparametrization symmetry, and the maximal-chaos bound provide the standard bridge to nearly-AdS2 quantum gravity [8, 9, 10].

This analytical control also makes SYK an attractive target for quantum simulation [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17]. At the same time, its fermionic formulation creates a practical obstacle on qubit-based hardware: standard fermion-to-qubit encodings convert generic fermionic interaction terms into Pauli strings whose support can grow with system size, contributing substantially to circuit depth and gate cost [11, 12]. For complex SYK, each qq-body term together with its conjugate maps under the Jordan–Wigner encoding to 2q2^{q} Pauli strings of weight up to O⁡(N)O(N), reduced to O⁡(q​log⁡N)O(q\log N) by the Bravyi–Kitaev encoding [18, 19]. A spin or hard-core-boson formulation avoids this particular nonlocal encoding, since each term of the spin model introduced below expands into the same number of Pauli strings, all of weight exactly qq. The key question is whether the SYK-like physics of interest remains accessible in the spin model.

Here we study a U⁡(1)U(1)-symmetric spin analogue of complex SYK. Spin and hard-core-boson relatives of SYK have a substantial history: hard-core bosonic all-to-all models, including the q=4q=4 member of the family studied here, display glassy behavior, while more recent spin-SYK constructions exhibit strong quantum chaos and SYK-like thermodynamic behavior in appropriate regimes [20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26]. In the model we consider, each cluster contains NN spin-1/21/2 degrees of freedom with random charge-conserving qq-body interactions, and multiple clusters can be coupled into a one-dimensional chain. The conserved quantity is total magnetization, which plays the role of fermionic charge. This construction is useful for three complementary reasons. First, it admits analytically controlled limits connected to complex SYK. Second, at finite NN and qq it supports nontrivial many-body phenomena including spin ordering and quantum-chaotic spectra. Third, coupled clusters support conserved-charge transport and provide a setting in which entanglement growth can limit classical tensor-network methods. Related SYK-chain constructions display diffusive transport, spatial scrambling, and nontrivial entanglement dynamics [27, 28, 5, 29].

The large-NN and large-qq limits serve as analytical benchmarks. At leading order in the large-qq expansion, the spin model inherits the saddle-point structure of complex SYK, with magnetic field playing the role of chemical potential and magnetization per spin corresponding to fermionic charge density measured relative to half filling. The precise extent to which this correspondence survives at finite NN and finite qq is therefore an important question. In particular, glassiness can obstruct the self-averaging saddle-point description even when spectral diagnostics continue to indicate quantum chaos. The relation between SYK-like behavior and glassiness has been analyzed both in fermionic SYK and in hard-core-boson/spin variants [20, 30, 22, 31, 32, 33], and the crossover from spin-liquid to spin-glass behavior has been studied in detail in random quantum Heisenberg magnets [34, 35, 36].

In particular, glassiness can obstruct the self-averaging saddle-point description even when spectral diagnostics continue to indicate quantum chaos. The relation between SYK-like behavior and glassiness has been analyzed both in fermionic SYK and in hard-core-boson/spin variants [20, 30, 22, 31, 32, 33], and the crossover from spin-liquid to spin-glass behavior has been studied in detail in random quantum Heisenberg magnets [34, 35, 36].

We address this finite-size regime using exact diagonalization. We use a U⁡(1)U(1)-invariant Edwards–Anderson (spin-glass) susceptibility that remains nonzero in finite systems even though U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry forces transverse one-point functions to vanish. Applied to the ground state, accessible system sizes show qualitatively different finite-size trends between q=2,4q=2,4 and q=6q=6. We separately analyze bulk-spectrum level statistics and the spectral form factor and find random-matrix behavior consistent with the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble at half filling and the Gaussian unitary ensemble in the adjacent magnetization sector. Adjacent-gap ratios and spectral form factors are standard finite-size probes of random-matrix universality in chaotic many-body systems and have been used extensively in dense and sparse SYK models [37, 38, 39, 40]. Because the ordering diagnostic is evaluated in the ground state while the level statistics probe the bulk of the spectrum, these results should be viewed as complementary.

We then turn to coupled clusters. A local magnetization imbalance can spread from cluster to cluster while the total U⁡(1)U(1) charge remains conserved. Matrix-product-state simulations of a small-cluster regime show domain-wall broadening consistent with diffusive transport, in the spirit of transport studies in generalized and coupled SYK models [27, 5, 41]. We treat this transport calculation as a proof of principle that motivates further study of the low-temperature regime, where, by the correspondence with complex SYK, one expects Planckian dynamics: relaxation and scrambling times set by β\beta, with the Lyapunov exponent approaching the chaos bound 2​π​T2\pi T [8, 2, 42, 43, 44]. Establishing this for the spin model requires an analysis of its own retarded ladder kernel, which we do not carry out here. We argue that quantum simulation is a promising route to probing this low-temperature regime.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1): Photometric-redshift pipeline overview and validation
papers.abstract: We present the pipeline design of the photometric redshift processing function for Data Release 1 (DR1) of the $Euclid$ mission, and the validation and performance of our cosmology-related products that are released as part of DR1-Foundation. The $Euclid$ mission aims to constrain the equation-of-state parameter of dark energy, $w$, to percent-level accuracy through the measurement of large-scale structure via weak gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering. As part of DR1-Foundation we release determinations of photometric redshifts (photo-$z$), corrected photometry, and object classes that are used to form the basis of the cosmological samples. The release furthermore includes estimates of the spectral energy distributions of stars and galaxies for the careful modelling of the point-spread function for weak-lensing measurement. We estimate the performance of the photo-$z$ point estimates and probability distribution functions using overlapping spectroscopic redshifts, which are weighted to match different flux-limited target samples. We find that the current performance is somewhat below mission design requirements ($40\%$ in scatter and a factor of 2 in outlier fraction) at the nominal survey depth ($I_{\rm E}<24.5$), but closely matching requirements at slightly brighter magnitudes ($I_{\rm E}<24$), consistent with pre-launch analyses and the slightly shallower external data (up to $0.3\,\mathrm{mag}$) with respect to end-of-mission expectations. Data from Rubin-LSST will help alleviate this issue by the time of the final cosmology analyses. The other cosmology-related outputs are tested to the extent that is possible with currently available comparison data. This paper is partnered by an article describing the measurement of the physical properties of galaxies for the purpose of non-cosmological science.

papers.intro:
Data Release 1 of the Euclid mission (Euclid Data Release 1 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Aussel and others 2026, DR1,) is the first major release, following the smaller Early Release Observations (Cuillandre et al. 2025) and Quick Data Releases (Euclid Collaboration: Aussel et al. 2026; Beaulieu et al. 2026, Q1 and Q2) data sets. It comprises the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) with data of the same depth as the Q1 release; the Euclid Deep Fields (EDFs), which cover the same area as Q1 but to greater depth; and numerous calibration observations, including the Euclid Auxiliary Fields (EAFs) for photo-zz and colour gradient calibration.

In this work we present an overview of the photometric redshift processing function (PHZ PF), developed by the organisation unit for photometric redshifts (OU-PHZ) and the Swiss science data centre (SDC-CH), and its output products that are released as part of DR1-Foundation. In particular, we focus on aspects that are new with respect to the Q1 pipeline (which is described in detail in Euclid Collaboration: Tucci et al. 2026, EC:T26 hereafter), the most significant difference being the availability of two of the photo-zz EAFs and the resulting implementation of the pre-launch baseline strategy (see Sect. 2.3.2 and Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025). This overview can be found in Sect. 2, along with a description of the two main tools used in the PHZ PF and developed alongside it, Phosphoros and NNPZ. The construction of the reference data sets from the EAF that are required by NNPZ is provided in Sect. 3.

DR1 represents the first opportunity to measure constraints for cosmological parameters such as the matter density, Ωm\Omega_{\rm m}, amplitude of the power spectrum, σ8\sigma_{8}, and the dark energy equation-of-state parameter, ww (Chevallier and Polarski 2001, e.g.), with Euclid data. It will mark the first weak-lensing analysis from a stage IV experiment, following the stage III weak lensing experiments, such as the Dark Energy Survey (DES, Abbott et al. 2018), the Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS, de Jong et al. 2013), and Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Programme (HSC-SSP, Aihara et al. 2018). Cosmological parameters from Euclid’s photometric data set will be measured through the combination of 22-point functions using both galaxy ellipticities and positions. They will form a so-called 3×\times2pt analysis of cosmic shear, galaxy–galaxy lensing, and galaxy clustering, as has become common in the literature (Krause et al. 2017, e.g.,). Among the key ingredients in these analyses are the redshifts of the galaxies used as probes of the large-scale structure, which rely largely on the photometric redshift (photo-zz) method (Bolzonella et al. 2000; Benítez 2000; Collister and Lahav 2004; Salvato et al. 2019, e.g.,). The statistical precision of the anticipated final-mission weak lensing measurements places requirements on the quality of such photo-zz and, in turn, requirements on the Euclid survey design and depths of the photometry (Laureijs et al. 2011).

They will form a so-called 3×\times2pt analysis of cosmic shear, galaxy–galaxy lensing, and galaxy clustering, as has become common in the literature (Krause et al. 2017, e.g.,). Among the key ingredients in these analyses are the redshifts of the galaxies used as probes of the large-scale structure, which rely largely on the photometric redshift (photo-zz) method (Bolzonella et al. 2000; Benítez 2000; Collister and Lahav 2004; Salvato et al. 2019, e.g.,). The statistical precision of the anticipated final-mission weak lensing measurements places requirements on the quality of such photo-zz and, in turn, requirements on the Euclid survey design and depths of the photometry (Laureijs et al. 2011).

The role of photo-zz in 3×\times2pt analyses is twofold: to place galaxies in meaningfully-separated bins in redshift (redshift tomography); and to calibrate the distributions in redshift of the galaxies, n⁡(z)n(z), in each bin. The first of these tasks implies requirements on the precision and accuracy of single-value best estimates for each galaxy’s redshift (‘point estimates’). These are expressed via the dispersion in the scaled redshift difference between the point estimate and spectroscopic redshift, σ⁡(δ​z)<0.05\sigma(\delta z)<0.05, and the fraction of outlier galaxies with photo-zz point estimates very different from their true redshift (|δ​z|>0.15|\delta z|>0.15), foutliers<10%f_{\rm outliers}<10\% (Amara and Réfrégier 2007; Laureijs et al. 2011); with δ​z\delta z the normalised difference, given by (zphot−zspec)/(1+zspec)(z_{\rm phot}-z_{\rm spec})/(1+z_{\rm spec}). These requirements can be similarly expressed through their redshift probability distribution functions, zzPDFs, following Euclid Collaboration: Desprez et al. (2020). These requirements are easily met in deep extra-galactic fields at the target magnitude limit of samples for cosmic shear (IE<24.5I_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}<24.5 in the case of Euclid), where high signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) data across many bands are available (Hartley et al. 2022; Weaver et al. 2022; Taylor et al. 2023, e.g.,). However, they remain a considerable challenge for the wide-field areas where the analyses are carried out (Tanaka et al. 2018; Euclid Collaboration: Desprez et al. 2020; Duncan 2022). Moreover, galaxies hosting AGN can remain hidden among the galaxy samples and will require careful treatment for the overall requirements to be met (Shirley et al. 2026).

Moreover, galaxies hosting AGN can remain hidden among the galaxy samples and will require careful treatment for the overall requirements to be met (Shirley et al. 2026).

In the second task, the requirement on the accuracy of the mean redshift for n⁡(z)n(z) in each tomographic bin is among the most stringent of all the Euclid design requirements, at δ​z/(1+z)<0.002\delta z/(1+z)<0.002. Multiple complementary strategies will be required to reach this performance, including photometric-space calibration approaches (Masters et al. 2015) and inference through angular clustering (Newman 2008). Stage III weak lensing experiments have already achieved impressive accuracy through the sophisticated application of these techniques with the support of simulated data sets (Wright et al. 2025a; d’Assignies et al. 2026; Yin et al. 2025). However, even the most tightly constrained n⁡(z)n(z) produced to date fall far from the required accuracy in stage IV experiments such as Euclid. In this paper we focus on the photo-zz performance required for the first of the tasks (presented in Sect. 4.3), while the calibration of n⁡(z)n(z) for cosmological inference will be presented in a separate paper, which will appear alongside the full Euclid DR1 release. The photo-zz point estimates for a flux-limited IE<24.5I_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}<24.5 sample are validated against the requirements in Sect. 4.1.

papers.title: Topology-Aware 4D Gaussian Splatting for Egocentric Videos
papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic scenes and objects from monocular egocentric video is crucial for embodied AI, yet existing 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) approaches struggle with everyday interactions involving topological changes, such as cutting, assembly, opening, or closing. Since 4DGS methods rely on deforming a fixed representation, events that split, merge, or reveal surfaces cause severe visual artifacts. To address this challenge, we introduce TopoEgo, the first benchmark dedicated to topological changes in egocentric video (covering fission, fusion, open, and close), alongside Topo-4DGS, a topology-aware reconstruction method. Topo4DGS jointly models part-level motion and time-varying surface support by assigning independent rigid transformations to interacting parts and dynamically activating or deactivating Gaussians as surfaces appear, disappear, or separate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Topo-4DGS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 4DGS approaches across topological changes, especially on post-event frames. Code and data will be made publicly available.

Dynamic 3D reconstruction from egocentric videos is important for robotics and AR applications, as it directly captures the physics and geometry of human-object interactions [29, 24]. However, everyday manipulation rarely involves purely rigid motion; it inherently induces complex object transformations and topological changes, such as cutting, assembling components, and opening containers (see Fig. 1 and 2). Because egocentric videos capture daily activities from the actors’ viewpoint, such events are ubiquitous. Our analysis identifies them in over 68.8%68.8\% of Ego4D [8] and over 80.0%80.0\% of EPIC-KITCHENS [6] annotated videos. Dynamically reconstructing these interactions in 3D requires more than estimating object motion: a method must determine which parts move together and adapt its geometric representation as surfaces are created, exposed, or concealed.

However, everyday manipulation rarely involves purely rigid motion; it inherently induces complex object transformations and topological changes, such as cutting, assembling components, and opening containers (see Fig. 1 and 2). Because egocentric videos capture daily activities from the actors’ viewpoint, such events are ubiquitous. Our analysis identifies them in over 68.8%68.8\% of Ego4D [8] and over 80.0%80.0\% of EPIC-KITCHENS [6] annotated videos. Dynamically reconstructing these interactions in 3D requires more than estimating object motion: a method must determine which parts move together and adapt its geometric representation as surfaces are created, exposed, or concealed.

In particular, topological events violate the persistence assumptions of Gaussian-based monocular 4D reconstruction methods in two ways. First, motion structure may change: regions that initially move together can become independent, whereas canonical deformation methods continuously deform fixed geometry [28, 26], tracking-based methods preserve primitive identities [17], and EgoGaussian [29] assigns a single rigid motion to each object. Second, surface support, i.e., the set of 3D surface locations represented by an object’s Gaussian primitives, may change as surfaces are created, exposed, or concealed, causing persistent canonical primitives to produce missing geometry or ghosting [28, 26, 17] (Fig. 1). However, topology-changing reconstruction remains largely underexplored: existing benchmarks rely on controlled capture with synchronized views or depth [19], and none systematically evaluate topological changes in real-world egocentric video.

To enable systematic evaluation of reconstruction across topological events, we introduce TopoEgo, a benchmark curated from EPIC-KITCHENS [6] and Ego4D [8], two of the largest egocentric video datasets. TopoEgo captures diverse, in-the-wild instances of fission, fusion, open, and close, spanning changes in both object connectivity and surface visibility (see Fig. 2). To address this challenging benchmark, we introduce Topo-4DGS, a topology-aware reconstruction method that explicitly models the two consequences of topological events: changes in part-level motion and variations in surface support. This leads to Topo-4DGS’s two main components. First, Motion Bifurcation enables parts that initially move together to follow independent rigid motions after an event. Second, Topological Boundary Resolution updates the represented surface support by adding or removing Gaussians as surfaces are created, exposed, or concealed.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Pushing back the borders of the invisible with Euclid. Discovery of fifteen resolved low-surface-brightness stellar systems from the Milky Way to the Local Volume
papers.abstract: We searched within the first data release of the Euclid Wide Survey (~1900 deg^2) for resolved stellar systems between distances from 10 kpc and several Mpc, using an isochrone filtering technique. We detect 15 systems that have never been resolved into stars before. Five are new discoveries, three in the Milky Way halo and two beyond the Local Group. The remaining ten are dwarf galaxies that were previously catalogued as unresolved sources in shallower ground-based surveys and lack reliable distance measures. We measured distance moduli for all 15 systems, and half-light radii, ellipticities, position angles, absolute magnitudes, and stellar masses for 14 of them. In the Milky Way halo, Ursa Minor II, at ~20 kpc, has Mv ~ +2.0 and a stellar mass of ~40 Msun, and is one of the least luminous stellar systems known. Fornax 7 is located near the tidal limit of the Fornax dwarf spheroidal galaxy and may be physically associated with it. Eridanus V lies at ~165 kpc and has a stellar mass of ~550 Msun, which places it in the region of the size-luminosity plane where globular clusters and ultra-faint dwarf galaxies overlap. Beyond the Local Group, the 12 dwarf galaxies lie at distances of 3--5.5 Mpc. Three of them reach or exceed a mean surface brightness within the half-light radius of mu_V~28 mag/arcsec^2, a regime in which almost no galaxies at these distances were previously known. Ten of them are candidate members of the M81 group: eight have three-dimensional distances from M81 smaller than or comparable to the radius of its zero-velocity surface, and two lie close to the peripheral member NGC 4236, one of which is a candidate satellite of this galaxy. These results demonstrate Euclid's transformative potential for low-surface-brightness science, enabling the study of an unprecedented range of environments from the MW halo out to the Local Volume within a single, homogeneous survey.

papers.intro:
A complete map of the satellite population of the Milky Way (MW) is a longstanding challenge in Galactic astronomy, with significant cosmological implications. While the first identifications of dwarf galaxies orbiting the MW, specifically the Sculptor and Fornax dwarfs, date back nearly a century (Shapley 1938), the field has experienced a profound renaissance over the last two decades. The advent of wide-field digital sky surveys, coupled with the development of automated detection algorithms for mining deep datasets in search of over-densities of resolved stars, has led to a rapid surge in the census of known MW satellites (Willman et al. 2005a; Willman et al. 2005b; Belokurov et al. 2007; Walsh et al. 2009; Cerny et al. 2023, e.g.,). Large-scale photometric surveys, such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (York et al. 2000, SDSS;), Panoramic Survey Telescope & Rapid Response System (Chambers et al. 2016, Pan-STARRS1;), and the Dark Energy Survey (DES Collaboration: Abbott et al. 2016, DES;), have been responsible for the majority of these recent discoveries (Belokurov et al. 2007; Laevens et al. 2015b; Laevens et al. 2015a; Bechtol et al. 2015; Koposov et al. 2015). These surveys have allowed us to probe the faintest end of the galactic luminosity function, uncovering the realm of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (Simon 2019, UFDs;)11 1 We follow the definition of Simon (2019) that denoted UFDs as those galaxies with a total luminosity L<105​L⊙L<10^{5}\,L_{\odot} or MV>−7.7M_{V}>-7.7..

In the current Λ\Lambda cold dark matter (Λ\LambdaCDM) cosmological paradigm (see Bertone & Hooper 2018; Condon & Matthews 2018; Peebles 2025, and references therein), local (z≃0z\simeq 0) dwarf galaxies are considered as the living relics of the hierarchical assembly process leading to the formation of large galaxies. Since the faintest among them appear as those whose mass budget is most dominated by dark matter (Mateo 1998; McConnachie 2012; Simon 2019), they serve as unique laboratories for addressing current small-scale challenges to the Λ\LambdaCDM model (Bullock & Boylan-Kolchin 2017).

The current census reaches approximately 50 confirmed dwarf satellites of the MW and about 550 dwarfs in the Local Volume (LV), within 6 Mpc from the Sun (Pace 2025). However, many works suggest that the total population of MW satellites remains significantly underestimated (Jethwa et al. 2018; Newton et al. 2018; Drlica-Wagner et al. 2020; Santos-Santos et al. 2026; Tan et al. 2026, e.g.), implying that the most elusive, diffuse, and distant systems have yet to be detected. The primary barrier to discovery is their extremely low surface brightness, which keeps a vast population of UFDs below the detection limits of current ground-based facilities. Beyond the MW halo, our knowledge of isolated dwarfs or of the satellite populations around different hosts in the LV is even more incomplete, given the higher distances involved, creating a significant observational bias. A telling example is offered by the Andromeda galaxy (M31), whose satellite system has been progressively extended to ever fainter dwarf members (Martin et al. 2006; Martin et al. 2013; Richardson et al. 2011; Arias et al. 2025; Smith et al. 2025; Doliva-Dolinsky et al. 2026; Sakowska et al. 2026), yet down to a brighter limit than in the MW, owing to M31’s greater distance (Doliva-Dolinsky et al. 2023). In particular, the faintest known dwarf satellite of M31 is more than four magnitudes brighter than the faintest MW satellite (Pace 2025, in MVM_{V},). This illustrates how the accessible faint end of the satellite luminosity function becomes increasingly truncated as host distance grows, leaving the faint dwarf populations in the LV largely uncharted.

Extending the study of UFDs and classical dwarfs beyond the immediate vicinity of the MW is therefore crucial to testing Λ\LambdaCDM predictions across a diverse range of host masses, morphologies, and environmental conditions. Beyond the Local Group (LG), considerable effort has been devoted in recent years to building censuses of satellites and isolated dwarfs around nearby hosts. Deep resolved-star surveys of individual groups, such as Centaurus A (Crnojević et al. 2016) and M81 (Okamoto et al. 2019; Gozman et al. 2024), and of nearby MW-mass or low-mass spirals (Carlin et al. 2016; Carlin et al. 2024; Smercina et al. 2018; Mutlu-Pakdil et al. 2024, e.g.,), have detected satellites close to the transition between classical dwarfs and UFDs, but each of them covers only the virial volume of one or a few hosts. In parallel, a growing number of isolated dwarfs in the LV has been discovered and resolved into stars (see, e.g., Jones et al. 2023; Jones et al. 2024; Karachentsev et al. 2024; Karachentsev et al. 2025, and references therein). Deep, wide-field space-based imaging, combining low-surface-brightness sensitivity with stable and homogeneous image quality, therefore offers a major opportunity to extend satellite censuses to fainter luminosities and around hosts well beyond the MW. In this context, the Euclid mission (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025) represents a transformative step forward for local low-surface brightness astronomy. Euclid’s unique combination of a vast survey area (≃\simeq14 00014\,000 deg2 at the end of the six-year mission), high spatial resolution in the visible (IEI_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}) with the VIS instrument (Euclid Collaboration: Cropper et al. 2025), and deep near-infrared (YEY_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, JEJ_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, HEH_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}) photometry with the NISP instrument (Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al. 2025), provides an unprecedented discovery space, thanks to the unrivaled sensitivity of searches based on exploring the surface density field as traced by individual resolved stars down to very faint magnitude limits. Unlike previous surveys, Euclid is uniquely positioned to bridge the gap between different scales: it possesses the sensitivity to detect the most elusive UFDs within the MW halo and the resolution required to identify dwarf galaxies by star counts at much larger distances. Furthermore, it explores large swaths of sky, making it the first optical-IR imaging space telescope operating in survey mode.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). The PHZ processing function for the physical properties of galaxies
papers.abstract: Euclid is a European Space Agency mission mapping the extragalactic sky, aiming to provide the most-accurate 3D view of the Universe at optical and near-infrared wavelengths, by measuring the photometric redshifts of billions of galaxies. Within the Euclid Consortium, this task is executed by the PHZ Organisation Unit. PHZ takes as input the multi-wavelength photometry of Euclid and ground-based data, and returns as output the source classification, photometric redshifts for the Euclid core science (i.e., cosmology), and photometric redshifts plus physical parameters and absolute magnitudes for non-cosmological science. As part of the first Euclid Data Release (DR1), we describe the details of the DR1 pipeline for non-cosmological science, along with the released data products, and their validation. The non-cosmological science data products are obtained with NNPZ, a nearest-neighbour algorithm developed within PHZ that infers the properties of each target galaxy from its closest matches, in colour-magnitude space, within a reference sample of galaxies with known redshifts and physical parameters. We built this reference sample from Euclid observations of COSMOS, one of the Euclid Auxiliary Fields, labelling each galaxy with redshifts and physical parameters derived from the COSMOS2020 multi-wavelength photometry, consistently with the Euclid core-science results. Combined with the adjustments and priors required to generalise the results across the entire extragalactic sky, this approach yields high-quality and internally consistent data products. We tested the performance using both internal metrics and comparisons to ancillary data sets (e.g., COSMOS2020, 3D-HST, and DESI) and scaling relations (e.g., the star-forming main sequence); the results are in line with expectations and pre-DR1 simulations for both the Euclid Wide Survey and Euclid Deep Fields.

papers.intro:
Euclid is a European Space Agency mission designed to map the large-scale distribution of matter in the Universe. The spacecraft carries two instruments: the visible imaging instrument (Euclid Collaboration: Cropper et al. 2025, VIS,) and the Near-Infrared (NIR) Spectrometer and Photometer (Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al. 2025, NISP,), which together provide high-resolution optical imaging and NIR imaging and spectroscopy over approximately 11 000​deg2$11\,000$\,\mathrm{deg}^{2} of the extragalactic sky, the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS). At the end of the nominal mission, the EWS will reach a uniform depth of 24.524.5 AB magnitudes in the visible band and fainter than 24.024.0 in the NIR bands (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022). Although Euclid was primarily designed to constrain dark energy and dark matter through weak gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering, the resulting data set is a substantial resource for non-cosmological science as well (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025).

At the end of the nominal mission, the EWS will reach a uniform depth of 24.524.5 AB magnitudes in the visible band and fainter than 24.024.0 in the NIR bands (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022). Although Euclid was primarily designed to constrain dark energy and dark matter through weak gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering, the resulting data set is a substantial resource for non-cosmological science as well (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025).

Achieving the mission’s full scientific potential requires photometric redshifts – or photo-zzs – for billions of galaxies. These will be used both to reconstruct the three-dimensional distribution of matter and to trace galaxy evolution across a wide range of cosmic time. To meet the required precision, Euclid incorporates multi-band photometry from ground-based surveys, including the Dark Energy Survey (Flaugher et al. 2015; DES Collaboration: Abbott et al. 2016, DES,), the Ultraviolet Near Infrared Optical Northern Survey (Gwyn et al. 2025, UNIONS,), and, in future, the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (Ivezic et al. 2008, LSST,).

The processing of these data is managed by the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS), organised into self-contained processing functions (PFs). The PHZ PF is responsible for photometric redshifts, physical parameters (PPs) of galaxies, source classification, spectral energy distribution (SED) estimation, and tomographic binning. The PPs– stellar masses, SFR, metallicities, and others – are central to the non-cosmological science cases that aim to reconstruct the assembly history of the Universe. For this purpose, PHZ developed a machine-learning algorithm, the Nearest-Neighbour Photometric Redshifts (Tanaka et al. 2018; Euclid Collaboration: Enia et al. 2024; Euclid Collaboration: Tucci et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Enia et al. 2026, NNPZ,). NNPZ estimates multi-dimensional posterior distributions of photo-zzs and PPs by searching, in colour–magnitude space, for the nearest neighbours of each target galaxy within a pre-defined reference sample of objects with known properties.

In this paper, we describe the PHZ pipeline for photometric redshifts and galaxy PPs used for the first ∼1900​deg2\sim 1900\,\mathrm{deg}^{2} of the Euclid Data Release 1 (2026). The accuracy and precision of the released data products are validated against large spectroscopic samples from external surveys, demonstrating their reliability for a broad range of astrophysical applications. This paper is structured as follows. In Sect. 2, we describe the DR1 data and the ancillary data sets used to evaluate performance. In Sect. 3, we describe the PHZ pipeline for recovering photo-zzs and PPs for non-cosmological science, and the products stored in the Euclid Archive System (Euclid Collaboration: Aussel and others 2026, EAS,). In Sect. 4, we validate the results against spectroscopic redshifts and H​α\mathrm{H}\,\alpha-estimated SFRs, while checking the relation between stellar masses and SFR, the star-forming main-sequence (SFMS). In Sect. 5, we present our conclusions.

papers.title: Singlet-triplet superconductivity from repulsive interactions in a $p$-wave magnet
papers.abstract: Motivated by recent proposals of $p$-wave magnets, which host odd-parity spin splitting, we study electrons near Van Hove singularities with local repulsive interactions. We demonstrate how the symmetry of the $p$-wave spin splitting governs the competition among instabilities. Using a parquet renormalization group (pRG) analysis of a simple one-sublattice model of a $p$-wave magnet, we find that superconductivity is the leading instability over the entire phase diagram for purely repulsive interactions. The resulting superconducting state is generically a mixture of spin-singlet and spin-triplet pairing and approaches an equal-weight mixture when $T_c$ is small compared with the energy offset between each Van Hove electron and its inversion partner. Extending the pRG analysis to a more realistic two-sublattice model, we find that superconductivity remains the leading instability, while the sublattice degree of freedom leads to a competition among various singlet-triplet pairing channels and even a finite-momentum equal-spin pair-density wave. Our mechanism applies broadly to odd-parity magnets and opens a natural route to nodal topological superconductivity.

papers.title: A self-shadowing black hole accretion disk at sub-Eddington luminosities
papers.abstract: Accretion onto black holes powers some of the most energetic sources in the Universe, yet its behaviour across the luminosity range remains poorly understood. Specifically, as the luminosity approaches the Eddington limit ($L_{\rm Edd}$), the inner accretion disk is expected to depart from the standard thin-disk solution, becoming vertically extended. The luminosity threshold and observational signatures of this transition remain, however, uncertain. We present multiwavelength spectroscopy obtained during the decay of a black hole X-ray binary outburst. At the peak ($\sim 0.2\,L_{\rm Edd}$), a cool optical and near-infrared spectrum dominated by strong recombination lines of hydrogen and He I is observed. However, as the luminosity decreases, it switches to a hot, highly irradiated, nearly featureless spectrum. This puzzling behavior reveals the emergence of a vertically extended inner disk at the outburst peak, shielding the outer regions from high-energy radiation produced near the black hole; a scenario supported by contemporaneous X-ray spectra. Observations of similar systems suggest that this phenomenon may be common among black hole accretion disks. Self-shadowing structures at luminosities well below $L_{\rm Edd}$ have major implications for black hole accretion flows and their observational properties, affecting inferred black hole spins, X-ray polarization measurements, and the physical conditions of the outer disk and its associated outflows.

papers.title: Observational constraints on CO sequestration and disk mass in the planet-hosting PDS 70 disk
papers.abstract: Exoplanets accrete gas, dust, and ice from their natal environment, setting the chemical composition of their atmospheres and interiors. The abundance of the major volatiles in disks can be used to possibly link exoplanet atmospheres to their formation location in the disk. In this work, we aim to quantify the peak CO abundance and disk mass of the PDS 70 disk, the first disk with a direct confirmation of two accreting planets in its dust cavity. We present the first detection of N$_2$H$^+$ and C$^{17}$O in this disk. The C$^{17}$O emission shows marginal statistical evidence for an azimuthal asymmetry trailing that previously seen in the continuum emission. We then compare the disk integrated fluxes of N$_2$H$^+$, CO isotopologues, and the continuum to an existing grid of thermochemical models. We find that the derived disk mass drops by a factor of $\sim 3.4$ from $0.039^{+0.067}_{-0.018}$ M$_{\odot}$ to $0.011^{+0.011}_{-0.006}$ M$_{\odot}$ if the C$^{17}$O line flux is included in the fitting procedure; the quoted intervals do not include systematic uncertainties. CO on the other hand is sequestered with an effective abundance of $(4.8^{+4.3}_{-2.7} - 17^{+8}_{-8}) \times 10^{-6}$ relative to H$_2$ in the probed disk layers after accounting for CO freeze-out and isotope selective CO photodissociation for the adopted chemical network and ionization prescription. The range in peak CO abundances reflects the uncertainty in the N$_2$H$^+$ emission, assuming either optically thin emission at 21 K or optically thick emission. Therefore, the PDS 70 planets are possibly accreting the final portion of their atmospheres from the outer disk molecular layer where CO is sequestered. Thus, CO sequestering may need to be considered when interpreting the chemical composition of planetary atmospheres.

papers.title: Quantum Hall Fabry-P\'erot Interferometry in Monolayer WSe$_2$
papers.abstract: Electronic Fabry-P\'erot interferometers provide a powerful probe of coherent quantum Hall edge transport, yet the presence of multiple spin and valley degrees of freedom in existing van der Waals material platforms can complicate their interpretation. Monolayer WSe$_2$ offers a distinct opportunity because strong spin-orbit coupling and spin-valley locking lift these degeneracies, producing intrinsically single-component Landau levels. Here we realize the first gate-defined quantum Hall Fabry-P\'erot interferometer in monolayer WSe$_2$. By continuously tuning the cavity size in a single device, we observe robust Aharonov-Bohm (AB) interference of quantum Hall edge channels across the interferometer; the observed predominance in the AB regime is consistent with a weak bulk-edge coupling ($\Delta \approx 0.034$) estimated by electrostatics. Moreover, temperature and bias dependence measurements consistently yield an edge velocity $v \approx (4.9 \pm 0.2) \times 10^4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Our results establish monolayer WSe$_2$ as a clean, flavor-resolved platform for quantum Hall interferometry and provide a foundation for future studies of single-component fractional quantum Hall states and interferometric probes of anyonic statistics in transition-metal dichalcogenides.

papers.title: Dark matter alters dwarf galaxy sizes and morphologies
papers.abstract: Dwarf galaxies are the most dark-matter-dominated systems in the Universe, serving as unique laboratories for exploring the fundamental nature of the dark sector. Although the observed diversity in dwarf galaxy sizes and morphologies suggests an interplay between dark matter and baryonic physics, this relationship has remained largely unquantified in existing models. Here, we utilize a set of novel cosmological simulations with baryons to demonstrate how dark matter physics directly drives the structural evolution of these galaxies. By comparing the same systems across cold dark matter and varied self-interacting dark matter models, we find that the evolution of the central density of dark matter significantly impacts a galaxy's half-light radius, but the signal is dependent on morphology. This causal link establishes galaxy size as a direct signature of the underlying dark matter microphysics. Our findings provide a predictive framework for decoding dark matter particle properties from galactic shapes, offering a roadmap for upcoming wide-field surveys, such as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time, to probe the dark sector through the statistical analysis of galaxy populations.

papers.title: Variations in the Extinction Curve at High Galactic Latitudes as seen by the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument
papers.abstract: The dust extinction curve, characterized by the total-to-selective extinction ratio, $R(V)$, varies with grain size and composition. Accurate $R(V)$ values are crucial for dereddening astronomical colors and understanding the interstellar medium. We measure extinction toward stars with Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) spectroscopy using a machine-learning-based relative of the "pair method," matching reddened and unreddened stars. We use XGBoost to predict stars' intrinsic colors from their spectroscopic parameters ($T_\mathrm{eff}$, $\log g$, $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]$) and subtract them from observed colors to measure reddening in combinations of the $g$, $r$, $z$, $W1$, and $W2$ bands. This approach directly measures reddening, unlike the common thermal-emission-based method of Schlegel et al. (1998; SFD). The reddening is accurate to roughly 0.02 mag in $g-r$ and $r-z$. We develop a forward model to map $g-r$ and $g-W1$ reddenings to $R(V)$ and find significant variation in $R(V)$, with $\sigma_\mathrm{NMAD}(R(V)) = 0.23$, in dusty regions ($E(g-r) > 0.1$) at high Galactic latitudes observed by DESI. In this footprint, $R(V)$ is bimodal, with modes at 2.9 and 3.4, likely due to large-spatial-scale correlations in the shape of the extinction curve combined with the relatively small number of distinct sightlines with substantial reddening. We find no strong relationship between $R(V)$ and other tracers of the interstellar medium, such as thermal emission, dust temperature, spectral emissivity index $\beta$, and $H\alpha$. However, the error in the SFD-predicted extinction correlates well with $R(V)$, implying that a single optical reddening combined with the far-infrared dust brightness can predict variations in the extinction curve.

papers.intro:
Dust is a major source of systematic uncertainty for many current and future cosmology experiments. For example, by reddening and extinguishing starlight, dust changes the measured distances to supernovae (R. Tripp 58, D. Brout & D. Scolnic 7) and imprints spurious structure on the observed distribution of galaxies [51]. This effect can limit the accuracy to which the expansion history of the universe can be measured [5], while scatter in the correction contributes to the noise budget of large-scale clustering measurements [33, 72].

This effect can limit the accuracy to which the expansion history of the universe can be measured [5], while scatter in the correction contributes to the noise budget of large-scale clustering measurements [33, 72].

Correcting the effects of dust extinction requires not only accounting for the amount of extinction but also for the shape of the extinction curve [53, 52], which varies across the sky and encodes the physical properties of dust [19].

Today, corrections for the effects of dust extinction are most often performed using measurements of the thermal brightness of dust (e.g., from Planck; Planck Collaboration et al. 48) or of the intensity of the 21 cm line emission from neutral hydrogen [30, 40]. The conversion of these measurements into dust extinction depends on quantities like the dust temperature, the extinction curve, and the dust-to-gas ratio. Systematic errors in those quantities now limit the accuracy to which dust corrections can be made [52, 72]. Improved correction for dust extinction must be made by other approaches.

Fortunately, direct extinction measurements via the “pair method” offer a promising alternative to these indirect measurements. In the pair method, the spectral types of a number of stars are measured. Stars with the same spectral type are expected to have the same intrinsic colors. The reddening of stars, as given by the difference between the observed colors of stars and the intrinsic colors of stars of the same spectral type, is attributed to dust. By building up a large sample of stars, we can map the distribution of dust in the Milky Way.

The pair method has a long history in astronomy, dating back to the work of [59]. A common approach is to directly compare reddened stars with lightly reddened or unreddened stars to determine extinction [59, 57, 6, 43, e.g.,]. A related approach involves training a mathematical model on unreddened stars and using it to predict instrinsic colors of similar reddened stars so that the difference between the observed and predicted colors provides extinction due to dust [52, 66, 54, e.g.,]. Related approaches also work for galaxies [47, e.g.,]. Another common approach is to obtain a prediction for the intrinsic color using a stellar atmosphere model (calibrated to observational stellar data) and difference it with the observed colors of reddened stars to obtain extinction (E. Extinction depends on wavelength and this dependence is described by the extinction curve, which is often parameterized by a single number: the total-to-selective extinction ratio, R⁡(V)R(V) [8]. The shape of the extinction curve probes the properties of dust grains. Variation in R⁡(V)R(V) is most commonly attributed to the grain size distribution: high R⁡(V)R(V) sightlines have flatter optical extinction curves, indicating a grain population weighted toward larger sizes [62, 19]. Other proposed drivers include the growth of ice mantles and grain coagulation in dense environments [63, 65], and the processing of grains by ultraviolet photons or differences in grain composition and chemistry [32, 45].

The mapping of R⁡(V)R(V) over large areas of the sky has been done by two principal approaches. The first approach involves measuring reddenings in several colors and converting their ratio into R⁡(V)R(V) using an assumed family of extinction curves. Here, the stellar type is determined beforehand, so the extinction measurement and the stellar type determination are separate steps. [54] took this approach, combining APOGEE spectroscopy with Pan-STARRS1, 2MASS, and WISE photometry to map R⁡(V)R(V) over a low Galactic latitude footprint. Similarly, R. Zhang et al. [68] combined LAMOST spectroscopy with Gaia, Pan-STARRS1, SDSS, 2MASS, and WISE photometry to map R⁡(V)R(V) over the northern sky, with reliable measurements concentrated at low and intermediate Galactic latitudes. The second approach involves fitting the shape of the extinction curve simultaneously with the stellar parameters. [69] applied this to Gaia XP spectrophotometry and mapped R⁡(V)R(V) over the whole sky, including the high Galactic latitude regime where extragalactic surveys operate. However, at the low resolution (R<100R<100) of those data, stellar type and extinction curve are covariant, complicating the analysis. In this work, we instead use the first approach, using the largest spectroscopic data set ever employed at high Galactic latitudes.

In this work, we use the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) [41], which has currently observed more than 40 million galaxies and 10 million stars. We use these stars in a pair-method-like approach to map dust. Recent work by [72], henceforth Z25, also computed reddening based on DESI spectroscopy and photometry, and published a dust map that improves dramatically on the traditional SFD thermal dust map [56]. They show that on large scales, 80% of the observed fluctuations in the density of a particular tracer of the large scale structure is explained by errors in the SFD dust map; errors in dust maps are the dominant source of noise in today’s cosmological measurements at large scales. Adoption of a dust map directly based on optical extinction measurements eliminates these errors.

The work of Z25 has focused on delivering the extinction corrections necessary to mitigate extinction systematics in the DESI cosmology analysis. Our work differs from theirs in two ways. First, Z25 fit theoretical stellar atmosphere models to observed spectra for predicting intrinsic colors, while we use empirically-derived intrinsic colors from low-reddening calibration stars. Second, Z25 focus on reporting improvements over SFD maps, while we extend our results to the shape of the extinction curve and its variation over the DESI footprint.

papers.title: When Should Semantic Priors Enter Partially-Identified Causal Discovery?
papers.abstract: Observational causal discovery often leaves causal di- rections unresolved or unstable. Large language mod- els (LLMs) can provide semantic information to resolve these directions, but incorrect proposals can exclude the true causal graph and invalidate downstream inference. We study three separate decisions: where to allocate semantic queries, which proposals to admit, and which causal graphs to retain. Our framework distinguishes population non-identifiability from finite-sample insta- bility, evaluates semantic orientation against statistical and random controls, and examines calibrated admis- sion and error-tolerant DAG retention. Experiments across benchmark networks show that semantic infor- mation improves recovery over coin-flip orientations, but targeting unstable edges has no established ad- vantage over matched-random allocation. The tested admission certificate cannot support nontrivial admis- sion with the available calibration tasks. Moreover, downstream retention depends on reference adequacy: learned references contain the true DAG in only three of 80 planned tasks. These findings separate the value of semantic information from the reliability of its alloca- tion, admission, and retention, and identify calibration size and reference adequacy as key limitations.

papers.title: A Multi-Prover Interactive Protocol for Certification of Resolution Refutations
papers.abstract: A resolution refutation of a SAT-formula $\varphi$ is an independently checkable certificate proving that $\varphi$ is unsatisfiable. However, the refutations of $\varphi$ can be exponentially larger than $\varphi$. So, a verifier needs worst-case exponential time in the size of $\varphi$ to check their correctness. We present ResCertify, an interactive probabilistic protocol in which the verifier interacts with multiple independent, untrusted provers (MIP) to check the refutation with very low probability of error. The verifier runs in linear time in the size of $\varphi$. The provers require time $\mathcal{O}(n \cdot |\Phi|)$, where $\Phi$ is the resolution refutation and $n$ is the number of variables of $\varphi$. If they can be trusted to act as a multilinear oracle on certain queries, a single prover suffices, and the runtime can be improved to $\mathcal{O}(|\Phi|)$. Finally, while the focus of our work is theoretical, we also report on a proof-of-concept implementation of ResCertify.
papers.intro:
Certifying SAT-solvers produce either a satisfying assignment or a proof of unsatisfiability in some proof system, e.g. resolution (see [14] for a survey). The proof is usually called an UNSAT certificate.

UNSAT certificates produced by modern SAT-solvers may be very large, in extreme cases petabytes [13]. We are interested in scenarios in which the SAT-solver runs on a powerful machine able to store large certificates, but the certificate is checked by an independent verifier only able to invest polynomial time in the size of the formula (not in the size of the certificate!). In this case, checking the certificate, or even fetching it, can be infeasible. For example, resolution proofs can be exponential in the size of the formula. Further, there is little hope of solving this problem by finding another proof system with polynomial size proofs, because that would imply 𝖭𝖯=𝖼𝗈𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}=\mathsf{coNP}.

Interactive proof protocols provide a theoretical solution to this problem [10, 2, 18, 1]. Intuitively, instead of fetching and checking the certificate, the verifier asks questions about it of an agent, called a prover, which we can imagine running on the same machine as the SAT-solver. The questions are selected following an interactive protocol. The protocol guarantees that the verifier employs only randomized polynomial time, accepts every correct certificate (completeness), and rejects every faulty certificate with high probability (soundness).11 1 The verifier rejects a certificate iff the answers given by the prover are incompatible with a correct certificate; this can happen because the certificate is faulty, or because it is correct but the provers give wrong answers to the verifier’s questions.

The Davis-Putnam procedure is a significant improvement over brute force, but generates much larger resolution proofs than modern techniques. In this paper we address the following question: Is there an interactive proof system whose prover has linear overhead for arbitrary resolution proofs? We show that the answer is affirmative if we move from single-prover to multiple-prover interactive proof systems (MIP). In this setting, the verifier asks questions to multiple provers (in our case just two) who, crucially, are not allowed to exchange information.
