To the best of our knowledge, no interactive protocol specific to automated reasoning has yet been proposed or implemented, besides the ones proposed by Couillard et al. [6] and Czerner et al. [7]. There exist multiple works on verifying generic computations without re-executing them [24, 28, 20, 26], but with numerical applications in mind. There is also extensive research on probabilistically checkable proofs (PCPs), which has produced PCP protocols for algebraic constraint satisfaction problems with quasi-optimal provers (see e.g. [3]), with applications to cryptographic protocols. None of these papers considers the problem of certifying the output of a SAT-solver, and we are not aware of any implementations. Other advances have been made in the field of zero-knowledge proofs [27, 16, 21], which, in the context of SAT-solving, would amount to proving the existence of a satisfying assignment without revealing information about it.

papers.title: BirdDreams: Joint Perspective and BEV Video Generation for a Plausible, Reactive Driving World Model
papers.abstract: Driving world models aim to simulate how a scene unfolds under different ego actions. This requires plausible motion of surrounding vehicles as well as precise ego-trajectory control. Learning vehicle motion from perspective video alone is challenging because motion is entangled with appearance and vehicles can be occluded. Prior work therefore conditions video generation on layouts that specify vehicle motion, providing control over surrounding vehicles but requiring their future trajectories as inputs. We introduce BirdDreams, an autoregressive driving world model that jointly generates perspective video and a schematic bird's-eye-view (BEV) video, making scene layout part of the predicted future. The BEV, rendered from scene annotations for training, depicts roads and vehicles as simple shapes at a fixed metric scale, providing a top-down view of their positions and motion with reduced occlusion between vehicles. Perspective video, by contrast, retains scene details that the BEV omits, such as traffic signals and object appearance. Joint attention between two video diffusion transformers, one per stream, lets each stream inform the other during generation. The predicted BEV also provides a geometric interface for ego control: we translate and rotate its latest frame along an input ego trajectory and use the resulting frames as a soft condition that shows how the scene would appear to move if only the ego vehicle moved. At inference, BirdDreams generates both videos from a single camera image without requiring an HD map or vehicle-state inputs. On PhysicalAI-AV and nuScenes, BirdDreams follows input ego trajectories more faithfully than prior driving world models and generates more plausible ego motion without ego-action conditioning. Human evaluation shows that BirdDreams outperforms a perspective-only baseline in generating realistic surrounding-vehicle behavior.

papers.intro:
Simulation allows autonomous driving systems to be tested in rare, dangerous scenarios that are difficult to reproduce safely on real roads. Driving world models learn from real driving videos to synthesize realistic future observations conditioned on ego actions [11, 34]. From the same initial observation, they can simulate how a scene unfolds under different ego maneuvers. Such simulation requires the model to predict plausible responses of surrounding vehicles to the ego maneuver while generating ego motion that follows the input trajectory. At an intersection, for example, an ego vehicle proceeding instead of yielding may cause a crossing vehicle to slow down or change course.

Recent driving world models such as OmniDreams [4] condition video generation on external scene layouts that specify road geometry and surrounding-vehicle motion. Replaying these layouts from driving logs fixes surrounding vehicles to their recorded trajectories, so they cannot react to changes in the ego maneuver. A separate traffic model can generate new trajectories, but leaves interaction prediction outside the video world model [49]. Without external scene-layout inputs, the world model must learn surrounding-vehicle motion from perspective video. This is difficult because motion is entangled with texture and lighting, occlusion often hides vehicles, and the same pixel displacement can correspond to different speeds depending on a vehicle’s distance from the camera. In our OmniDreams baseline trained without surrounding-vehicle trajectories as inputs, vehicles can disappear or make implausible maneuvers at complex intersections (Fig. 6).

Joint prediction combines the BEV’s representation of vehicle motion with this visual information from perspective video.

Accurately following an ego trajectory specified in meters also remains challenging for video world models. Even with trajectory conditioning, subtle steering maneuvers may not be faithfully reproduced in the generated ego motion. We use the predicted BEV as an action interface for video generation. In an ego-centered, orthographic BEV at a fixed metric scale, a change in ego position shifts the scene by a uniform number of pixels, and a change in heading rotates it about the ego vehicle. Our BEV-aware action conditioning uses these transformations to reproject the latest predicted BEV frame into the ego coordinate frame at each pose along the input trajectory. The resulting frames show how the scene would appear to move if the surroundings stayed fixed. They serve as a soft condition for the BEV branch, and the perspective branch attends to the conditioned BEV features through joint attention. The model predicts how surrounding vehicles move and interact in both videos. Without ego-action conditioning, ego motion is also predicted as part of the rollout.

papers.title: Spontaneous mechanical patterning in active elastic tissues with stress feedback
papers.abstract: The active mechanics of biological tissues is often governed by embedded active contractile fibers responding to mechanical feedback. We introduce a minimal model of a solid-like tissue where the mechanics is controlled by feedback of local active and elastic stresses on fiber organization. The resulting tissue generically exhibits a bistable response to external strain and spontaneously segregates into domains of orthogonally aligned fibers. Our theory thus provides a minimal mechanical feedback mechanism generating orthogonal structural alignment ubiquitous in biological tissues.

papers.title: Feedback-induced mechanical bistability and perpendicular-domain formation in active elastic tissues
papers.abstract: Contractile fibers in muscle tissues are highly aligned over the scale of many cells. Muscle layers surrounding organs with an inner lumen are often arranged in orthogonal directions. Here, we study a minimal mechanism of how structural order and its patterning into orthogonally aligned domains can emerge from mechanical feedback alone. The central idea is that contractile fibers align in the direction of the local active and elastic stresses, a feedback motivated by the maturation of muscle fibers under tension. We thus model muscle tissue as an active nematic solid with stress feedback: an elastic medium with embedded contractile fibers that are reinforced along the directions of the local tissue stresses. We find that the feedback from the contractile fiber stress is self-amplifying and drives spontaneous fiber alignment. Feedback from the elastic stress couples the alignment to the mechanical boundary conditions and tissue geometry. Depending on the mechanical boundary conditions, the elastic-stress feedback stabilizes two orthogonally aligned tissue states, resulting in a structurally and mechanically bistable tissue that shows a hysteretic stress-strain response. In spatially extended tissues, this bistability gives rise to orthogonally aligned domains separated by domain walls. In an annulus surrounding a pressurized lumen, a radially aligned inner domain and a circumferentially aligned outer domain stably coexist because the domain wall is pinned at a position that results in the fibers carrying the lumen pressure. Our results show that stress feedback can pattern structural order by coupling spontaneous alignment to the tissue geometry. Our mechanism thus provides a purely mechanical route to orthogonal fiber patterning in muscle tissues.

papers.intro:
During the development of muscle tissue, the contractile machinery of cells self-organizes into remarkable structural order. Muscle fibers almost perfectly align along a common axis over hundreds or thousands of cells, allowing for effective directional force generation. This type of order is found in vivo in cardiac, skeletal, and smooth muscle [1], in entire organisms, such as Hydra [2], and in vitro in engineered skeletal and cardiac muscle tissues [3, 4, 5], as well as in cardiac organoids [6].

Muscle fibers almost perfectly align along a common axis over hundreds or thousands of cells, allowing for effective directional force generation. It has been suggested that this structural organization emerges through mechanical feedback [7, 8, 5, 9, 10, 11]. Aligned fibers assemble de novo from initially unaligned cytoskeletal material over hours to days [7, 4, 8, 5], and their assembly, maturation, and orientation are mechanosensitive. Myofibrils, the elongated contractile actomyosin bundles that make muscle contraction possible, assemble only under tension in developing Drosophila flight muscle [7] and along the directions of maximal principal stress in cardiac muscle cells on micropatterned substrates [8]. The formation of sarcomeres, the basic contractile unit of mature cardiac and skeletal muscle fibers, is argued to be mediated by the forces transmitted along the fiber [11]. On the molecular level, such tension feedback may be implemented through force-sensitive molecules, the catch-bond behavior of myosin-actin binding, or the load-dependent reinforcement of focal adhesions and cell–cell junctions [12, 13, 11, 14].

In many organs, the structural order of muscle tissue is precisely patterned to allow force generation not only along a single axis but in several directions. Examples are the myocardium of the heart [15], the smooth muscle cells of the gut [16] and of the arterial wall [17], and the epithelial fibers of Hydra [2, 18]. In particular, muscle layers that surround organs with an inner lumen, are frequently arranged in orthogonally aligned structures. For instance, the intestine of chicken consists of an inner circumferential and an outer longitudinal smooth-muscle layer [16]. Similarly, the Drosophila midgut is enclosed by an inner layer of circular and an outer layer of longitudinal visceral muscles [19]. In Hydra, whose body wall encloses a central gastric cavity, the ectodermal actomyosin fibers run along the body axis, while the endodermal ones run circumferentially [2]. Cardiac organoids with a central lumen similarly develop circumferentially and radially aligned regions [6]. It remains unclear whether a generic mechanical-feedback mechanism may generate this type of perpendicular alignment.

Different theoretical models have been introduced to study the interplay between the alignment of contractile fibers and mechanical feedback. At the subcellular scale, models of sarcomere and myofibril self-assembly explore how contractile units nucleate and order within a single fiber [20, 11]. At the cellular scale, physical models describe how adherent cells and their stress fibers orient in response to the mechanics of their environment [14] and how cell shape and feedback between actin fibers and focal adhesions orient precursory myofibrils [21]. At the tissue scale, extensive previous work has focused on modeling tissue as active nematic fluids where cells flow and rearrange to release stress [22]. Here, in contrast, we seek to describe muscle tissue that structurally orders but does not change shape significantly. Moreover, cell proliferation and intercalation are negligible in these tissues after an initial growth phase [23, 24]. We therefore describe the large-scale tissue response as elastic and model tissues as active solids.

In the setting of active solids, numerical models of the left ventricle have been used to simulate different fiber-alignment mechanisms based on local tissue strains and stresses [25, 26, 27, 28, 29]. Moreover, models of adherent cells that sense the stiffness and strain of their elastic substrate have shown that elastic interactions transmitted through the substrate can drive cell alignment [30, 31, 32, 33, 32]. Coupling to a strain-stiffening substrate, such mechanosensitivity of cells can create bistability in cellular tractions [34]. Moreover, the nematic alignment of stress fibers has been modeled as the ordering of force dipoles in an elastic background [35]. At the tissue scale, models where fibers reorient in the direction of principal strain reproduce the alignment of endothelial actin in pressurized vessels [36]. The folding of engineered cell sheets with prescribed cellular alignment is captured by modeling the tissue as an active contractile elastic sheet [37]. These models differ in the mechanical quantity to which the fiber alignment is coupled. In models of adherent cells, cells sense the strain in their elastic environment [30, 31]. Since this environment is deformed by both external loads and the contraction of the cells themselves, this microscopic strain coupling effectively encompasses, when coarse-graining to the tissue scale, coupling to both the elastic and active stresses [35]. Other models reorient the fibers based on the local tissue strain, as for endothelial tubes [36] and classical numerical models of the fiber architecture of the left ventricle [25, 26, 27, 28]. Given the diverse mechanisms of mechanosensitivity discussed above, and local tension created by both active and elastic stresses, we consider a generic coupling of the fiber orientation to active and elastic stresses, where the elastic stress is related to the tissue strain. When coupling equally to active and elastic stress, this coupling becomes a coupling to the total stress [43, 44, 45, 29]. papers.title: Nitride crystalline barrier epitaxial SIS Josephson junctions by MBE
papers.abstract: Superconductor-insulator-superconductor Josephson junctions with crystalline tunnel barriers have remained elusive by epitaxial techniques such as MOCVD or MBE that produce the junction materials and devices powering today's electronic and photonic systems like transistors and lasers. Here, we overcome the key materials hurdle to realize the first functional nitride crystalline barrier Josephson junctions by MBE. Despite an AlN barrier thickness of approximately 4.5 nm, the NbN/AlN/NbN trilayers exhibit coherent Josephson tunneling with critical current densities of approximately 17 A/cm2, an IcRn product of approximately 2.5 mV, and a superconducting gap voltage of approximately 3.7 mV with a BCS-like gap evolution with temperature. Hysteretic current-voltage characteristics and Fraunhofer current modulation with magnetic field establish underdamped SIS Josephson behavior. The realization of crystalline barrier Josephson junctions by MBE opens the doors to a richer materials palette with alloys and superlattice electrodes and tunnel barriers, as well as potential monolithic integration of superconducting quantum circuits with active electronic and photonic devices such as HEMTs and lasers.

papers.title: SAVE: Less is More in Agentic Video Reasoning
papers.abstract: Agentic video-reasoning frameworks iteratively explore a video, choosing what to observe based on the query and evidence gathered so far. Existing methods are typically evaluated with different backbones, preprocessing pipelines, and computational budgets, making it difficult to determine which components actually drive performance, how much they cost, and whether agentic inference is preferable to native video reasoning in the first place. We conduct a controlled evaluation of a diverse set of recent agentic video-reasoning systems across two strong contemporary backbones, with explicit token and monetary-cost accounting. Across Gemini 3 Flash and Gemma 4, most existing agentic frameworks fail to consistently improve over native video inference and often increase computational cost. We investigate two primary questions: (1) How much agentic framework complexity is necessary for effective video reasoning? (2) When, if at all, is agentic video reasoning preferable to just using the backbone directly? To answer the first question, we introduce a deliberately minimal Active Exploration Baseline and show that it remains competitive with substantially more elaborate agents. We then propose targeted extensions to this baseline, yielding SAVE (Simple Agentic Video Explorer). SAVE outperforms all evaluated prior agentic methods in five of six backbone-benchmark settings. Turning to the second question, our results indicate that the advantage of agentic exploration grows when dense processing would otherwise represent answer-relevant events too sparsely, particularly for long videos and temporally concentrated evidence. Overall, our results suggest that agentic video reasoning should favor simple frameworks over increasingly elaborate pipelines and focus primarily on long-form video, where selective evidence acquisition offers the clearest advantage over native inference.

papers.intro:
Long-form video reasoning remains a fundamental challenge for modern vision-language models because it requires processing large amounts of temporally structured information, performing complex visual reasoning, and integrating evidence over long time horizons. In videos, the observations needed to answer a question may be distributed across thousands of frames, creating a tension between reasoning quality and computational efficiency: densely processing the entire video is expensive, while aggressive downsampling or compression risks discarding critical evidence. Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs), including GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024), and Gemini 3 (Google DeepMind, 2025), have substantially improved video understanding, but efficient and accurate reasoning remains challenging.

This makes it difficult to determine which components of the agentic framework actually drive performance, what constitutes an effective video agent, and whether agentic inference is preferable to native video reasoning in the first place.

To address those questions, we conduct, to the best of our knowledge, the most comprehensive controlled evaluation to date of contemporary agentic video reasoning frameworks under shared frontier backbones. We systematically evaluate both Gemini 3 Flash (Google DeepMind, 2025) and the open-weight Gemma 4 (Gemma Team, 2026), adapting a diverse set of recent methods to use the same underlying backbone, evaluating them on a common suite of video reasoning benchmarks, and explicitly accounting for computational cost. papers.title: The SDSS-V Black Hole Mapper Reverberation Mapping Project: Short Lags in the COSMOS Field
papers.abstract: We present the first reverberation mapping (RM) measurements in the COSMOS field included in the SDSS-V Black Hole Mapper Reverberation Mapping Project. Using $\sim$6 months of plate-based spectroscopy (from late 2020 to mid-2021) and accompanying ZTF+DECam \emph{gri}-band photometric light curves, we analyze the variability of over 250 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) out to $z \sim 3$. We successfully recover reliable $\lesssim$ 200d time lags for 22 AGNs ($z \lesssim 2.5$) in H$\alpha$, H$\beta$, MgII, or CIV, using a combination of multiple lag detection methods and significance tests. Our measurements are consistent with the radius-luminosity relations from recent large-scale RM programs, providing measured masses of $10^{7-9} M_{\odot}$ for these AGNs. These results and upcoming long-baseline SDSS-V spectroscopy lay the groundwork for large-sample AGN studies in conjunction with other facilities covering the COSMOS field, including the Vera C. Rubin Observatory and Roman Space Telescope.

papers.intro:
Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) represent a prime population for constraining supermassive black hole (SMBH) growth across cosmic time. AGN SMBH mass estimation capitalizes on the signature multi-band, multi-timescale variability within AGNs, well-described by Gaussian random processes [32, 33, 55, e.g.,]. In particular, the reverberation mapping [10, RM;] method assumes the signal from the central engine close to the SMBH is reverberated throughout the system, with the reprocessing of radiation dominated by light travel time [47]. While the origin of said variability remains under debate, possibly originating from instabilities within the accretion disk [5, 30, 46, 71, e.g.,], estimating a time lag between two regions within the AGN can nonetheless provide an approximate distance. Short time lags between two photometric bands can be used to estimate the size of the accretion disk [15, e.g.,], while a lag between the photometric continuum and spectroscopic broad line light curves grant a size for the broad-line region [47, BLR;]. Assuming a virial BLR, a property which may be violated in certain unique systems [18, 61, e.g.,], combining the BLR radius and BLR velocity (estimated from the broad lines), produces a SMBH mass estimate MBHM_{\rm BH}.

papers.title: Higher order schemes for the numerical solution of integro-differential equation-based age-of-infection models with time-dependent contact rates
papers.abstract:
Age-of-infection models, formulated as integro-differential equations (IDEs), provide elegant mathematical descriptions for the spread of infectious diseases. In contrast to ordinary differential equation (ODE)-based models, IDE-based models can accommodate general distributions of transition times between disease stages. Yet, the accurate numerical assessment of the solution of IDE models remains challenging.
  Here, we extend a recently proposed fixed-point method based on Gregory quadrature. We generalize the formulation to time-dependent contact rates whose changes at discrete time points are represented by continuously differentiable sigmoidal interpolants, and suggest additional finite difference approximations to obtain higher-order schemes for susceptible, infected and recovered subpopulations. The resulting numerical schemes achieve convergence orders of two, three and four for all three subpopulations, enabling accurate and flexible simulations of IDE-based epidemic models with general sojourn time distributions and changing contact patterns.

papers.intro:
Ordinary differential equation (ODE) models are among the most popular tools for describing and analyzing infectious disease dynamics in a population [18]. These models allow for the computation of reproduction numbers and (endemic) equilibria; however, they implicitly assume exponentially distributed sojourn times in the different disease states, an assumption that is often unrealistic [16]. More complex sojourn-time distributions can be represented within the ODE framework using the Linear Chain Trick (LCT), which yields Erlang-distributed transition times [25], or its generalizations [19, 20, 21]. Although these approaches provide greater modeling flexibility and can reveal dynamics absent from simpler ODE models [30], they require the introduction of auxiliary states. This increases the dimensionality of the model and can lead to intricate systems, particularly when complex sojourn-time distributions are considered.

A mathematically direct and more elegant alternative to expanded ODE models is provided by integro-differential equation-based (IDE) models which accommodate general sojourn-time distributions without introducing auxiliary states. IDE-based epidemic models were already considered by Kermack and McKendrick [22] and by Hethcote and Tudor [17]. These models have also commonly been referred to as age-of-infection models [6, 4, 2, 14, 29].

A substantial body of analytical work has established the theoretical foundations for SIR-type age-of-infection models. These contributions include analyses of the classical Kermack–McKendrick model [7], final-size relations [8], reproduction numbers and final sizes under heterogeneous mixing [6], endemic equilibria [10], and the dynamics of disease-specific models [5]. More recently, the COVID-19 pandemic motivated the development of more advanced models that distinguish between symptomatic and asymptomatic infections [1, 34]. Further work also demonstrated that the long-term dynamics can depend on the distributional shape of the infectious period [32]. Despite this extensive foundation, important questions concerning the accurate and efficient numerical solution of nonlinear IDE-based epidemic models remain open. The lack of established numerical methods represents a practical barrier to the broader use of these models, particularly when compared with the wide range of mature integration schemes available for ODE models.

Numerical methods for IDE-based epidemic models are a field of active research, and the absence of user-friendly computational tools remains a recognized limitation [15]. An early contribution was the nonstandard scheme developed by Lubuma and Terefe for an SIS model [24]. Building on this, Messina, Pezzella, and Vecchio introduced a nonstandard finite difference scheme that applies modified left- and right-rectangle rules to different terms of the integral equation [26, 29]. This construction resolves the nonlinear coupling between the susceptible population and the force of infection while preserving positivity, monotonicity, and boundedness independently of the step size hh. The scheme was subsequently applied to models incorporating heterogeneous population mixing [28] and behavioral changes in contact patterns [13], and it underlies the EPITIME computational framework for behavioral epidemic modeling [12]. We further extended the approach to a SECIR-type IDE model that includes disease-related deaths and established preservation properties for its eight compartments and the flows between them [34]. Despite these advantages, the nonstandard scheme is only first-order convergent.

papers.title: Nearly Computable Numbers with Additional Properties
papers.abstract:
A real number is called \emph{nearly computable} if it is the limit of a computable sequence of rational (or dyadic) numbers that has the additional property that for any computable subsequence the sequence of differences of consecutive elements converges to $0$ computably. The main result of this article provides methods for constructing nearly computable numbers with additional properties. The main result is proved by an infinite injury priority argument. Using these methods, we construct nearly computable numbers with several different additional properties:
  - a nearly computable number that is not divergence bounded computable,
  - for any left-computable number $\alpha$ that is neither in the least nor in the highest Solovay degree, a left-computable, nearly computable number that is Solovay incomparable with $\alpha$,
  - a nearly computable number $\gamma$ that can be written as the difference of two left-computable numbers but has the property that for any two left-computable numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$ wih $\gamma=\alpha-\beta$ both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are Martin-L\"of random.
  We also look at two classes of nearly computable numbers: the class $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{dlnc}}$ of differences of real numbers that are nearly computable and left-computable, and the class $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{wnc}}$ of nearly computable numbers that can be written as the difference of two left-computable numbers. Both classes form real closed fields, in fact, $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{dlnc}}$ is closed under computable functions with open domain that are Lipschitz continuous or differentiable. Finally, we show that $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{dlnc}}$ is a proper subset of $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{wnc}}$.

papers.title: Priority-Based Network Access with Strict-Priority Scheduling in PLCA Multidrop Networks
papers.abstract: Shared-medium Ethernet is gaining renewed attention across industrial domains, driven by the adoption of 10BASE-T1S. In such multidrop networks, collision-free and deterministic medium access is achieved through Physical Layer Collision Avoidance (PLCA). However, PLCA follows a node-based cyclic access structure that does not account for traffic priority, leading to high access latency for time-sensitive traffic and limited scalability with increasing network size. Existing PLCA extensions improve latency for selected devices but remain restricted to node-based access and do not support network-wide traffic differentiation. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a priority-based network access and scheduling mechanism for multidrop networks. The proposed approach decouples medium access from node-based ordering and enables class-based prioritization, allowing high-priority traffic from any device to be transmitted ahead of lower-priority traffic. It further supports a configuration that emulates Strict Priority (SP) scheduling, providing low and bounded access latency for highest-priority traffic. Analytical bounds on the worst-case access latency are derived, validated, and shown to be tight. Performance evaluation demonstrates that the proposed mechanism reduces the maximum observed access latency for high-priority traffic by over 65% compared to PLCA, with latency increasing by less than 1% as the network grows from 8 to 40 devices.

Shared-medium Ethernet is re-emerging across diverse domains, including industrial automation, robotics, and in-vehicle networks. In automotive systems, Ethernet has become the dominant in-vehicle communication technology, driven by the transition toward zonal architectures [1]. Similarly, industrial networks are transitioning from heterogeneous, task-specific fieldbus systems to unified Ethernet-based infrastructures, eliminating the need for dedicated gateways and enabling seamless integration of edge computing and virtualized control [2].

Physical Layer Collision Avoidance (PLCA), standardized in 10BASE-T1S [4][5], addresses these requirements by assigning exclusive transmission opportunities to devices, thereby eliminating collisions and providing bounded access latency.

Despite these advantages, PLCA exhibits fundamental limitations. Medium access is strictly ordered according to node identifiers (IDs), without considering traffic priority. As a result, latency-sensitive traffic may experience significant delays while waiting for transmissions from lower-priority traffic. Moreover, due to its cyclic access structure, the worst-case access latency of PLCA grows linearly with the number of devices, limiting its scalability in large networks. The IEEE 802.3 PLCA Enhancements Study Group is exploring enhancements to address these limitations, including support for differentiated services and improvements in latency performance and scalability [6].

Several extensions have been proposed to introduce prioritization and differentiated service into PLCA networks. Some approaches prioritize selected devices by modifying their access order [7, 8] or transmission frequency [9, 10, 11]. Others regulate transmissions according to packet priorities or flow timing requirements [12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. While these approaches improve service differentiation, they still retain device-associated transmission opportunities. Consequently, medium access for high-priority traffic remains affected by the access opportunities assigned to its transmitting device, limiting the ability to provide priority access independently of which device generates the traffic.

This paper analyzes the access latency of PLCA and its variant, PLCA with node prioritization (PLCA-NP), highlighting the impact of node-based access on latency and scalability. To address these limitations, we introduce a priority-based network access and scheduling mechanism for shared-medium multidrop networks. The proposed mechanism assigns transmission opportunities to traffic classes rather than individual devices. Any device with pending traffic of the corresponding class can participate in its transmission opportunity, with contention resolved through a deterministic ID-based tree mechanism. This enables network-wide traffic differentiation, allowing high-priority traffic from any device to gain access ahead of pending lower-priority traffic. Furthermore, a configuration that emulates Strict Priority (SP) scheduling is introduced, providing low and bounded access latency for the highest-priority traffic.

This paper substantially extends our previous work in [17] as follows. First, we provide a formal worst-case latency analysis of the resolution mechanism. Second, building on these results, we formally derive the resulting worst-case access latency, covering the single-packet assumption as well as the general multi-packet case and the worst-case queueing delay. Third, we validate the derived bounds through an exhaustive search over all possible resolution scenarios, confirming that the bounds are both valid and tight. Fourth, we provide a comprehensive performance evaluation across a wider range of network sizes and traffic loads. Finally, we refine the proposed mechanism along two aspects: we introduce two strategies for handling interrupted resolution processes, an aspect not discussed in [17], and we retain the BEACON message from standard PLCA to ensure robust synchronization for devices joining or rejoining during an ongoing cycle.

papers.title: Directed Domain Wall Motion by Radio-Frequency Currents
papers.abstract: Magnetic domain walls (DWs) are central to emerging spintronic technologies for memory, logic and neuromorphic computing, where their controlled displacement is a key functionality. While current-induced DW motion driven by spin-orbit torques is well established under direct currents, it remains unclear how radio-frequency (RF) currents couple to DWs and whether they can generate directed motion under a symmetric periodic drive. Here we show that RF currents drive DW oscillations, which can be rectified into directed motion through symmetry breaking. Using time-resolved and static magneto-optical Kerr microscopy, we demonstrate that RF spin-orbit torques efficiently excite low-frequency DW oscillations well below the ferromagnetic resonance frequency. Whereas these oscillations remain symmetric in the absence of perturbations, symmetry breaking by a transverse magnetic field produces self-propulsion, while symmetry breaking by an initial current pulse gives rise to sustained DW motion. We further show that in initially uniform magnetic states, RF-driven expansion of a pulse-generated edge domain ultimately results in efficient RF-assisted magnetic switching. Together, these results establish a general framework for understanding how RF-driven DW oscillations are rectified into directed motion, providing new opportunities for their high-frequency control.

papers.title: Energetic Particle Confinement In Black Hole Accretion Disks
papers.abstract: Using tracer particles propagating in the environment provided by general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations, this paper addresses fundamental questions related to the confinement and acceleration properties in accretion disks around compact objects. By varying the spin parameter of the central black hole and the accretion regime of the disk, a comprehensive picture is obtained for particles whose Larmor radius is comparable to the gravitational radius of the system. It is found that such particles can escape the system at the outermost boundary of the simulations, though, depending on the accretion regime, the time it takes them to escape, and the energetic dynamics along the trajectory can vary significantly. Dynamics near the black hole are even more sensitive to environmental details as black holes with higher spin values generate stronger magnetic fields, which influence particle motion in non-trivial ways. The primary acceleration mechanism is identified as turbulent scattering, with the jet-sheath emerging as the dominant site for particle energization

papers.intro:
The environment surrounding massive black holes (BHs) is a leading candidate site for the acceleration of energetic charged particles, as revealed by their multi-messenger signatures (Boulanger et al., 2018, Rieger and Levinson, 2018, de Mello Neto, 2022, Globus and Blandford, 2025, e.g.,). A recent detection of particular interest was reported by the IceCube Collaboration (Collaboration et al., 2022), which identified an excess in the neutrino flux in the energy range (1−15)(1-15) TeV originating from a region of the sky coincident with the Seyfert II active galactic nucleus (AGN) NGC 1068 (Bland-Hawthorn et al., 1997, Padovani et al., 2024). Analysis of this source (Padovani et al., 2024), in particular with regard to its bright X-ray emission but weak gamma-ray counterpart, suggests that a compact (r≲30​rgr\lesssim 30\;r_{g}) region around the BH, commonly referred to as the “corona”, is the most likely origin of the observed neutrino flux. The overall properties of such a region can be constrained through phenomenological arguments, but the details of its composition remain uncertain, with a growing body of literature exploring these unresolved aspects (Murase, 2022a, Eichmann et al., 2022, Fiorillo et al., 2024, Das et al., 2024, Padovani et al., 2024, Lemoine and Rieger, 2025, e.g.,). Given the experimental challenges with directly probing such environments, numerical simulations provide a fundamental instrument for investigating the phenomena occurring within these systems. The present paper is one such study, in which accretion disks with Advection Dominated Accretion Flows (ADAFs) (Narayan et al., 2012, Abramowicz and Fragile, 2013, Yuan and Narayan, 2014), the Magnetically Arrested Disk (MAD) (Narayan et al., 2003) and the Standard And Normal Evolution (SANE) (Narayan et al., 2012) disk configuration, are simulated using the equations of General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) (Shibata and Sekiguchi, 2005, Mizuno and Rezzolla, 2024). SANE and MAD states represent limiting magnetization regimes of magnetized accretion flows in which the horizon-threading magnetic flux remains respectively subcritical or saturates at dynamically important values, respectively. The distinction is most clearly realized in geometrically thick, advective flows, where magnetic-flux advection is efficient, although analogous magnetically arrested states may arise in radiatively efficient disks provided sufficient net poloidal flux is supplied. It is worth noting that the nomenclature ”Magnetically Arrested Disk” can be somewhat misleading, as accretion is only ever temporarily suppressed and resumes after a transient time in a periodic fashion. While we use the SANE and MAD labels for convenience in the following, we also highlight which fundamental properties of the flows or of the magnetic fields, including the dependence on BH spin, are at play in each instance, so that the results are not strictly tied to the specific type of simulation, but provide deeper insight into the underlying physics.

Once the accretion rate and angular momentum transport in our simulations reach a quasi-steady regime, energetic tracer particles are injected and evolved self-consistently with the disk in order to investigate their transport and propagation properties. These particles respond to the electromagnetic fields generated by the plasma flow, and obey the laws of General Relativity (GR) to account for strong gravitational effects. At the moment, these particles are completely passive and do not exert any feedback on their environment. In GRMHD simulations, the normalization length is set by the gravitational radius (rg=G​M/c2=1.5×105​(M/M⊙)r_{g}=GM/c^{2}=1.5\times 10^{5}(M/M_{\odot}) cm, with GG the gravitational constant, MM the BH mass and cc the speed of light) The ratio of the Larmor radius (rLr_{L}, defined below) of the energetic particles to the gravitational radius, is what determines the scaling of the results of our simulations. Namely, the dynamics observed in these simulations are representative of any system in which particles move with GR dynamics and satisfy the ratio rL/rGr_{L}/r_{G} set by our parameters. For the purposes of this paper, the “corona” is defined as a region of gravitationally bound plasma near the black hole (within ∼30​rg\sim 30\;r_{g}) that satisfies the Bernoulli parameter criterion defined later and that is strongly magnetized. This definition allows flexibility in identifying the corona’s structure but explicitly excludes magnetized outflows (winds and jets) that are more common in ADAF simulations and that do not match observational constraints from NGC 1068 (Padovani et al., 2024). IV presents the analysis of particle escape and infall times, including comparisons with standard estimates, and examines the mechanisms of particle acceleration, with a focus on turbulent scattering. Sec. V discusses the implications for high-energy astrophysics, including the potential role of these flows in accelerating cosmic rays and producing high-energy neutrinos. Finally, Sec. papers.title: EQUIP-RPT: A framework for objective evaluation of quantitative imaging methods in radiopharmaceutical therapies
papers.abstract:
Quantitative imaging (QI) provides a non-invasive approach for dosimetry and quantitative response assessment in radiopharmaceutical therapies (RPTs). QI methods are being developed for instrumentation, acquisition, reconstruction, and image analysis. However, a key barrier to routine adoption of these methods is that evidence demonstrating reliable performance of QI methods on clinically relevant quantification tasks in RPTs remains limited. Our goal is to outline the Evaluation of Quantitative Imaging Performance in Radiopharmaceutical Therapy (EQUIP-RPT) framework, a structured approach for objective, task-based evaluation of QI methods for RPTs.
  We outline the EQUIP-RPT framework based on image-science and task-based image-quality evaluation methodology, practical considerations, and recent literature. The framework is organized around four linked design steps: (i) specification of the quantification task, (ii) design of the study population and imaging protocol, (iii) task-specific information extraction, and (iv) selection of figures of merit (FoMs).
  The EQUIP-RPT framework is presented in the context of four quantification tasks in RPT: activity uptake, absorbed dose, volumetric tumor burden, and lesion-level longitudinal quantifications. The framework distinguishes two paradigms for task-specific information extraction and organizes FoMs according to the performance attributes they characterize. We describe key elements to apply the EQUIP-RPT framework in simulation, physical phantom, and clinical studies. Finally, we show how EQUIP-RPT can be used to generate a quantitative claim based on the evaluation study.
  The EQUIP-RPT framework is designed to provide a structured approach for objective task-based evaluation of QI methods in RPTs, thereby facilitating clinical translation of these methods.

papers.title: Learning Motion-Appearance Coupling Priors for Solving Video Inverse Problems
papers.abstract: Reconstructing video from degraded measurements requires priors that capture both frame appearance and temporal dynamics. Many recent approaches combine pretrained image diffusion priors with motion guidance, sidestepping the costs of training large video models. Temporal consistency is often enforced via photometric losses or warping-based constraints, which implicitly assume that motion explains frame-to-frame or latent-to-latent changes up to small deviations, an assumption that fails under occlusions, lighting changes, and non-rigid deformation. In this paper, we propose to learn the coupling between motion and frame appearance as a generative prior. We learn the distribution of motion-induced appearance residuals with a conditional diffusion model and use it to regularize reconstruction in video inverse problems. Our motion-appearance prior acts as a plug-in regularizer for diffusion-based video reconstruction, preserving the benefits of image diffusion models while remaining compatible with existing appearance regularization techniques. Experiments on dynamic video inverse problems show that reconstruction with a learnt motion-appearance coupling prior outperforms photometric-consistency and noise-warping baselines, and that the approach also transfers to cardiac MRI reconstruction.

papers.title: Finite Element Approximation of Three-Dimensional Elliptic Optimal Control Problems with Curve-Supported Controls
papers.abstract: We consider a linear-quadratic elliptic optimal control problem in three dimensions with a box-constrained control supported on a compact embedded $C^{1,1}$ curve strictly contained in a bounded convex polyhedral domain. The right-hand side of the state equation is a measure supported on the curve, and the state is singular along it. We establish well-posedness and first-order optimality conditions and derive curve-adapted weighted inequalities and finite element error estimates for the singular state. For continuous piecewise linear finite elements on quasi-uniform tetrahedral meshes and variational discretization of the control, assuming exact integration over the curve, we prove the almost quadratic estimate $\|\bar q-\bar q_h\|_{L^2(\gamma)}\le Ch^2(1+\abs{\ln h})^3$. The proof of this estimate requires new results, which are of independent interest. The convergence rate observed in a numerical experiment is consistent with the predicted algebraic order.

papers.title: Orthogonal Code-Based Parallel Signaling for PLCA in Shared-Medium Ethernet
papers.abstract: Physical Layer Collision Avoidance (PLCA) enables collision-free channel access in shared-medium Ethernet by granting each node an exclusive transmission opportunity (TO) in a sequential, cyclic manner. This sequential, node-based access structure, however, is the root cause of PLCA's fundamental limitations, causing access latency to grow with network size and idle TOs to accumulate when traffic is sparse, a limitation inherited by existing PLCA extensions. To address this, we propose OC-PLCA, an orthogonal code-based parallel signaling mechanism for PLCA. Rather than signaling sequentially, all nodes with pending traffic transmit their unique Walsh-Hadamard code simultaneously to signal their intent to transmit. Since these codes are mutually orthogonal, each node independently identifies the complete set of active nodes, allowing the transmission cycle to include only active nodes and eliminating idle TOs entirely. We further investigate the impact of quantization on active node detection, and propose a grouping-based extension that preserves unambiguous detection for networks of an arbitrary number of nodes. Theoretical analysis shows that OC-PLCA reduces signaling overhead by 88% for an 8-node network, with the reduction growing as network size increases. Simulation results confirm significant reductions in observed access latency across a range of network loads and heterogeneous node activity.

papers.intro:
Shared-medium Ethernet is increasingly adopted across automotive and industrial environments, as well as emerging domains such as humanoid robotics. In automotive networks, the shift towards zonal architectures has made Ethernet a dominant in-vehicle communication technology, progressively replacing legacy technologies such as the Controller Area Network (CAN)[1]. A crucial enabler of this transition is the standardization of Physical Layer Collision Avoidance (PLCA) in 10BASE-T1S [2, 3]. PLCA grants each node on the shared channel an exclusive transmission opportunity (TO) in a sequential, cyclic manner. During its TO, a node signals its intent to transmit; otherwise, the cycle advances to the next node. By ensuring that at most one node accesses the channel at any given time, PLCA eliminates collisions and bounds access latency, making it attractive for latency-sensitive and safety-critical applications.

A crucial enabler of this transition is the standardization of Physical Layer Collision Avoidance (PLCA) in 10BASE-T1S [2, 3]. PLCA grants each node on the shared channel an exclusive transmission opportunity (TO) in a sequential, cyclic manner. During its TO, a node signals its intent to transmit; otherwise, the cycle advances to the next node. By ensuring that at most one node accesses the channel at any given time, PLCA eliminates collisions and bounds access latency, making it attractive for latency-sensitive and safety-critical applications.

This sequential, node-based access structure, however, is the root cause of PLCA’s fundamental limitations, resulting in suboptimal access performance under both light and heavy load conditions. Under heavy load, the worst-case access latency grows directly with the number of nodes on the network, limiting scalability in large deployments. Under light load, the cycle nonetheless advances through every device regardless of whether it has pending traffic, introducing substantial idle time on the channel that likewise grows with network size.

papers.title: Learning-Based Interpolation of Detector Gaps in Photon-Counting X-ray Imaging
papers.abstract: Image detectors assembled from tiled modules have physical gaps in the field of view that must be filled before downstream processing such as phase retrieval or tomographic reconstruction. Unlike natural-image inpainting, detector-gap interpolation must leave all other pixels unmodified and preserve the intensity statistics of the filled region, since even a small shift in mean intensity can cause ring artifacts after reconstruction. We adapted two generative models, a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP) and a conditional Pix2Pix model, to this task. We implemented a masking strategy that restricts all changes to the gap pixels and loss terms that constrain the mean intensity and the intensity distribution of the filled region. Both models were trained on nanoCT projections with simulated gaps and compared with linear interpolation, Navier--Stokes inpainting, and the deep image-inpainting network MADF, quantitatively on simulated gaps and visually on real detector gaps. WGAN-GP and Pix2Pix achieved the best perceptual similarity (LPIPS) and histogram distance and, apart from linear interpolation, the shortest inference time. Pix2Pix required about five times fewer training GPU-hours than WGAN-GP. Ablation studies showed that masking the network output contributes by far the most to plausible inpainting results. Applied to sinograms, Pix2Pix produced the most natural gap filling but improved the reconstruction only slightly compared with linear interpolation. The source code and the weights of the final Pix2Pix model are available at https://github.com/J-3TO/detectorGapRemoval_Pix2Pix.

Photon-counting detectors offer several advantages over conventional detectors, but are commonly designed with individual detector tiles arranged into a larger panel, introducing physical gaps in the field of view. These gaps do not provide imaging information and can cause errors in subsequent processing steps, which propagate into artifacts in the reconstructed tomographic images.

Several classical algorithms exist to fill image gaps. Linear interpolation is fast but transmits only smooth, low-frequency information into the gap and fails to reproduce the surrounding texture. More sophisticated inpainting techniques, such as the fast-marching method of Telea [18] or the Navier–Stokes-based approach [2], better preserve local structure, but are slower, require manual parameter tuning, and still struggle to reproduce realistic texture.

Specifically for detector gaps, Brun et al. proposed a physics-informed approach: the masked measurement is reconstructed iteratively and forward-projected, and the forward-projected values are combined with partial-differential-equation-based inpainting to fill the gap [4]. papers.title: Quota-Based Traffic Classification for Bounded Jitter in Multi-CQF under Redundancy Mechanisms
papers.abstract: The demand for deterministic and reliable communication is rapidly increasing in industrial networks. Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) addresses these requirements through deterministic scheduling and redundancy mechanisms such as Multiple Cyclic Queuing and Forwarding (Multi-CQF) and Frame Replication and Elimination for Reliability (FRER). Multi-CQF guarantees bounded end-to-end (E2E) latency and jitter, while FRER provides seamless fault tolerance through redundant forwarding. With static traffic classification, redundant paths with different hop counts can exhibit different E2E latency ranges. This can amplify jitter when a failure causes packets to be delivered over a longer redundant path. To address this, we propose a quota-based traffic classification mechanism that adapts class assignments hop-by-hop using a common E2E latency budget derived from the primary path, thereby mitigating jitter amplification. Simulation results show that the proposed mechanism reduces jitter amplification by up to 70% and latency degradation by up to 41% compared to static classification.

papers.title: Machine-accelerated extraction of experimental superconducting parameters for physical insight and prediction across thousands of materials
papers.abstract: New superconductors could unlock next-generation technologies from nuclear fusion to lossless electronics. Machine learning can predict candidate superconductors but lacks validated experimental training data beyond the critical temperature. Here we present AutoSuperCon, a database of eight superconducting parameters, containing 20354 entries for 6793 superconductors. The data were extracted from over 47000 arXiv preprints using a large language model and validated against reference datasets ($R^2 = 0.96$ with NIMS SuperCon). Using AutoSuperCon, we show that median gap ratios rise from 3.6 in conventional superconductors to 6.4 in cuprates, 28% of upper critical fields exceed the Pauli limit, and critical temperatures lie below a ceiling proportional to the superfluid density. Further, we train composition-based predictors for the critical temperature ($R^2_{\log}=0.83$) and the upper critical field ($R^2_{\log}=0.69$), boosted by transfer learning. Within known superconducting families, composition alone is sufficient to screen candidates for both parameters. AutoSuperCon thus enables physical insight and data-driven discovery across thousands of superconductors.

Discovering new superconductors with desirable properties would advance technologies from high-efficiency electronics to medical imaging to nuclear fusion. However, superconductor discovery has historically owed more to chance than design [1]. For example, neither cuprate [2] nor iron-based [3] superconductors were predicted by theory. The same is true even for most conventional superconductors, whose phonon-mediated pairing is quantitatively described by the Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) theory [4] and its extensions. Such models are typically trained on materials from the NIMS SuperCon dataset [11], a compilation of superconductors and their critical temperatures.

papers.title: Early Reflections on How Large Language Models are Reshaping Software Engineering Research
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are radically reshaping software engineering (SE) research. Yet, their steep financial and computational costs raise questions about who participates in that change, and who does not. By analysing all 1,918 papers published in the ICSE 2019-2026 Research and SEIP tracks, we uncover a shifting and highly concentrated research landscape. China and the US dominate LLM-based SE research, appearing in 74% of LLM-based publications between 2023-2026, yet they diverge sharply in their use of commercial versus open-weight models. Beneath this national dominance lies extreme institutional concentration: just 5 institutions in China and 7 in the US appear in more than half of their respective nations' LLM-based output. In the US, only half of the unique institutions active in 2023-2026 participated in LLM-based research, whereas Singapore displays broader usage, with 11 of 15 active institutions participating in LLM-based work. Furthermore, across 2023-2026 Research-track papers, industry involvement is more prevalent in LLM-based work (23.4% vs 16.9%), and academia-only papers make up a smaller share (63.4% vs 70.9%). Crucially, we expose a gap in model usage across industry and academia. SEIP track papers lean strongly towards commercial LLMs, with 77.4% featuring them and 40.5% using them exclusively. In contrast, only 21.2% of Research-track work relies strictly on commercial models, making greater use of open-weight models that typically support more sustainable and reproducible experiments. However, this divide warrants reflection on the extent to which SE research aligns with industry practice.

These costs risk contributing to geographical and institutional disparities in access to the computational resources required to participate in research [1]. As early as 2021, industry-developed AI models were, on average, 29 times larger than those developed in academia [2]. More recently, a 2025 questionnaire of 57 authors of LLM-based ICSE papers found that more than half were uncertain about their ability to sustain the costs of experiments involving commercial LLMs [3]. papers.title: RUMI: A Robotiq-Matched Universal Manipulation Interface for Robot Learning with Augmented Reality and Haptic Feedback
papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require carefully controlled contact forces for successful execution, yet large-scale, force-aware datasets remain scarce. Handheld interfaces can help by transmitting interaction forces directly through the operator's arm, but most existing designs are tailored to simple linear grippers and do not match the nonlinear mechanics of widely used robotic grippers. We present RUMI, a handheld universal manipulation interface matched to the Robotiq 2F-85 with exchangeable fingertip sensors that preserves the target gripper geometry while enabling natural input before contact and force measurement after contact. By integrating the tracking system into a virtual reality headset, our method provides real-time augmented reality feedback about the kinematic feasibility of motion on the target robot platform. We further introduce a haptic feedback mechanism that supports force-aware teleoperation for simulated and real robots. A user study shows fewer episodes containing joint-limit violations with live robot visualization and pose initialization (3/50) than without augmented reality (16/50). We additionally train imitation policies from demonstrations, collected using two different fingertip modalities enabled by the gripper-matched hardware, and assess the haptic interface's capability for collecting force-aware teleoperation datasets in simulation.

This is increasingly relevant for large visuomotor policies, whose performance depends on the scale and quality of their demonstration data [3]. papers.title: Frequency-dependent time delays in Sgr A* from a broadband VLA observation
papers.abstract: Frequency-dependent radio time delays have been measured in Sgr A* light curves, with higher-frequency emission generally leading lower-frequency emission. These lags have been interpreted in terms of an organized jet-like outflow, expanding plasma components, or magnetic-flux eruptions, although their origin and recurrence remain uncertain. We aim to search for and quantify frequency-dependent radio time delays in a new high-cadence Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA) observation of Sgr A*. Using the improved broad 12-37 GHz frequency coverage, we measured the timing of the dominant variability feature and compared the resulting lag-wavelength slope with previous measurements. Sgr A* was observed with the VLA on 28 May 2022 in the Ku, K, and Ka bands over a 6-hour track. We extracted both band-averaged and 2 GHz subband light curves and measured the delays using a peak-time method and a locally normalized cross-correlation function. The light curves show one broad variability feature, with the maximum occurring progressively later at lower observing frequencies. Both timing methods recover a positive lag-wavelength relation, with a slope of order 40 min/cm. This value agrees with time lag results reported over more than 15 years from the first VLA observations at 22-43 GHz to later multifrequency VLA and ALMA campaigns. The sign and magnitude of the estimated delay are consistent with outward propagation through an optically thick synchrotron-emitting region. The recurrence of comparable delays over almost two decades suggests that frequency-dependent radio lags are a persistent feature of Sgr A* variability. Broadband, multi-epoch VLA monitoring of Sgr A* provides a useful probe of its radio variability, but robust lag measurements require high cadence and improved (u,v) coverage of both Sgr A* and the surrounding extended emission such as by combining different VLA configurations.

Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*) is the compact radio source associated with the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way. Its mass, M≃4×106​M⊙M\simeq 4\times 10^{6}\,M_{\odot}, is constrained by stellar orbital measurements (Ghez et al. 2008; Gillessen et al. 2009; GRAVITY Collaboration et al. 2020). Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) observations at ∼230\sim 230 GHz have resolved the emission on horizon scales, revealing a ring-like morphology with a central brightness depression (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al. 2022a; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al. 2022b; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al. 2022c; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al. 2022d; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al. 2022e; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al. 2022f), interpreted as the black hole shadow (Falcke et al. 2000). At radio to submillimeter wavelengths, the spectral energy distribution of Sgr A* rises toward a peak around 1–2 THz, consistent with self-absorbed synchrotron emission (Falcke et al. 1998). The source is optically thick at lower radio frequencies and becomes increasingly optically thin at higher frequencies, so multifrequency observations probe different depths in the compact emitting region. Jet models for Sgr A* reproduce its flat radio spectrum as a superposition of self-absorbed synchrotron components (Blandford and Königl 1979; Falcke et al. 1993). Based on this model, Falcke (1999, Sec. 3.3.) predicted frequency-dependent time lags and sizes as a signature of a jet-like outflow. Very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) measurements also show that the apparent size decreases with the observed wavelength once interstellar scattering is accounted for, indicating that higher frequencies sample smaller spatial scales closer to the black hole (Bower et al. 2006; Doeleman et al. 2008; Issaoun et al. 2019).

Sgr A* is variable throughout the electromagnetic spectrum, with short infrared and X-ray flares and lower-amplitude radio and millimeter variability on timescales from minutes to hours (Dexter et al. 2014; Witzel et al. 2018; Wielgus et al. 2022). GRAVITY resolved loop-like centroid motion and polarization-angle rotation during bright near-infrared flares, consistent with compact emission evolving on dynamical timescales close to the black hole (GRAVITY Collaboration et al. 2018; GRAVITY Collaboration et al. 2023). At millimeter wavelengths, ALMA observations show variability on timescales of tens of minutes to hours (Wielgus et al. 2022). In addition to the characteristic variability timescale, time delays have also been measured between light curves observed at different frequencies. Yusef-Zadeh et al. (2006) reported that the peak of a flare at 43 GHz preceded that at 22 GHz by 20–40 min. They explained the delay using the expanding cloud model of van der Laan (1966), in which an initially optically thick synchrotron-emitting component expands and first becomes optically thin at higher frequencies and subsequently at lower frequencies. Falcke et al. (2009) interpreted frequency-dependent size and lag relations in terms of the jet model and derived a moderately relativistic outflow velocity with γ​β∼2\gamma\beta\sim 2. More recently, general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations by Vos et al. (2024) showed that outward-propagating magnetic-flux eruptions in the jet-disk boundary can produce lower-frequency delays through the combined effects of plasma propagation and evolving synchrotron opacity. Using simultaneous Very Large Array (VLA) and ALMA observations between 19 and 100 GHz, Brinkerink et al. (2015) measured a lag–wavelength slope of 42±14​min​cm−142\pm 14\penalty\ \mathrm{min\,cm^{-1}}. Assuming that the variability traces an outflow, the estimated lag and intrinsic size–frequency relation implied mildly relativistic flow speeds. In a subsequent multi-epoch VLA study between 18 and 48 GHz, Brinkerink et al. (2021) find positive lag slopes in five of eight epochs. Their synthetic data analysis was consistent with a persistent lag relation of approximately 40​min​cm−140\penalty\ \mathrm{min\,cm^{-1}}, which they interpreted as evidence of a mildly relativistic outflow. At lower frequencies, Michail et al. (2021) measured a delay of approximately 20 min between 9.948 and 8.052 GHz within a single VLA receiver band and epoch. At millimeter wavelengths, Miyazaki et al. (2013) estimated a much shorter lag of -2.56 min between 102 and 90 GHz, with the lower-frequency light curve leading the higher-frequency one. This change in lag behavior at higher frequencies may be expected as the emission approaches the transition from the optically thick to the optically thin synchrotron regime (Falcke et al. 2009; Brinkerink et al. 2015). At even higher frequencies, Wielgus et al. (2022) report no measurable lag between the 213213 and 229229 GHz ALMA light curves; however, the fractional frequency separation Δ​ν/ν\Delta\nu/\nu between these bands is small, and the resulting sensitivity may not be sufficient to rule out detectable time delays across the broader submillimeter range. Finally, Brinkerink et al. (2021) argue that short-timescale variability correlated across several frequency bands can introduce a zero-lag component in cross-correlation curves, while uncorrelated noise can bias the recovered lags toward smaller values.

papers.title: oMEGACat. XI. Kinematic Characterization of Omega Centauri's Subpopulations: A Flattened Primordial Component
papers.abstract: Omega Centauri ($\omega$ Cen; NGC 5139), the likely stripped nucleus of a dwarf galaxy accreted by the Milky Way, is one of the few galactic nuclei resolvable into individual stars. Because of its long relaxation time, the kinematics of its stars may still retain memory of how this nucleus formed. We combine HST proper motions and MUSE line-of-sight velocities from the oMEGACat survey to compare populations defined by abundance variations (the chromosome map), metallicity, and age within the half-light radius. The chromosome-map division separates two dynamically distinct components. The primordial stars have a flattened dispersion field, with kinematic ellipticity $\epsilon \approx 0.7$ ($\sigma_{\rm minor} / \sigma_{\rm major} \approx 0.8$), which we recover independently in the line-of-sight velocities and the proper motions. The enriched stars are consistent with $\epsilon=0$ in the line-of-sight velocities and are no more flattened than the full sample in the proper motions, and the two components show no strong difference in rotation. Metallicity bins show no comparable structure, because each bin mixes stars from both components, and the age-metallicity sample covers only the cluster core, where it cannot test for the flattening. The present-day central concentration of the most enriched (P2) stars suggests that they formed more centrally concentrated than the primordial stars, independent of assembly scenario. These results favor a picture in which the primordial stars retain the flattened orbital structure of the progenitor, while the enriched stars fell inward as dense clumps or formed in compact, centrally concentrated starbursts.

papers.intro:
Omega Centauri (ω\omega Cen; NGC 5139) is the most massive globular cluster in the Milky Way (MW), with a mass of approximately 33–4×106​M☉4\times 10^{6}\,M_{\sun} [7, 33]. Unlike typical globular clusters (GCs), ω\omega Cen exhibits complex stellar populations, spanning more than 1 dex in metallicity [55, 87, 88], and an age spread of ∼\sim3 Gyr [122, 19]. These characteristics strongly suggest that ω\omega Cen is the remnant nuclear star cluster (NSC) of a dwarf galaxy that was accreted and stripped by the MW [65, 11, 86, 93, 108]. Furthermore, recent astrometric detections of fast-moving central stars support the presence of an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) of ≳8200​M☉\gtrsim 8200\,M_{\sun} at its core [46], a hallmark of galactic nuclei. Understanding the formation and evolution of ω\omega Cen can therefore constrain the processes governing NSC formation and the assembly history of the MW (e.g., the Gaia-Enceladus/Sausage (GSE) merger; D. Massari et al. 78, G. Limberg et al. 69, which C. F. P. Laporte & M. D. A. Orkney 63 date to ∼\sim11 Gyr ago and associate with a coeval burst of GC formation).

Decades of photometric and spectroscopic studies have revealed that ω\omega Cen hosts multiple, distinct populations of stars [90, 65, 9, 55, 73, 12, e.g.,]. The oMEGACat survey11 1 https://omegacatalog.github.io/ [87, 47] has since mapped the metallicity [88], age [19], helium enhancement [20], and chemical abundance [127] distributions of these populations, as well as the intracluster medium [126].

Clontz et al. [21]. The P2 population is characterized by extreme helium enhancement (Δ​Y∼0.15\Delta Y\sim 0.15), nitrogen and sodium enrichment, and oxygen depletion [89, 95, 55, 73, 74, 20, 127]. By linking the chromosome map on the red giant branch (RGB) to the subgiant branch (SGB) age–metallicity relation (AMR), C. Clontz et al. [21] demonstrated a ∼\sim1 Gyr age gap between the P1 populations and the P2 populations across all metallicities, which requires an extended formation history [102, 103, 74, 12, e.g.,]. The true population count is likely even finer than this three-way split: A. Bellini et al. [12] identify at least 15 subpopulations along the main sequence (MS), F. Akbaba et al. [2] recover ten distinct populations from clustering in abundance space, while C. Clontz et al. [21] identify 14 subpopulations through data-driven clustering in photometry and metallicity.

The labels P1 and P2 echo the primordial and enriched populations of typical GCs, but differ from them in important ways: P2’s helium enhancement lies at the extreme of the range seen in GCs, and both P1 and P2 span a wide range in [Fe/H][\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}] [55, 73] and in age [21], whereas the populations of typical clusters share a single metallicity and are close to coeval [6]. The scenarios proposed for the multiple populations of typical clusters therefore may not apply to ω\omega Cen’s P1 and P2.

Stellar kinematics probe the assembly history of stellar systems. In particular, the multiple stellar populations observed in typical GCs have long been known to exhibit distinct spatial distributions [64, 66, 82, e.g.,] and kinematic properties [23, 83, 68, 26, 24, 67, e.g.,]. These differences can provide clues about the formation mechanisms of the various populations, such as whether they formed in situ or were accreted from external sources (e.g., pristine gas from the surroundings, A. Standard models predict that P2 forms from enriched ejecta left behind by P1 stars, which settle into a compact, rotating, centrally concentrated configuration before undergoing star formation [10, 79]. Hydrodynamical simulations of second-generation formation from asymptotic giant branch (AGB) ejecta mixed with accreted low-density pristine gas likewise produce a compact, centrally concentrated second generation [128]. The specific enrichment channel is debated, with proposed sources including AGB stars [31, 27, e.g.,], interacting binaries [28], fast-rotating massive stars [29], and supermassive or accreting extremely massive stars [30, 42, 41] [see 101, 6, for critical assessments], and most predict that P2 is more centrally concentrated than P1, since enriched ejecta settle toward the cluster center. Recent observations, however, present a more mixed view: among dynamically young clusters, some have a centrally concentrated enriched population, some a centrally concentrated primordial population, and some fully mixed populations [66].

Large proper-motion and MUSE samples now show that kinematic differences between the populations are common. In most clusters the P2 stars have enhanced radial anisotropy compared to the P1 stars, which is consistent with the P2 stars being more centrally concentrated [83, 68, 26, 24]. The evidence for a rotation difference is similarly mixed, with no universal, consistent difference in rotation between P1 and P2 stars across clusters [23, 26, 67]. These differences are weaker in dynamically older clusters [26, 24], and some clusters show no significant difference or the opposite sense [75, e.g.,].

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Euclid Lens Identification Pipeline and Scientific Exploration (ECLIPSE) D: Photometric redshifts and the first census of strong lenses in the galaxy evolution framework
papers.abstract: The Euclid mission is revolutionising the study of strong gravitational lenses by providing high-resolution imaging over an unprecedented survey area, increasing the number of known lenses by two orders of magnitude compared to previous surveys. Characterising this sample of lens-galaxies requires accurate measurements of their physical properties. However, standard catalogue photometry often blends the light from the foreground lens and the lensed background source, limiting the reliability of derived galaxy parameters. We present a homogeneous catalogue of photometric redshifts and physical properties for 9538 galaxy-scale strong lenses identified in Euclid's DR1 strong-lens sample. We use deblended multiwavelength photometry obtained from the lens modelling of Euclid and ground-based images with PyAutoLens. The photometric redshifts of the lens galaxies are estimated using the template-fitting code Phosphoros. The stellar masses, SFRs, stellar ages, and metallicities are inferred through SED fitting with Prospector, adopting a flexible non-parametric SFH and a Salpeter IMF. The robustness of the inferred parameters is assessed through comparisons with spectroscopic redshifts and external galaxy surveys. The sample of lenses spans a broad redshift range of $0.13\lesssim z_{\rm phot} \lesssim 1.98$, with a median $z_{\rm phot} = 0.68^{+0.33}_{-0.29}$. The sample is dominated by massive quiescent galaxies with a $M_\ast$ range $[10^{10},\,10^{12.1}]\,M_\odot$ and a median $\log_{10}(M_\ast/M_\odot) = 11.39^{+0.29}_{-0.33}$. This catalogue represents one of the first large-scale characterisations of strong-lens galaxies in the Euclid era. By combining deblended photometry with homogeneous photometric redshift and SED-fitting analyses, it provides a foundation for studies of galaxy evolution, lens-galaxy scaling relations, and the connection between stellar and total mass in strong lenses.

papers.intro:
The Euclid space mission will transform observational cosmology by surveying 14 000​deg214{\,}000\penalty\ \mathrm{deg}^{2} of the extragalactic sky with high-resolution optical imaging and near-infrared (NIR) photometry (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022; Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025). Over the next few years, Euclid is expected to resolve approximately 1.5 billion galaxies (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025) and discover about 170 000 galaxy–galaxy strong lenses (Collett 2015), nearly two orders of magnitude more galaxy-scale lenses than previously known. This unprecedented sample will enable robust statistical studies of the strong-lens population, provide independent probes of cosmology (Sharma et al. 2023) and time-delay cosmography, test dark matter models on small scales through the detection of low-mass subhalos (O’Riordan et al. 2023; Vegetti et al. 2024), and constrain the internal structure and assembly histories of massive galaxies (Shajib et al. 2025).

Over the next few years, Euclid is expected to resolve approximately 1.5 billion galaxies (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025) and discover about 170 000 galaxy–galaxy strong lenses (Collett 2015), nearly two orders of magnitude more galaxy-scale lenses than previously known. This unprecedented sample will enable robust statistical studies of the strong-lens population, provide independent probes of cosmology (Sharma et al. 2023) and time-delay cosmography, test dark matter models on small scales through the detection of low-mass subhalos (O’Riordan et al. 2023; Vegetti et al. 2024), and constrain the internal structure and assembly histories of massive galaxies (Shajib et al. 2025).

Characterising the lens galaxies requires not only accurate lens models, but also robust measurements of their physical properties. The lens redshift sets the physical scale of the lens, while spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting provides stellar masses, star-formation rates (SFRs), luminosities, and rest-frame colours. These measurements enable statistical studies of the lens population and comparisons with the general galaxy population.
