The lens redshift sets the physical scale of the lens, while spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting provides stellar masses, star-formation rates (SFRs), luminosities, and rest-frame colours. These measurements enable statistical studies of the lens population and comparisons with the general galaxy population.

While spectroscopic observations provide the most reliable redshift measurements, they are not available for the vast majority of strong lenses that will be discovered by current and future imaging surveys. Consequently, accurate photometric redshifts and homogeneous SED-derived physical properties have become essential for exploiting these samples statistically. Within the context of Euclid, accurate photometric redshifts are also a fundamental requirement for achieving the mission’s primary cosmological goals, including weak gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering. To meet the mission requirements on redshift precision [i.e. σz<0.05​(1+z)\sigma_{z}<0.05\penalty\ (1+z)], the fraction of catastrophic outliers (Amara & Réfrégier 2007; Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025, typically <10%<10\%;), and the calibration of the mean redshift in tomographic bins (Ma et al. 2006; Huterer et al. 2006; Amara & Réfrégier 2007; Kitching et al. 2008; Euclid Collaboration: Tucci et al. 2026), Euclid combines high-resolution VIS imaging (Euclid Collaboration: Cropper et al. 2025) and near-infrared NISP photometry (Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al. 2025) with complementary multi-band optical data from ground-based surveys. The resulting homogeneous photometric data set enables robust photometric redshift estimates and the derivation of galaxy physical properties for billions of sources across the extragalactic sky.

Strong-lens systems represent a particularly challenging subset of the Euclid galaxy population because their observed photometry contains contributions from multiple objects at different redshifts. In particular, accurate photometric redshift estimation for the foreground lens galaxies is complicated by contamination from lensed source light, and crowded environments. The reliability of the inferred photometric redshift, zphotz_{\rm phot}, and stellar population properties depends sensitively on the lens-to-source surface brightness ratio, with significant degradation in systems dominated by lensed-source source emission. At the same time, lensing magnification enables the detection of intrinsically faint, high-redshift background galaxies that would otherwise remain inaccessible, extending such studies into the early Universe. Therefore, a proper characterisation of strong-lens systems requires sophisticated deblending and template-fitting techniques, validated through spectroscopic constraints.

Therefore, a proper characterisation of strong-lens systems requires sophisticated deblending and template-fitting techniques, validated through spectroscopic constraints.

This paper presents the photometric redshift estimation and multiwavelength characterisation of the first large sample of strong gravitational lenses discovered by Euclid. Precise redshift estimates are essential for nearly all strong lensing applications, from deriving lens masses and physical scales to studying the galaxy populations responsible for the lensing. The methodology adopted here was developed, tested, and validated using 328 galaxy–galaxy strong lenses presented in the Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1; Euclid Collaboration: Walmsley et al. 2026a; Euclid Collaboration: Rojas et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. 2026c; Euclid Collaboration: Li et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Holloway et al. 2026b; Euclid Collaboration: Ecker et al. 2026), consisting of Grade A or B lens candidates with a successful lens model. We apply this methodology to the DR1 sample of similar Grade A and B lens candidates, identified using improved machine-learning models for lens discovery (Euclid Collaboration: Vincken et al. 2026b; Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. 2026b; Euclid Collaboration: Fogliardi et al. 2026). Building on the methods established with the Q1 strong-lens sample, Euclid Collaboration: Holloway et al. (2026a) describes the discovery and validation of the DR1 lens candidates, Euclid Collaboration: Nightingale et al. (2026) presents the lens-mass modelling of the systems, and Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. (2026a) introduces the full DR1 strong-lens catalogue. Here, we derive photometric redshifts and characterise the lens galaxies through measurements of their stellar populations, structural parameters, and scaling relations. Together, these studies provide a comprehensive characterisation of the largest sample of galaxy-scale strong lenses currently known, all discovered by Euclid, and establish the framework for exploiting the much larger lens samples expected from future Euclid data releases.

papers.title: Identification of extragalactic radio sources in the VISTA survey of the Magellanic Clouds using an unsupervised machine learning algorithm
papers.abstract: The Magellanic Clouds benefit from a wealth of data across the electromagnetic spectrum, but extracting extragalactic sources from these crowded fields is a less than straightforward endeavour. We used an unsupervised machine learning algorithm (t-distributed stochastic neighbourhood embedding; t-SNE) to classify 6,652 and 1,356 sources in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, respectively, that were detected in the VISTA Survey of the Magellanic Clouds (VMC) and the Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) survey with the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP). Multi-wavelength photometry and colours from optical to radio were used as features to cluster similar sources together in 2D space on a t-SNE map. We used previously classified sources to separate the clusters into five classes: AGN, low-redshift galaxies, blazars, dusty stellar objects (e.g. young stellar objects, planetary nebul{\ae} etc) and high proper-motion stars. Previous photometric classifications from the literature match with specific clusters identified, as well as provide insight on areas of the t-SNE map for which there are no previous classifications. This work shows that the combination of unsupervised machine learning with photometry from optical to radio has proven adept at separating the stellar from the extragalactic, and the AGN from the galaxies. Our associated new spectroscopy with SALT includes new discoveries of AGN up to redshift 3.3 and Magellanic emission-line objects.

papers.intro:
Identifying extragalactic sources from sky fields crowded with stars, such as the Galactic Plane and the Magellanic Clouds, is a less than straightforward and time consuming endeavour. As wider and deeper photometric surveys become available in these parts of the sky allowing us to better sample source’s spectral energy distribution (SED), this challenge becomes viable. However, various factors, such as emission lines, dust and variability of a source’s flux between measurements at different wavelengths, can cause some stellar sources to masquerade as extragalactic sources and vice versa (Hony et al., 2011; Pennock et al., 2022, e.g.).

Identifying extragalactic sources from sky fields crowded with stars, such as the Galactic Plane and the Magellanic Clouds, is a less than straightforward and time consuming endeavour. As wider and deeper photometric surveys become available in these parts of the sky allowing us to better sample source’s spectral energy distribution (SED), this challenge becomes viable. However, various factors, such as emission lines, dust and variability of a source’s flux between measurements at different wavelengths, can cause some stellar sources to masquerade as extragalactic sources and vice versa (Hony et al., 2011; Pennock et al., 2022, e.g.).

Extragalactic sources, in particular active galactic nuclei (AGN), are capable of emitting across the entire electromagnetic spectrum. Emission observed at different wavelengths relate to different parts of an AGN’s structure, such as the accretion disk observed in the optical/UV, the dusty torus (or obscuring structure) in the infrared and the presence jets and/or lobes in the radio. Photometry in the infrared is a powerful tool in identifying AGN in particular as the dusty torus has a distinct bump-like shape in an SED which helps isolate these sources in colour–colour and colour–magnitude diagrams (Werner et al., 2004; Stern et al., 2012; Mateos et al., 2012; Assef et al., 2013; Nikutta et al., 2014, e.g.). A radio detection is also a strong sign that we are observing an AGN, though it should be noted that star formation in galaxies and stellar sources (e.g. planetary nebulæ young stellar objects) are also capable of emitting in the radio, though they tend to be much weaker than AGN and exhibit flatter radio spectral slopes (Joseph et al., 2019, e.g.).

The Magellanic Clouds (including the Magellanic Bridge that links them) span ∼\sim 100 sq. degrees on the sky and benefit from a plethora of all-sky and Magellanic specific surveys from X-ray to radio. They have been observed in the near-infrared (near-IR) with the VISTA Magellanic Clouds survey (Cioni et al., 2011, VMC;) which showcases a great improvement in depth and angular resolution compared to previous IR surveys, and has detected stars encompassing most phases of evolution such as main sequence stars, red giant branch (RGB) stars, red clump stars, RR Lyræ and Cepheid variables, asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, post-AGB stars, planetary nebulæ (PNe) and supernova remnants (SNRs) (Gullieuszik et al., 2012; Cioni et al., 2013; Ripepi et al., 2015; Zivkov et al., 2018; Groenewegen et al., 2019; Zivkov et al., 2020; Groenewegen et al., 2020; Cusano et al., 2021; Choudhury et al., 2021, e.g.). The VMC has also had success in discovering background extragalactic sources (Cioni et al., 2013; Ivanov et al., 2016; Pennock et al., 2022; Ivanov et al., 2024). This is due to the benefits from all-sky surveys such as WISE (Wright et al., 2010; Cutri et al., 2013) and Magellanic Clouds specific surveys with the Spitzer Space Telescope as part of the Spitzer Agents of Galaxy Evolution (SAGE) survey of the LMC (Meixner et al., 2006) and SMC (Gordon et al., 2011), both at mid-IR wavelengths that have been used to identify AGN (Lacy et al., 2004; Donley et al., 2012; Stern et al., 2012, e.g.). Furthermore, the Clouds have been observed in the radio as part of the Evolutionary Map of the Universe all-sky (Joseph et al., 2019; Pennock et al., 2021, EMU;) survey. The combination of all these data has great potential for discovery of the more unusual and extreme cases of AGN, such as SAGE0536AGN (van Loon and Sansom, 2015; Pennock et al., 2022), which is a dusty AGN with one of the strongest 10μ\mum silicate emissions currently known.

The area of the Magellanic Clouds, contains hundreds of millions of sources to sort through, which would be an extremely time-consuming task. Machine learning has been put to good use in astronomy to learn patterns in large datasets and separate different classes of sources (Storrie-Lombardi et al., 1992; Farrah et al., 2009; Geach, 2012; Dieleman et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2020; Pennock et al., 2022; Rimoldini et al., 2023; Pennock et al., 2025; Prathap et al., 2026, e.g.). Supervised machine learning, such as applied to the Magellanic Clouds in Pennock et al. (2025), uses a training set from which to learn patterns which can then be applied to unseen data. However, such techniques only classify sources into previously known categories, and does not deal well with the fluctuations in real astrophysical numbers for the different classes. Unsupervised machine learning requires no training set and learns from all the data to structure and separate sources. Unsupervised machine learning is used to be able to combine a multitude of features that are not necessarily easily combined through human comparison between different diagrams and selection functions, which means it can identify groupings that are unbiased from human selection upfront. In Pennock et al. (2022) an unsupervised machine learning algorithm called t-SNE (t-distributed stochastic neighbourhood embedding) was used to cluster similar sources to find sources behind the SMC that were similar to the unusual AGN, SAGE0536AGN and SAGE0534AGN, whose emission appeared to be mostly from their AGN. This paper is a continuation of the t-SNE work but will look at all the sources, instead of a small subset, as well as expanding this technique to the LMC, in the aim of exploring the populations of radio detected sources, especially the AGN, in the crowded field of the Magellanic Clouds that have a large variety of different object types, from nebulae to high-z AGN, with a particular focus on what the near-IR and radio bands can do to separate these different populations.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Euclid Lens Identification Pipeline and Scientific Exploration (ECLIPSE) A: Strong lens catalogue overview
papers.abstract: We present 15 072 high-confidence strong lens candidates in Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1), spanning 2000 deg$^2$. These comprise 6073 grade A ('sure lens') and 8999 grade B ('probable lens') systems, which we publish alongside a further 9010 grade C ('possible lens') candidates. With more high-confidence candidates than all previous catalogues combined, this sample establishes a large, homogeneous data set of galaxy-scale strong lenses with high-resolution imaging, transforming strong lensing from a field of rare discoveries to a robust statistical tool for astrophysics and cosmology. Of the roughly 900 million sources in DR1, we searched the 68 million passing our catalogue selection using a bespoke discovery pipeline that synthesises scores from five machine-learning models with visual classifications from around 7000 citizen scientists and 67 strong lensing experts. Beyond classical Einstein rings, our catalogue includes 84 candidate double-source-plane lenses and over 1000 candidate disc lenses, two exotic classes with few previously known examples, as well as several hundred candidate lensed AGN and quasars. We deliver automated lens models for the combined grade A+B systems, and photometric redshifts and stellar population properties for the deflector galaxies, providing immediate science-ready data products. We find that the majority of the deflector galaxies are massive and quiescent, with stellar masses of $\log_{10}(M_\ast /M_\odot) = 11.39^{+0.29}_{-0.33}$ (Salpeter initial mass function; 16th-84th percentile range). The deflector galaxies span a range of photometric redshifts ($z=0.68 ^{+0.33}_{-0.29}$), extending to higher redshifts than previous ground-based lens samples, and the lenses have a typical Einstein radius of $0.85 ^{+0.44}_{-0.24}$ arcsec. Extrapolating by area, we expect over 100 000 high-confidence strong lens candidates in the Euclid Wide Survey.

papers.intro:
Strong gravitational lensing is the general relativistic phenomenon in which massive objects warp spacetime sufficiently to bend the light from a background source into multiple images, arcs, Einstein rings, and Einstein crosses (Einstein 1936). These cosmic mirages are unique and powerful probes of astrophysics and cosmology. Strong lensing is one of the most robust methods of accurately measuring the total mass of galaxies, providing a unique probe of their underlying mass distributions without a reliance on luminous matter. In addition to producing multiple images, the strong lensing effect acts as a cosmic telescope, magnifying the light from the background source. This opens new windows into galaxies in the early Universe, enabling the observation of objects too distant and faint to otherwise be detectable. Strong lensing is also sensitive to the composition and expansion history of the Universe, and hence can be used to constrain cosmological parameters, including the Hubble constant when there is a time-variable background source. We refer interested readers to Shajib et al. (2024) for a review of applications of galaxy-scale strong lensing to astrophysics and cosmology.

Historically, strong lensing has been a data-starved field due to its inherent rarity. Strong lensing requires a near-perfect alignment of the observer, a foreground deflector galaxy, and a background source – a rare configuration that occurs in fewer than 0.1% of observed galaxies. Additionally, galaxy-scale strong lenses are hard to detect: the average radius of an Einstein ring is theoretically expected to be just 0.4​″ (Collett 2015), meaning that a large fraction of strong lenses are unresolvable from the ground. The compounded effect of intrinsic rarity and small angular size has limited the growth of strong lens samples in the optical and near-infrared (NIR). Generally, previous imaging surveys have either been ground-based (e.g., Gavazzi et al. 2014; Jacobs et al. 2019a; Jacobs et al. 2019b; Petrillo et al. 2019; Cañameras et al. 2020; Storfer et al. 2024; Storfer et al. 2026), and therefore limited by resolution, or were conducted by high-resolution space telescopes, such as Hubble (HST) and James Webb (JWST; e.g., Garvin et al. 2022; Petit et al. 2025; Nightingale et al. 2025; Mahler et al. 2025; Hogg et al. 2025), which have a limited field of view. Figure 1 illustrates this trade-off, showing the number of lenses found by previous optical and NIR imaging surveys as a function of survey area and lens number density. Wide-area ground-based searches have so far produced the largest samples, with the largest homogeneous catalogue previously identified from imaging containing around 3000 lens candidates across 19 00019\,000 deg2 (Storfer et al. 2024).

However, Euclid (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025) is perfectly designed to overcome these challenges. The Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) will cover an area of 14 00014\,000 deg2 over the nominal six-year mission, mitigating the intrinsic rarity, while its high-resolution imaging (with a 0.1​″ pixel scale in the VIS instrument) is sufficient to resolve a substantial fraction of the lenses that would otherwise go undetected. As a result, Euclid will revolutionise the field of strong lens discoveries, being forecast to image around 170 000170\,000 galaxy-scale strong lenses – over an order of magnitude more than what was previously known (Collett 2015). Euclid DR1 (Euclid Data Release 1 2026) covers approximately 20002000 deg2 and represents an important milestone towards the survey’s final data set. Making up 15% of the full survey area, forecasts suggest that around 23 00023\,000 strong lenses should be discoverable within DR1. The prospect of such a massive sample offers unprecedented scientific opportunities, but extracting these rare systems from the tens of millions of non-lenses in the data is a non-trivial task. With true lenses outnumbered by ordinary galaxies by thousands to one, discovering even a majority of the strong lenses is not guaranteed. Maximising the potential from this wealth of data therefore requires a highly automated, robust, and concerted search effort.

Our DR1 strong lens search builds upon the ‘Strong Lens Discovery Engine’ (SLDE; Euclid Collaboration: Walmsley et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Rojas et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. 2026b; Euclid Collaboration: Li et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Holloway et al. 2026b; Euclid Collaboration: Ecker et al. 2026), a lens-finding pipeline that led to the discovery of approximately 600 galaxy-scale strong lens candidates in the Euclid Quick Release 1 (Q1; Euclid Quick Release Q1 2025). Q1 consists of just seven days worth of Euclid observations spanning 63 deg2, serving as a test-bed for developing and refining the pipeline in preparation for DR1. While the overall approach of combining multiple complementary machine-learning (ML) models with the power of crowd-sourced visual inspection remains the same, the DR1 search benefits from improved ML models (Euclid Collaboration: Vincken et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. 2026a; Euclid Collaboration: Fogliardi et al., in prep.), optimisation of visual inspection time (Euclid Collaboration: Holloway et al. 2026a), and is informed by lessons learnt from objects missed in the initial Q1 search (Euclid Collaboration: Ecker et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Xu et al. 2026).

The most robust approach, fitting physical mass and light profiles with posteriors inferred through sampling, is traditionally a system-by-system manual process that would be fundamentally infeasible at the scale of DR1. papers.title: A statistical study of ionized outflows in low-mass galaxies from DESI DR1
papers.abstract: We present a statistical analysis of ionized gas outflows in a large sample of low-mass ($\mathrm{log(M_{*}/M_{\odot})\lesssim10}$) galaxies at $z<0.45$ from the first data release of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI DR1). Using [OIII] and H$\alpha$ emission lines, we identify $\sim5800$ dwarf galaxies with robust signatures of ionized outflows. Most are star-forming systems above the star-forming main sequence, with a smaller fraction of composites and AGN hosts. The derived mass-loading factors span $\eta=0.001-1$, with a median $\eta\sim0.01$, consistent with previous studies at similar stellar masses. These values are $1$--$2$ dex lower than predicted by cosmological simulations, suggesting that the ionized phase traces only a minor fraction of the total outflow mass. Outflow velocities are sufficient to enrich the circumgalactic medium in $\gtrsim80\%$ of cases, while escape into the intergalactic medium appears efficient mainly in composite and AGN hosts. We find that mass-loading factors decrease with stellar mass, broadly reproducing simulated trends despite the normalization offset. Comparing individual detections with stacked spectra of the general low-mass star-forming population, we find systematically lower mass-loading factors in the stacks, although the difference decreases toward larger offsets above the star-forming main sequence. Together with a positive correlation between mass-loading factor and specific star-formation rate, this suggests that enhanced star formation and burstiness regulate feedback efficiency and shape galactic winds. Our results highlight the role of ionized outflows in the baryon cycle of low-mass galaxies and the need for multiphase studies to fully understand feedback in galaxy evolution.

papers.intro:
Stellar and active galactic nuclei (AGNs) feedback are considered a fundamental component of galaxies’ evolution. In fact, they play a leading role in regulating their baryon cycle by producing large-scale winds able to heat or remove a significant amount of gas from the interstellar medium (ISM), possibly polluting the surrounding circum- and intergalactic medium (CGM and IGM) with metal-enriched material (see e.g., Péroux & Howk 2020; Tacconi et al. 2020). Their ability to regulate or completely stop star formation is required by cosmological simulations to match both the low- and high-mass ends of the predicted halo mass function to the observed luminosity function of galaxies, thought to be primarily shaped by star-formation and AGN feedback, respectively (e.g., Silk & Mamon 2012; Behroozi et al. 2013; Pillepich et al. 2018). At the same time, they are needed to explain a number of fundamental scaling relations (e.g., Mannucci et al. 2009; McGaugh 2012; Somerville & Davé 2015; Curti et al. 2020), or the observed black hole-galaxy co-evolution (e.g., Kormendy & Ho 2013; King & Pounds 2015).

Nearby low-mass galaxies (with stellar mass lower than 1010​M⊙10^{10}\penalty\ M_{\rm{\odot}}; e.g., McCormick et al. 2018; Marasco et al. 2023) are particularly interesting for investigating outflow-driven processes. Their shallow gravitational potential wells allow galactic winds to efficiently expel gas and dust out of their stellar disk (e.g., Christensen et al. 2018; McCormick et al. 2018; Romano et al. 2023; Romano et al. 2024). Additionally, their low metallicities and compact nature make them excellent analogs of distant galaxies, offering valuable insight into mechanisms shaping galaxy evolution in the high-redshift Universe (e.g., Izotov et al. 2021; Shivaei et al. 2022). The general theoretical consensus is that stellar feedback dominates in low-mass galaxies, with high-mass stars exploding as supernovae and injecting energy and momentum in the ISM, accelerating the surrounding gas and producing galactic-scale outflows (e.g., Hopkins et al. 2012; Muratov et al. 2015; Hayward & Hopkins 2017; Nelson et al. 2019). This is also supported by observational studies which detect star-formation driven outflows in dwarf starbursting galaxies (e.g., Strickland & Stevens 2000; Cicone et al. 2016; Martín-Navarro & Mezcua 2018; Romano et al. 2023; Carniani et al. 2024; Hagedorn et al. 2026). On the other hand, over the past decade, evidence for AGN activity in nearby dwarf galaxies has been growing, as witnessed by thousands of detections via optical and infrared tracers (e.g., Reines et al. 2013; Sartori et al. 2015; Kaviraj et al. 2019; Manzano-King et al. 2019; Pucha et al. 2025; Rodríguez Morales et al. 2025; Rodríguez Morales et al. 2026). This challenges the current paradigm for which AGN feedback is not an important channel of star formation regulation in low-mass galaxies, and is being further theoretically investigated (e.g., Dashyan et al. 2018; Trebitsch et al. 2018; Koudmani et al. 2019; Arjona-Gálvez et al. 2024).

Given their multi-phase nature (e.g., Cicone et al. 2018; Fluetsch et al. 2019), different techniques, instruments, and gas tracers have been adopted for their characterization, covering the whole electromagnetic spectrum from the rest-frame UV/optical and far-infrared (FIR) emission (for the warm, ionized, and cold atomic and molecular gas; e.g., Erb et al. 2012; Heckman et al. 2015; Cicone et al. 2016; Roberts-Borsani et al. 2020; Calabrò et al. 2022; Concas et al. 2022; Hagedorn et al. 2026), to the X-ray emission (for the more hot phase; e.g., Ott et al. 2005; Tombesi et al. 2015; McQuinn et al. 2018). papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Euclid Lens Identification Pipeline and Scientific Exploration (ECLIPSE) B: Discovery pipeline overview
papers.abstract: We present the method used to identify the $15\,000$ high-grade galaxy-galaxy strong lens candidates in Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Given that lenses are intrinsically rare systems and the DR1 data set is vast, this lens search was conducted in a number of stages: a catalogue-level cut; a machine-learning and ensemble search; a two-stage citizen-science search, and finally grading of lens candidates by strong lens researchers. In this paper, we describe each search stage and their respective results. This search was enabled by the automated classification of over 68 million objects by neural networks, more than 4.5 million classifications of $300\,000$ objects by citizen-scientist volunteers, and the inspection of over $30\,000$ objects by strong lens researchers. We find this multi-stage approach helps maximise the number of lenses identified, while minimising inspection requirements of both citizen scientists and strong lens researchers. We measure a completeness in our comprehensive search of $0.73_{-0.15}^{+0.08}$ to grade A ('definite') systems and $0.34_{-0.06}^{+0.05}$ to grade A+B ('definite' + 'probable') systems. Our search therefore identifies the majority of the definitive strong lens systems in the DR1 area with the remainder likely to be fainter or more ambiguous cases. We find that researcher grading remains subjective; in this work we implement calibration to account for biases of individual inspectors and highlight the benefit of lens modelling (ECLIPSE-C) in determining the nature of a lens candidate. This paper forms part of the ECLIPSE series, here focussing on the discovery pipeline used to identify lens candidates in Euclid DR1; an overview of the lenses discovered is presented in ECLIPSE-A.

papers.intro:
Gravitational lensing, the deflection of light from a background source by a foreground mass, can be used as a probe of both astrophysics and cosmology. Strong gravitational lenses are systems in which this deflection is sufficiently strong that multiple images of the same background source are produced. Such systems can be used to constrain the Hubble constant (Refsdal 1964; Treu et al. 2022; TDCOSMO Collaboration et al. 2025), evolution of dark energy (Collett and Auger 2014; Li et al. 2024; Shajib et al. 2025), initial mass function (IMF, Leier et al. 2016; Newman et al. 2017; Sonnenfeld 2025), galaxy mass profiles (Koopmans et al. 2006; Sonnenfeld et al. 2013), and probe the large-scale distribution of matter via line-of-sight shear (Fleury et al. 2026), amongst many other science applications. However, such systems are very rare with extragalactic strong lensing requiring the close angular alignment of the background source (e.g. a galaxy, quasar, or supernova), and a foreground massive galaxy (e.g. a galaxy, galaxy group, or cluster).

The Euclid satellite will detect 1.5 billion galaxies over the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS, Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022; Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025). With an area of 14 000​deg214\,000\deg^{2} (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025), an IEI_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E} PSF with a full-width at half-maximum of 0.16​″ (Euclid Collaboration: Cropper et al. 2025; Euclid Collaboration: McCracken et al. 2026), as well as three near-infrared bands providing crucial colour information (Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al. 2025), the survey will revolutionise the field of strong lensing and is expected to identify more than 100 000100\,000 galaxy–galaxy lenses (Collett 2015). However, given their complexity and wide range of configurations, identifying these systems is a significant challenge. Historically, strong lenses were identified using arc-finding algorithms (Seidel and Bartelmann 2007; Gavazzi et al. 2014; Sonnenfeld et al. 2018). However, successively larger data volumes meant that citizen-science (Marshall et al. 2016; More et al. 2016), and more recently machine-learning methods (ML, e.g., Schuldt et al. 2025; González et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. 2026b), have been relied upon.

The Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1, Euclid Quick Release Q1 2025; Euclid Collaboration: Aussel et al. 2026), comprising 63.1​deg263.1\deg^{2} of imaging, provided an opportunity to test state-of-the-art strong lens classifiers and demonstrate the revolutionary potential of lens finding in Euclid. The systematic search was presented in the Strong Lens Discovery Engine series (Euclid Collaboration: Walmsley et al. 2026, Euclid Collaboration: Rojas et al. 2026, Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. 2026b, Euclid Collaboration: Li et al. 2026, Euclid Collaboration: Holloway et al. 2026b, Euclid Collaboration: Ecker et al. 2026, SLDE A–F respectively) and identified approximately 600600 high-grade lens systems.

The Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1, Euclid Quick Release Q1 2025; Euclid Collaboration: Aussel et al. 2026), comprising 63.1​deg263.1\deg^{2} of imaging, provided an opportunity to test state-of-the-art strong lens classifiers and demonstrate the revolutionary potential of lens finding in Euclid. The systematic search was presented in the Strong Lens Discovery Engine series (Euclid Collaboration: Walmsley et al. 2026, Euclid Collaboration: Rojas et al. 2026, Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. 2026b, Euclid Collaboration: Li et al. 2026, Euclid Collaboration: Holloway et al. 2026b, Euclid Collaboration: Ecker et al. 2026, SLDE A–F respectively) and identified approximately 600600 high-grade lens systems.

The Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1; Euclid Data Release 1 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Aussel and others 2026), which consists of 2000​deg2{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}2000}\deg^{2} of area, presents a unique opportunity to identify over 10 00010\,000 galaxy-scale lens systems across a homogeneous data set. This represents a significant advancement in the field of strong lensing, but identifying these lenses presents a number of challenges. Firstly, the data volume is vast, requiring scalable search techniques to analyse such large data sets. Secondly, the total number of detectable lenses in DR1 is comparable to the inspection budget of strong lens researchers, ∼104\sim 10^{4}, i.e., the total number of systems that inspectors could plausibly grade.11 1 Following the completion of a lens search, it is common for researchers to grade lens candidates according to their likelihood that they are truly lenses. Given this is a time-consuming process this can become a limiting factor for a large-scale lens search. The sample flagged for expert grading must therefore have very high purity to ensure that the majority of lens candidates are identified. This paper presents the discovery pipeline used to tackle these challenges, from ML to citizen inspection to grading of high-scoring candidates by strong lens researchers. This discovery pipeline was tuned to maximise the lens purity of systems inspected by experts, without compromising on the completeness of high-grade lenses.

The DR1 lens search differs from the Q1 search in a number of ways. While both searches include an ML classification, citizen-science classification and expert grading stage, the DR1 search includes two citizen-science inspection stages to further refine the lens sample. Secondly, the DR1 ML classification utilised networks retrained on a much larger sample of real lenses, including lenses within the DR1 area. Thirdly the DR1 classification pipeline measured and equitably accounted for the variation in performance of the ML classifiers in order to maximise the number of lenses identified. Finally, the DR1 galaxy selection was loosened with respect to Q1 (Sect. 2.3.1) to ensure low-redshift lenses were not excluded (Euclid Collaboration: Ecker et al. 2026).

This paper is part of the ECLIPSE series that describes the DR1 lens search and catalogue. Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. (2026c) presents the galaxy–galaxy strong lens catalogue, focussing on the nature of the lenses identified, and their properties. Euclid Collaboration: Nightingale et al. (2026) presents modelling results for the high-confidence lenses, and Euclid Collaboration: Nersesian et al. (2026) describes the photometric redshifts and physical properties of the strong lens candidates. We point to further papers for detailed description of aspects of the search and lens catalogue. Euclid Collaboration: Li et al. (2026, in prep.) and Euclid Collaboration: Ecker et al. (2026, in prep.) present the Euclid double-source plane lenses and edge-on lenses, respectively and Euclid Collaboration: Wielders et al. (in prep.) presents automated modelling of the multi-galaxy lens sample, i.e. strong lenses with more than one lens galaxy. Euclid Collaboration: Vincken et al. (in prep.) compares the behaviour of the different ML lens classifiers and Euclid Collaboration: Fogliardi et al. (in prep.) investigates the impact of training choices on ML lens classification performance. Alongside the modelling results, Euclid Collaboration: Vincken et al. (in prep) presents segmentation maps, which mask the lens, source, and background objects in the surroundings of each lens candidate.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Euclid Lens Identification Pipeline and Scientific Exploration (ECLIPSE) C: Lens modelling pipeline overview
papers.abstract: Galaxy-scale strong lenses provide precise measurements of galaxy mass distributions, magnified views of distant galaxies, and a competitive cosmological probe. Historically, such studies have been limited to hundreds of lenses, with automated modelling methods proving difficult to scale. We present automated lens modelling of 15 072 strong-lens candidates from Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1), over an order of magnitude larger than any previously modelled sample. Using PyAutoLens-JAX, we perform three fits with multi-Gaussian expansion (MGE), pixelised, and S\'ersic representations of the source, adopting an isothermal ellipsoid mass model with external shear. These fits provide foreground lens-light subtraction, adaptive Delaunay source reconstructions, and deblended photometry. More than 20 expert inspectors visually assess the resulting models, and each model is assigned the classification on which at least 75% of its inspectors agree. Of the 6073 grade A (secure) lens candidates, inspectors classify 4098 (67.5%) as successfully modelled, 580 (9.6%) as failures, 317 (5.2%) as multi-galaxy lenses, 15 (0.2%) as double-source-plane lenses, and 7 (0.1%) as unsure if lens, while 1032 (17.0%) reach no consensus and 24 (0.4%) have incomplete models. For the 8999 grade B (probable) candidates, the modelling success rate falls to 43.1%, primarily reflecting an increase in cases without consensus (37.6%), rather than a comparable increase in agreed failures (12.9%). Successfully modelled grade A and B systems have a median effective Einstein radius of 0.85 arcsec and a median total $I_E$-band source magnification of 8.1. We publicly release the successful lens models, their inferred properties, and magnified-source reconstructions through the ECLIPSE catalogue, demonstrating automated modelling at Euclid sample sizes and enabling population-level strong-lensing science.

papers.intro:
Galaxy-scale strong gravitational lensing occurs when a foreground galaxy aligns closely along the line of sight with a more distant background source. The mass of the foreground galaxy curves space-time, deflecting and magnifying the light of the source into multiple images, arcs, or, in the most aligned configurations, complete Einstein rings (Kochanek, 2006; Treu, 2010). Each such system encodes an unusually rich set of astrophysical measurements: the total mass and dark matter distribution of the foreground galaxy (Bolton et al., 2008; Vegetti et al., 2014; Oguri et al., 2014; Sonnenfeld et al., 2015), and a magnified view of a high-redshift source that would otherwise be inaccessible (Swinbank et al., 2015; Atek et al., 2015; Dye et al., 2018; Rizzo et al., 2020; Amvrosiadis et al., 2025). Strong lenses also provide cosmological constraints on the Hubble constant through time delays (Suyu et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2020; Birrer et al., 2020), the matter density and dark energy through double-source-plane systems (Collett & Auger, 2014; Sahu et al., 2025; Euclid Collaboration: Li et al., 2026), and cosmic shear through line-of-sight perturbations (Birrer et al., 2017; Birrer et al., 2018; Hogg et al., 2026; Fleury et al., 2026), for which Euclid’s upcoming weak-lensing catalogue further enables cross-correlations with galaxy shapes and tests for systematic errors in shear measurements (Hogg et al., 2023; Fleury et al., 2026).

The mass of the foreground galaxy curves space-time, deflecting and magnifying the light of the source into multiple images, arcs, or, in the most aligned configurations, complete Einstein rings (Kochanek, 2006; Treu, 2010). Each such system encodes an unusually rich set of astrophysical measurements: the total mass and dark matter distribution of the foreground galaxy (Bolton et al., 2008; Vegetti et al., 2014; Oguri et al., 2014; Sonnenfeld et al., 2015), and a magnified view of a high-redshift source that would otherwise be inaccessible (Swinbank et al., 2015; Atek et al., 2015; Dye et al., 2018; Rizzo et al., 2020; Amvrosiadis et al., 2025). Strong lenses also provide cosmological constraints on the Hubble constant through time delays (Suyu et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2020; Birrer et al., 2020), the matter density and dark energy through double-source-plane systems (Collett & Auger, 2014; Sahu et al., 2025; Euclid Collaboration: Li et al., 2026), and cosmic shear through line-of-sight perturbations (Birrer et al., 2017; Birrer et al., 2018; Hogg et al., 2026; Fleury et al., 2026), for which Euclid’s upcoming weak-lensing catalogue further enables cross-correlations with galaxy shapes and tests for systematic errors in shear measurements (Hogg et al., 2023; Fleury et al., 2026).

Extracting that information requires strong lens modelling, a simultaneous analysis of the light of the foreground lens galaxy, its mass distribution, and the unlensed surface brightness of the background source. Conceptually, a model of the light of the source is forward ray-traced via general relativity, with its path distorted by a mass model of the foreground lens galaxy. This produces an image of the lensed source, which is added to a model image of the light of the foreground lens and compared to the data. Lens modelling puts this process in an inference procedure, varying the model parameters to determine the combination of lens light, mass, and source light that best reproduces the observed strong lens system (Warren & Dye, 2003; Suyu et al., 2006; Vegetti & Koopmans, 2009; Nightingale et al., 2018; Birrer & Amara, 2018; Vernardos & Koopmans, 2022; Galan et al., 2022, e.g.); see also the review by Shajib et al. (2024).

(2024).

As strong lens samples have grown, scaling lens modelling has posed a significant challenge. Dedicated strong lens surveys discovered hundreds of lenses (Bolton et al., 2008; Treu et al., 2011; Brownstein et al., 2012; Gavazzi et al., 2014; Shu et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2022), with modelling performed successfully but typically on a lens-by-lens basis using procedures that relied heavily on manual human intervention. Automated and uniform modelling pipelines have since been introduced (Nightingale et al., 2018; Nightingale et al., 2021) and demonstrated on real data (Shajib et al., 2019; Etherington et al., 2022; Schuldt et al., 2023), although these relied on manual preprocessing steps that have only recently been automated (Shajib et al., 2025; Euclid Collaboration: Vincken et al., 2026a). Automated modelling has also been demonstrated for lensed quasars (Ertl et al., 2023; Schmidt et al., 2023). Despite the availability of samples containing hundreds of strong lenses, automated modelling studies have generally been demonstrated on fewer than about 100 systems, highlighting the difficulty of scaling lens modelling to survey-sized data sets. Nightingale et al. (2025) present lens models for 419 strong lens candidates discovered with the James Webb Space Telescope as part of the COSMOS-Web Lens Survey (COWLS).

The Euclid mission (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al., 2022; Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al., 2025) will provide high-resolution imaging from its visible instrument (VIS), with a pixel scale of 0.1​″ and point-spread function (PSF) full width at half maximum (FWHM) of approximately 0.16​″ (Euclid Collaboration: Cropper et al., 2025; Euclid Collaboration: McCracken et al., 2026a), across 14 000​deg214\,000\,\deg^{2} of sky, alongside three near-infrared bands from its Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) that provide crucial colour information (Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al., 2025). This combination of image quality and survey scale is expected to yield in excess of 100 000100\,000 galaxy-scale strong lenses (Collett, 2015), transitioning strong lensing into the era of large statistical samples. The precise number depends on the lens and source populations assumed and on how lenses are identified (Holloway et al., 2023; Ferrami & Wyithe, 2024). The VIS imaging is sufficiently resolved to measure key lensing quantities directly from the data, including Einstein radii, lens-galaxy mass distributions, and the morphologies of lensed source galaxies.

Euclid DR1 (Euclid Data Release 1), covering approximately 2000​deg22000\,\deg^{2}, already represents a major step towards this goal and is expected to contain more strong lenses than all previous samples combined. Automated modelling of Euclid lenses has already been demonstrated on the Early Release Observations (Acevedo Barroso et al., 2025; O’Riordan et al., 2025) and, at larger scale, by the Strong Lens Discovery Engine (SLDE) collaboration on approximately 500 grade A and B lenses discovered in Q1 (Euclid Collaboration: Walmsley et al., 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Rojas et al., 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al., 2026b; Euclid Collaboration: Li et al., 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Holloway et al., 2026a; Euclid Collaboration: Ecker et al., 2026). Grade A denotes a secure lens with unambiguous lensing features, and grade B a probable lens requiring additional evidence to confirm its lensing nature. In the ECLIPSE catalogue and discovery pipeline (Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al., 2026a; Euclid Collaboration: Holloway et al., 2026b), both grades are assigned solely from visual inspection of the imaging, before lens modelling.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1): VIS processing and data products
papers.abstract: This paper describes the characteristics of the Euclid visible imager (VIS) data delivered as part of the Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). This data set contains 42092 calibrated frames. Validated nominal exposures cover 2092 deg$^2$ of sky. We outline the minor changes made to the VIS processing function (PF) since previous releases. For the wide survey, the photometric and astrometric accuracy of the reference stellar sample $(18.5 < I_{\rm E} < 19.8)$ is excellent. The internal and external astrometric dispersions are 0.08 and 0.18 mas, respectively, at the quadrant level, and 3.4 and 5.6 mas at the source level. The corresponding internal and external photometric dispersions are 0.76 and 1.4 mmag at the quadrant level, and 11 and 25 mmag at the source level. We characterise remaining astrometric and photometric systematic effects: focal-plane-dependent variations; time-dependent photometric offsets; and colour-dependent centroid shifts. The noise floor in the deepest VIS images appears to be set by the extended diffuse light of faint galaxies. Globally, the DR1 VIS data meet pre-launch mission requirements and the 42092 images it contains provide our first substantial look at the sky as seen by VIS.

papers.intro:
The ESA Euclid mission aims to improve our understanding of dark energy by precisely measuring the shapes and positions of an unprecedentedly large sample of galaxies (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025). A key element of Euclid is the VIS (VIS) camera (Euclid Collaboration: Cropper et al. 2025). This paper describes the processing and characteristics of the VIS images delivered as part of the Euclid DR1 (Euclid Data Release 1 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Aussel et al. 2026, DR1;), which were processed by the Euclid SGS (Euclid Collaboration: Ruffenach et al. 2026, SGS;). Previously, Q1 (Q1; Euclid Collaboration: McCracken et al. 2026, hereafter 8) and Q2 (Beaulieu et al. 2026, Q2;) provided 61.361.3 and 4.8​deg24.8\,\mathrm{deg}^{2} of VIS data, respectively. DR1 data contain nominal VIS exposures over 2092.2 deg2\mathrm{deg}^{2} spanning the EWS (EWS) and EDS (EDS) areas, and also include the data in the COSMOS area and other calibration fields. DR1 comprises principally survey data taken from 14 February 2024 to 21 May 2025. It also includes calibration fields and observations taken before the survey started during the PV (PV) phase. This paper presents a description of the characteristics of the VIS DR1 data set, an assessment of the performance of the VIS PF pipeline, and a detailed discussion of the global properties of the processed VIS DR1 data.

This paper describes the processing and characteristics of the VIS images delivered as part of the Euclid DR1 (Euclid Data Release 1 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Aussel et al. 2026, DR1;), which were processed by the Euclid SGS (Euclid Collaboration: Ruffenach et al. 2026, SGS;). Previously, Q1 (Q1; Euclid Collaboration: McCracken et al. 2026, hereafter 8) and Q2 (Beaulieu et al. 2026, Q2;) provided 61.361.3 and 4.8​deg24.8\,\mathrm{deg}^{2} of VIS data, respectively. DR1 data contain nominal VIS exposures over 2092.2 deg2\mathrm{deg}^{2} spanning the EWS (EWS) and EDS (EDS) areas, and also include the data in the COSMOS area and other calibration fields. DR1 comprises principally survey data taken from 14 February 2024 to 21 May 2025. It also includes calibration fields and observations taken before the survey started during the PV (PV) phase. This paper presents a description of the characteristics of the VIS DR1 data set, an assessment of the performance of the VIS PF pipeline, and a detailed discussion of the global properties of the processed VIS DR1 data.

The plan of this paper is as follows: Sect. 2 summarises the VIS PF and outlines the differences compared to Q1 (Q1) processing; Sect. 3 explains how DR1 input data were validated; Sect. 4 presents an investigation of the global performance of all the VIS images in DR1 and Sect. 5 outlines some remaining problems. Conclusions are presented in Sect. 6.

papers.title: Elastic tricriticality at the collapse of magnetic order in a valence fluctuating Eu-based compound
papers.abstract: Spin and charge fluctuations are key for understanding the properties of materials with strongly correlated electrons, but their coupling to the atomic crystal lattice is often assumed to be weak and perturbative. In this work, we demonstrate that at tricritical points (TCPs), that are associated with electronic correlations, a coupling to crystal elasticity is generically non-perturbative. It will modify the tricritical universality class leading to elastic tricriticality, characterized by a compressibility that diverges in a universal manner with the correlation length. To test this scenario experimentally, we use single crystals of EuPd$_2$(Si$_{1-x}$Ge$_x$)$_2$, where, depending on $x$ and pressure, magnetic order collapses due to strong valence fluctuations. First, we confirm the presence of a TCP for $x \approx 0.1$ by using complementary probes, in particular, measurements of relative length changes under control of temperature and He-gas pressure. Second, by studying the elastic response, we uncover clear signatures of elastic tricriticality, notably a drastically enhanced compressibility.

papers.title: Euclid: Data Release 1 (DR1) -- Bayesian 3D shape inference of star-forming galaxy populations
papers.abstract: Understanding the intrinsic 3D shapes of galaxies provides crucial insights into their formation and evolution, but determining these from projections remains challenging. We apply a Bayesian inference framework to optical images of galaxies from the Euclid Data Release 1, leveraging its large sample size to test the scalability and robustness of this methodology. Applying Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) sampling to S\'ersic axis ratios and effective radii, we constrain the population-level mean 3D ellipticity, triaxiality, and size, together with their covariances for $40\,864\,304$ star-forming galaxies with stellar masses $M_\ast=10^{9}$--$10^{10.5}M_\odot$ at redshifts $0<z<1.2$. Our sample size exceeds previous shape inference studies by factors of $440$--$52\,800$ relative to early observations by JWST, and factors of $440$--$17\,600$ relative to legacy observations from HST in overlapping mass-redshift bins, enabling finer binning alongside improved statistical constraints on shape evolution. We additionally include over 9 million galaxies at $z<0.5$, a regime historically limited by sample size in previous shape inference studies. We recover key evolutionary trends identified in previous smaller-sample studies. We find high ellipticities ($\mu_E \sim 0.600$--$0.821$) across all bins, indicating that the underlying 3D shape distributions are statistically dominated by flattened geometries. Most notably, we recover the decline of the prolate fraction towards $z=0$ at low masses ($M_\ast=10^{9}$--$10^{9.5}M_\odot$) reported by previous studies. This trend is seen consistently in comparable analyses of independent data sets spanning different depths and resolution regimes, showing that it is not an artefact of small-sample statistics, suggesting it may be a genuine feature of galaxy evolution. We also identify future methodological improvements for subsequent Euclid data releases.

papers.intro:
The study of galaxy 3D geometries through projected shapes spans nearly a century, and remains crucial to understanding how the diverse morphologies seen today formed and evolved. Such studies assume that galaxies can be approximated as 3D ellipsoids classified by their degree of flattening in certain directions. Hubble (1926) demonstrated that nearby galaxies have projected ellipticities too round to be explained by randomly orientated disc galaxies alone, leading to his well-known classification system, and the introduction of the flattened ‘lenticular’ galaxy class (de Vaucouleurs 1959; Sandage 1961). Subsequent analyses incorporated projected axis ratios for late- and early-type galaxies (Sandage et al. 1970; Binney 1978; Noerdlinger 1979, e.g.,). This eventually led to more ‘triaxial’ models to explain the kinematics of nearby elliptical galaxies (Contopoulos 1956; Stark 1977; Binney 1978, e.g.,).

Subsequent analyses incorporated projected axis ratios for late- and early-type galaxies (Sandage et al. 1970; Binney 1978; Noerdlinger 1979, e.g.,). This eventually led to more ‘triaxial’ models to explain the kinematics of nearby elliptical galaxies (Contopoulos 1956; Stark 1977; Binney 1978, e.g.,).

Modern imaging has enabled statistical inference of intrinsic 3D galaxy shapes from projected measurements, revealing several robust trends in the local Universe (Lambas et al. 1992; Alam and Ryden 2002; Ryden 2004; Vincent and Ryden 2005; Méndez-Abreu et al. 2010; Costantin et al. 2018, e.g.,). In particular: intrinsic roundness increases with luminosity and stellar mass (Padilla and Strauss 2008; Rodríguez and Padilla 2013); spiral discs are thicker and less circular than previously assumed, with thickness increasing with luminosity (Rodríguez and Padilla 2013); massive elliptical galaxies are more spherical than their low-mass counterparts, as confirmed by stellar kinematics (Binney 1985; Franx et al. 1991; Ryden 1992; Tremblay and Merritt 1995; Emsellem et al. 2011; Cappellari 2016, e.g.,); and local dwarf galaxies span a wide range of morphologies, including both discs and spheroids (Caldwell 1983; Ichikawa et al. 1986; Ferguson and Sandage 1989; Ferguson and Binggeli 1994; Sánchez-Janssen et al. 2010; Kado-Fong et al. 2021, e.g.,).

The HST-CANDELS and JWST-CEERS studies firmly establish the prolate-to-disc evolutionary trend, but are limited by relatively small samples – often only a few hundred galaxies per mass-redshift bin. Large-scale surveys such as Euclid (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025) provide an opportunity to test the robustness and scalability of the 69 methodology on a far larger sample and in a different observational regime. Aimed at probing the evolution of the dark Universe, Euclid is delivering high-quality imaging and spectroscopic data for millions of galaxies across a wide range of redshifts. papers.title: Robo-SWE: An Executable Issue-Resolution Dataset Mined from Robot Software Repositories
papers.abstract: Coding agents are evaluated mostly on general-purpose software, but domain-specific systems require domain-aware evaluation. Robot software is a particularly challenging case: Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) packages have their own build tools, simulators and learning frameworks are built on physics engines, and behavior that depends on timing and hardware is hard to test. We present Robo-SWE, a dataset of 236 executable issue-resolution tasks mined from merged pull requests in 28 public robotics repositories in four domains: ROS 2 systems, simulation and physics engines, robotics algorithm libraries, and robot-learning frameworks. Each task contains the original issue text, a container recipe for the repository at the commit before the fix, the developers' fix, and the developers' tests, which fail before the fix and pass after it in repeated offline runs. The dataset also keeps a provenance ledger of all 1,567 candidate pull requests, with the stage each reached and the reason for every rejection, and, as a first use, 3,540 graded attempts by five coding-agent setups with recorded patches and 3,529 available trajectories. Across three runs per primary setup, resolve rates range from 45.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 to 56.5% for Claude Opus 5.5; GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 54.1% at maximum effort and 52.5% at medium effort, and GPT-6 Astra 51.4%. GLM-5.3 resolves 46.2%, and Kimi K3.1 Pro 43.9%. The tasks are validated by execution; verification of their fairness by human reviewers is future work. The dataset and public leaderboard are available online.

papers.intro:
Robot software consists of large, interdependent stacks of reusable components [1]. A mobile manipulator built on the Robot Operating System (ROS), in its current generation ROS 2 [2], combines navigation, control, perception, hardware drivers, and middleware across C++ and Python packages built with colcon and CMake. Development depends on simulators and physics engines, while robot-learning frameworks add substantial codebases for policies trained in simulation before deployment to hardware [3, 4]. Maintaining these stacks is central to robotics engineering, yet testing them is difficult: behavior depends on timing, concurrency, and hardware, and practitioners still rely heavily on field testing [5].

Development depends on simulators and physics engines, while robot-learning frameworks add substantial codebases for policies trained in simulation before deployment to hardware [3, 4]. Maintaining these stacks is central to robotics engineering, yet testing them is difficult: behavior depends on timing, concurrency, and hardware, and practitioners still rely heavily on field testing [5].

These characteristics distinguish robot-software repair from repair in self-contained applications. Correctness spans packages and processes: a patch may compile yet violate a ROS message or lifecycle contract, change launch-time behavior, or fail only with a particular simulator, middleware, timing, or hardware configuration. Reproducing a task therefore requires more than checking out source and running unit tests. Evaluation must preserve the domain toolchain and execution environment, account for concurrency and nondeterminism, and separate infrastructure failures from incorrect repairs; otherwise, scores may measure environment mismatch rather than an agent’s repair ability.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Near-infrared processing and data products
papers.abstract: The Euclid near-infrared processing function (NIR PF) converts the raw observations acquired by the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) into calibrated images and source-level products. Following the first implementation delivered with the Euclid Quick Data Release 1 (Q1), the NIR PF has been revised for the first major Euclid Data Release (DR1), with improvements to detector-level processing, calibration, image reconstruction, and quality control. The DR1 processing includes observations covering more than $1900\,\rm{deg}^2$ and has produced $71\,659$ calibrated near-infrared (NIR) images. We assess the performance of the processing chain through extensive astrometric and photometric validation. The astrometric solution reaches an average root-mean-square (RMS) of 10 mas, remaining below 20 mas for 99% of the dithers in all three NISP bands. Temporal variations in the instrumental throughput are typically corrected to a level of 2 mmag RMS, while the relative photometric accuracy reaches 0.9% for sources brighter than 19 mag in $Y_\mathrm{E}$, $J_\mathrm{E}$, and $H_\mathrm{E}$, and the residual spatial variations of the photometric calibration across the focal plane are at the level of approximately 10 mmag for the entire sample. Despite some remaining limitations, the DR1 NIR imaging products are consistent with the required astrometric and photometric performance over the large area covered by this release.

papers.intro:
The ESA Euclid space mission, launched on 1 July 2023, is conducting a wide and deep survey of the extragalactic sky to investigate the nature of dark matter and dark energy and the evolution of the large-scale structure of the Universe (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al., 2025). Euclid is equipped with two complementary instruments: the visible imager (Euclid Collaboration: Cropper et al., 2025, VIS,); and the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al., 2025, NISP,), which provides both near-infrared imaging and slitless spectroscopy. The NISP photometric channel covers the wavelength range from 950–2021 nm through the three broad-band filters YEY_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, JEJ_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, and HEH_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E} (Euclid Collaboration: Schirmer et al., 2022), using 16 HAWAII-2RG (H2RG) near-infrared detectors of 2048 ×\times 2048 pixels each, with a pixel scale of 0.3​″ and a field of view of 0.57 deg2{\rm deg}^{2}.

The NIR PF is the Euclid SGS (SGS) block (Euclid Collaboration: Ruffenach et al., 2026) responsible for transforming the raw NISP photometric observations into calibrated imaging products through a sequence of detector-level corrections, calibration, and image-processing steps, ultimately producing calibrated images and associated source-level products. The first implementation of the NIR PF was described in the context of the Euclid Quick Data Release 1 (Q1; Euclid Collaboration: Polenta et al., 2026, hereafter 19), which provided NISP imaging over 63.1 deg2{\rm deg}^{2} and served as the first large-scale validation of the processing chain. Building on this experience, the NIR PF has been revised and extended for the first major Euclid Data Release (Euclid Data Release 1, 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Aussel and others, 2026, DR1;). The DR1 processing includes observations acquired between 1 October 2023 and 21 May 2025, covering a total area of more than 1900 deg2{\rm deg}^{2} across the EWS (EWS) and the EDS (EDS), as well as the COSMOS field and dedicated calibration fields (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al., 2022; Euclid Collaboration: Tereno et al., 2026). In total, the DR1 processing produced 71 65971\,659 calibrated NIR images.

papers.title: PolicySniff: Inferring Agent Policy States through Shared-GPU Execution
papers.abstract: LLM agents apply approval settings, such as whether to ask before a consequential tool call, through instructions in their system prompt, and operators keep these settings confidential by restricting access to prompts and responses. Audits check whether an agent obeys its setting, not whether a neighboring process can infer which setting is deployed. PolicySniff infers an agent's approval-policy state through shared-GPU execution. A co-resident attacker that knows the candidate settings and the task first profiles both settings, then times only its own GPU kernels while the agent processes the task. The policy prefix is cached before capture, so the attacker observes processing of a task suffix that is identical under both settings. On an eager sparse mixture-of-experts runtime, where each selected expert runs as separate work, a frozen and blinded study identified the deployed setting at 94.17% balanced accuracy on its primary estimand. Across all authorization conditions, accuracy was 88.82% on tasks for which both settings produce the same decision and 91.98% on tasks where they differ. Hardware replays of expert routing show that its temporal density and layer-and-bucket alignment carry the policy information. Behavioral compliance does not imply configuration confidentiality: deployments that keep their approval setting private should measure its distinguishability on the serving runtime and enforce authorization outside the model.

papers.intro:
LLM agents use tools to act on their users’ behalf, including sending messages, modifying files, and executing code [1]. Agent frameworks govern access to these tools and resources, while the model selects actions in pursuit of a task. Permission to reach a resource leaves further authorization questions: which data may be sent, to whom, and for what purpose. A documented agent incident illustrates this gap: a domain allowlist admitted a request that uploaded private files to an attacker’s account on an approved service [2]. Deployments combine environmental restrictions with instructions and approval checks that constrain how the agent uses its access [3, 4]. When the model itself decides whether to act or ask for confirmation, the applicable approval rule forms part of its prompt context.

That rule is useful information for an attacker. Agents read external documents, web pages, and tool results to complete their tasks, and prompt injection uses such content to redirect their actions [5, 1]. Knowing which deployments let the model proceed without confirmation can guide the selection of targets for these attempts. In the setting we study, candidate approval rules are known, while the deployed choice, prompt, and responses remain private. The reconnaissance target is the identity of the active rule. Its recovery reveals an authorization-relevant configuration even if the attacker cannot reconstruct the prompt or observe an action that distinguishes the candidates.

papers.title: GOOSELoc: A Multimodal Benchmark for Ground-to-Aerial Localization in Unstructured Off-Road Terrain
papers.abstract: Cross-view pose estimation estimates a ground camera's geographic pose by matching onboard sensor data with geo-referenced overhead imagery. This is particularly relevant when GNSS is unreliable, for example under forest canopy or in urban canyons. Existing metric cross-view benchmarks, such as VIGOR and cross-view KITTI, are dominated by urban and road scenes with strong human-made structure without off-road terrain. We introduce GOOSELoc, a multimodal benchmark for ground-to-aerial localization in unstructured environments, including forests, fields, and rural tracks. GOOSELoc comprises 9,356 scenes recorded across all four seasons around Munich, Germany, pairing geo-referenced aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB imagery and 3D LiDAR point clouds. Paved/unpaved labels enable analyzing the impact of terrain structure, while the seasonal recordings allow studying the appearance gap to mostly summer-captured orthophotos. To assess the transferability of existing methods, we adapt and fine-tune four state-of-the-art cross-view localization baselines on GOOSELoc. Despite task-specific fine-tuning, the performance degrades substantially in off-road environments. We therefore propose a multimodal baseline combining surround-view imagery and LiDAR geometry, improving localization performance and providing a stronger reference for future work. Data and baselines are released at https://gooseloc.github.io.

papers.intro:
Accurate geo-localization is one of the cornerstones of modern navigation and underpins the safe transportation of goods and people. Systems deployed in cars, trucks, and UAVs rely predominantly on Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS). However, GNSS signals degrade systematically in environments where direct sky visibility is obstructed: urban canyon effects limit accuracy in dense cities [2], and tree canopies together with uneven terrain cause comparable or worse degradation in forested and off-road areas [35, 44]. Robust backup systems are therefore required, particularly for the off-road domain, where these conditions are the norm rather than the exception.

Accurate geo-localization is one of the cornerstones of modern navigation and underpins the safe transportation of goods and people. Systems deployed in cars, trucks, and UAVs rely predominantly on Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS). However, GNSS signals degrade systematically in environments where direct sky visibility is obstructed: urban canyon effects limit accuracy in dense cities [2], and tree canopies together with uneven terrain cause comparable or worse degradation in forested and off-road areas [35, 44]. Robust backup systems are therefore required, particularly for the off-road domain, where these conditions are the norm rather than the exception.

Cross-view geo-localization [15] is a computer-vision-based alternative: it estimates a ground sensor’s pose by relating its observations to globally available, geo-referenced aerial imagery, yielding absolute positions. Existing benchmarks address two task formulations. Retrieval-oriented datasets such as CVUSA [36, 41] and CVACT [16] pair ground panoramas with aerial tiles and treat localization as nearest-neighbor matching against a tile database, where the recoverable position is bounded by the tile size. Metric pose estimation is targeted by VIGOR [46], which additionally supports retrieval, and by the cross-view extension of KITTI [7] introduced by Shi et al. [26], both targeting sub-tile localization at the meter level. These benchmarks share a limitation that reflects their origin: all target urban, road-centric settings, with imagery captured from street-view panoramas or road-going vehicles along paved roads. Even datasets that include rural imagery, CVUSA for instance, capture it along highways and paved roads. Off-road perception itself is well studied [34, 11, 19], but almost exclusively for segmentation and navigation rather than ground-to-aerial localization. Whereas urban and road scenes provide stable, human-made cross-view anchors such as buildings, lane markings and signage [4], unstructured terrain is dominated by vegetation whose appearance varies strongly with the season and shifts continuously between recordings, a well-documented source of degradation for place recognition and pose estimation [18, 23]. papers.title: HybridCT: ML Accelerated Tomography for Climate Relevant 3D Cloud Observations
papers.abstract: Low-level clouds are one of the largest sources of uncertainty in climate predictions, partly because we lack detailed three-dimensional (3D) measurements of their internal structure. Here, we present HybridCT, a cloud tomographic reconstruction scheme accelerated by machine learning (ML) that recovers 3D cloud extinction directly from passive multi-angle observations. An ML emulator maps radiances from multiple viewing angles to cloud optical thickness (COT), producing path-integrated projections, and a Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART) explicitly inverts these projections to retrieve 3D extinction. Training observations are generated from synthetic 3D cloud fields using radiative transfer simulations for nine viewing angles between $\pm$70$^{\circ}$. HybridCT reconstructs extinction with RMSE 13.3 km$^{-1}$ in 3.5 s, compared to 22.7 km$^{-1}$ in approx. 30 min for the state-of-the-art physics-based tomography framework AT3D, a speedup exceeding 500$\times$. HybridCT thus provides a scalable route toward large-scale observations of 3D cloud structure relevant to radiative-budget interpretation and evaluation of high-resolution cloud simulations.

papers.intro:
Low-level clouds strongly influence Earth’s radiation budget and remain one of the largest sources of uncertainty in climate feedbacks and future warming projections [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Many processes governing cloud evolution and radiative effects are inherently 3D, yet satellite observations involve a fundamental tradeoff: Vertically resolved measurements provide detailed profiles but only along limited sampling tracks, while passive imagers provide broad spatial and temporal coverage but mostly of column-integrated or cloud-top properties. This limits our ability to observe cloud depth, internal structure, and organization over large areas. Recent studies suggest that such 3D information could improve understanding of cloud processes, radiative effects, and the evaluation of high-resolution atmospheric models [6, 7]. Multi-angle tomography can address this observational gap. Multiple views of the same cloud provide complementary geometric information for reconstructing 3D structure [8, 9, 10]. The main obstacle is computational: physics-based tomography requires repeated 3D radiative-transfer calculations that are expensive for realistic cloud scenes [11, 12]. This limits the number and size of cloud fields that can be processed, and consequently the use of tomography for large observational datasets. While machine learning (ML) is increasingly used to derive 3D cloud structure from 2D observations, we distinguish tomography from other 3D reconstruction techniques, like radiance mapping/extrapolation of single view points [13, 14, 15]. Tomography requires multi-angle observations that constrain 3D information geometrically and assumes the cloud field remains static across viewing angles. Prior works using multi-angle observations include 3DeepCT [16] and VIPCT [17] for extinction, and NeMF [18] for microphysical properties. However, these approaches do not explicitly constrain geometry, but learn to extrapolate 3D structure through supervised learning with simulated ground truth cloud volumes. For real observations, ground truth volumes are not available. ProbCT [19] partially addresses this through a 3D radiative transfer solver that compares real imagery against renderings from predicted volumes. However, this is again limited by the computational constraint of 3D radiative transfer calculations. Neural radiance fields [20] instead constrain volumes via differentiable rendering, but are optimized per scene and require higher angular sampling and spatial resolutions than spaceborne multi-angle instruments currently provide. papers.title: 3D radiative transfer of K-series lines of He-like ions with SKIRT
papers.abstract: High-resolution X-ray spectroscopy with XRISM has resolved line profiles of highly ionised ions, including P Cygni profiles, in many systems containing compact objects. To interpret these line profiles, forward modelling with three-dimensional radiative transfer (3D RT) calculations including the relevant ionic processes is required. Following our previous work on the Lyman-series lines of H-like ions, we present the implementation of the K-series lines of He-like ions with Z = 2-30 in the open-source Monte Carlo RT code SKIRT, providing a numerical tool for interpreting highresolution X-ray spectra of photoionised plasmas. Building upon the framework developed for H-like ions, we incorporate the resonance scattering (RS) and radiative recombination (RR) channels. We also implement the inner-shell ionisation (II) channel of Li-like ions for the production of He-like lines. We resolve fine-structure levels and account for level populations, frequency redistribution, phase function, and linear polarisation through transition-specific Mueller matrices. The implementation reproduces the expected RT effects in He-like lines. The Fe xxv w and y lines, dominated by the RS channel, develop optically thick line-profile distortions and P Cygni profiles in an outflowing plasma, whereas the x and z lines, dominated by the RR and II channels, do not exhibit such behaviour. The line intensities from the RS and RR channels agree well with Cloudy. The II channel further enhances the z line, which is not yet included in Cloudy. The linear polarisation calculations reproduce the analytical and experimental angular dependence of resonance scattering on a line-by-line basis. This extension to He-like lines, together with our previous implementation of H-like lines, enables 3D RT modelling of the major X-ray lines, providing a tool for constraining gas kinematics around compact objects observed with XRISM.

papers.intro:
In systems containing compact objects such as black holes (BHs) and neutron stars (NSs), part of the gravitational energy released by mass accretion is converted into extreme-UV and X-ray radiation (Done et al., 2007). This intense radiation in turn drives mass outflows through radiatively driven winds (Proga & Kallman, 2002). The wind velocity provides information about the transport of matter and kinetic energy from accretion into the surrounding environment. Revealing the gas kinematics around compact objects is therefore crucial for understanding the circulation of matter and energy in the Universe.

The wind velocity provides information about the transport of matter and kinetic energy from accretion into the surrounding environment. Revealing the gas kinematics around compact objects is therefore crucial for understanding the circulation of matter and energy in the Universe.

High-resolution X-ray spectroscopy is a powerful tool for this purpose because the velocity structure is imprinted on spectral line profiles. This approach has been enabled by the advent of the X-ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission (XRISM; Tashiro et al. 2025), which allows line profiles to be studied in unprecedented detail. Indeed, XRISM has revealed P Cygni profiles in H-like and He-like lines of S, Ar, Ca, and Fe in many compact-object systems (XRISM Collaboration et al., 2024; XRISM Collaboration et al., 2025a; XRISM Collaboration et al., 2025b; Tsujimoto et al., 2025; Chakraborty et al., 2025; Mizumoto et al., 2026), whereas previous X-ray telescopes detected them only in systems with exceptionally high outflow velocities (Brandt & Schulz, 2000).

Spectral line profiles are modified by interactions between photons and outflowing gas in three-dimensional (3D) geometries. Interpreting the observed line profiles therefore requires 3D radiative transfer (RT) calculations. Although one-dimensional (1D) RT codes, such as SPEX (Kaastra et al., 2024), Cloudy (Gunasekera et al., 2025), and XSTAR (Ko & Kallman, 1994), have been widely used in X-ray studies, Monte Carlo RT (MCRT) codes offer clear advantages for treating complex 3D geometries and velocity fields (Steinacker et al., 2013; Noebauer & Sim, 2019).

SKIRT (Camps & Baes, 2015; Baes & Camps, 2015; Camps & Baes, 2020) is a state-of-the-art MCRT code with flexible 3D geometries, radiation sources, spatial grids, detectors, and interfaces to hydrodynamical simulations. The code is available as open-source software11 1 https://github.com/SKIRT/SKIRT9 and is supported by extensive documentation and tutorials22 2 https://skirt.ugent.be. Modern acceleration techniques, including peel-off, forced scattering, continuous absorption, composite biasing, and explicit absorption (Baes et al., 2011; Baes et al., 2016; Baes et al., 2022), make it well suited to interpreting high-resolution observations at feasible computational cost. The code was originally developed for dust radiative transfer from the sub-mm to ultraviolet bands (Baes et al., 2003) and has since been extended to other wavelength regimes, including molecular and atomic excitation in the millimetre band (Matsumoto et al., 2023) and several X-ray processes involving neutral matter, free electrons, and bound electrons (Vander Meulen et al., 2023; Vander Meulen et al., 2024).
