papers.title: EP250226a: A fast X-ray transient associated with GRB 250226A and its multiwavelength afterglow properties
papers.abstract: Recent advances in fast X-ray transient studies have been driven by the wide-field, sensitive soft X-ray monitoring capabilities of the Einstein Probe (EP), enabling the prompt detection and localization of previously underexplored events. EP observations offer new opportunities to investigate the origins, emission mechanisms, and population properties of newly discovered fast X-ray transients. We present multiwavelength observations of EP250226a, an extragalactic fast X-ray transient associated with GRB 250226A. We jointly analyze the prompt emission from soft X-rays to gamma rays and the X-ray afterglow spectra. We collect optical photometric data, perform empirical and afterglow model-based analyses, and present optical-to-infrared spectroscopy, measuring the equivalent widths of absorption lines. The spectroscopic redshift is $z = 3.314$, and the isotropic-equivalent gamma-ray energy is $E_\mathrm{iso}\simeq7.32\times10^{53}$ erg. Its location in the Amati diagram is consistent with a massive-star core-collapse origin (Type II GRB). The fluence ratio $\rm{S}(25-50\,\rm{keV})/\rm{S}(50-100\,\rm{keV})=0.57\pm0.06$ supports its classification as a classical GRB. The X-ray and optical afterglows show achromatic behavior. Among the models considered, a top-hat jet propagating into a uniform interstellar medium best describes the multiwavelength afterglow. This model suggests a highly collimated, nearly on-axis jet, with an isotropic-equivalent kinetic energy of $E_\mathrm{k,iso}\simeq4.07\times10^{55}$ erg, a gamma-ray radiative efficiency of $\eta_{\gamma}\simeq 1.77\%$, and a low magnetic-field energy fraction of $\log \epsilon_\mathrm{B,FS} \simeq -6.52$. EP250226a exhibits typical long-duration GRB properties, with the first soft X-ray peak coinciding with the gamma-ray prompt emission, while the soft X-ray emission lasts significantly longer than the gamma-ray emission.

papers.intro:
Fast X-ray transients are a heterogeneous class of high-energy transients characterized by soft X-ray emission on timescales ranging from seconds to thousands of seconds (Heise and in’t Zand 2004; Heise and in’t Zand 2010; Alp and Larsson 2020; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2026b). Their physical origins span a wide variety of Galactic and extragalactic phenomena, making them an important population for understanding the dynamic high-energy universe (Heise and in’t Zand 2004; Jonker et al. 2013; Bauer et al. 2017; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2023; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2026b; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2026a; van Hoof et al. 2026). To date, a substantial fraction of extragalactic fast X-ray transients have been discovered through systematic searches of historical X-ray archives (Bauer et al. 2017; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2022; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2023, e.g.,). Although a small number of extragalactic fast X-ray transients were previously detected by several soft X-ray missions (Heise et al. 2001; Sakamoto et al. 2005; Negoro et al. 2016, e.g.,), the lack of rapid localization and timely multiwavelength follow-up observations has prevented detailed characterization of their physical properties and progenitor systems.

Their physical origins span a wide variety of Galactic and extragalactic phenomena, making them an important population for understanding the dynamic high-energy universe (Heise and in’t Zand 2004; Jonker et al. 2013; Bauer et al. 2017; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2023; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2026b; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2026a; van Hoof et al. 2026). To date, a substantial fraction of extragalactic fast X-ray transients have been discovered through systematic searches of historical X-ray archives (Bauer et al. 2017; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2022; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2023, e.g.,). The Einstein Probe (EP) mission was recently launched to survey the soft X-ray sky in the 0.5–4 keV band and to provide rapid X-ray follow-up observations in the 0.5–10 keV energy range (Yuan et al. 2025). The Wide-field X-ray Telescope (Yuan et al. 2022, WXT;) provides an instantaneous field of view of approximately 3,600 square degrees and enables near real-time detection and arcminute localization of X-ray transients. Autonomous follow-up observations with the Follow-up X-ray Telescope (Chen et al. 2021, FXT;) further improve the localization accuracy to the arcsecond level. Together with rapid-response observations from both space-based and ground-based facilities, EP has fundamentally expanded the discovery space of extragalactic fast X-ray transients.

An increasing number of EP-discovered fast X-ray transients have now been found to be temporally and spatially associated with gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) (Zhao et al. 2026; Yin et al. 2025; Levan et al. 2025; Liu et al. 2025; Jiang et al. 2025c; Yin et al. 2024, e.g.,). Likewise, the Space-based multi-band astronomical Variable Objects Monitor (Wei et al. 2016; Cordier et al. 2026, SVOM;), equipped with the wide-field instrument ECLAIRs with a field of view of approximately 2 sr and a low-energy threshold down to 4 keV (Godet et al. 2014; Godet et al. 2026), is also discovering soft and faint GRBs that further bridge the observational connection between fast X-ray transients and the classical GRB population (Schneider et al. 2026). For some subclasses of extragalactic fast X-ray transients, such as ‘CDF-S XT1’-like events, the inferred intrinsic event rate can be comparable to those of orphan and low-luminosity GRBs (Bauer et al. 2017; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2022; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2023).

Likewise, the Space-based multi-band astronomical Variable Objects Monitor (Wei et al. 2016; Cordier et al. 2026, SVOM;), equipped with the wide-field instrument ECLAIRs with a field of view of approximately 2 sr and a low-energy threshold down to 4 keV (Godet et al. 2014; Godet et al. 2026), is also discovering soft and faint GRBs that further bridge the observational connection between fast X-ray transients and the classical GRB population (Schneider et al. 2026). For some subclasses of extragalactic fast X-ray transients, such as ‘CDF-S XT1’-like events, the inferred intrinsic event rate can be comparable to those of orphan and low-luminosity GRBs (Bauer et al. 2017; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2022; Quirola-Vásquez et al. 2023).

Among the diverse fast X-ray transient population, one important subclass is physically associated with long-duration GRBs. In these events, the prompt emission is generally attributed to internal energy dissipation processes within relativistic jets (Rees and Meszaros 1994; Paczynski and Xu 1994; Sari and Piran 1997; Piran 2004; Zhang et al. 2006). The prompt emission is generally detected by GRB-triggering instruments, such as the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (Meegan et al. 2009, Fermi/GBM;), which covers an energy range of 8 keV-40 MeV, and the Swift Burst Alert Telescope (Gehrels et al. 2004; Barthelmy 2004; Barthelmy et al. 2005, Swift/BAT;), which operates over 15–150 keV. In contrast, EP provides sensitive triggering in the soft X-ray band (0.5–4 keV), extending the observational window to lower energies than those accessible to previous GRB-triggering instruments. This unique capability enables the detection and characterization of soft X-ray emission associated with GRBs, offering new insights into the early emission mechanisms. A distinguishing feature of EP-detected GRBs is that the soft X-ray emission lasts longer than the gamma-ray emission (Liu et al. 2025; Wu et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2026; van Hoof et al. 2026). Following the prompt phase, broadband afterglow emission is produced as the relativistic ejecta interact with the circumburst medium, where shock-accelerated electrons radiate predominantly through synchrotron processes (Sari and Piran 1997; Sari et al. 1998; Mészáros and Rees 1997; Piran 1999; Gao et al. 2013; Kumar and Zhang 2015; Zhang 2018). Multiwavelength observations of the prompt and afterglow emission therefore provide powerful diagnostics of the jet energetics, geometry, radiation mechanisms, and the circumburst environment. Consequently, establishing whether a newly discovered fast X-ray transient belongs to the GRB population is essential for understanding its physical origin.

EP250226a/GRB 250226A was discovered by EP as a bright fast X-ray transient and subsequently triggered extensive follow-up observations across the electromagnetic spectrum. The event was also independently detected by several gamma-ray instruments (see Sections 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3 for details of the gamma-ray observations), providing further evidence for a connection with the GRB population. We investigate whether EP250226a can be robustly classified as a long-duration GRB and explore its physical nature through comprehensive multiwavelength analyses. In this paper, we present X-ray and gamma-ray observations of the prompt emission, X-ray and optical observations of the afterglow, together with optical spectroscopic measurements of the transient. We perform detailed spectral analyses of the prompt emission and broadband modeling of the afterglow to constrain the properties of the relativistic jet and its surrounding environment. This event serves as a representative example of the growing population of EP-discovered fast X-ray transients that can be physically linked to classical GRBs, illustrating the new discovery space opened by sensitive soft X-ray transient surveys.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). An overview of the Science Ground Segment architecture and operations
papers.abstract: The Euclid mission is designed to address fundamental questions on the nature of dark energy and dark matter by mapping the extragalactic sky with a wide-area survey complemented by targeted deep observations. The required scientific performance places stringent demands on the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS), which transforms raw telemetry into calibrated, validated, and scientifically exploitable products. The SGS is a distributed system comprising the Euclid Science Operations Centre, the Science Data Centres, Instrument Operation Teams, and supporting Organisation Units, within a common architectural and procedural framework. This paper presents the SGS as implemented for Data Release 1 (DR1), describing its organisation, architecture, processing functions, and operational model. We outline the main components of the SGS common infrastructure. A key element is the Euclid Archive System (EAS), the central metadata repository based on a common data model. It comprises a Distributed Storage System, providing scalable storage of data files across the Science Data Centres; a Data Processing System used by the pipelines to register and access files and their lineage; and a Science Archive, distributing validated data products. Processing is coordinated by a common orchestration framework based on the Infrastructure Abstraction Layer, providing workflow management and resource abstraction of distributed compute clusters. Software development, integration, and deployment are supported by the Common Development Environment. We describe daily operations, calibration, and quality control, followed by the DR1 production campaign, including processing flows, validation strategy, and computational and data volumes. This infrastructure enabled Euclid DR1, involving 35 million jobs across nine Science Data Centres and 6.7 million core-hours, demonstrating robustness and scalability of the SGS.

papers.intro:
The Euclid mission of the European Space Agency (ESA), conducted in partnership with the Euclid Consortium (EC), is designed to investigate the nature of dark energy and dark matter by mapping the geometry and growth of large-scale structure over a substantial fraction of the extragalactic sky (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025). By combining weak gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering probes over billions of galaxies, Euclid aims to deliver percent-level constraints on cosmological parameters and to test deviations from the standard cosmological model. Achieving these objectives requires unprecedented control of systematic effects, uniform survey coverage, and homogeneous data processing throughout the life of the mission. Beyond its primary cosmological objectives, Euclid will also enable a broad range of legacy science. These include studies of Solar System objects and exoplanets, transient and variable phenomena, stellar populations in the Milky Way, galaxy formation and evolution, large-scale galaxy environments, and the identification and characterisation of rare and distant galaxies in the early Universe.

(2025) and the Near-Infrared Spectrophotometer (NISP) described in Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al. (2025), over a nominal duration of six years. The statistical power of the mission is directly tied to the survey area, depth, and stability of the instrument response. Consequently, scientific return critically depends not only on instrument performance in flight, but also on the ability of the SGS to process, calibrate, validate, archive, and distribute data products with traceable quality and reproducibility.

Another defining challenge is the distributed nature of the EC. It is composed of numerous institutes across multiple countries, operating Science Data Centres (SDCs) with heterogeneous computing infrastructures. The SGS must federate these resources into a coherent production system, ensuring consistent software versions, data models, configuration control, and operational procedures. This federated approach increases resilience and scalability, but requires strong architectural principles and rigorous interface management.

The purpose of the Euclid SGS (Pasian et al. 2012) is to transform raw telemetry into validated, science-ready data products and to deliver them to the EC and the broader community according to the mission data release plan. In operational terms, it encompasses survey planning support, instrument and calibration data processing, routine and reprocessing pipelines, quality control, archiving, and user support. It also provides the technical and organisational framework that ensures traceability from pixel-level measurements to high-level cosmological products.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). NIR astrometric calibration
papers.abstract: This paper presents the methodology and results of the astrometric calibration applied to the Euclid Near-Infrared (NIR) images in the Euclid Data Release 1, focusing on the techniques used to model and correct instrumental distortions, as well as the assessment of calibration quality. This work details the calibration pipeline, including quality control tests, and the evaluation of astrometric residuals against the Gaia DR3 catalogue and internal consistency metrics based on data encompassing more than one year of Euclid operation: the achieved accuracy is 30 mas for 97% of the total area, thus exceeding the requirements for Data Release 1. For the remaining 3%, accuracy declines due to a persistence correction issue: a method to correct the issue is presented. Furthermore, we discuss the stability of the solution over time, its dependence on source properties and instrument configuration, and outline the improvements planned for future Euclid data releases to enhance the astrometric calibration accuracy and efficiency.

papers.intro:
Accurate astrometric calibration is essential for the success of the Euclid mission (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al., 2025), which enables the precise mapping of celestial sources across its detectors. The astrometric calibration process ensures the reliable alignment of observed images with external reference catalogues, such as Gaia DR3 (Gaia Collaboration: Vallenari et al., 2023), and maintains internal consistency among multiple dithered images. Euclid’s Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al., 2025, NISP:) features three imaging channels: YEY_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, JEJ_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, and HEH_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}. An array of 16 HAWAII-2RG (H2RG) detectors, each with 2048x2048 pixels and a plate scale of 0.3​″ pixel-1, provides a field of view of 0.57 deg2\mathrm{deg}^{2}. We recall that within Euclid, a dithering sequence operating mode is termed a single observation, and the individual exposures (dithers) of each observation are archived under an Observation ID (OBSID hereafter). In the wide survey, each OBSID consists of four dithers; the self-calibration field consists of 76 dithers (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al., 2025; Euclid Collaboration: Polenta et al., 2026b). In DR1 (Euclid Data Release 1, 2026), NISP calibrated images and associated catalogues are available for both single dithers and stacked products (Euclid Collaboration: Polenta et al., 2026a).

An array of 16 HAWAII-2RG (H2RG) detectors, each with 2048x2048 pixels and a plate scale of 0.3​″ pixel-1, provides a field of view of 0.57 deg2\mathrm{deg}^{2}. We recall that within Euclid, a dithering sequence operating mode is termed a single observation, and the individual exposures (dithers) of each observation are archived under an Observation ID (OBSID hereafter). In the wide survey, each OBSID consists of four dithers; the self-calibration field consists of 76 dithers (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al., 2025; Euclid Collaboration: Polenta et al., 2026b). In DR1 (Euclid Data Release 1, 2026), NISP calibrated images and associated catalogues are available for both single dithers and stacked products (Euclid Collaboration: Polenta et al., 2026a).

For the initial data releases (DR1 and DR2), the astrometric calibration requirement is set as a root mean square (RMS) of 200 mas for both RA and Dec, compared to the external reference (absolute astrometry), and 100 mas for the positions of the same sources observed within a dither sequence (relative astrometry). The ultimate aim of the final release (DR3) is to achieve an RMS of 30 mas on each axis for both relative and absolute astrometry, corresponding to 0.1 pixels. An additional requirement pertains to geometric distortion, which must be calibrated to within 0.015% over scales of 3 arcmin. This paper focuses on the methods used to model and correct instrumental distortions in images from the NISP photometric channel (NISP-P) and assesses the calibration quality achieved in the Euclid DR1, covering an area of 1900 deg2\mathrm{deg}^{2} (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al., 2022). The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 summarises the astrometric calibration module of the NIR processing function (NIR-PF) pipeline and its quality control tests. Section 3 presents the results obtained in the DR1, evaluating astrometric residuals against external catalogues and internal consistency metrics based on more than 1 year of Euclid operations. This analysis shows that the astrometric calibration meets the requirements on the RMS and on the geometric distortion accuracy, described in Sect. 3.3. The stability of the astrometric solution over time and its dependence on source properties and instrument configuration are also discussed in Sect. 3.3. Section 4 outlines the enhancements already implemented for Euclid Data Release 2, as well as additional improvements that may further refine the calibration accuracy and efficiency in later data releases. To support the use of the calibrated data products, for each parameter described in the text we also give the corresponding keyword in the NIR_AstrometricCalibration module of the NIR-PF (NIR_Astrometry hereafter).

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) - NISP-P point-spread function modelling pipelines
papers.abstract: The images collected in photometric mode by the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) instrument of the Euclid satellite are used to model the point-spread function (PSF) of a selection of sources detected in single and combined frames. We used Q1 and DR1 data to improve the development of the PSF module of the near-infrared processing function (NIR PF) and to refine the models currently provided. We explored a few methods normally used to evaluate the quality of the derived models and discuss possible variations related to the position of the sources in the focal plane and to the wavelength and time of the observations. The procedure of fitting the PSF profile, compared to other methods used for flux estimation, such as aperture photometry, indicates that updated models are better than those provided by Q1 images. The current results are in agreement with several key requirements defined for the mission, but there is still room for further improvements, which we plan to investigate and implement in future releases.

papers.intro:
The Euclid mission (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025) of the European Space Agency started the nominal observations on 14 February 2024. It has already provided us with data from the Euclid Quick Release Q1 (2025), which covers 63.1 deg2 of the sky (Euclid Collaboration: Aussel et al. 2026). Data products for the Euclid Data Release 1 (2026, DR1,) are now available and comprise about 1900 deg2 (Euclid Collaboration: Aussel and others 2026). The observations include data acquired with the two Euclid instruments: the visible imager (Euclid Collaboration: Cropper et al. 2025, VIS,) and the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al. 2025, NISP,). The NISP instrument was designed to perform slitless spectroscopy and to collect images in three photometric passbands in the near-infrared (NIR): YEY_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, JEJ_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, and HEH_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E} (Euclid Collaboration: Schirmer et al. 2022), reaching a median depth of mABm_{\rm AB} = 24.4 mag for 5σ\sigma point-like sources (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022).

It has already provided us with data from the Euclid Quick Release Q1 (2025), which covers 63.1 deg2 of the sky (Euclid Collaboration: Aussel et al. 2026). Data products for the Euclid Data Release 1 (2026, DR1,) are now available and comprise about 1900 deg2 (Euclid Collaboration: Aussel and others 2026). The observations include data acquired with the two Euclid instruments: the visible imager (Euclid Collaboration: Cropper et al. 2025, VIS,) and the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al. 2025, NISP,). The NISP instrument was designed to perform slitless spectroscopy and to collect images in three photometric passbands in the near-infrared (NIR): YEY_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, JEJ_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, and HEH_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E} (Euclid Collaboration: Schirmer et al. 2022), reaching a median depth of mABm_{\rm AB} = 24.4 mag for 5σ\sigma point-like sources (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022).

To achieve scientific goals, Euclid needs to measure the shapes and colours of galaxies with high precision (Laureijs et al. 2011), which in turn requires precise models of the point-spread function (PSF) across the entire field of view (FoV). The primary purpose of the VIS instrument is to measure weak gravitational lensing, also known as cosmic shear. While VIS measures shapes, NISP measures the brightness of galaxies in the infrared bands (photometry) and spreads their light into spectra (slitless spectroscopy). To map the three-dimensional distribution of the Universe, we need to know how far away these galaxies are. This is done by measuring their flux across different wavelength bands to estimate their photometric redshift (photo-zz). If the PSF is poorly modelled, the measurement of how much light falls into a specific pixel will be wrong, skewing the colour measurements and resulting in incorrect distance estimates.

The observation strategy of the mission consists of taking a sequence of pointings, each comprising multiple exposures following a predefined dithering pattern (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022). In the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), the pointings include a set of four dithered exposures in each spectroscopic and photometric channel, while deep fields and calibration fields require repeated visits and a much larger number of exposures. The single-dither exposures are processed by dedicated pipelines, which apply pre-processing steps, perform astrometric and photometric calibrations, resample and combine single exposures in stacked images, extract catalogues, and model the PSF profile11 1 Here, the PSF profile or PSF shape is the two-dimensional brightness pattern (or one-dimensional cross-section) of a single point source after passing through an optical system, defining its sharpness, symmetry, and degree of blurring. of point-like sources extracted from individual and stacked frames.

Instead of using traditional optical charge-coupled devices, Euclid NIR data was acquired with HgCdTe H2RG complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) detectors, arranged in a matrix of 4×\times4 in the focal plane array (FPA). In this architecture, an infrared-sensitive semiconductor layer is bonded directly to a readout integrated circuit, enabling independent, non-destructive sampling of each pixel (see Kubik et al. 2016, for more details). Given the diffraction limit of the 1.2 m primary mirror and a pixel scale of ∼\sim 0.3​″ across the three photometric passbands, the sampling falls below the Nyquist criterion, resulting in an undersampled PSF (see also Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al. 2025, for an overview of the PSF generated by the NISP instrument). Consequently, a dedicated code is required to accurately model and process these undersampled profiles.

Here we describe the NIR_PointSpreadFunction module of the near-infrared processing function (Euclid Collaboration: Polenta et al. 2026b; Euclid Collaboration: Polenta et al. 2026a, NIR PF,) developed to model the PSF profile of point-like sources observed by NISP under undersampled conditions. Using data collected during Q1 and DR1 observations, we discuss recent improvements in the code and demonstrate its performance through photometric measurements based on PSF models derived from single-dither exposures and stacked images.

This paper is structured as follows. In Sect. 2 we present the observation data used and some key requirements for optimal mission performance. In Sect. 3, we describe the NIR PSF module and the procedure adopted to derive the PSF models. In Sect. 4, we present the models obtained on the basis of individual exposures and stacked frames, explore their application to fitting the PSF profile, discuss possible refinements, and evaluate the dependencies on position, wavelength, and time. A brief summary and some final remarks are provided in Sect. 5. Finally, in the Appendices from A to E we present additional tables and plots that illustrate complementary results.

papers.title: Euclid: Data Release 1 (DR1) - First NISP emission-line maps: Methodology, validation, and applications to galaxy evolution
papers.abstract: We demonstrate the capability of the slitless spectroscopic mode of the Euclid Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) to produce emission-line maps analogous to narrow-band images with user-defined central wavelengths. We present the first such maps of galaxies at $0.4 < z < 0.9$, constructed from blue-grism exposures obtained during the Euclid performance-verification observations of the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) field in November 2023. We demonstrate the use of these maps for identifying star-forming clumps, measuring radial star-formation profiles, detecting projected internal velocity gradients, deblending the H$\alpha$--[N II] complex, and assessing spectroscopic redshift measurements. As a first statistical application, we reconstruct the galaxy mass--metallicity relation for 885 galaxies observed with the blue grism at $0.4 < z < 0.9$ by deblending the H$\alpha$--[N II] complex in the emission-line maps, and measure stacked H$\alpha$ radial profiles for 2634 galaxies over the same redshift range. The mass--metallicity relation is consistent with that obtained from the Euclid 1D spectroscopic measurements, demonstrating overall agreement between the two deblending approaches. The recovered H$\alpha$ radial profiles broadly follow the $Y_{\mathrm{E}}$ stellar continuum but remain modestly more extended after matching the $Y_{\mathrm{E}}$ images to the H$\alpha$ PSF, consistent with previous results in the literature. Across the four $Y_{\mathrm{E}}$ size bins, we measure a mean $R_{50,\mathrm{H}\alpha}/R_{50,Y_{\mathrm{E}}}=1.15$.

papers.intro:
The Near-infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al. 2025, NISP;) on board Euclid (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025) performs slitless spectroscopy, dispersing the light from every source across the 0.5​deg​20.5\,{\rm deg}\textsuperscript{2} field of view. Its blue spectroscopic channel covers 926–1366 nm with a dispersion of 1.24 nm pixel-1 and a resolving power of R=440R=440–900 for a 0.′′50\aas@@fstack{\prime\prime}5-diameter source. The red channel covers 1206–1892 nm with a dispersion of 1.37 nm pixel-1 and R=550R=550–740 (Euclid Collaboration: Gillard et al. 2026). The native detector sampling is 0.′′30\aas@@fstack{\prime\prime}3 pixel-1.

The Euclid Wide Survey (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022, EWS;) will cover 14 00014\,000 deg2 by the end of the nominal mission using four red-grism exposures obtained at different dispersion orientations (0∘0^{\circ}, 180∘180^{\circ}, −4∘-4^{\circ}, and OPEN184∘)184^{\circ}). The EWS requirement is a 3.5​σ3.5\,\sigma emission-line flux sensitivity of 2×10−16​erg​s−1​cm−22\times 10^{-16}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}} at 1.6​µ​m1.6\,$\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ for a 0.5​″-diameter source, with the first on-sky measurements confirming that NISP meets this requirement (Euclid Collaboration: Le Brun et al. 2026). The Euclid Deep Survey (EDS) will cover approximately 50 deg2 through repeated observations with both the red and blue grisms over the nominal 6-year mission (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022; Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025). At the end of the mission, the EDS is expected to reach line-flux sensitivities of 5×10−17​erg​s−1​cm−25\times 10^{-17}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}} and 6×10−17​erg​s−1​cm−26\times 10^{-17}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}} with the red and blue grisms, respectively (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025).

The performance of NISP for slitless one-dimensional (1D) spectroscopy on real data is described in Euclid Collaboration: Copin et al. (2026), and the effects of galaxy morphology on spectral extraction and emission-line detectability have been investigated using simulations in Euclid Collaboration: Gabarra et al. (2023); we also refer to Walsh et al. (2010), Momcheva et al. (2016), and Ryan et al. (2018) for further discussion of slitless spectroscopy. Here, we address the complementary problem of reconstructing two-dimensional (2D) emission-line maps from the dispersed NISP observations. In slitless observations, the stellar continuum produces extended spectral traces that may overlap across the field, whereas strong emission lines appear as relatively compact features superimposed on these traces. After subtracting the stellar continuum and mapping the line signal back onto sky coordinates, it is possible to reconstruct a 2D image of the line-emitting regions. Related techniques for recovering spatially resolved emission-line information have been demonstrated with slitless observations from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and James Webb Space Telescope (Nelson et al. 2012; Matharu et al. 2024; Estrada-Carpenter et al. 2024, JWST; for example). In addition, a spectral datacube can be reconstructed from the combination of many slitless spectroscopic exposures with different dispersion orientations (Griggio et al. 2026; Zhang and Sinigaglia 2026).

Spatial information is lost in conventional spectroscopic extractions when a 2D spectrogram is collapsed into a 1D spectrum. For resolved galaxies, spatial and spectral features are superimposed along the dispersion direction, such that emission from distinct regions or nearby spectral features can become confused during the 1D extraction. The relative orientation of spatial features in a resolved galaxy with respect to the dispersion direction depends on the position angle of the observations and the grism orientation. This further complicates the interpretation when spectrograms are co-added. In contrast, emission-line maps preserve the spatial distribution of the line emission, facilitating its interpretation and enabling spatially resolved studies.

papers.title: Characterizations of products of projective spaces and quadrics
papers.abstract: We characterize products of projective spaces and smooth quadrics using Schur functors and positivity of vector bundles. First, we obtain characterizations of projective spaces and smooth quadrics using positivity of arbitrary Schur functors of extensions of a unipotent bundle by the tangent bundle, generalizing several existing results. We then prove that almost nef regular foliations whose direct sum is a subbundle of the tangent bundle determine a product decomposition, if the corresponding Schur functors admit suitable positive Schur submodules. For smooth weak Fano varieties similar results are obtained by replacing almost nefness and individual integrability of the foliations by the integrability of their total image. As special cases, we obtain product analogues of well-known characterizations of projective spaces and quadrics.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Colouring Euclid with external ground-based imaging data
papers.abstract: Accurate photometric-redshift estimation and calibration of the weak-lensing point-spread function (PSF) for Euclid require complementary ground-based optical imaging with high photometric precision and spatial homogeneity. The Organisation Unit for External Data (OU-EXT) integrates heterogeneous ground-based surveys into the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS), delivering uniformly calibrated, co-added images, and associated PSF models. To minimise systematics in spectral energy distribution (SED) reconstruction and photometric-redshift estimation, these data must achieve relative photometric stability at the $\sim$10 mmag level on Euclid-tile scales. We present the ground-based imaging component of Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1), comprising $\sim2500$ deg$^2$ across the wide, deep, and auxiliary fields. We summarise the OU-EXT production workflow and validation framework, and quantify the achieved data quality of the co-added products in terms of depth, photometric zero-point stability, and spatial colour homogeneity. In the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), the point-source $10\sigma$ depths in the $griz$ bands reach 24.8/24.3/24.0/23.0 AB mag, with the deep fields extending 1--2 magnitudes deeper. Most EWS DR1 tiles meet the 10 mmag relative photometric requirement, with 1.1% and 1.5% showing offsets exceeding 50 mmag in the northern and southern hemispheres, respectively. Spatial colour variations remain typically below 5--10 mmag across the southern EWS footprint, while larger residual structures of 10--25 mmag appear in some northern regions. These results demonstrate that the EXT production chain provides a largely homogeneous framework for integrating ground-based datasets into Euclid, while identifying calibration and co-addition limitations that have to be addressed in DR2 to meet the mission's most stringent cosmological requirements. (Abridged)

papers.intro:
The Euclid mission (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025) is an ongoing project of the European Space Agency (ESA), carried out in collaboration with the Euclid Consortium, with the primary goal of constraining the nature of dark energy and its role in cosmic acceleration. Following its successful launch in 2023, the observatory has been continuously acquiring data at an unprecedented rate.

However, the onboard imaging instruments, VIS (Euclid Collaboration: Cropper et al. 2025) and NISP (Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al. 2025), provide only limited spectral coverage, resulting in coarse sampling of the spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of detected sources. A precise characterisation of galaxy SEDs is essential for accurate photometric-redshift (photo-zz) estimation (Bolzonella et al. 2000; Abdalla et al. 2008), which underpins galaxy clustering measurements, and weak lensing analyses – both key methods for the Euclid primary scientific goals.

OU-EXT coordinates the ingestion, homogenisation, calibration, and processing of the ground-based imaging used to complement the Euclid VIS and NISP observations. Multiple coordinated ground-based observing campaigns therefore contribute to the Euclid survey footprint. In the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), the northern hemisphere is covered by the Ultraviolet Near Infrared Optical Northern Survey (Gwyn et al. 2025, UNIONS;), while the southern hemisphere is currently covered by DES (DES Collaboration: Abbott, T. et al. 2016) and will eventually be complemented by deeper LSST observations (Ivezić et al. 2019). While Euclid itself delivers a vast and homogeneous space-based dataset, the incorporation of ground-based ancillary data introduces an additional layer of complexity. OU-EXT must combine observations obtained under varying atmospheric conditions, from different observing sites, instrumental passbands, survey strategies, and data-reduction pipelines into a single, consistently calibrated framework. The resulting external dataset spans a data volume several times larger than that delivered by the spacecraft alone, making its homogenisation, photometric recalibration, and quality control a central technical challenge for the mission. Moreover, even small spatial variations in the photometric calibration can introduce position-dependent biases in galaxy colours and colour–redshift relations, which can propagate into photometric-redshift estimates and ultimately into cosmological parameter inference. Ensuring photometric calibration homogeneity across the Euclid footprint is therefore not only a data-quality objective, but an essential requirement for controlling systematic uncertainties in the mission’s cosmological analyses.

We describe the characteristics of the DR1 external data, including observations covering the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), as well as the data used in the Euclid Auxiliary Fields (EAFs) and Euclid Deep Fields (EDFs). We present the co-addition strategy adopted within the SGS, the generation of stacked data products, and a quantitative assessment of the resulting data quality across the DR1 footprint.

This paper provides a detailed description of the processing and calibration steps applied to the ground-based optical imaging datasets released in DR1 (Euclid Data Release 1 2026). We describe the characteristics of the DR1 external data, including observations covering the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), as well as the data used in the Euclid Auxiliary Fields (EAFs) and Euclid Deep Fields (EDFs). We present the co-addition strategy adopted within the SGS, the generation of stacked data products, and a quantitative assessment of the resulting data quality across the DR1 footprint.

The structure of this paper is as follows. We begin by describing the role of OU-EXT within the SGS, outlining its responsibilities in the acquisition, homogenisation, calibration, and validation of ground-based imaging data (Sect. 2). We then present the datasets included in DR1, detailing their survey origins, sky coverage, and observational characteristics (Sect. 3). Next, we describe the co-addition pipeline implemented within the SGS for both images and point-spread function (PSF) models (Sect. 4). In Sect. 5, we assess the data quality of the released co-added images and their associated PSF models, providing a quantitative evaluation of the photometric performance achieved across the DR1 footprint. We discuss the DR1 validation outcome, identified limitations, and improvements planned for future releases in Sect. 6, and summarise our main conclusions in Sect. 7. Appendices A–D provide additional information on SEF flag propagation, reference catalogues, and the spatial distributions of depth and photometric stability. Magnitudes are reported using the AB magnitude system (Oke & Gunn 1983).

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1): Calibration strategy and observations
papers.abstract: This paper reviews how Euclid's top-level calibration requirements were translated into a calibration plan, how this plan is implemented and maintained during the survey, and how it performs in the current DR1 release. We show that DR1 already meets or exceeds most end-of-mission spectrophotometric calibration requirements. The construction of spectroscopically complete and pure samples relies on ongoing data acquisition for the Euclid Deep Survey, while point-spread-function modelling and shear calibration are still converging to their stringent accuracy requirements. With all DR1 data reprocessed with the DR1 pipeline configuration, more subtle effects have been detected and characterised, and correction strategies have been developed for DR2. These include improved absolute flux calibration, astrometry, charge-persistence correction, shutter effects, wavelength calibration, and spectrophotometric corrections for water-ice contamination. Finally, synthetic photometric transformations between Euclid and each of Roman, the James Webb Space Telescope, and the Chinese Space-station Survey Telescope, are presented.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1): Spacecraft performance in the L2 environment
papers.abstract: The Euclid mission was designed around the need for thermo-optical and mechanical stability, stray-light suppression, low outgassing, and precise guiding. After three years in space, a wealth of data is available to assess the performance in these areas. We review the L2 halo-orbit design and consumables budget. Solar stray-light gradually increases by 14\% per year and is consistent with meteoroid puncturing, but remains low overall. Data loss from high solar activity has declined notably since the maximum of the 25th Solar cycle passed. The thermodynamical response of the optical elements to a thermal step impulse follows sigmoidal growth curves, entering the asymptotic equilibration regime after 21--46 hours. Water-ice contamination has affected data from both instruments and requires continued monitoring; we review detection and decontamination methods, and Euclid's contamination history. High-precision measurements of the zodiacal background reveal, at eight sigma significance, the subtle modulation caused by the changing perspective on the dust distribution due to the L2 halo-orbit libration. These data also show that conservative pre-launch estimates overestimated the out-of-field stray-light by factors of 4 (H band) to 27 (I band). Telemetry data demonstrate excellent guiding, and enable highly significant detections of solar radiation pressure and of thermal-emission recoil from Euclid's unilluminated dark sides. Lastly, we present a list of 34 meteoroid impacts, discuss their mechanical and optical signatures, and derive a minimum detectable impactor mass of 5e-7 g.

papers.intro:
Euclid’s mission specifications include extraordinary optical stability and image quality, to achieve the best possible shear measurements from space (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025). These manifested in numerous key characteristics, among others the following that affect calibration of mission data: (i) a silicon-carbide structure for all relevant opto-mechanical parts of the scientific PLM (PLM); (ii) an eclipse-free halo orbit around the Sun–Earth L2 point, offering maximum thermal stability; (iii) a survey design minimising thermal disturbances; (iv) a spacecraft design that minimises outgassing and molecular contamination of optical surfaces; and (v) minimal levels of optical in- and out-of-field stray light.

These manifested in numerous key characteristics, among others the following that affect calibration of mission data: (i) a silicon-carbide structure for all relevant opto-mechanical parts of the scientific PLM (PLM); (ii) an eclipse-free halo orbit around the Sun–Earth L2 point, offering maximum thermal stability; (iii) a survey design minimising thermal disturbances; (iv) a spacecraft design that minimises outgassing and molecular contamination of optical surfaces; and (v) minimal levels of optical in- and out-of-field stray light.

In this paper we present a science-centred perspective of Euclid’s technical performance after three years in orbit. While this is already half the nominal mission’s duration, DR1 (Euclid Data Release 1 2026) just begins to deliver on Euclid’s promise. In Sect. 2 we demonstrate that the spacecraft is in excellent operational condition, delivering a maximum of scientifically useful data with operational time exceeding 99%. In Sect. 3 we review Euclid’s sensitivity to solar stray light and X-ray emission from solar flares. In Sect. 4 we model the thermal response and equilibration timescales of opto-mechanical elements to a thermal step impulse. Section 5 covers molecular contamination by water ice, which was expected and explicitly folded into the calibration plan; although its effect on the optical and photometric performance remained highly uncertain until in-flight data became available. We present detection methods and our decontamination strategies, and in Sect. 6 the spacecraft’s actual in-flight contamination history. In Sect. 7 we use monthly observations of the self-calibration field to compare the background’s time-variability against ZB (ZB) model predictions. In Sect. 8 we review the guiding performance in terms of RPE (RPE), and use the corrective torques from the cold-gas thrusters to determine SRP (SRP) and TER (TER). Finally, we discuss the mechanical and optical signatures of meteoroid impacts in Sect. 9, and conclude in Sect. 10.

papers.title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?
papers.abstract: Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. Each task requires agents to implement core systems from a minimal starting point and evaluates them against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. Additionally, through extensive red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we expose reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework and develop Breakwater, an extension of Harbor that blocks all attacks tested in our study. Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, suggesting it may have the skills needed to reach the singularity. The remaining agents average only 0.58. Our vision is for Singularity-Bench to track how much of AI development agents can already automate and when they may transition from assisting to taking end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.

Frontier AI agents are rapidly gaining both capability and autonomy, with increasing success on realistic tasks that require sustained work over long horizons (Jimenez et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Kwa et al., 2026). Recent work on recursive self-improvement (RSI) suggests that these gains are beginning to extend beyond completing tasks to improving the agent systems themselves (Robeyns et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026c). These advances call for a benchmark that measures how much of AI development agents can already automate and tracks how close they are to the singularity, the point at which they can fully take charge of the process.

As AI agents become more capable, design choices that made earlier benchmarks tractable increasingly limit their ability to measure further progress.

1. Restricted action spaces. Restricting the action space isolates specific skills and makes failures easier to interpret. Many benchmarks therefore fix most of the development stack. RSI Bench includes a pre-training data-curation task (Mahmoud et al., 2026); autoresearch permits architecture and optimizer changes within one training script (Karpathy, 2026); and Φ\Phi-Bench includes both localized and whole-repository optimization (Φ -Bench contributors, 2026). For stronger agents, however, these constraints can reduce AI development to tuning an existing system’s hyperparameters, preventing agents from discovering more consequential improvements elsewhere in the stack.

KernelBench and PTXBench evaluate kernels in isolation (Ouyang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a), while training and inference benchmarks often use small models, single-GPU settings, or simplified workloads (Karpathy, 2026; Rank et al., 2026; Yeon et al., 2026). 3. Unreliable verification. Reference solutions and finite tests enable fast, reproducible verification when outputs are well specified (Jimenez et al., 2024; Merrill et al., 2026). They may not suffice when capable agents build end-to-end systems. Tests can fail to distinguish genuine improvements from unintended shortcuts, while agent-written code may inspect hidden tests, access unintended resources, or invoke another agent during evaluation. Verification must cover both functional correctness and execution integrity.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) Euclid photometric masks
papers.abstract: This paper describes the Euclid DR1 photometric masks, which trace spatial variations in the survey properties (e.g. satellite position angles, integration time, sky tiling, and survey footprint); in the instrumental performance of Euclid and the external data (EXT) it uses (e.g. survey coverage, depth, PSF width, quality flags, systematic effects and astrometric uncertainties); and in possible contamination from sky emission (e.g. galactic extinction and zodiacal light emission). Among this, the effective coverage mask is particularly important as it defines the effective survey area and can be used to exclude spurious objects when selecting Euclid photometric samples for scientific analyses. The Euclid photometric masks are built for each observed sky region (tile) and are provided as full-sky HEALPix maps (nested ordering and explicit indexing) at Nside = 16 384, equating to a resolution of 12"88, for both the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) and Euclid Deep Survey (EDS). We estimate the total area of the DR1 EWS (EDS) to be 2008.8 (74.7) deg$^2$ and find that 82 (81)\% of this area is preserved by the effective coverage mask. We observe that Euclid's instrumental properties are consistent with expectations, showing only minor relative variations across the sky. For DR1 EWS the standard deviation of the depth (computed for a 2" aperture and at 5 $\sigma$) is below 0.2 AB mag, with median values of 25.69, 24.14, 24.3, and 24.29 for the Euclid IE, YE, JE, and HE bands. Finally, we expect these photometric masks to be key to many science applications and in particular for cosmological analyses.

papers.intro:
The Euclid satellite mission (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025), launched in July 2023, aims to constrain the main cosmological parameters through two primary cosmological probes: gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering (Amendola et al. 2018; Euclid Collaboration: Blanchard et al. 2020). To this end, it will collect data over the 14 000 deg2\text{deg}^{2} Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) and the approximately 63​deg263\,\text{deg}^{2} Euclid Deep Survey (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022, EDS;)11 1 https://www.cosmos.esa.int/web/euclid/euclid-survey.

The Euclid satellite mission (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025), launched in July 2023, aims to constrain the main cosmological parameters through two primary cosmological probes: gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering (Amendola et al. 2018; Euclid Collaboration: Blanchard et al. 2020). To this end, it will collect data over the 14 000 deg2\text{deg}^{2} Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) and the approximately 63​deg263\,\text{deg}^{2} Euclid Deep Survey (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022, EDS;)11 1 https://www.cosmos.esa.int/web/euclid/euclid-survey.

Euclid has two instruments (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022): the Visible instrument (Euclid Collaboration: Cropper et al. 2025, VIS,) and the Near Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al. 2025, NISP,). VIS was designed to provide exquisite imaging in the optical domain for galaxy detection and shear measurements. It consists of a single visible band, IEI_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}. NISP provides photometric imaging in three bands, YEY_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, JEJ_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, and HEH_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, for detecting distant galaxies, as well as spectroscopic redshifts for galaxy clustering. The Euclid data are combined with external data (referred to as ‘EXT’, see Euclid Collaboration: Corcho-Caballero et al. 2026, for more details) from ground-based photometric surveys such as the Dark Energy Survey (Abbott et al. 2021, DES,), the Canada-France Imaging Survey (Ibata et al. 2017, CFIS,), the Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System on Maui (Magnier et al. 2020, Pan-STARRS,), The Waterloo-Hawaii-IfA G-band Survey (WHIGS), and the Wide Imaging with Subaru HSC of the Euclid Sky (Aihara et al. 2018, WHISHES,) to determine photometric redshifts for all VIS- and NISP-detected objects (Euclid Collaboration: Hartley et al. 2026).

The processing of Euclid data (see Euclid Collaboration: Ruffenach et al. 2026, for a detailed description) is organised within the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS) into pipelines and processing functions (PFs). Each PF is developed and maintained by a corresponding Organisational Unit (OU) within the SGS. This paper describes the OU-LE3 (Organizational Unit Level 3) VMPZ-ID (Visibility Mask PhotoZ-Internal Data) PF (Processing Function) and associated pipelines contributing to the core products of Euclid Data Release 1 (Euclid Data Release 1 2026, DR1), also known as DR1 Foundation. An overview of the DR1 Foundation products is given in Euclid Collaboration: Aussel et al. (2026b). The DR1 sky survey (Euclid Collaboration: Tereno et al. 2026) comprises about 2000​deg22000\,{\rm deg}^{2} of the EWS and the three EDS subfields: Euclid Deep Field Fornax (EDF-F), South (EDF-S), and North (EDF-N). Some Euclid Auxiliary Fields and calibration fields are also released.

The main VMPZ-ID products are HEALPix22 2 Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelation of a sphere, see https://healpix.sourceforge.io/ (Górski et al. 2005) sky maps, which are called photometric masks hereafter, tracking spatial variations in the properties of the Euclid survey, the instrumental performance of VIS and NISP, the quality of EXT data, and foreground sky emission. These variations could propagate into the final Euclid catalogues and bias the estimation of cosmological parameters, as reported for other photometric surveys, such as KiDS and DES (see Weaverdyck et al. 2026; Yan et al. 2025, and references therein). These masks will be also useful in selecting Euclid galaxy samples for statistical studies in non-cosmological analyses.

papers.title: Metadata for the Flux Density Calibration of the April 2021 and March 2022 Event Horizon Telescope Science Data
papers.abstract: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) has been conducting science observations annually since 2021 after the initial campaigns in 2017 and 2018. In this memo, we report on the metadata associated to the observations from 2021 April and 2022 March at 1.3mm wavelengths. We follow a similar path for the collection, processing, and validation of the metadata used for the initial amplitude calibration of the 2018 EHT data. In this release, we introduce some differences regarding the treatment of sensitivities and gain curves for some stations. In addition, we describe the changes to the EHT array since 2018.

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) is a continually improving array that has been performing yearly science observations since 2021, following the successful 2017 and 2018 campaigns. In this release, we build on the framework set in place in those campaigns for the treatment of the Level 1 (L1) processing of the metadata used for amplitude calibration (Issaoun et al., 2017a; Janssen et al., 2019; Koay et al., 2023a), highlighting the changes made in the 2021 and 2022 campaigns.

The 2021 observations marked the return of EHT operations after the restrictions imposed by the COVID-19 pandemic. Significant adjustments were needed to enable a new EHT campaign, such as controlling some telescopes remotely. For example, the Greenland Telescope (GLT) operations required coordination of efforts between the GLT staff in Taiwan and engineers employed by the Pituffik Space Base in Greenland (Chen et al., 2023), who had no previous experience with telescope operations. In addition, both the NOrthern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) operated by the Institut de Radio Astronomie Millimétrique (IRAM) in France, and the University of Arizona 12-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak (KT) joined the EHT observations for the first time in that year. The Large Millimeter Telescope Alfonso Serrano (LMT) in Mexico returned to operations on time for the 2022 campaign, although relying on a crystal clock rather than a maser, which was unavailable due to extended maintenance. Thus, a total of 10 and 11 stations participated in the 2021 and 2022 EHT campaigns, respectively. This makes a total of eight single-dish stations (APEX, IRAM 30 m, SPT, LMT, SMT, JCMT, GLT and KT) and three phased arrays (ALMA, SMA and NOEMA).

papers.title: Towards Democratising Low-Data Medical Image Classification: CPU-Trainable ZACH-ViT and Its Geometric Variants
papers.abstract: Medical image classification in resource-constrained settings must contend with limited annotations and computational capacity. We evaluate four ZACH-ViT variants with linear, Euclidean prototype, Poincare and spherical heads alongside two compact multiple-instance-learning baselines. All models are trained from scratch with fewer than 260,000 parameters across seven MedMNIST+ datasets and three external benchmarks (PCam, ISIC2017 and Shenzhen tuberculosis radiographs). The low-data protocol uses 50 training images per class and five seeds, with validation-selected checkpoints at 23 and 47 epochs; a full-data reference uses one seed. Compact-TransMIL achieves the highest ten-dataset mean test Macro-F1 at 23 epochs (53.34%) and with full data (73.93%). At 47 epochs, ZACH-Linear narrowly leads (57.76% versus 57.54% for Compact-TransMIL). Extending training improves Macro-F1 in 239 of 300 paired comparisons. On ISIC2017, hZACH-Spherical has the highest 47-epoch low-data Macro-F1 (44.09% with SD 4.09%), whereas ZACH-EuclideanProto leads with full data (51.27%). We additionally conduct 40 CPU-only training runs on ISIC2017 and Shenzhen using four CPU threads; model-only single-image inference requires approximately 4-9 ms, while image decoding and preprocessing substantially increase end-to-end latency. The results demonstrate the feasibility of CPU-only training on the tested platform and the task- and regime-dependence of compact medical imaging under strict resource constraints.

papers.intro:
Medical image analysis is fundamentally constrained by two distinct resources: labelled examples and computational capacity. Large pretrained visual backbones can be highly effective when appropriate weights and hardware accelerators are available, but they do not address the more foundational question of what can be learned from scratch using few annotated cases and a minimal computational footprint. Earlier work on compact transformers established data and parameter efficiency as explicit architectural objectives (Hassani et al., 2021). However, the term accessible AI is only meaningful if tied to measurable properties: the number of labels used for training, instantiated model parameters, training time, memory footprint, inference latency, and the often-overlooked cost of image preprocessing.

However, the term accessible AI is only meaningful if tied to measurable properties: the number of labels used for training, instantiated model parameters, training time, memory footprint, inference latency, and the often-overlooked cost of image preprocessing.

ZACH-ViT was previously introduced as a compact vision transformer that eschews learned positional embeddings and dedicated class tokens, relying instead on global averaging over patch tokens and adaptive residual projections (Angelakis, 2026c). Its geometric extensions replace the standard final classifier with Euclidean or curved prototype heads (Angelakis, 2026a). Subsequent investigations have explored clean-versus-adversarial behaviour, corruption sensitivity, geometric boundary effects, and quantized deployment (Angelakis and Gomez-Barrero, 2026c; Angelakis and Gomez-Barrero, 2026b; Angelakis, 2026b). These prior studies establish the architecture and its boundaries; the present paper does not claim to introduce ZACH-ViT or its geometric heads anew.

A critical remaining question is how these compact architectures perform across diverse medical imaging benchmarks, under extended training budgets, and when trained entirely without GPU acceleration. To address this, we study ten datasets, incorporating three additional classification benchmarks with distinct image sources: PCam histopathology patches, ISIC2017 dermoscopy images, and Shenzhen radiographs. Rather than comparing against unrestricted pretrained systems, we constrain all evaluated models to a strict sub-0.26-million-parameter regime. This is a deliberately narrow, resource-conditioned comparison, not a claim of unrestricted state-of-the-art performance.

We structure our contributions around four main axes: (i) Beyond-MedMNIST evaluation. A ten-dataset, 224×\times224 benchmark comprising four canonical ZACH classifier heads and two compact MIL-inspired baselines, all trained from scratch under an identical parameter ceiling. (ii) Low-data budget analysis. Five seed-matched 50-per-class training subsets per dataset, yielding 23- and 47-epoch validation-selected checkpoints from a single 47-epoch trajectory, alongside separately reported exact-epoch controls. (iii) Explicit regime and failure analysis. A single-seed full-training-data reference, per-class recall checks, known dataset-integrity flags, and transparent accounting for unequal training updates and class balance. (iv) Measured CPU feasibility. Forty additional CPU-only real-data training runs of the four ZACH heads, combined with six-model synthetic resource profiles and trained-model inference timings that explicitly separate model execution from input decoding.

papers.title: Quantitative flocking of Cucker-Smale flocks under time-delay and noise
papers.abstract: We study the asymptotic flocking dynamics of the delayed stochastic Cucker-Smale (in short, DSCS) model driven by agent-wise independent, component-wise multiplicative Brownian noise. The simultaneous interplay of stochastic perturbations and time delay yields fundamental challenges to asymptotic stochastic flocking analysis, as the communication weight may lose a uniform positive lower bound, while the velocity moment is no longer monotone. To overcome these difficulties, we present a sufficient framework and an analytical tool combining the method of time-varying effective region and Lyapunov functional approach with time-delay corrections. This approach avoids any reliance on uniformly positive communication weights or monotone velocity moments. The proposed approach recovers sufficiently strong effective velocity alignment despite stochastic fluctuations and delay effects. As a consequence, we establish the mean-square stochastic flocking with an explicit polynomial convergence rate. The admissible decay exponent is determined by the communication kernel exponent and the orders of the spatial and velocity history moments. These results establish a quantitative theory for long-time stochastic flocking under simultaneous delay and multiplicative noise, and we provide a positive answer to an open problem raised by~[R. Erban, J. Haskovec, Y. Sun, SIAM J. Appl. Math., 76, 1535--1557 (2016)]. We also develop robust analytical tools applicable to delayed stochastic collective dynamics with degenerate communications.

papers.intro:
Collective behaviors are ubiquitous in interacting particle systems, where simple communications between agents may lead to coherent macroscopic patterns such as alignment, aggregation, synchronization, and flocking. Such emergent behaviors have often been observed in biological swarms, animal groups, robotic networks, opinion dynamics, and other multi-agent systems [12, 17, 35, 36, 39]. Over the past several decades, mathematical models for such collective dynamics have attracted considerable attention, leading to significant progress on the local and global well-posedness, asymptotic behavior, and mean-field description of various alignment models [3, 12, 22, 31, 32, 33, 36]. Among them, the Cucker-Smale (CS) model has become one of the most influential paradigms for self-organized flocking through pairwise velocity alignment. In this paper, we focus on the quantitative flocking analysis of a delayed stochastic Cucker-Smale (DSCS) model. To set the stage, we begin with the deterministic CS model [12, 13].

papers.title: Double Blandford: Resistive GRMHD simulations of accreting black holes simultaneously launch winds and jets
papers.abstract: Magnetic fields can launch outflows through the Blandford-Znajek (BZ) or the Blandford-Payne (BP) mechanism in accreting black hole systems. Despite the dominant launching mechanism still being unclear, the BP process has been insufficiently studied in general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations due to difficulties in generating and maintaining the required large-scale magnetic field geometry. Here, we set up six resistive GRMHD simulations of thin accretion disks with BHAC. The accretion disks in two simulations become magnetically arrested, while the others stay in the standard and normal evolution (SANE) regime. All simulations form jets and winds. The jets are parabolic and collimated by the outer sub-relativistic disk wind; a power law relating the jet width $x$ to the height $z$ as $x\propto z^\mathcal{K}$ yields exponents between 0.52 and 0.64. Among the SANE simulations, the setup with spin parameter $a_* = -0.9375$ has the strongest and most efficient jet, as it accumulates the most magnetic flux at the black hole horizon. For a highly spinning black hole with $a_*=0.9375$, the BZ jet power is $\gtrsim3$ times greater than the disk wind power. The simulated wind regions consist of a highly magnetized region, where the magnetization parameter $\sigma\gg1$, and a less magnetized region. A fast outflow with the potential to reach Lorentz factors up to $\Gamma_\infty\approx25$ propagates in the former region, but because the Lorentz force acts against the disk, it cannot remove a measurable amount of mass from the disk. In the less-magnetized region, a centrifugally driven slower wind efficiently carries away disk material.

Magnetic fields are a vital component of accretion processes around black holes. In accretion disks, magnetic fields, either dragged inwards or generated through dynamo processes (Lubow et al., 1994; Brandenburg et al., 1995; Spruit and Uzdensky, 2005; Jacquemin-Ide et al., 2024, e.g.,), facilitate the angular momentum transfer through the magnetorotational instability (Balbus and Hawley, 1991, MRI,).

Magnetic fields are a vital component of accretion processes around black holes. In accretion disks, magnetic fields, either dragged inwards or generated through dynamo processes (Lubow et al., 1994; Brandenburg et al., 1995; Spruit and Uzdensky, 2005; Jacquemin-Ide et al., 2024, e.g.,), facilitate the angular momentum transfer through the magnetorotational instability (Balbus and Hawley, 1991, MRI,).

Moreover, magnetic fields can launch outflows, which not only provide another avenue for removing angular momentum but also for a variety of observational phenomena. Magnetic fields can launch outflows through the Blandford-Znajek (Blandford and Znajek, 1977, BZ,) or the Blandford-Payne (Blandford and Payne, 1982, BP,) mechanism. In the BZ mechanism, magnetic fields threading a spinning black hole extract its rotational energy to power outflows, while in the BP process, magnetic fields threading the accretion disk extract the disk’s rotational energy to launch outflows loaded with disk material. These outflows are observed in the form of jets and winds across multiple energy bands (Russell et al., 2019; Giustini et al., 2023, for a review, see e.g., Blandford et al. 2019; Muñoz-Darias et al. 2026; Ribeiro and da Rocha 2026).

In the BZ mechanism, magnetic fields threading a spinning black hole extract its rotational energy to power outflows, while in the BP process, magnetic fields threading the accretion disk extract the disk’s rotational energy to launch outflows loaded with disk material. These outflows are observed in the form of jets and winds across multiple energy bands (Russell et al., 2019; Giustini et al., 2023, for a review, see e.g., Blandford et al. 2019; Muñoz-Darias et al. 2026; Ribeiro and da Rocha 2026).

There is clear observational evidence for the simultaneous presence of radio jets and mass-loaded winds in radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGNs), in radio-loud broad-absorption-line quasars, and in black hole X-ray binaries (Gregg et al., 2000; Miller et al., 2006; Tombesi et al., 2010; Tombesi et al., 2014; Muñoz-Darias et al., 2017; Sánchez-Sierras et al., 2023, e.g.,). However, which mechanisms are responsible for jet- and wind- launching is still an open question. In particular, assuming BZ and BP processes are responsible for jet- and wind- launching, which process dominates energetically and how the two processes interact remains poorly constrained by observations (Russell et al., 2013a, e.g.,). Both launching mechanisms operate close to the black hole, and observationally resolving the actual launch site is feasible only for a few select cases, such as the low-luminosity AGN M87* (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2019; EHT MWL Science Working Group et al., 2021, which shows no indication for a classical thin-disk or disk-launched outflow however).

On the theoretical side, magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations have become a prominent tool for elucidating jet-launching mechanisms. However, while properties of BZ-driven outflows, such as their power and dependence on parameters like black hole spin, have been repeatedly studied in general-relativistic MHD (GRMHD) simulations (Tchekhovskoy et al., 2011; Tchekhovskoy and McKinney, 2012; Morales Teixeira et al., 2018; Dhruv et al., 2025, e.g.,), studies of the BP mechanism have been limited to Newtonian or special relativistic MHD simulations (Kato et al., 2002; Zanni et al., 2007; Porth and Fendt, 2010, e.g.,). In GRMHD simulations, generating and maintaining the magnetic field geometry required for BP outflows has proven to be challenging, such that disk winds are often pressure driven in those simulations (Hawley and Krolik, 2006; Vourellis and Fendt, 2021).

In GRMHD simulations, generating and maintaining the magnetic field geometry required for BP outflows has proven to be challenging, such that disk winds are often pressure driven in those simulations (Hawley and Krolik, 2006; Vourellis and Fendt, 2021).

One way to maintain the magnetic field geometry is a departure from ideal MHD. In ideal MHD, magnetic field lines are frozen into the underlying plasma. Consequently, magnetic flux is dragged inward until it saturates, choking off the accretion process and forming a magnetically arrested disk (Narayan et al., 2003, MAD, ). Resistive MHD lifts the frozen-in condition, which enables the accreting matter to cross magnetic flux surfaces and form a steady-state accretion stream in which inward advection of field lines is balanced by outward diffusion. In simulations, resistivity is either prescribed (Striani et al., 2016; Ripperda et al., 2020; Moran et al., 2025, e.g.,), or numerical (Ripperda et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2023, in ideal GRMHD simulations, e.g.,), the latter resulting from the finite resolution when evolving the MHD equations (Rembiasz et al., 2017). Resistive MHD also allows magnetic field lines to reconnect, which has been connected to flux eruptions observed for Sgr A∗ (Dexter et al., 2020; Porth et al., 2021; Nathanail et al., 2022; Scepi et al., 2022, e.g.,). Hence, non-ideal MHD facilitated by, e.g., resistivity, majorly impacts observations.

Consequently, magnetic flux is dragged inward until it saturates, choking off the accretion process and forming a magnetically arrested disk (Narayan et al., 2003, MAD, ). Resistive MHD lifts the frozen-in condition, which enables the accreting matter to cross magnetic flux surfaces and form a steady-state accretion stream in which inward advection of field lines is balanced by outward diffusion. In simulations, resistivity is either prescribed (Striani et al., 2016; Ripperda et al., 2020; Moran et al., 2025, e.g.,), or numerical (Ripperda et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2023, in ideal GRMHD simulations, e.g.,), the latter resulting from the finite resolution when evolving the MHD equations (Rembiasz et al., 2017). Resistive MHD also allows magnetic field lines to reconnect, which has been connected to flux eruptions observed for Sgr A∗ (Dexter et al., 2020; Porth et al., 2021; Nathanail et al., 2022; Scepi et al., 2022, e.g.,). Hence, non-ideal MHD facilitated by, e.g., resistivity, majorly impacts observations.

Despite the importance of resistivity in accretion, few global resistive GRMHD simulations exist, especially those featuring thin accretion disks capable of launching BP-driven outflows. Vourellis et al. (2019) and Vourellis and Fendt (2021) ran resistive GRMHD simulations of thin accretion disks using rHARM3D, which yielded outflows in the form of jets and winds. However, turbulence in their simulated accretion flows prevented BP-driven outflows from forming. Thus, uncertainty remains about the properties of BP winds and their relationship to BZ-driven jets in GRMHD. We aim to address this knowledge gap by running resistive GRMHD simulations of thin accretion disks with BP and BZ-driven outflows. We structure our paper as follows: We outline the simulation setups in section 2 and detail the results in section 3. We discuss the results further in section 4, and conclude with section 5.

papers.title: Transferable Neuromorphic Protection for Distribution Networks
papers.abstract: Protection of converter-dominated distribution networks is challenging due to limited fault currents, operating-mode transitions, bidirectional power flow, and heterogeneous network configurations. This paper proposes a scale-invariant neuromorphic protection framework to enable transferable protection decisions across such networks. The framework integrates asset-based normalization, multi-domain disturbance representation, event-driven spike encoding, leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) dynamics, adaptive threshold regulation, and directional supervision within a unified mathematical formulation. Local voltage, current, active power, and reactive power measurements are transformed into dimensionless disturbance representations, while latency encoding and membrane integration capture disturbance intensity and temporal evolution. The framework is evaluated across four heterogeneous network configurations: a two-DER inverter-interfaced microgrid, an islanded ring microgrid, the IEEE 13-node feeder, and the CIGRE European medium-voltage benchmark. Across 480 cases, it achieves a median operating time of 7.6 ms, with 94.2 % of cases operating within one power cycle. The results demonstrate selective protection across different electrical ratings and network topologies using a common parameterization without network-specific retuning, highlighting the potential of neuromorphic processing for physically interpretable, communication-free protection of converter-dominated distribution networks.
papers.intro:
The growing integration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) is reshaping the protection requirements of modern distribution networks. In contrast to conventional synchronous generators, power-electronic converters generally impose limits on fault-current contribution through their control and protection mechanisms, potentially complicating fault detection under certain operating conditions. The challenge is further compounded by transitions between grid-connected and islanded operation, network reconfiguration, and bidirectional power flow [1, 2]. These characteristics can reduce the sensitivity and compromise the coordination of conventional protection schemes in heterogeneous, converter-dominated networks[3, 4, 5]. Accordingly, developing protection mechanisms that accommodate variations in equipment ratings, network configurations, and operating conditions without fundamental redesign remains an important research objective [6].

Several approaches have been investigated to address these challenges, including adaptive protection, differential protection, signal-processing-based methods, and time-domain techniques [6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. For instance, Samkari and Johnson proposed a time-domain protection scheme for microgrids comprising aggregated inverter-based distributed energy resources, demonstrating the potential of time-domain approaches for converter-dominated systems [10]. Furthermore, reviews of IBR protection have highlighted the need to assess emerging methods in terms of implementation feasibility, validation maturity, and generalization across diverse power-system conditions [4, 11]. Despite their contributions to specific protection problems, developing a common protection-processing architecture applicable to heterogeneous networks remains an open challenge. In particular, successful validation on one network does not necessarily demonstrate that the underlying decision mechanism can be transferred to systems with different electrical ratings, topologies, and operating conditions [12, 13].
