papers.intro:
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) (oshea2015introductionconvolutionalneuralnetworks) have become foundational to a wide range of applications, including medical imaging, autonomous driving, robotics, surveillance, and mobile vision systems. The growing demand for real time, on device intelligence has shifted many CNN workloads from data centers to edge platforms, where processing data locally reduces latency, communication costs, and privacy concerns. However, edge devices such as embedded GPUs, FPGAs, and custom ASICs provide only limited memory capacity, power budgets and memory bandwidth (9708948). This makes computational efficiency and low memory consumption essential. In many image processing tasks on edge deployment scenarios, model weights reside permanently in device memory while input feature maps, for example in the form of input images, are streamed at runtime. Due to the limited memory capacity of edge devices, memory footprint reduction by storing only non-zero model weights explicitly via sparse matrix formats becomes an attractive approach for reducing memory traffic and improving inference efficiency.

This makes computational efficiency and low memory consumption essential. In many image processing tasks on edge deployment scenarios, model weights reside permanently in device memory while input feature maps, for example in the form of input images, are streamed at runtime. Due to the limited memory capacity of edge devices, memory footprint reduction by storing only non-zero model weights explicitly via sparse matrix formats becomes an attractive approach for reducing memory traffic and improving inference efficiency.

One of the most promising strategies for reducing the memory footprint and computational cost of CNNs on resource-constrained hardware is weight sparsification (raihan2020sparse; stamenovic2021weightblockunitexploring). By pruning a large fraction of the learned weights to zero, sparse networks can substantially reduce both floating-point operations (FLOPs) and memory traffic during inference (liu2024efficientexpertpruningsparse; hoefler2021sparsitydeeplearningpruning). Consequently, recent research has focused on pruning networks to extreme sparsity levels, typically between 90%90\% and 99%99\% (kuznedelev2023accurateneuralnetworkpruning). However, translating these theoretical savings into practical performance gains remains challenging because sparse implementations incur additional execution overhead. In particular, irregular sparsity patterns require indirect accesses to locate non-zero weights and produce uneven workloads across processing elements, resulting in load imbalance and reduced memory efficiency (gale2020sparsegpukernelsdeep; 10.1145/1654059.1654078).

For a sparse convolution (sparse weights, dense images), We identify two principal obstacles to high performance: (1) inefficient sparse weight access, whereby non-contiguous weight layouts generate memory transactions that underutilize memory bandwidth, and (2) workload imbalance, arising because different output channels or spatial tiles encounter varying numbers of non-zero weights, causing some processing elements to idle while others remain saturated. We propose a packed weight representation that addresses the first challenge by enabling coalesced, single-transaction access and improved cache utilization, together with a thread mapping strategy that helps equalize load across threads for the second challenge.

papers.title: Data Archive for 2D and 3D Electrical Impedance Tomography with moderate conductivity contrast phantoms
papers.abstract: This document describes open Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) measurement data that were collected from biomedical imaging inspired phantoms with moderate conductivity contrasts. The data were collected with the KIT4 and KIT5 EIT measurement devices at the University of Eastern Finland, and are intended for EIT image reconstruction algorithm development and testing. The data from thoracic imaging inspired cylindrical and chest-shaped phantoms are suitable for 2D algorithms, and the data from an intracerebral hemorrhage imaging inspired head-shaped phantom with resistive skull are suitable for 3D algorithms. In addition to the measurement data, computational meshes and example reconstruction codes are provided and sample reconstructions included.

papers.title: Characterising a population of fast-declining SNe Ia in galaxy cluster cores
papers.abstract: Galaxy cluster cores, characterised by old stellar population and suppressed star-formation are ideal for studying the environmental dependence of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia). It is unclear whether the diversity of SNe Ia, parametrised by light curve stretch, stems from distinct explosion mechanisms or varying initial conditions, both closely tied to progenitor age. We analyse the light curve stretch and colour distribution of photometrically identified SNe Ia within the galaxy clusters cores, utilising the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) archival data. Using the AMPEL platform, we filter 89,025 ZTF transients spatially coincident with our galaxy cluster catalogues to identify 4,969 likely SN Ia candidates. We split this sample into three populations: core cluster SNe Ia $r \le 0.5R_{500}$, outer-core cluster SNe Ia $0.5R_{500}< r\le 2R_{500}$, and a reference population of non-cluster SN Ia. We present the largest sample of photometrically identified cluster SNe Ia to date, notably isolating a population of 242 SNe Ia within innermost cluster cores $r \le 0.5R_{500}$. This fast-declining SN Ia population is statistically different from the outer-core cluster and field SN Ia population at $\sim4\sigma$ level. A marginal statistical preference for a bimodal distribution over a unimodal one $\Delta AIC$ of 1.53 and 2.3 for each catalogue, indicate cluster cores almost entirely host fast-declining SNe Ia. Conversely, the colour distribution show no significant environmental variation. By filtering out the prompt SN Ia population, cluster cores provide an environment to directly probe the delayed SN Ia progenitor channel. Our observations support a two-population model where progenitor age drives the light curve stretch diversity. The low-stretch values observed in core cluster SNe Ia suggest sub-Chandrasekhar mass double degenerate systems as their likely progenitors.

papers.intro:
A Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) is a specific class of stellar explosion occurring in a binary system involving at least one carbon-oxygen white dwarf (Hoyle and Fowler, 1960). The explosion is triggered by the white dwarf’s interaction with its companion, either through accretion from a non-degenerate star or a merger with another white dwarf. This interaction initiates a thermonuclear runaway, which completely disrupts the white dwarf and produces the observed SN Ia. The intrinsic diversity of the majority of observed SNe Ia can be corrected by a relationship between their peak luminosity and their photometric light curve properties (Phillips, 1993; Hamuy et al., 1996; Tripp, 1998), specifically the stretch (x1x_{1}) and colour (cc) (Guy et al., 2005). Applying these corrections reduces the dispersion in SN Ia brightness from ≈\approx 0.40 mag to ≈\approx 0.15 mag, allowing distances to SNe Ia to be estimated within ≈6%\approx 6\% accuracy. This standardisable nature of SNe Ia enabled the fundamental discovery of the accelerated expansion of the universe (Riess et al., 1998; Perlmutter et al., 1999) and have rendered SNe Ia as the most important cosmological distance indicator.

As crucial SNe Ia have been to cosmology, several open questions remain regarding their progenitor systems, evolutionary pathways and explosion mechanisms. Currently accepted models for the progenitor systems fall into two categories: the single degenerate (SD) model (Whelan and Iben, 1973) where the companion is a non-degenerate star, typically a main-sequence or red giant, that facilitates mass transfer via Roche lobe overflow, and the double degenerate (DD) model (Webbink, 1984), where a binary white dwarf system evolves through the emission of gravitational waves, leading to orbital decay and the eventual merger of the two compact objects. The fundamental assumption behind using SNe Ia as cosmological distance indicators is that they remain standardisable candles across redshift and progenitor environment. A strategy to validate this assumption and investigate any environmental effect of SN Ia properties is to look for SNe Ia in unique environments such as galaxy clusters. Galaxy clusters are predominantly composed of early-type elliptical galaxies characterised by minimal star formation and low dust content (Draine and Salpeter, 1979; McGee and Balogh, 2010). Furthermore, the cores of galaxy clusters exhibit distinct physical properties compared to their outer regions and field environments, such as cluster cores (≤0.5​R500\leq 0.5R_{500}) being more metal-rich than rest of the clusters (Mantz et al., 2017; Romero-Gómez et al., 2023), and galaxies near the virial radius (1​R2001\,R_{200}) featuring younger mean stellar population ages (by 15±4%15\pm 4\%) relative to core galaxies (von der Linden et al., 2010; Smith et al., 2006). Consequently, evaluating SNe Ia partitioned across cluster cores, outer cores, and the field provides an ideal test bed to investigate the progenitor systems and host environment dependence of SN Ia properties.

A fundamental approach to constrain the progenitor scenarios involve measuring their delay time distribution (DTD). The DTD traces the SN Ia rate over time that would follow a brief burst of star formation, with different progenitor scenarios predicting different DTDs. The field SN Ia rate measurements suggest the existence of two SN Ia populations following a burst of star formation, a prompt population that explodes within ≈100−500\approx 100-500 Myr, and a delayed channel that produces SNe Ia on timescales in order of 5 Gyr (Mannucci et al., 2005; Sullivan et al., 2006a; Scannapieco and Bildsten, 2005; Smith et al., 2012). In galaxy clusters, the stellar population is assumed to have been formed in a single brief burst at a redshift of z≈3z\approx 3 (Eisenhardt et al., 2008; Kurk et al., 2009; Mancone et al., 2010). This simple star-formation history (SFH) allows for a more accurate derivation of the DTD, compared to the uncertainties inherent in determining the complex SFH of field galaxies. Assuming an instantaneous star-formation burst at zf=3z_{f}=3, the SNe Ia rate in galaxy clusters peaks at short delay times (≤5​Gyr\leq 5\text{Gyr}, corresponding to 1.45≤z≤31.45\leq z\leq 3), and at longer delay times (≥5​Gyr\geq 5\text{Gyr}, corresponding to z≤1.45z\leq 1.45) the rate almost remains a constant (see Fig. 2 in Maoz et al. 2010). Furthermore, the cluster DTD analysis by Maoz et al. (2010) demonstrates that pure SD or DD model yields poor fit to the observed DTD. Instead, the observed rate can be reproduced by a combination of the prompt SD and the delayed channel, under which assumption the vast majority of SNe Ia at z<1.5z<1.5 originate from DD systems. If this scenario holds, studying SNe Ia in galaxy clusters in the nearby redshift regime could potentially isolate the delayed progenitor channel.

papers.title: Euclid data release 1 (DR1) - SIR spectroscopic calibration
papers.abstract: The Euclid space mission is dedicated to probing the nature of dark energy and dark matter, through a comprehensive mapping of the Universe's large-scale structure. Central to these cosmological goals are the spectra produced by the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) and reduced by the scientific pipelines of the SIR (Spectral near InfraRed) processing function. Due to the intrinsic complexity of slitless spectroscopic data, scientific observations cannot be self-calibrated by the science pipelines. Consequently, the development of dedicated SIR calibration pipelines, utilising specific pointing sequences and observation fields, is essential. The resulting calibration products are fundamental to ensuring that reduced spectra are characterised within requirements in both wavelength and flux. This paper provides a detailed description of the SIR calibration pipelines responsible for generating the products utilised by the science pipelines for Data Release 1 (DR1). A significant challenge in these calibration tasks arises from the requirement to model the entire focal plane as a unified entity. Such a global modelling approach is critical for maintaining astrometric and spectroscopic continuity across the entire field of view. DR1 provides more than 170 millions validated spectra in both red- and blue-grism modes. The accuracy of the reduced spectra is strictly dependent on the performance of the calibration pipelines. Comprehensive analyses of the calibration products and the resulting science spectra demonstrate that current outputs successfully meet the mission requirements. Nevertheless, specific areas for optimisation have been identified; ongoing development is focused on addressing these critical points to further enhance data quality for future data releases.

papers.title: BrickFlow: Connectivity-Guided Brick Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Given a set of LEGO parts and an image of an assembled object, our task is to infer the pose of each part to assemble the object. In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors. To learn a prior over how parts fit together, we train a set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies. We then finetune this model to inject image conditioning, using 1% as much data. However, while the learned flow captures global structure, it does not enforce connectivity. To address this, we introduce an analytic connectivity-field guidance to pull predictions toward connected assemblies at test time. Through this, we demonstrate improved build quality with model size, pretraining, and guidance. We make our models and data available for research purposes at https://kulits.github.io/BrickFlow/

Imagine opening a new set of LEGO to find a box full of pieces, but no instructions. All you have is the picture on the front of the box. You can identify a number of parts visible on the surface, but the image only reveals the outside. The internal structure must be inferred: which bricks support which, what fills the spaces you cannot see. Every piece must end up with a precise position and orientation satisfying discrete connector-defined constraints. This is the problem we address: given an inventory of parts and a single image of the completed assembly, recover the 6D pose of each piece (see Fig. 1).

You can identify a number of parts visible on the surface, but the image only reveals the outside. The internal structure must be inferred: which bricks support which, what fills the spaces you cannot see. Every piece must end up with a precise position and orientation satisfying discrete connector-defined constraints. This is the problem we address: given an inventory of parts and a single image of the completed assembly, recover the 6D pose of each piece (see Fig. 1).

While sharing some of the ambiguities of traditional monocular 3D reconstruction – such as from occlusion – the task presents unique challenges. Though it is possible to computationally verify the validity of a given assembly, figuring out how to go from parts to structure requires understanding not just how pieces fit together, but how they fit together jointly, over possibly many at once. Contributing to this complexity, our assembly domain spans thousands of parts which connect in diverse ways.

papers.title: ArchSpace: Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing LLM Architecture Research
papers.abstract: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.

papers.intro:
Architecture forms the foundation of a large language model (LLM), shaping its performance, scaling behavior, and efficiency during training and inference. When teams such as DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi release new open models, they also introduce architectural changes and innovations. Validating these designs involves costly training experiments. However, the experiments and trade-offs behind most models remain inaccessible, leaving the community with little account of which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. An open and complete record of validation would therefore be as valuable to subsequent research as a new idea itself.

papers.title: The full Gaia colour-magnitude diagram with white dwarfs reveals a declining Milky Way star formation history
papers.abstract: White dwarfs (WDs) provide a fossil record of the Milky Way star formation history (SFH) through the combined effects of stellar evolution and cooling. They have, however, generally been modelled in isolation from the non-degenerate population, so that no single self-consistent set of Galactic assumptions has been required to reproduce both. We present CALOMERA, a semi-analytic chemo-dynamical population synthesis framework in which the vertical density profiles of mono-age subpopulations are computed self-consistently with the Galactic potential and coupled to modern WD cooling sequences, metallicity-dependent progenitor lifetimes and synthetic photometry. We calibrate 18 parameters describing the initial mass function, SFH, initial-final mass relation and WD population against a Gaia DR3 sample of $7.98\times10^{6}$ stars within 1 kpc, including $1.1\times10^{5}$ WDs. The calibrated model reproduces the star counts in each colour-magnitude diagram region to within 3% and the total number count to within 0.5%, compared with the 81% excess in the predicted WD count obtained with the previous main-sequence-only calibration. The recovered SFH peaks early, declines exponentially thereafter, and includes two recent bursts, located at $\tau\approx2.4$ and $0.5$ Gyr. Three cooling libraries (Montr\'{e}al, BaSTI and LPCODE) yield comparably good fits, with differences confined to ${\rm M_G}\gtrsim15$ mag. The predicted luminosity function is in reasonable agreement with the 100 pc Gaia WD sample. We further predict the Galactic WD distribution and differential number counts for surveys of varying depth. Extending the framework to the substellar regime using ATMO models, we predict the Galactic L, T, and Y dwarf populations and their contribution to the deep JWST fields.

papers.intro:
White dwarfs (WDs) are the end products of the evolution of the vast majority of stars. Because all stars with initial masses below ∼\sim8–11 M⊙ end their lives as WDs, the local WD population samples nearly every generation of star formation in the Milky Way (MW) disc and therefore constitutes a fundamental fossil record of its evolution. Their use as Galactic clocks rests on the fact that, once nuclear burning ceases, WD evolution is governed by cooling at essentially constant radius, a process that can be modelled from first principles (Mestel, 1952). Consequently, the faint end of the white dwarf luminosity function (WDLF) has long been used to estimate the age of the Galactic disc (Schmidt, 1959; Liebert et al., 1988; Rowell, 2013; Tremblay et al., 2014, e.g.,), while the detailed distribution of WDs in the colour–magnitude diagram (CMD) encodes information about the MW star formation history (SFH), stellar mass loss, and Galactic structure. Over the past two decades, rapid progress in WD observations, culminating in the era of the Gaia mission (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2016), together with major theoretical advances, has transformed this classical framework into a precision tool for Galactic archaeology (Tremblay et al., 2024, e.g.,).

Observationally, WD studies have progressed from small, extremely local spectroscopic samples confined to the nearest few tens of parsecs (McCook and Sion, 1999; Gianninas et al., 2011; Limoges et al., 2013, e.g.,) to homogeneous wide-area surveys. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (York et al., 2000, SDSS,) increased the known spectroscopic WD sample by an order of magnitude, enabling population-level studies of atmospheric types, mass distributions, and luminosity functions (Kleinman et al., 2004; Kepler et al., 2015, e.g.,). The decisive step came with Gaia, whose astrometry and photometry resolved the WD sequence in the CMD with unprecedented clarity, expanded the census to more than 350 000 candidates (Gentile Fusillo et al., 2021), and enabled nearly complete volume-limited samples in the Solar neighbourhood (Gentile Fusillo et al., 2021; Golovin et al., 2023; O’Brien et al., 2024, e.g.,). These data also revealed rich structure within the WD sequence, including signatures of crystallisation, spectral evolution, unresolved binaries, and mass-dependent cooling (Tremblay et al., 2019; Bédard et al., 2020; El-Badry et al., 2021, e.g.,). Ongoing spectroscopic programmes with the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (Levi et al., 2019, DESI,) and the WHT Enhanced Area Velocity Explorer (Jin et al., 2024, WEAVE,) are extending these samples further. Deeper photometric and spectroscopic coverage is expected from the 4-metre Multi-Object Spectroscopic Telescope (de Jong et al., 2012, 4MOST,) and the Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (Ivezić et al., 2019, LSST,), which together will turn WDs from a sparse, poorly accessible population into one of the principal tools of Galactic stellar population studies.

In parallel, WD evolutionary theory has advanced substantially. Modern cooling models treat neutrino losses at high luminosities, gravothermal cooling at intermediate stages, and the effects of core crystallisation, e.g., latent heat release, chemical phase separation, and the sedimentation of heavy species such as 22Ne, all of which introduce cooling delays at advanced ages (Althaus et al., 2010; Salaris et al., 2010; García-Berro et al., 2010; Tremblay et al., 2019; Camisassa et al., 2021). Improved conductive opacities (Blouin et al., 2020), more accurate treatments of convective coupling in the envelope (Tremblay et al., 2015), element diffusion (Bauer and Bildsten, 2019; Rolland et al., 2020), and high-density atmospheric physics (Blouin et al., 2019) have further refined cooling time-scales (Sahu et al., 2025, see also). Together with improved constraints on the initial–final mass relation (Weidemann, 2000; Cummings et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2026, IFMR; e.g.,), which links a progenitor to its WD mass, these developments have made WD ages and masses considerably more robust than they were two decades ago (Fontaine et al., 2001; Althaus et al., 2010; Salaris et al., 2010; Tremblay et al., 2024, e.g.,). As a result, WDs have become powerful and independent tracers of the age, SFH, and evolution of the Milky Way (García-Berro and Oswalt, 2016; Fantin et al., 2019; Roberts et al., 2025, e.g.,).

The MW star formation history is imprinted in its stellar populations, but directly inferring it from star counts is not straightforward because robust stellar age determination remains challenging. Indirect reconstruction techniques have therefore been developed that do not require individual ages. Traditional approaches include fitting the CMD (Mor et al., 2019; Ruiz-Lara et al., 2020; del Alcázar-Julià et al., 2025; Alzate-Trujillo et al., 2026, e.g.,) and modelling chemical abundance distributions and enrichment laws (Rocha-Pinto et al., 2000; Snaith et al., 2015). Although details differ between methods, many studies converge on a broadly declining SFH, with enhanced star formation at early times (∼\sim8–13 Gyr ago), a period of suppressed activity at ∼\sim6–8 Gyr, and renewed star formation more recently, in some cases with multiple bursts (Mor et al., 2019; Ruiz-Lara et al., 2020; Sysoliatina and Just, 2021, e.g.,).

papers.title: A Unified Interpretable Semantic Framework for Multi-Modal Fiber Sensing Under Data Scarcity
papers.abstract: We propose a unified interpretable semantic framework for multi-modal fiber sensing under data scarcity. The framework maps heterogeneous measurements from state of-polarization (SOP) monitoring, distributed acoustic sensing (DAS), and optical time-domain reflectometry (OTDR) into a shared set of physics-grounded semantic descriptors capturing impulsiveness, persistence, structural characteristics, and energy concentration. Inference is performed through reasoning over semantic class profiles, optionally assisted by retrieval of semantically similar examples to resolve ambiguity and support adaptation without model retraining. Experimental validation on real SOP, DAS, and OTDR datasets demonstrates robust performance across sensing modalities, achieving accuracies of 95.0%, 91.1%, and 94.6%, respectively, while providing transparent and physically interpretable decisions. The proposed framework establishes a unified and data efficient approach for optical fiber sensing in evolving and data scarce deployment environments.

papers.title: Continual Event Recognition for Autonomous Optical Network Monitoring
papers.abstract: Autonomous optical networks require monitoring systems capable of adapting to evolving disturbances without repeated retraining or service interruption. We propose a continual event recognition framework for state-of-polarization (SOP)-based optical monitoring based on prototype representations, open-set recognition, and few-shot prototype registration. The framework supports recognition of known disturbances, detection and integration of novel events, and investigates whether overlapping disturbances can be inferred through compositional reasoning from existing prototypes. Experimental validation on a 2600-km ROADM-based optical testbed demonstrates 99.82% closed-set recognition accuracy, successful adaptation to novel disturbances without encoder retraining, and reveals that overlapping optical disturbances exhibit varying degrees of latent compositionality. While some overlaps can be recognized in a zero-shot manner through prototype composition, others require explicit few-shot registration. These results establish continual event recognition as a promising paradigm for future autonomous optical network monitoring systems.

papers.title: VISTA: View-Independent micro-Doppler Reconstruction with Multistatic ISAC
papers.abstract: The micro-Doppler (uD) spectrum provides detailed characteristics of target movement, making it highly valuable for applications such as target classification and human activity recognition. However, traditional Integrated Sensing And Communication (ISAC) systems are highly view-dependent and limited by blind spots and angle dependencies. Existing approaches rely on either configuration-specific solutions or data-driven models. The former results in poor generalization when device deployments or target orientations change, while the latter requires acquiring extensive multi-view datasets, which is time-consuming and not always feasible. To address these limitations, in this work we propose VISTA, a novel method for reconstructing the uD spectrogram in an absolute coordinate frame, yielding view-independent Doppler features that are invariant to the spatial distribution of ISAC nodes. We formulate the uD estimation as a sparse reconstruction problem that jointly leverages measurements from all ISAC receivers. This is solved using a modified Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) algorithm, which iteratively alternates between jointly selecting candidate velocity vectors across all receivers (RXs) and independently estimating the complex channel gain amplitudes for each RX. Our results show that, provided sufficient spatial diversity, VISTA successfully reconstructs the targets' absolute uD spectrograms with a median error \leq 0.69 m/s for speeds \leq 15 m/s.

papers.title: Probe Dynamics in Active Baths via Trajectory-Response Relations
papers.abstract: Passive probes in active baths can undergo spontaneous motion driven by nonequilibrium forces that depend on probe velocity and interaction geometry. Using trajectory-response relations that express the bath response to a probe in terms of free-particle displacement statistics, we investigate the dynamics of freely moving probes weakly coupled to ideal active baths. The mean force exerted by the bath defines a velocity-space potential whose minima describe the stable states. By analyzing how the mean force depends on the probe velocity, we identify stable resting and moving states and determine the parameter regime in which they coexist. For elliptical interactions, the resting state becomes unstable first along the narrow axis, resulting in direction selection already at the linear-response level. For fourfold interactions, linear friction remains isotropic, while the nonlinear dependence of the mean force on probe velocity selects axial or diagonal motion and produces directional multistability. We further show that the trajectory-response relations extend to higher orders in the probe strength, where multi-interval free-particle trajectory statistics become relevant. For a Gaussian probe, these higher-order terms shift the speed of the stable moving state.

papers.intro:
Active matter is driven out of equilibrium by constituents that consume energy to sustain motion or mechanical stresses, including motile microorganisms, motor–filament assemblies, and synthetic self-propelled colloids [52, 37, 5, 5, 6]. The interplay of this local driving with interactions gives rise to collective motion [67, 66], phase separation [64, 12, 11], and spontaneous flows [56]. Activity also changes how particles accumulate near and exert forces on boundaries and immersed objects, making the mechanical effects of an active medium sensitive to its surroundings [65, 61, 42, 20].

Experiments in microbial suspensions have revealed enhanced diffusion and non-Gaussian displacements [69, 32, 39, 24, 23]. Further studies have demonstrated non-Gaussian transport in motile-cell carpets [22], transient superdiffusion in bacterial turbulence [70], and persistent memory in active granular media [10]. Theoretical descriptions connect tracer transport to swimmer–tracer encounters and activity-driven forces [8, 16], as well as interaction-induced memory in crowded active suspensions [53].

To describe driven tracers and probes in these nonequilibrium media, theoretical approaches incorporate friction, noise, and memory through stationary distributions and dynamical correlations conditioned on the probe configuration or motion [15, 33, 34, 46, 47]. A striking response in active baths is negative drag, for which the bath force has a component along the probe velocity and transfers positive mechanical power to the probe [18, 21, 30]. The velocity dependence of this force can destabilize rest and generate spontaneous motion even for a symmetric passive object in an inversion-symmetric bath [28, 47]. Determining the mean force as a function of velocity is therefore central to identifying resting and moving states and their stability.

We use the trajectory–response relations established in the companion Letter [68] to analyze freely translating probe dynamics in active baths. We first introduce the model and the relations connecting the density perturbation and mean force to the free-particle self-intermediate scattering function (self-ISF). The resulting mean force describes the quasistatic dynamics of a freely translating probe and defines its velocity-space potential (Sec. II). We then use this description to analyze the coexistence of resting and moving states (Sec. III) and the selection of motion directions by interaction geometry (Sec. IV). Extending the response to higher orders in probe strength allows us to examine the correction to the moving speed and connect the higher-order response to correlations between successive displacement intervals (Sec. V). We conclude with a discussion in Sec. VI.

papers.title: Theory of interferometric background suppression for highly sensitive electro-optic sampling
papers.abstract: In electro-optic (EO) sampling, increasing the probe power enhances the EO signal, but the usable power can be limited by photodetector saturation caused by the much larger probe background independent of the applied electric field. Here, we propose a method for suppressing this background through destructive interference between an EO-modulated probe and an unmodulated reference beam. Using a Jones-matrix model, we compare five detection configurations and identify balanced detection as suitable for maintaining a linear weak-field response under strong background suppression. This suppression allows higher input optical power to be used without saturating the photodiodes, thereby enhancing the EO signal. Under a per-photodiode saturation constraint, the optimized signal enhancement scales approximately as the square root of the total input power. For a total input power of 5 W and a saturation limit of 5 mW per photodiode, the optimized configuration yields an approximately 12-fold signal enhancement over conventional balanced detection.

papers.intro:
Electro-optic (EO) sampling detects electric fields through the field-induced birefringence of an EO crystal, which produces a phase retardation in an optical probe. EO sampling was initially developed for subpicosecond measurements of electrical transients [32] and subsequently extended to coherent detection of far-infrared fields [2] and to free-space sampling of terahertz (THz) pulses [36]. It is now used for field-resolved measurements from THz to optical frequencies [4]. By providing access to both the amplitude and phase of the electric field, EO sampling enables the determination of complex optical constants in time-domain spectroscopy [9, 17]. Its applications also include field-resolved molecular spectroscopy [26, 20] and studies of ultrafast current dynamics through THz emission spectroscopy [15, 29]. Beyond spectroscopy, EO sampling has been used to characterize transient electric fields generated in laser–plasma interactions [24] and electric fields associated with ultrashort relativistic electron bunches [5, 21, 22, 11]. It has further been extended to direct sampling of vacuum electric-field fluctuations [27].

Detecting weak electromagnetic fields remains challenging, particularly when the available field strength is limited by source output, sample absorption, or unwanted sample excitation. The EO-induced modulation can be increased by using a crystal with a larger EO coefficient or a longer interaction length. However, the available EO materials are limited, and increasing the interaction length involves a trade-off between sensitivity and bandwidth because of absorption and dispersive effects, including velocity mismatch between the THz field and the optical probe [10, 4]. Increasing the probe power raises both the EO-induced signal and the much larger field-independent background, which can saturate the photodetector before the useful signal becomes sufficiently large. Preferential suppression of this background before photodetection therefore allows higher probe powers and hence larger EO signals while maintaining linear detector operation [3].

Several optical readout strategies have been developed for this purpose. Spectral post-filtering can reduce shot noise by rejecting probe spectral components that contribute little to the EO signal [25]. Polarization-based approaches include operation near the extinction point of crossed polarizers [13, 37], subtraction of signals acquired at opposite optical biases [6, 14], balanced phase-offset detection [23], and selective attenuation of the dominant field-independent polarization component [16]. In the ideal weak-field limit, attenuating only the field-independent amplitude by a factor bb (0<b<10<b<1) reduces the background intensity by a factor of b2b^{2} and the linear EO signal by a factor of bb, thereby enhancing the background-normalized modulation by a factor of 1/b1/b at fixed incident probe power [16]. More recently, Stromberg and Heilweil experimentally demonstrated amplification of EO-detected THz signals using optical-bias-based detection schemes [30]. In practice, imperfect polarization extinction, residual crystal birefringence, and scattered light limit the achievable suppression and determine the optimal operating point [13, 37, 6]. These limitations motivate complementary methods for suppressing the field-independent probe component.

An optical interferometer offers such a route by canceling this background through destructive interference. A prominent example is laser-interferometric gravitational-wave detection, where destructive interference suppresses the strong optical carrier at the dark output port while differential phase shifts produce a measurable signal [1]. Related approaches have been applied to background suppression in absorption and vibrational spectroscopy [31, 28]. Interferometric EO readout has also been demonstrated using a modified Sagnac interferometer to detect THz-induced phase shifts [8], cross-polarized spectral-domain interferometry to extend the dynamic range [12], and integrated Mach–Zehnder THz sensors [35]. These implementations primarily employ interferometry for phase readout or dynamic-range extension; in contrast, interferometric suppression of the field-independent probe background before polarization analysis in bulk-crystal EO sampling has received comparatively limited attention. The sensitivity-enhancement mechanism shares the same general principle as polarization filtering [16], namely, suppression of the field-independent background before photodetection. Unlike purely polarization-based readout, however, interference with an independent, unmodulated reference beam also enables EO-induced optical phase shifts to be converted into intensity changes even when the probe polarization state remains unchanged.

In this work, we theoretically investigate an interferometric background-suppression scheme for EO sampling under photodetector-saturation constraints. Using a Jones-matrix formalism, we compare five representative EO detection configurations and examine their weak-field responses as functions of amplitude and phase imbalances. The analysis shows that balanced detection retains a first-order response to the THz electric field at finite amplitude imbalance, while its differential output eliminates even-order contributions; complete background cancellation, in contrast, leaves a cubic leading response. We further determine the amplitude imbalance that maximizes the differential EO signal for different phase imbalances under photodetector-saturation constraints and quantify the resulting enhancement relative to conventional balanced detection.

The analysis shows that balanced detection retains a first-order response to the THz electric field at finite amplitude imbalance, while its differential output eliminates even-order contributions; complete background cancellation, in contrast, leaves a cubic leading response. We further determine the amplitude imbalance that maximizes the differential EO signal for different phase imbalances under photodetector-saturation constraints and quantify the resulting enhancement relative to conventional balanced detection.

papers.title: Signatures of CH$_4$ and NH$_3$ in the atmosphere of $\beta$ Pictoris b
papers.abstract: $\beta$ Pictoris is a nearby (19.7 pc), young ($\sim$ 24 Myr), bright ($V = 3.85$) planetary system hosting three directly imaged planets. Previous high-resolution spectroscopy of $\beta$ Pic b has detected H$_2$O and CO, but not CH$_4$ or NH$_3$. Combining observations across a broad wavelength range has been shown to maximise sensitivity to such weak molecular signals. We searched for previously undetected molecular species in the atmosphere of $\beta$ Pic b using high-resolution near-infrared spectra. We combined 44 CRIRES+ spectral settings covering the H, K, L, and M bands and cross-correlated the extracted planetary spectra with molecular templates. For species with uncertain detectability, we weighted the observations by their molecular information content and data quality, independent of the measured candidate-species cross-correlation functions. We recover H$_2$O and CO at cross-correlation S/N values of approximately 200 and 50, respectively. We additionally identify tentative CH$_4$ and NH$_3$ signals near the expected radial velocity of $\beta$ Pic b, with S/N values of approximately 5.3 and 5.7. Equivalent extractions at the same projected separation on the opposite side of the star show no comparable peaks. We classify the CH$_4$ and NH$_3$ signals as tentative because their cross-correlation S/N values do not fully account for possible residual systematics. If confirmed, these would be the first detections of both species in the atmosphere of $\beta$ Pic b.

papers.intro:
High-resolution spectroscopy (HRS) has become a powerful tool for characterising the atmospheres of exoplanets. HRS resolves molecular bands into tens to hundreds of individual lines, and cross-correlating the observed spectra with a model template enhances the signal for a given species. HRS is highly complementary to low-resolution spectroscopy because, in addition to probing abundant atmospheric species, it is sensitive to species present at relatively low abundances. It has been applied to transiting and close-in planets, where the planet’s changing radial velocity shifts its lines relative to the stellar and telluric ones (Greene et al., 2016; Sing, 2018; Kempton and Knutson, 2024, e.g.), and it can also be combined with high-contrast imaging (HCI) to study giant planets at wide separations (>10>10 au) that are spatially resolved from their host stars (Snellen et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2021b; Janson et al., 2025; Denis et al., 2025, e.g.). This synergy enables robust and precise measurements of elemental abundance ratios, rotational and radial velocities, and orbital trajectories, all of which are key diagnostics for investigating planet formation pathways, interactions with circumplanetary discs, and the dynamical and migration histories of planetary systems (Konopacky et al., 2013; Snellen et al., 2014; Maire et al., 2021, e.g.).

β\beta Pictoris is one of the most remarkable and extensively studied planetary systems. It is a nearby (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2016, 19.7 pc;), young (Luhman, 2024, 24.7−0.6+0.924.7^{+0.9}_{-0.6} Myr;), bright (V=3.85V=3.85) A6V star surrounded by three known giant planets discovered through direct imaging or interferometry (Lagrange et al., 2010; Lagrange et al., 2019; Nowak et al., 2020; Gibbs et al., 2026; Sutlieff et al., 2026). β\beta Pic b is the second planet in order of increasing orbital separation from the host star. Its mass is estimated to be 7–12 MJupM_{\mathrm{Jup}}, and it has a semi-major axis of ∼\sim10 au (Lacour et al., 2021; Brandt et al., 2021), making it a widely separated super-Jupiter. Owing to its suitability for high-contrast HRS, β\beta Pic b has been the subject of numerous atmospheric studies. Using CRyogenic high-resolution InfraRed Echelle Spectrograph (Kaeufl et al., 2004; Dorn et al., 2023, CRIRES+, R∼50 000R\sim 50\,000–100 000100\,000;) K-band observations, Landman et al. (2024) reported detections of H2O and CO. A study in the M-band led by Parker et al. (2024) later confirmed the presence of the species that were claimed to have been detected in the K-band, and reported a tentative detection of SiO. Janson et al. (2025) investigated the system in the L and M bands, confirming the presence of H2O but not that of SiO. Finally, the recent K-band study by González Picos et al. (2026) detected 13CO and measured a 12CO/13CO ratio consistent with that of the local interstellar medium and lower than the solar photospheric value.

papers.title: Astrometric modeling of unresolved variable binary systems
papers.abstract: Gaia DR4 will, for the first time, provide epoch astrometry. When analysing these data, binary sources must be treated carefully, as modelling their astrometry as single stars can bias parallax and proper motion estimates. We developed the vimbinary tool, a framework to simulate and interpret epoch astrometry of unresolved binary systems and to evaluate the impact of model assumptions on the resulting astrometric parameters. We simulated Gaia DR4-like epoch astrometry for a sample of 17 well-characterised unresolved binary systems, including both non-pulsating binaries and systems containing one photometric variable component - variability-induced movers (VIMs). We show that both binary motion and the VIM effect can significantly impact parallax and proper motion measurements, with the magnitude of the effect strongly dependent on the orbital period, photocentric amplitude, and flux ratio of the specific system. We also show that larger time coverage does not necessarily improve parallax precision, in contrast to proper motion, for which precision generally improves with longer baselines. Instead, parallaxes retrieved with binary-system fitting are more accurate than those obtained within the single-star framework.

papers.intro:
The Gaia third data release (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2016; Gaia Collaboration et al., 2023b, DR3,) provided 800 000 binary solutions (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2023a), which represents a significant increase in the total number of known binaries. Nevertheless, the whole catalogue contains about 1.5 billion sources with at least a five-parameter (single-star) solution; given the expected binary fraction of at least 50% for Sun-like stars, rising to nearly 100% for the most massive stars (Moe and Di Stefano, 2017; Fulton and Petigura, 2018; Offner et al., 2023), the majority of binary systems likely remain undetected. This misrepresentation affects the quality of the solutions and the accuracy of the retrieved parameters.

This misrepresentation affects the quality of the solutions and the accuracy of the retrieved parameters.

The upcoming DR4 is expected to become groundbreaking for binary searches. Not only is it expected to contain a drastically increased number of binary solutions compared to DR3, but the community will also have access to epoch astrometry for the first time. This will allow users to conduct more targeted studies and to use complementary data, moving beyond the binary detection performed in DR3 (Halbwachs et al., 2023), which applied sharp cuts to avoid suspicious solutions. Here, we focus on the treatment of binary systems in epoch astrometry in preparation for the DR4.

A specific type of binary systemin detectable with Gaia astrometry are the so-called variability-induced movers (VIMs). These systems are defined as unresolved binary systems containing one photometrically variable component. As the flux of the variable component changes, its contribution to the total flux varies, which shifts the position of the photocentre back and forth between the two components (see Fig. 1). This effect was first studied by Wielen (1996) in the context of the Hipparcos mission, with possible extension to Gaia. Such missions provide an efficient way to detect these systems because they require a large number of highly precise astrometric measurements over a long time span.

Cepheids are prime VIM candidates because they exhibit a high fraction of binary or multiple systems (Evans et al., 2015; Sana, 2017; Kervella et al., 2019b), and their pulsational variability is continuous and stable over time, making them particularly suitable for this method (Wielen, 1996). Moreover, observations of Cepheids with this approach are especially important as Cepheids are a cornerstone of the cosmic distance ladder. Their period–luminosity (PL) relation (Leavitt, 1908; Leavitt and Pickering, 1912) provides one of the primary routes to determine the Hubble constant (H0H_{0}) (Riess et al., 2022; Breuval et al., 2024; H0DN Collaboration et al., 2026). In the Gaia DR4 era, we expect to obtain precise parallaxes for a large sample of Cepheids to calibrate this relation. In addition, Cepheid masses suffer from discrepancies between values derived from evolutionary models and those inferred from pulsation calculations (Neilson et al., 2011). Binary systems provide a way to measure Cepheid masses dynamically, helping to calibrate and constrain these models.

The second, RX Cam, already suspected to host a companion (Szabados, 1992), was fitted with a full Keplerian solution. However, as noted by Shetye et al. (2024), the derived orbital period coincides with the 33-month time span of DR3, which raises concerns about the robustness of the solution. Nevertheless, Groenewegen (2013) derived an orbital period of 1113.8 d by using radial velocities, comparable to the 33-month duration of DR3. The validity of the RX Cam orbital solution therefore remains an open question. No Cepheids were treated as VIMs in DR3, likely reflecting the limited number of VIM solutions in the catalogue (869 in total) and the fact that Cepheids are generally distant objects, so their apparent orbital motion often remains small.

papers.title: The Gaia-alerted 2024--2025 brightening of V346 Nor
papers.abstract: Young stellar objects (YSOs) build their final mass through a highly unsteady, episodic accretion process, often accompanied by outflow and ejection events. Objects undergoing episodic high-accretion states are known as eruptive YSOs. V346 Nor is an embedded eruptive YSO that underwent a sudden optical brightening in 2024 July that triggered an alert from the Gaia Photometric Science Alert system. With the aim of characterizing the physical processes behind this recent brightening event, we analyze new and archival photometric and spectroscopic monitoring data. We study how the brightness, colors, and spectral features changed with time in the past decade. We also fitted an accretion disk model to the observations in which the stellar mass--accretion rate product $M_{\star}\dot{M}$ and the line-of-sight extinction $A_V$ are free parameters. The accretion rate in V346 Nor has been higher ($M_{\star}\dot{M} \sim 10^{-4}\,M_{\odot}^2\,$yr$^{-1}$) since 2021 than during any previous historical peak, although it was relatively constant during the 2025 February-May brightness maximum, which was driven instead by a drop in extinction from $A_V \approx 20$\,mag to $10$\,mag. V346 Nor has accreted about 2\% of the stellar mass since its outburst. A P Cygni profile in H$\alpha$ indicates a strong outflowing wind reminiscent of classical FUors. The variability of the CaII infrared triplet lines and transient CO bandhead emission point to a highly unstable inner disk and accretion region. The persistence of forbidden line emission indicates ongoing jet activity. The brightness and color variations of V346 Nor are the result of a superposition of changes in the accretion rate and the line-of-sight extinction. With record-high accretion levels and strong wind and jet activity, V346 Nor is in one of its most active phases since its original outburst in the 1970s.

papers.intro:
Young stellar objects (YSOs) build their final mass in an unsteady process that involves episodic (eruptive) accretion from the circumstellar disk onto the central object, often accompanied by repeated outflow and ejection events as well (Reipurth and Bally, 2001; Fischer et al., 2023). The physical driver of these eruptions is thought to be thermal or gravitational instabilities in the circumstellar disk, which cause a runaway increase in the accretion rate that can persist for years to decades (Bell and Lin, 1994; Vorobyov and Basu, 2006, e.g.,). Eruptive YSOs are broadly classified by their outburst amplitudes, timescales, and spectroscopic properties.

FU Orionis objects (FUors) brighten by 4–6 magnitudes over months to years and remain elevated for decades, with accretion rates of 10−5−10−4,M⊙​y​r−110^{-5}-10^{-4},M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1} (Szabó et al., 2021, e.g.,), probably proceeding through a boundary layer (Popham et al., 1996; Labdon et al., 2021; Carvalho et al., 2024). EX Lupi-type objects (EXors) undergo shorter, repetitive bursts of 1–3 magnitudes over weeks to months, but their spectra are consistent with magnetospheric accretion operating at an elevated rate (Sicilia-Aguilar et al., 2012; Sicilia-Aguilar et al., 2015; Pouilly et al., 2024). V1647 Ori-type objects (MNors) bridge these two classes in terms of timescales, variability amplitudes, and spectral properties. The same magnetospheric accretion mechanism works in them as in EXors, but they likely represent a younger, more deeply embedded evolutionary stage (Hamaguchi et al., 2012; Contreras Peña et al., 2017). EX Lupi-type objects (EXors) undergo shorter, repetitive bursts of 1–3 magnitudes over weeks to months, but their spectra are consistent with magnetospheric accretion operating at an elevated rate (Sicilia-Aguilar et al., 2012; Sicilia-Aguilar et al., 2015; Pouilly et al., 2024). V1647 Ori-type objects (MNors) bridge these two classes in terms of timescales, variability amplitudes, and spectral properties. The same magnetospheric accretion mechanism works in them as in EXors, but they likely represent a younger, more deeply embedded evolutionary stage (Hamaguchi et al., 2012; Contreras Peña et al., 2017). An up-to-date list of currently known young eruptive stars is available in the OYCAT11 1 http://starformation.synology.me:5002/OYCAT/main.html catalog (Contreras Peña et al., 2025).

YSOs currently accreting at extremely high rates may be bona fide FUors (if an outburst was observed), FUor-like objects (if the brightening was not directly observed), or peculiar objects (if they show only some of the properties typical of FUors). Their optical and infrared spectra show a characteristic multi-temperature structure, dominated by absorption features forming in the cooler atmosphere of a hot, optically thick accretion disk, including CO bandhead absorption in the near-infrared and P Cygni profiles in Hα\alpha (Connelley and Reipurth, 2018; Portnoi et al., 2026).

It reached a broad maximum brightness between 1990 and 2000 and displayed a deep minimum between 2008 and 2013. This fading was interpreted by Kraus et al. (2016) and Kóspál et al. (2017b) as a temporary halt in the accretion rate. The peak accretion rate of V346 Nor was 10−4​M⊙10^{-4}\,M_{\odot} yr-1, reached in 1992, while during the minimum in 2010, this value went below 4×10−7​M⊙4\times 10^{-7}\,M_{\odot} yr-1. Using ALMA data from 2014-2015, Kóspál et al. (2017a) measured the radial velocity profile in the disk and pseudo-disk and found that the infall rate in the pseudo-disk is 6×10−6​M⊙6\times 10^{-6}\,M_{\odot} yr-1. They concluded that the mismatch between the disk-to-star accretion and the envelope-to-disk infall may be the cause of the eruptive nature of the object.

The optical and near-infrared spectra of FUors is dominated by the inner active accretion disk (Liu et al., 2022). FUors typically have absorption features owing to the temperature profile in the active accretion disk, which is hot in the midplane and colder on the surface, the opposite of what is usual for regular, normally accreting T Tauri stars. V346 Nor is peculiar in this respect, because it displays emission lines as well. Most emission lines in its spectrum are forbidden metallic and H2 lines, typical jet tracers (Kóspál et al., 2020). Such lines are observable not only toward the source, but also about 5′′5^{\prime\prime} away to the south, at the position of the Herbig-Haro object HH 57 (Reipurth et al., 1997), indicating both more recent and older ejection activities.

V346 Nor underwent a sudden optical brightening in 2024 July that triggered an alert from the Gaia Photometric Science Alert system of the Gaia astrometric space mission (Hodgkin et al., 2021), where it appeared under the name Gaia24chn. Motivated by this alert, here we present results based on new and archival photometric and spectroscopic monitoring data from various optical and near-infrared instruments and draw conclusions about the physical processes behind this recent brightening. In Sec. 2 we present details of the observations we obtained for V346 Nor and their reduction. In Sec. 3 we present the resulting light curves, spectral energy distributions (SEDs), analyze the variability spectral features and fit an accretion disk model to the data. In Sec. 4, we summarize our conclusions.

papers.title: La Silla-QUEST RR Lyrae Survey III: The Shape of the Outer Virgo Overdensity
papers.abstract: Using the La Silla-QUEST and Gaia surveys, we identify 256 RR Lyrae stars (RRLS) in the Outer Virgo Overdensity (OVOD). These show that the OVOD has a signifcantly larger and more complex shape than previously recognized. The OVOD lies at an average distance of $\sim 85$ kpc, has a long dimension of $\sim 57^\circ$ ($\sim 85$ kpc), and a width that varies from $\sim 10^\circ $ ($\sim 15$ kpc) to $\sim 35^\circ $ ($\sim 50$ kpc) in a prominent bulge. Because it bends by $\sim 35^\circ$ from a great circle, it does not appear to be a stellar stream. The type ab RRLS (RRab) span a large range in period, with a mean of $0.59$ days, and only $19\pm 3 \%$ lie near the locus of Oosterhoff II variables in the Bailey diagram. The overall large number of RRLS along with a mean RRab metallicity ([Fe/H]) of -1.60 and $1 \sigma$ dispersion of 0.32, as inferred from the RRab periods, suggest that the OVOD progenitor was a large dwarf galaxy. The hypothesis that the OVOD may be a shell produced by the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger \citep{chandra2023} is supported by the $\sim 70^\circ$ angle that the southern extension of the OVOD makes with the orbits of red giants in its central part. The complex shape of the overall RRLS distribution, including a small north-south distance gradient, may also indicate, however, that we are seeing a blended, composite structure projected on the sky.

papers.intro:
Observations of the Galactic halo over the past 5 decades have provided increasingly strong evidence that most of the stars and globular clusters in the halo originated in dwarf galaxies that were disrupted while merging with the Milky Way (MW). Similarly, numerous investigations over the last two decades have shown that the same is true of the halos of M31 and other galaxies. These results have become some of the strongest observational evidence in favor of the hierarchical picture of galaxy formation in which massive galaxies, such as the MW, have grown through a multitude of mergers with smaller systems. The observational and theoretical studies that have led to this picture are discussed in reviews by, for example, S. R. Majewski [51], K. Freeman & J. Bland-Hawthorn [35], H. Mo et al. [58], H. J. Newberg & J. L. Carlin [62], J. S. Bullock & M. Boylan-Kolchin [17], A. W. McConnachie et al. [56], J. D. Simon [73], A. Helmi [40], A. J. Deason & V. Belokurov [26], A. Bonaca & A. M. Price-Whelan [13].

Price-Whelan [13].

Although the mechanism by which galaxies acquire their stellar halos has been arguably identified, important properties of the MW’s merger history may be still unknown. For example, there is continuing debate about what is widely considered the largest merger in the MW’s history, the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (GSE) merger. It was firmly identified by V. Belokurov et al. [10] and A. Helmi et al. [41], although some earlier evidence existed for a large, near-radial merger [28, 16, 59, 18, e.g.,]. The GSE is thought to have happened ≳8\gtrsim 8 Gyr ago, because the stars in the GSE are of that age [37, 15, e.g.,], and because this merger is estimated to be sufficiently large to have puffed up a pre-existing thin disk into the thick disk, which is composed of old stars. An alternative picture has been proposed by T. Donlon et al. [31], T. Donlon et al. [30], who argued that the kinematics of the local halo stars are best explained if the merger, which they termed the Virgo Radial Merger (VRM), occurred ≲3\lesssim 3 Gyr ago. On the basis of the chemical compositions of the stars, T. Donlon et al. [29] and H. Liu et al. [48] have argued that more than one large merger may have occurred. These issues and other pieces of the GSE “puzzle” have been reviewed in depth by A. J. Deason & V. Belokurov [26]. Clearly, much remains to be learned about it and other properties of the Galactic halo.

Their origins have already been investigated in some detail [18, 22, e.g.,], yet, as we demonstrate here, there is still more to be learned about them. More substructures also likely remain to be mapped in the outer halo.

[69] consisted of finding 73 probable type ab RRLS (RRab) in the range 65≤d☉≤9565\leq\rm d_{\sun}\leq 95 kpc that lie in an approximately elliptical region of the sky spanning ∼150​deg2\sim 150\,\rm deg^{2}. Although the OVOD is close to the leading stream of the Sgr Stream when projected on the sky, B. Sesar et al. [69] argued that the OVOD is a separate halo substructure because it is ∼20\sim 20 kpc more distant than the Stream and offset from its mid-plane. B. Sesar et al. [69] used the term “outer” to distinguish this overdensity from the previously discovered and already well-researched Virgo Overdensity (VOD)[80, 63, 43, 14, e.g.,]. The VOD is a much closer overdensity, 10≲d☉≲2510\lesssim\rm d_{\sun}\lesssim 25 kpc, which may or may not be debris from the same merger event as the OVOD. The VOD contains several moving groups of stars, and its properties motivated the VRM hypothesis by T. Donlon et al. [31][18, see also]. papers.title: VISTA Magellanic Clouds deep observations of Classical Cepheids: Precision distances and a collision-driven SMC
papers.abstract: The central regions of the Magellanic Clouds are crucial for understanding galaxy interactions and calibrating the cosmic distance scale, yet they remain observationally challenging due to extreme stellar crowding. We utilised deep VISTA observations (VMCDeep) to determine the highest-precision near-infrared Period-Luminosity (PL) and Period-Wesenheit (PW) relations to date for Classical Cepheids (delta Cep class, DCEPs) in the dense central regions of the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC). We analysed J and Ks time-series data covering the central 1.77 deg^2 of each galaxy. Utilising approximately 40 epochs per filter and PSF-based photometry, we derived high-quality light curves for 573 and 2090 DCEPs in the LMC and SMC, respectively. We derived exceptionally precise PL and PW relations, exhibiting the lowest photometric dispersion published so far for the Magellanic Clouds. Fourier parameters calculated from the light curves indicate that pulsational models incorporating a mildly non-canonical mass-luminosity relation and a mixing-length parameter of alpha = 1.7 best reproduce the observations. Age derivations confirm a bimodal star formation history in the SMC centre. Crucially, we discovered a striking line-of-sight spatial dichotomy within the young SMC DCEP population (t < 116 Myr), which is bifurcated into two distinct structures separated by ~4 kpc. This provides independent stellar evidence tracing a recent direct collision with the LMC. Finally, by unifying fundamental and first-overtone pulsators, we derived a highly constrained relative distance between the Clouds. Comparing this to detached eclipsing binary distances, our data suggest a moderate metallicity correction for the Leavitt Law with gamma ~ -0.2 mag/dex.

papers.intro:
The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC, MCs) represent our nearest pair of interacting dwarf irregular galaxies, currently located at distances of approximately 50–60 kpc (de Grijs et al., 2014; de Grijs and Bono, 2015, e.g.). Due to their proximity and the possibility of studying their stars in great detail, the LMC and SMC are important objects for a variety of astrophysical topics. In particular, the MCs (especially the LMC) serve as primary anchors for calibrating the cosmic distance ladder (e.g. Freedman and Madore, 2010; Freedman et al., 2011; Riess et al., 2016, and references therein). Among the various tracers, Classical Cepheids (δ\delta Cep class, DCEPs hereafter) are of paramount importance, due to the tight correlation between their pulsation periods and luminosities or Leavitt Law (Leavitt and Pickering, 1912; Freedman and Madore, 2010), which makes them the most relevant standard candles in the cosmic distance scale and eventually to the estimate of the Hubble constant H0H_{0} (Riess et al., 2016; Riess et al., 2022, e.g.). In addition, DCEPs are excellent tracers of the young stellar population (between 50–300 Myrs) both in the Milky Way (MW) and in the MCs. Indeed, they have been extensively used to trace the spiral arms of the MW (e.g. Chen et al., 2019a; Gaia Collaboration et al., 2023; Drimmel et al., 2025, and references therein) and the Galactic radial abundance gradients (e.g. Luck, 2018; da Silva et al., 2023; Trentin et al., 2024a; Trentin et al., 2026, and references therein). In the MCs, the DCEPs have been employed to calculate the viewing angles and the three-dimensional geometry of both the LMC and SMC (e.g. Subramanian and Subramaniam, 2015; Jacyszyn-Dobrzeniecka et al., 2016; Ripepi et al., 2017; Ripepi et al., 2022, and references therein).

Large-scale surveys often lose completeness in these high-density regions; for example, the Survey of the Magellanic Clouds Stellar History (SMASH) shows a distinct lack of stars in the LMC centre due to crowding effects (Nidever et al., 2017; Choi et al., 2018), while the STEP survey (Ripepi et al., 2014; Gatto et al., 2021, the SMC in Time: Evolution of a Prototype interacting late-type dwarf galaxy) discussed the effect of crowding in the SMC. Even the Gaia mission exhibits at least 50% incompleteness within a 2.5 deg radius of the LMC centre (Jiménez-Arranz et al., 2023; Rathore et al., 2025). Furthermore, optical monitoring by the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE) has faced challenges where blending effects can mimic line-of-sight extensions (Jacyszyn-Dobrzeniecka et al., 2016; Cusano et al., 2021).

papers.title: Low effective-temperature diminution of H$\alpha$ emission from metallic centrifugal magnetospheres fed by ion-runaway winds
papers.abstract: Main-sequence B-stars with a strong magnetic field and moderately rapid rotation form centrifugal magnetospheres (CMs), which often exhibit distinct H$\alpha$ line emission, as well as circularly polarized radio. For CMs of early-type B-stars with $T_{\rm eff} \gtrsim 17$ kK, the onset and strength of the H$\alpha$ emission is well explained in terms of a centrifugal breakout (CBO) model, in which mass fed into the CM by the star's radiatively driven stellar wind builds up to a density that is sufficient for centrifugal forces to overwhelm magnetic confinement. The analysis here now argues that the observed diminution and disappearance of the H$\alpha$ emission for CM B-stars with $T_{\rm eff} \lesssim 17$ kK can be explained by the failure of their lower luminosity to drive hydrogen-rich winds; instead they develop an ion runaway of heavier metal ions that are the seat of line-driving, which thus feed a metallic CM (mCM) for which the requisite hydrogen is diminished or even absent. For mid-B-type stars in a narrow transition range of effective temperature $T_{\rm eff} \approx (16.8 \pm 0.3)$ kK, hydrogen can still be driven to a sufficient speed to coast into the inner CM, which we show can explain the reduced strength and width of H$\alpha$ line emission in the transition CM star $\rho$ Oph C. But even in regions with no hydrogen, the build-up of metal density to CBO levels can still drive the magnetic reconnection needed to produce the observed radio. We discuss whether such build-up of metals could give rise to direct observational signatures.

papers.intro:
Hot luminous, massive stars of spectral type O and B have dense, high-speed, radiatively driven stellar winds (Castor et al., 1975). In the subset (Grunhut et al., 2017; Sikora et al., 2019, ∼\sim10%;) of massive stars with strong (Aurière et al., 2007; Shultz et al., 2019, > 100>\,100 G;), globally ordered (Kochukhov et al., 2019, often essentially dipolar;) magnetic fields, the trapping of this wind outflow by closed magnetic loops leads to the formation of a circumstellar magnetosphere (Petit et al., 2013). Because of the angular momentum loss associated with their relatively strong, magnetised wind (ud-Doula et al., 2009), magnetic O-type stars are typically slow rotators, with trapped wind material falling back on a dynamical timescale, giving what is known as a “dynamical magnetosphere” (DM). Despite the short persistence timescale of plasma within DMs, the powerful winds of O-type stars are capable of maintaining a sufficiently high density for the DMs of magnetic O-type stars to be detectable via hydrogen emission.

papers.title: 3D dust attenuation effects in galaxies: structural biases and induced negative color gradients
papers.abstract: Radial surface brightness profiles (SBPs) and color gradients are useful tools for studying galaxy structure, formation, and evolution. While it is usually assumed that they are primarily driven by stellar properties, such as mass, age or metallicity, their dependence on 3D dust attenuation is not fully understood or accounted for. We analyze how 3D dust attenuation affects galaxy observations by hindering the estimation of intrinsic properties. We examine dust-induced shifts in surface brightness and color. Using SKIRT radiative transfer models, we simulated simple S\'ersic galaxies, with spherically-symmetric stellar densities, constant stellar-to-dust ratios, and a spatially constant spectral energy distribution (SED). We find that attenuated SBPs differ significantly from dust-free profiles, particularly in the central galaxy regions. These differences become more pronounced at bluer wavelengths and for higher core dust densities, leading to variations in the fitted S\'ersic index of up to ~25%. This can lead to incorrect conclusions about the intrinsic stellar distribution and mimic a central mass deficit. For galaxies with very centrally-dense dust distributions, a core-S\'ersic model results in a better fit of the attenuated SBP. For dust masses as low as ~2*10^6 $M_{\odot}$, dust-induced negative color gradients reach the same order of magnitude as those commonly observed in galaxies, which a dust-screen fails to account for. This occurs even for a spatially invariant SED and can lead to wrong conclusions about intrinsic stellar populations and related astrophysical questions, such as their formation histories or the mechanisms of inside-out star formation quenching. A full 3D approach is necessary to properly model attenuation effects, which, if not accounted for, can bias inferences made about stellar populations, their evolutionary histories, and spatial distributions.

Full radiative transfer is required to properly model the realistic 3D mixture of stars and dust, given that the SED recorded at a given projected radius rr is not identical to that of a simple or even composite stellar population (SSP and CSP, respectively), but rather depends on the complex interplay between the dust and star geometries, where absorption and scattering, both out and into the line-of-sight, play significant roles.

papers.title: A giant dark matter core extending far beyond the stars of a dwarf galaxy
papers.abstract: In the standard cosmological model, the distribution of cold dark matter (CDM) can be reshaped by baryonic processes through gravity, as gas outflows alter the central potential and transform steep cusps into nearly constant-density cores. However, such feedback-generated cores are generally expected to have sizes comparable to the visible stellar body of a galaxy. Here we report the discovery of an exceptionally extended dark matter core in a nearby gas-rich dwarf galaxy UGCA 320. We combine high-resolution MUSE H$\alpha$ kinematics in the inner region with high-, medium-, and low-resolution MeerKAT HI observations from the MHONGOOSE survey tracing the galaxy out to large radii. After accounting for an additional non-circular kinematic component identified in the central HI spectra, we construct an extended rotation curve to constrain the dark matter distribution. The resulting rotation curve is poorly reproduced by a cuspy Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) halo but well described by cored pseudo-isothermal (ISO) and Burkert halo models. Consistently, a fit with a generalized NFW model yields an inner density slope of $\gamma=0.36\pm0.12$, quantitatively supporting a shallow central density profile. The best-fit ISO model gives a dark matter core radius of $7.62\pm0.80$ kpc, approximately four times the stellar half-light radius and substantially larger than typically found in dwarf galaxies. We investigate the main systematic uncertainties and find that the resulting core radii remain large, all lying within 3$\sigma$ of the fiducial fit. The exceptionally large core in UGCA 320 may pose a challenge to the standard CDM paradigm. While its properties are broadly consistent with self-interacting dark matter (SIDM), they may be difficult to reconcile with warm and fuzzy dark matter models, as well as the stellar feedback-driven core formation scenario.

papers.intro:
Since discoveries that galaxies have flat rotation curves at large radii (e.g., Freeman 1970; Rubin & Ford 1970) rather than follow Kepler’s law, dark matter was proposed to account for the invisible mass (e.g., Ostriker et al. 1974; Einasto et al. 1974). In the standard Λ\LambdaCDM cosmology, small-scale structures collapse first and then hierarchically merge into larger systems (Press & Schechter, 1974; Springel et al., 2006). While this model successfully explains the large-scale structures of the Universe, it faces significant challenges on small scales (Weinberg et al., 2015; Bullock & Boylan-Kolchin, 2017; Sales et al., 2022).

Since discoveries that galaxies have flat rotation curves at large radii (e.g., Freeman 1970; Rubin & Ford 1970) rather than follow Kepler’s law, dark matter was proposed to account for the invisible mass (e.g., Ostriker et al. 1974; Einasto et al. 1974). In the standard Λ\LambdaCDM cosmology, small-scale structures collapse first and then hierarchically merge into larger systems (Press & Schechter, 1974; Springel et al., 2006). While this model successfully explains the large-scale structures of the Universe, it faces significant challenges on small scales (Weinberg et al., 2015; Bullock & Boylan-Kolchin, 2017; Sales et al., 2022).

These small-scale tensions emcompass the cusp-core problem (Moore, 1994; Flores & Primack, 1994), the diversity problem (Oman et al., 2015), the missing satellites problem (Klypin et al., 1999; Moore et al., 1999), and the too-big-to-fail problem (Boylan-Kolchin et al., 2011). Some of these issues, notably the missing satellites problem, have been alleviated by deeper observations and higher-resolution simulations that incorporate baryonic physics (e.g., Willman et al. 2005; Bechtol et al. 2015; Laevens et al. 2015; Buck et al. 2019; Santos-Santos et al. 2026). Others, however, remain unresolved. In this paper, we focus on the cusp-core problem. In dissipationless cold dark matter N-body simulations, the central density profiles of dark matter halos follow a cuspy form, well described by the Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) model (Navarro et al., 1996b; Navarro et al., 1997) as ρ∝r−1\rho\propto r^{-1}. In contrast, rotation curves derived from HI observations of dwarf and low surface brightness galaxies are shallower than these predictions and infer a constant-density core (Moore, 1994; de Blok & McGaugh, 1997; Oh et al., 2011), but with few exceptions (Shi et al., 2021, e.g.). To mitigate potential beam smearing effects, high-resolution long-slit Hα\alpha data (Swaters et al., 2000; McGaugh et al., 2001; de Blok et al., 2001; Spekkens et al., 2005; Zackrisson et al., 2006) have been used to derive rotation curves, yielding results consistent with those from HI. Furthermore, subsequent studies employing high-resolution two-dimensional velocity fields (de Naray et al., 2008; Oh et al., 2015; Korsaga et al., 2019) have eliminated concerns related to pointing offsets and non-circular motions, and they conclude that cored dark matter density profiles provide significantly better fits to the data than cuspy ones.

To address this long-standing tension encountered in Λ\LambdaCDM scenario, various alternative dark matter candidates — such as warm dark matter, self-interacting dark matter, and fuzzy dark matter — have been proposed. Warm dark matter possesses a non-zero thermal velocity, which erases the primordial power spectrum on small scales via free-streaming effect and lowers the central dark matter density due to an upper limit on phase-space density (Hogan & Dalcanton, 2000; Bode et al., 2001; Macciò et al., 2012; Viel et al., 2013). For self-interacting dark matter, its particles can transfer energy through elastic scatterings, turning a cusp into a core; moreover, cored halos are less bound than their cuspy counterparts of the same mass, making substructures more susceptible to tidal stripping (Spergel & Steinhardt, 2000; Kaplinghat et al., 2016; Tulin & Yu, 2018; Adhikari et al., 2025). With an ultralight mass, fuzzy dark matter exhibits prominent wave-like properties, and the quantum pressure predicted by quantum mechanics resists gravitational collapse, giving rise to a stable soliton core in the center (Hu et al., 2000; Schive et al., 2014; Eberhardt & Ferreira, 2025). A detailed introduction to dark matter can be found in the Discussion.
