For self-interacting dark matter, its particles can transfer energy through elastic scatterings, turning a cusp into a core; moreover, cored halos are less bound than their cuspy counterparts of the same mass, making substructures more susceptible to tidal stripping (Spergel & Steinhardt, 2000; Kaplinghat et al., 2016; Tulin & Yu, 2018; Adhikari et al., 2025). With an ultralight mass, fuzzy dark matter exhibits prominent wave-like properties, and the quantum pressure predicted by quantum mechanics resists gravitational collapse, giving rise to a stable soliton core in the center (Hu et al., 2000; Schive et al., 2014; Eberhardt & Ferreira, 2025). A detailed introduction to dark matter can be found in the Discussion.

As the discrepancy originates from dark-matter-only simulations that include only gravitational interactions, baryonic processes offer a possible solution within the Λ\LambdaCDM framework. One well-known mechanism is the non-adiabatic gravitational potential fluctuations driven by multiple, repeated bursts of star formation, which heat the orbits of dark matter particles and flatten the central dark matter density(Navarro et al., 1996a; Governato et al., 2010; Pontzen & Governato, 2012; Teyssier et al., 2013; Collins & Read, 2022). Subsequent cosmological simulations (Di Cintio et al., 2013) have confirmed that the inner density slope sensitively depends on the stellar-to-halo mass ratio M∗/MhaloM_{*}/M_{\mathrm{halo}}, and such feedback-induced cores can be efficiently produced when M∗/Mhalo∼5×10−3M_{*}/M_{\mathrm{halo}}\sim 5\times 10^{-3} — i.e., when the potential well is relatively shallow and the supernova feedback is strong enough to expel large amounts of gas (see also Chan et al. 2015; Tollet et al. 2016; Macciò et al. 2020; Lazar et al. 2020; Straight et al. 2025). Moreover, the sizes of such feedback-induced dark matter cores are generally found to be smaller than or comparable to the stellar distribution (Read et al., 2016; Lazar et al., 2020). Another heating mechanism involves the infall of compact, massive baryon clumps, which transfer energy and angular momentum to background dark matter particles in the central region via dynamical friction. This process can operate before stellar feedback becomes effective (El-Zant et al., 2001; El-Zant et al., 2004; Nipoti & Binney, 2014; Del Popolo & Pace, 2016).

papers.title: Model-dependent metallicities of young stellar populations in TIMER galaxies
papers.abstract: Stellar populations in the central regions of disc galaxies provide key constraints on their formation and secular evolution. We investigate the properties of young stellar populations in the centres of nearby barred galaxies from the TIMER survey, using four stellar population models, two based on empirical (MILES, X-Shooter) and two on theoretical (Starburst99, HR-pyPopStar) stellar libraries, complemented by independent gas-phase metallicities from emission-line diagnostics. The inferred stellar metallicities depend strongly on the adopted model. Measured as the 5th-to-95th percentile spread across the three galaxies analysed in detail, the empirical libraries recover variations of 1.11 and 0.98 dex, whereas the theoretical ones return 0.40 and 0.49 dex; the gas in the same regions spans 0.49 dex. Gas metallicities are indeed lower in the central star-forming regions, but the amplitude of that depression (about 0.3 dex in NGC 1097) exceeds what bar-driven inflow of disc gas can account for, given typical abundance gradients in literature. The age-metallicity relations consistently reveal two distinct components: an older population consistent with a self-enrichment scenario, and a younger population formed from gas inflows with a different chemical enrichment history. The empirical libraries produce a monotonic decline of metallicities from old to young populations, which would require a sustained inflow of metal-poor gas outpacing its own enrichment. The theoretical libraries instead recover a young component whose metallicity departs from the older populations only at the most recent ages and by a few tenths of a dex, compatible with a single dilution episode. Our results demonstrate that model choice critically affects inferred metallicities, with empirical stellar libraries recovering age-metallicity relations that demand physical conditions the gas measurements cannot sustain.

papers.intro:
Observations of extragalactic systems at low redshift show that massive disc galaxies generally display ordered kinematics and relatively smooth rotation curves. In contrast, disc galaxies observed at high redshift are significantly more turbulent, clumpy, and morphologically irregular (Förster Schreiber et al., 2006; Law et al., 2009). Recent studies based on JWST observations suggest that this transition may occur at redshifts around z∼4z\sim 4 (Ferreira et al. 2023, Huertas-Company et al. 2025). Understanding when and how this transformation took place, as well as identifying the physical mechanisms responsible for driving it, remains one of the key open questions in extragalactic astrophysics.

One way to study this settling process in extragalactic discs is to examine their central structures, such as bars, nuclear discs, and nuclear rings. Theoretical works show that bars only form hundreds of millions of years after the dynamical settling of the disc, and that the gravitational potential of the bar can cause the gas in the interstellar medium (ISM) to shock, lose angular momentum, and funnel down to the central region. This process will be of great importance in the formation of nuclear discs and nuclear rings.

The TIMER project (Time Inference with MUSE in Extragalactic Rings; Gadotti et al. 2019) was conceived precisely to investigate such processes by obtaining high-quality spectroscopic data for a sample of nearby barred galaxies. A key motivation is that bars can only form once discs are dynamically settled, so constraining their ages provides unique insight into the cosmic epoch of disc settling. With this approach, TIMER has delivered the first systematic bar age measurements (de Sá-Freitas et al. 2023; de Sá-Freitas et al. 2025), revealing both young and old bars spanning 1–13 Gyr in age. These results demonstrate that some discs were already dynamically mature at redshift z∼2z\sim 2, while others have only recently settled, in agreement with the observed redshift evolution of the bar fraction. Beyond bar ages, TIMER studies have also shown that bars quench star formation in their hosts and build up nuclear discs, with older bars tending to be stronger, longer, and associated with more massive central discs (de Sá-Freitas et al., 2025). TIMER has further revealed that bars are, on average, more metal-rich than their surroundings, and that the spatial distribution of stellar ages and metallicities across bars can now be reproduced in cosmological simulations (Neumann et al. 2020). In addition, the exquisite quality of the TIMER data enabled several breakthroughs beyond bar age properties. The project has provided the first systematic measurements of the stellar initial mass function (IMF) in star-forming regions of external galaxies, showing that while most regions are consistent with a Milky Way–like IMF, coherent spatial variations exist and can be linked to recent bursts of star formation (Martín-Navarro et al. 2024). TIMER has also uncovered evidence of stellar feedback in circumnuclear rings: in NGC 3351, young stars formed in the nuclear ring both heat the surrounding gas and drive outflows at ∼70\sim 70 km s-1, displacing the surrounding cold molecular gas (Leaman et al. 2019). Moreover, the project has presented suggestive evidence that nuclear discs, rather than classical bulges, dominate the central regions of massive discs, highlighting the central role of bar-driven secular evolution in shaping galaxy centers (Gadotti et al. 2020; Bittner et al. 2020). Finally, detailed studies of nuclear bars confirm that they form and evolve in a manner analogous to main bars, strengthening the picture of a “galaxy within a galaxy,” where nuclear discs and their nuclear bars mirror the dynamics of discs and main bars at larger scales (de Lorenzo-Cáceres et al. 2019; Méndez-Abreu et al. 2019; Bittner et al. 2021).

Their results indicate that nuclear discs and nuclear rings are part of the same physical component, with nuclear rings constituting the star-forming outer edge of stellar nuclear discs. The authors also find evidence of metal-poor young stellar populations in nuclear rings (or in the outer regions of nuclear discs, in galaxies in which both structures cannot be distinguished), which would be inconsistent with what is expected from the secular evolution of the interstellar medium of spiral galaxies (Ho et al., 2017). However, this inconsistency has been observed in various studies that utilise spectral fitting for the young stellar populations.

papers.title: A Multi-Cycle Treasury Survey of Andromeda: Comprehensive, All-Encompassing Spectroscopy, Imaging, and Mid-Infrared Mapping of the Nearest Giant Spiral
papers.abstract:
We propose a Multi-Cycle Treasury program of $\sim$800 hours that would survey Andromeda the way the Milky Way has been surveyed by APOGEE, Gaia, and WISE.
  - NIRSpec: spectra of $\sim$4,500 red giants and supergiants at S/N~80, sufficient for 16 elements at $\lesssim$0.05 dex precision and radial velocities to a few km s$^{-1}$.
  - NIRCam: $\sim$1,600 arcmin$^{2}$ in up to ten filters, reaching $\sim$20 million stars, every field imaged twice a year apart: two-epoch infrared photometry of the $\sim$500 Cepheids and $\sim$10$^{4}$ Miras in the footprint.
  - MIRI: $\sim$450 arcmin$^{2}$ in five filters at the depth of PHANGS.
  The observations are predominantly organized as twelve "bricks", each of three adjacent fields including two NIRSpec/MOS pointings, in which one instrument is prime and a second observes in parallel, so that roughly 40% of the exposure time comes at no charge. The bricks sample the nucleus, bulge, major axis to 29 kpc, minor axis, and inter-arm disk. In addition, a 100-hour grid of short NIRCam pointings with MIRI in parallel covers the HST-PHAT footprint. The result would be the first chemodynamical, star-formation, and dust map of an $L^{\star}$ galaxy other than our own built from individual stars, at a scale no single-cycle program can reach.

papers.title: PCLSegNet: Anatomy-Aware Deep Learning Framework for MRI-based Pancreatic Cyst Segmentation and Size Assessment
papers.abstract: Early detection and follow-up of pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) are crucial, as some of their subtypes, such as mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs) and intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms, carry a significant risk of malignant transformation. Although most AI studies investigating PCLs rely on computed tomography (CT) scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers superior soft tissue contrast, making it highly suitable for PCLs assessment. In this work, we propose an anatomy-aware two-stage deep learning framework for automated PCLs segmentation on abdominal MRI scans. First, a publicly available pancreas segmentation model is used to localize the pancreas. Then, we introduce the anatomyaware PCLSegNet, which incorporates anatomical priors as guidance for pancreas and PCLs segmentation. To address the class imbalance problem, we develop a Class-Specific ErrorWeighted (CSEW) loss function. Postprocessing is applied through anatomical constraints.Our proposed method outperforms multi-organ segmentation models such as TotalSegmentator, achieving substantially higher Dice scores for pancreas segmentation. Moreover, it also achieves a superior normalized surface Dice (NSD) and recall for PCLs segmentationcompared to other state-of-the-art models like nnU-Net, while also notably reducing the false negative rate, facilitating the automatic early detection and the noninvasive imaging-based assessment of PCLs.

papers.intro:
Pancreatic cancer is the third most common cause of cancer-related death, with incidence continuing to increase by approximately 1% annually over the past decade, and a contemporary 5-year survival rate of only 13% [1]. It can develop from pancreatic cystic neoplasms [2]. While the incidental detection rate of pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) on routine MRI is high (2.4–49.1%), clinical management remains challenging [3]. Guidelines [3, 4] recommend imaging surveillance or resection based on size and morphology. Nevertheless, interobserver variability in size measurement is significant (Cohen’s kappa 0.59), and up to nearly two-thirds of incidental PCLs are not included in routine reports [5, 6, 7]. Automated tools are thus essential to improve detection sensitivity, ensure reporting consistency, and facilitate evaluation during follow-up.

Accurate PCL segmentation remains difficult due to the high anatomical variability of the pancreas and the inherent heterogeneity of PCLs in shape, size, and distribution. To date, only a limited body of literature is available on PCL segmentation, and existing studies exhibit several clinical constraints. In [8], 2D and 3D U-Nets were trained on T2-weighted scans from 146 polycystic kidney disease patients, achieving Dice similarity coefficients (DSC) of 0.70–0.80; however, their model’s generalizability is limited by the specific patient cohort. In [9], a cascaded pipeline was proposed for PCLs in coronal MRCP images, reaching a mean DSC of 0.80 for lesions >5 mm. Yet, the MRCP sequence is not routinely included in abdominal MRI protocols, limiting its applicability for incidental PCLs.

The purpose of this study was to develop and evaluate an automated deep learning framework for the joint segmentation of the pancreas and PCLs on T2-weighted MRI. Furthermore, we aimed to automate the assessment of PCL size and anatomical location and to benchmark the framework’s performance against established state-of-the-art segmentation models to demonstrate its potential clinical utility in the assessment of incidental PCLs.

papers.title: IncR-3DSGG: Incremental Posed RGB Image Based 3D Scene Graph Generation via Privileged Depth Supervision
papers.abstract: Scene graphs provide a compact, structured representation of environments by capturing objects and their spatial or semantic relationships in a form suitable for embodied agents. Existing 3D scene graph generation methods often rely on depth sensing at inference, either to associate object instances across views via point cloud overlap or to compute inter-object relations from geometric cues, limiting deployment to platforms with depth sensors. We propose IncR-3DSGG, which builds 3D scene graphs incrementally from posed\footnote{RGB images with camera extrinsics estimated by an off-the-shelf visual SLAM system.} RGB images, eliminating the use of depth sensors at inference. Our method leverages a Parametric Relation Predictor (PRP) that learns to estimate pairwise distances and relative angles between objects from 2D visual features and 2D geometric cues, using 3D geometric supervision available only during training. These learned pairwise measurements are fused across views through Pose Graph Optimization (PGO)~\cite{grisetti2010tutorial} to recover metrically grounded 3D object positions and build a globally consistent 3D scene graph incrementally. On the real-world 3RScan~\cite{wald2019rio} dataset, our method attains $52.2$ mean object recall and $30.8$ mean predicate recall under the 3DSSG~\cite{wald2020learning} evaluation protocol, against $27.0$ and $17.6$ for MonoSSG~\cite{wu2023incremental}, while using no depth or reconstructed geometry at inference. This shows that relations and metrically grounded 3D object representations can be predicted from posed RGB images alone.

papers.intro:
Scene understanding is a crucial area in computer vision for various tasks like image captioning, visual question answering and embodied reasoning [14, 35, 13]. An embodied agent navigating in unknown environment must build and maintain a map of its surrounding to support reasoning, planning and interactions. Conventional approaches for environment representation rely on SLAM-based methods [3], which construct geometric or topological maps to support agent localization and path planning. While this approach is effective for metric navigation, such representations lack object-level and semantic-level understanding of the environment as they only capture where the agent is, but not what surrounds it or how entities relate to one another.

Conventional approaches for environment representation rely on SLAM-based methods [3], which construct geometric or topological maps to support agent localization and path planning. While this approach is effective for metric navigation, such representations lack object-level and semantic-level understanding of the environment as they only capture where the agent is, but not what surrounds it or how entities relate to one another.

Scene graphs provide compact yet expressive formalism [17, 5, 25], by encoding objects, their attributes and inter-object relationships as a structured graph. Unlike purely metric maps, scene graphs can capture hierarchical information spanning object instances, rooms and spatial relations, enabling higher-level reasoning for tasks such as object goal navigation, language-grounded planning and manipulation [16, 42, 13]. Compared to dense 3D point cloud representations, scene graphs are a substantially more memory-efficient format for storing environmental information while preserving the semantic and relational content necessary for high-level reasoning. This makes them well suited to embodied settings where perceptual data must be processed and stored incrementally under tight computational budget.

While 2D scene graph methods have made significant progress, they operate within the image plane. Hence, their spatial relationships remain viewpoint-dependent and inconsistent across camera perspectives [5], lacking the geometric grounding that navigation and manipulation require. 3D scene graphs address this by capturing view-consistent spatial/semantic relationships anchored in the physical world [16, 31].

Most prior work on 3D scene graphs assumes access to a complete 3D reconstruction or dense RGB-D sequences available a priori. The problem of incrementally building a scene graph as the agent actively explores has received comparatively limited attention, despite being the relevant setting for embodied AI. Moreover, methods that do operate incrementally such as SceneGraphFusion [44] and ConceptGraphs [13], rely on depth sensing at every frame to associate object instances across views via 3D point cloud overlap and to compute inter-object relations from geometric cues. papers.title: Covering numbers of metric spaces
papers.abstract: We propose and provide evidence for the following conjecture: the covering number of a product of metric spaces with the sum metric is greater than or equal to the product of their covering numbers. This generalizes Vizing's conjecture in graph theory. We prove an infinitesimal version of the conjecture for Finsler manifolds of dimension at least six.

papers.title: Generic equivariant simplicity of the spectrum of Laplace-type operators with finite symmetry
papers.abstract: We prove that for generic elements in three natural families of Laplace-type differential operators on smooth manifolds, which are equivariant with respect to a finite symmetry group, all the eigenspaces are irreducible representations. In other words, the spectrum of these operators is generically equivariantly simple. The three families of operators with symmetry are Schr\"odinger operators parametrized by the potential, going back to the work of Wigner, Laplace-Beltrami operators parametrized by invariant Riemannian metrics and conformal Laplacians parametrized by invariant metrics in a given conformal class. The latter two results extend prior work of Zelditch for certain free group actions and resolve, for finite group actions, a well-known open question raised by Guillemin and Yau. Our approach stems from methods developed by Wendl and Doan-Walpuski to address equivariant transversality in symplectic topology.

A celebrated result of Uhlenbeck [34] states that for a generic, in a suitable sense, Riemannian metric gg on a closed connected manifold of dimension at least 22, the associated Laplace-Beltrami operator Δg\Delta_{g} has a simple spectrum. That is, every eigenspace is of dimension one. Related results, extensions and alternative approaches to this result appeared in [1, 31, 7, 6, 8, 12, 33, 19, 10].

In problems of geometric and physical origin manifolds often appear with symmetries. It has therefore been of interest to establish whether or not a similar statement holds in an equivariant sense when the manifold is endowed with an action of a compact Lie group GG. Specifically, every eigenspace of the Laplace-Beltrami operator of a GG-invariant metric becomes a GG-representation, and one asks whether or not every such representation is irreducible for a generic GG-invariant metric. This question of generic equivariant simplicity of the spectrum or generic irreducibility of eigenspaces was asked by Guillemin [28] and by Yau [40, Problem 42]. It is reinforced by results of Donnelly [16, 15] stating for instance that for finite GG acting with trivial minimal isotropy group, a real irreducible representation ρ\rho asymptotically occupies deg⁡(ρ)2/(α​|G|)\deg(\rho)^{2}/(\alpha|G|) of the total dimension of the sum of the eigenspaces up to any given eigenvalue (here α=dimℝEndG⁡(ρ)∈{1,2,4}\alpha=\dim_{\mathbb{R}}\End_{G}(\rho)\in\{1,2,4\} depending on whether ρ\rho is of real, complex, or quaternionic type).

From the perspective of physics, this question corresponds to the classical notion of accidental degeneracy of energy levels of a quantum mechanical system with symmetry. For instance, as observed by Wigner [39], every multi-particle system composed of NN identical scalar particles admits a G=SNG=S_{N} symmetry by permutations. This forces a necessary degeneracy of the energy levels corresponding to irreducible GG-representations, and generic equivariant simplicity corresponds to the absence of further, accidental, degeneracy. We refer to [17] for further background on the physical aspects of this question.

papers.title: An EPTAS for Max-Cut on Interval Graphs
papers.abstract:
Max-Cut was shown NP-hard on interval graphs by Adhikary, Bose, Mukherjee, and Roy (SoCG 2021). The best previously known approximation ratio for this class, due to Ahn, DeHaan, Kim, and Lee (APPROX 2025), exceeded the Goemans--Williamson ratio of about $0.878$ by only $10^{-34}$. We give a deterministic efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme (EPTAS): for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate cut of an unweighted $n$-vertex interval graph can be found in time $2^{O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^3(2/\varepsilon))}n^2$. The same guarantee and running time hold for Max-Bisection. An FPTAS is impossible unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$.
  Our algorithm rests on a structural theorem: every interval graph with $m$ edges can be turned into an interval graph of clique-width $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(2/\varepsilon))$ by deleting at most $\varepsilon m$ edges. The construction combines endpoint-rank coordinates, length-dependent rounding, and a shifted dyadic hierarchy. Intervals intersecting cell boundaries at their own scales are isolated at small total edge cost; the interactions of remaining long intervals with smaller subproblems can be summarized by counts. The structural theorem also yields a randomized EPTAS via Lampis's scheme for bounded clique-width; our direct dynamic program is deterministic and handles Max-Bisection.
  Finally, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is NP-hard to approximate Max-Cut within $84/85+\varepsilon$ on unweighted chordal graphs, which contain interval graphs. Thus an approximation scheme for Max-Cut on chordal graphs would imply $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$.

It remains NP-complete for interval graphs of interval count four, that is, graphs with an interval representation that uses only four distinct lengths [15], and a preprint of Barsukov and Roy proves the same for interval count two [8]. For unit interval graphs, in which all intervals have the same length, the complexity is open [3, 23]; two polynomial-time algorithms proposed for this case were later reported to be incorrect (see [1, 32]). papers.title: Are We Ready for Snow-tonomous Driving? Challenges Toward Robust Automated Driving in Extreme Weather
papers.abstract:
Automated driving has gained remarkable momentum over the past decade, with both industry and academia investing substantial resources in developing perception and control solutions to advance vehicle autonomy. However, these efforts have largely focused on clear-weather scenarios, leaving harsh conditions, such as snow, rain, and fog, comparatively understudied. As a result, inclement weather remains one of the most significant hurdles for autonomous vehicles, often leading to substantial performance degradation in downstream perception and control tasks.
  In this paper, we present insights from the EU-funded Horizon Europe project ROADVIEW, which aims to develop robust, weather-aware perception and control modules for connected and automated vehicles operating under severe conditions, including snow, rain, and fog. Drawing on four years of large-scale development and real-world demonstrations across multiple vehicle platforms in different locations, we identify ten key challenges that hinder the development of weather-resilient autonomy, including data scarcity, domain shifts, limitations in multimodal perception, control robustness, and validation gaps, among others. We summarize these challenges and lessons learned toward enabling reliable snow-autonomous driving, highlighting critical directions for future research and standardization.

Severe weather is a natural phenomenon that poses significant challenges for current AVs. Sensors can become partially (or fully) occluded or contaminated by water droplets, mud, snow, and ice (see Fig. -1), leading to degraded sensor measurements and impaired perception performance. For example, 3D LiDAR scans can be severely affected by precipitation, which in turn degrades downstream tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation. Likewise, road surface conditions can deteriorate rapidly, for instance, due to ice formation or aquaplaning. This compromises tire–road friction and reduces controller reliability and safety. Testing and validation under such conditions remain particularly challenging, as severe weather is both sporadic and difficult to reproduce in a controlled and scalable manner.

papers.title: Progress on the MALTA CMOS Sensor: Edge-TCT Measurements for Parametric Pixel Simulation
papers.abstract: MALTA2 is a monolithic active pixel sensor, developed in the 180 nm CMOS imaging technology for radiation-hard applications in high-rate environments. This contribution summarizes recent developments in the characterization and simulation of MALTA2. The charge collection of a sensor on epitaxial silicon is studied with the Edge Transient Current Technique (Edge-TCT), using a digital readout, where the charge is reconstructed solely from binary hit data. In previous works, only specially designed analog output pixels at the matrix periphery were investigated. In contrast, the digital readout gives access to the full edge of the pixel matrix. Laser scans across neighboring pixels enable a two-dimensional parameterization of the charge collection. This parameterization serves as input to a parametric pixel simulation, which has been developed for chip design optimization and system-level studies. The simulation results are validated with test beam data.

Monolithic active pixel sensors (MAPS) have already demonstrated such improvements over hybrid detectors in terms of lower material budget, higher granularity and lower power consumption. papers.title: A hybrid machine learning-analog framework for downscaling unprecedented climate extremes
papers.abstract: Extreme weather events are critical for climate impact assessments. While physical models can simulate unprecedented extremes, for example, through ensemble boosting, this approach is computationally demanding, often restricting output to coarse spatial resolutions. Probabilistic generative downscaling offers a solution by enabling efficient sampling from the entire climate distribution, including its extreme tails. Here, we first demonstrate that machine learning generated regional climate model heatwaves over Paris are physically realistic. We then leverage an emulated machine learning dataset to perform analog-based downscaling of coarse global climate model ensemble boosting events. Our hybrid framework effectively bridges high-resolution regional detail with rare-event sampling, providing an efficient tool for extreme event downscaling and capturing multi-model uncertainty.

papers.intro:
Despite the computational effort dedicated to multi-model initiatives like the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project CMIP (Eyring et al., 2016), their generally coarse spatial scale limits their utility for impact assessments at local to regional scale, in urbanized areas, over complex topography, and along coastlines. Evaluating more localized risks related to heatwaves and compound events benefits from fine-scale detail (Clarke et al., 2022), yet practical analyses remain limited by the inherent scarcity of extreme events and the spatial resolution of standard global climate model outputs. To overcome the sample-size constraints, rare event algorithms such as ensemble boosting (Gessner et al., 2021) and the GKTL algorithm (Giardina et al., 2011) have emerged as tools for generating physically coherent extremes. Ensemble boosting addresses the sample-size constraints by perturbing the initial atmospheric conditions of targeted events days or weeks in advance. It efficiently samples low-probability, high-impact extremes while maintaining physical coherence within climate models. Yet, despite its conceptual efficiency, generating these large ensembles is computationally intensive, particularly in higher-resolution climate models (Balaji et al., 2017).

Dynamical downscaling of these boosted global climate samples presents an even greater technical and computational challenge. Running dynamical regional climate models over hundreds of boosted ensemble members to obtain high-resolution fields is computationally prohibitive. Consequently, extreme event storyline studies frequently rely directly on global climate model outputs (Fischer et al., 2023). While statistical downscaling is possible, statistical approaches struggle with unprecedented extremes, where observational analogs based on historical archives do not exist for future record-shattering extremes that exceed the historic range (Noyelle et al., 2025).

To bridge the gap between low-resolution ensemble-boosted simulations and fine-scale detail, we leverage machine learning emulators to sample climate extremes. Our approach combines physics-based GCM ensemble boosting with a general-purpose, temporally-consistent machine learning (ML) downscaling emulator to construct a large, physically consistent high-resolution climate dataset. By combining high-resolution ML-generated data with low-resolution physical extremes, coarse GCM extremes can be mapped to high-resolution regional states, and climate model uncertainty can be used to construct alternative storylines of extreme events.

We demonstrate the utility of this framework using Western European heatwaves studied in Fischer et al. (2023), centered on Paris, as a primary proof-of-concept. More specifically, by training the temporally consistent ML emulator EnScale (Schillinger et al., 2026) on physics-based GCM-RCM simulations, we create a library of physically consistent, fine-scale climate emulations. The emulator’s computational efficiency allows us to sample 8,000 summers, including extremes, across 8 different GCM-RCM combinations. We show that these ML-generated samples span the range of the most extreme boosted events, allowing us to perform analog matching to instantaneously downscale coarse boosted GCM events. Ultimately, our hybrid framework preserves spatio-temporal consistency while capturing multi-model variability at a fraction of the computational cost of traditional dynamical downscaling.

papers.title: Rotationally Symmetric Lattice Boltzmann Pseudopotential Methods for Porous Media Applications
papers.abstract: Pseudopotential models are a well established approach for multiphase and multicomponent simulations using the lattice Boltzmann method. Although not the most accurate, they are often chosen for ease of implementation and adaptability. A drawback of the models are spurious currents at the interfaces and particularly at solid walls which introduce numerical artifacts. An improved lattice Boltzmann pseudopotential model is presented. The discrete fluid density gradients in the coupling force are computed with rotationally symmetric gradient operators formulated as a convolution. As a result, spurious currents are reduced in settings where solid walls are unaligned with the lattice directions. Additionally, variations of introducing fluid-solid interaction either equally through both fluids or through a single fluid only are compared. Presented model variants are compared using droplets on walls as a common benchmark, analytically solvable capillary rise experiments (Jurin's law), and porous media imbibition as a practical application. Rotationally symmetric operators outperform the classical lattice weights approach in all tests in terms of accuracy, while avoiding extending the lattice to compute higher order gradients. The choice of the fluid-solid interaction variant depends on the problem under consideration and the desired properties of the resulting model.

papers.title: Immersive Sight-Restriction-Based Collision Prevention Using Generic Particle Systems in Virtual Reality
papers.abstract: Collision prevention systems (CPS) help VR users navigate their physical surroundings safely. Most approaches overlay conceptually distinct grids or add solid virtual counterparts of physical obstacles; both can reveal the physical space, as they either stand out visually or behave inconsistently during locomotion. We explore sight restriction as an alternative: a standard particle system visualizes the play area boundary as a fog-like cloud whose intensity scales with proximity and viewing direction. A pre-study (N=10) determined the distance at which the visualization must appear. In a main study (N=11), we compared this particle-based CPS with a grid-based solution, focusing on locomotion behavior: across 253 approach episodes, users interrupted their approach after a comparable distance once either visualization appeared. Although the particle boundary was visible three times as often, participants reported higher presence. We release our implementation as open source to support further work on immersive collision prevention.

papers.intro:
Collision prevention systems (CPSs), such as Meta’s Guardian (, 2024) or Valve’s Chaperone (34), are essential for safe virtual reality (VR) use (Huang et al., 2018b). They inform users about upcoming boundaries of their physical environment and prompt them to reorient. While it appears to be easy to effectively communicate these prompts, for instance, through a switch to passthrough, this would be at the cost of the immersive experience. In fact, CPSs often use virtual boundary visualizations in the first place to avoid reminding users of their physical surroundings. However, to communicate the prompt to reorient effectively yet immersive CPSs have to provide the flexibility to adapt to diverse scenarios, with respect to the virtual environment (VE), physical environment, and users’ current movement. Locomotion can cause different changes in the virtual and physical environment, which make it challenging to provide a logically coherent CPS visualization that dynamically adapts accordingly. Logical inconsistencies between CPS visualization and virtual environment, however, may break plausibility and presence, respectively (Slater and Steed, 2000). The perfect tradeoff between presence and effectiveness has not yet been found. State-of-the-art built-in systems mostly use grid-based boundary visualizations that appear at a certain proximity to the boundary (, 2024; 34). Their standardized appearance may be beneficial for efficient communication of the boundaries’ location, as confusion with visualizations of the actual VE is unlikely. However, this clear distinction will also likely cause breaks in presence. Another common approach is to trigger reorientation through virtual counterparts of physical obstacles (Sra et al., 2016). Building on intuitive collision avoidance, this approach also works with contextualized visualizations. However, it has limitations for teleportation-based VR applications, as this implies the sudden appearance of the virtual counterparts at the target location. Another prevention approach is based on sight restrictions, such as reducing the field of view (FOV) (Wu and Rosenberg, 2019). Restricting sight is conceptually a promising approach, as in reality, people also intuitively reduce their pace with increasing sight restrictions (Jeon et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2014). However, to our knowledge, no prior work has investigated a contextualized sight-restriction-based CPS. In reality, smoke and fog are two prominent causes of temporarily reduced sight. The higher their density, the less people can orient themselves, to the point where navigation is barely possible. The diverse and dynamic visual appearance of so-called aerosols also offers great advantages over solid virtual counterparts. We are used to different types of aerosols as well as different ways of their formation (Hinds and Zhu, 2022). Aerosols can be integrated into a wide range of virtual environments without introducing rigid geometric structures that are visually inconsistent with the scene. Their shape and appearance depend on the context and can change dynamically due to gusts of wind or the like. This provides a set of attributes that are needed for boundary visualizations. The question remains, however, whether aerosols can be used in VR to effectively communicate upcoming boundaries of physical space and prevent collisions while still providing an immersive alternative to standard grid-based solutions. Avoiding aerosols is not necessarily natural, as most aerosols can be passed through without harm in reality. Davis et al. showed that increasing smoke density in VR induces slowing the user’s speed (Davis et al., 2023). However, the task was still to traverse the aerosol. How users would intuitively respond to sight restrictions has not yet been investigated, especially at more severe levels. Rather, it was found that for CPS in general, users may intentionally cross boundary visualizations, because they have some sort of mental model of the physical environment (Tseng et al., 2024). As this finding applied to grid-based solutions that resemble the shape of the configured play area, it is unclear whether users would still apply this behavior when using more neutral cloud-based CPSs. papers.title: Radiation Hardness Assurance of Optical Coatings for the COMPASSO Iodine Reference
papers.abstract: The COMPASSO payload demonstrates compact iodine-based optical frequency references on the International Space Station (ISS), requiring optical windows and antireflective coatings that remain stable in the Low Earth Orbit (LEO) radiation environment. Radiation analysis was performed to quantify how trapped electrons, protons, and ions affect the fused-silica iodine cell and its coatings under mission-relevant shielding and exposure scenarios. The aim was to determine whether selected coatings meet the COMPASSO optical requirements after realistic LEO irradiation, identify degradation mechanisms linked to deposition technology and materials, and provide selection guidance for coatings used in spaceborne iodine spectroscopy and optical-clock payloads. Nominal and worst-case corpuscular environments for the ISS orbit were derived using AE8/AP8, CREME96, ESP, and ISO15390 models. Eight coating stacks produced by different deposition methods were exposed to proton and electron irradiation corresponding to the nominal and worst-case mission loads. Pre- and post-irradiation characterization included reflectance and transmittance measurements, together with visual and microscopic inspection. The tests led to the selection of a four-layer $\mathrm{Ta_2O_5/SiO_2}$ stack for the iodine cell optical window. Total ionizing dose levels for all layers of the selected coating were derived with GRAS, showing that the coating will not be affected by corpuscular radiation for years in the LEO ISS environment, including the COMPASSO mission at the ISS Bartolomeo platform.

papers.intro:
Optical systems used in space rely on resilient components in harsh environments. One key aspect is optical coatings, which have to withstand the radiation environment in space. Therefore, optics and its coatings must undergo analysis and testing regarding irradiation and the potential influence of low energy (<<1MeV) electrons and protons on optical parameters such as reflectance and transmittance [1, 2]. These aspects are also considered in future space-borne technologies, like satellite-operated optical clocks. These technologies are interesting for future generations of Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), such as Galileo, and for new GNSS architectures, such as the Kepler concept developed at DLR [3].

The payload is attached to the Bartolomeo platform outside the Columbus module of the International Space Station (ISS) on slot 2A, see Figure 2a in Steimle C. et al. [5]. The iodine references utilise the Doppler-free spectroscopy technique to resolve the iodine hyperfine structure near a wavelength of 532 nm [4].

papers.title: Video-Action Models for Data-Efficient Industrial Manipulation
papers.abstract: Industrial manipulation requires precise alignment and controlled handling of rigid, deformable, and flexible components. Yet, the benefits of pretrained visuomotor policies remain underexplored in settings where limited access to specialized hardware, components, and fixtures constrains demonstration collection and evaluation. Understanding task-specific data requirements is important for assessing their scalability across diverse processes on the factory floor. We investigate whether video pretraining can support reliable industrial manipulation with limited action data. We propose FLUX-mimic, a video-action model, motivated by the potential of video pretraining to capture motion and interaction patterns that enable sample-efficient training. FLUX-mimic is built on a backbone pretrained on large-scale web and industrial task data, and an action expert to generate robot trajectories. We train our policy by joint video-action training. Across four automotive manufacturing benchmark tasks and two bimanual robot platforms, FLUX-mimic outperforms all considered baselines on the dexterous robot platform and matches pi_{0.5}'s average success rate on the gripper-based robot platform. On a deformable part kitting task, FLUX-mimic reaches 77.5% success with as little as two hours of task-specific action-labeled demonstrations.

Physical foundation models have been shown to bridge web-scale pretraining and real-world deployment, allowing robots to acquire manipulation behaviors that are difficult to specify through hand-engineered rules and controllers. However, their adoption in industrial automation remains limited, as high task specificity with characteristic visual and physical properties and scarce demonstration data present significant hurdles. For example, in the automotive industry, typical tasks include inserting components into rigid fixtures with tight clearances, routing flexible cables through constrained geometry, and picking parts from unstructured bins into ordered slots (see Fig. ), yielding scenes with metal panels, foam and rubber components, wire harnesses, and densely populated trays. These tasks require precise control under visual and geometric variation, and are substantially different from standard web-scale priors.

papers.title: Authenticated Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in Outsourced Vector Databases
papers.abstract: Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search has become a fundamental query primitive in modern vector databases for managing large-scale embedding data. To support growing vector collections, organizations increasingly outsource database management and query processing to third-party clouds. However, untrusted service providers may return suboptimal or fabricated results, posing a serious threat to ANN search integrity. Existing authenticated ANN approaches face substantial scalability challenges. They typically require transmitting high-dimensional vectors for distance verification and rely on topology-agnostic authentication structures, resulting in excessive communication and verification overhead. In this paper, we propose VIDA, a novel and efficient scheme for authenticated graph-based ANN search. VIDA replaces raw vector transmission with compact vector commitments and employs an aggregated Inner Product Argument to efficiently verify multiple distance computations. Furthermore, we introduce MeST, a topology-aware authenticated data structure that aligns authentication paths with graph traversal, significantly reducing structural proof overhead. Additionally, we design a quantization-aware authentication strategy that exploits distance bounds for pruning, reducing the number of exact distances requiring cryptographic authentication. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed schemes substantially improve the efficiency of authenticated ANN search, achieving up to a $6.6\times$ speedup in end-to-end latency and reducing data transfer time by up to 99.2% compared with state-of-the-art methods.

papers.intro:
Driven by the rapid advancement of deep learning, massive volumes of unstructured data, such as text, images, and videos, are routinely transformed into high-dimensional vector embeddings to capture their underlying semantic relationships. To efficiently manage and query these immense datasets, specialized vector databases (e.g., Milvus [1], Qdrant [2], and Weaviate [3]) have emerged and are now widely deployed. Serving as the core retrieval engine for these systems, ANN search has established itself as a fundamental primitive in the era of artificial intelligence. Leveraging this capability, vector databases empower a wide range of data-intensive applications, including retrieval-augmented generation [4], recommendation systems [5], and semantic search [6]. To support ANN search on a massive scale, modern vector databases rely on advanced indexing structures, such as hashing [7], inverted files [8], and proximity graphs [9, 10]. In this paper, we focus on proximity-graph-based (or simply graph-based) indexing methods, as they achieve the best trade-off between search efficiency and recall [11].

To support ANN search on a massive scale, modern vector databases rely on advanced indexing structures, such as hashing [7], inverted files [8], and proximity graphs [9, 10]. In this paper, we focus on proximity-graph-based (or simply graph-based) indexing methods, as they achieve the best trade-off between search efficiency and recall [11].

With the exponential growth in dataset sizes and the continuous increase in vector dimensionality, maintaining massive vector databases locally has become prohibitively expensive for many data owners. Consequently, there is a growing trend to outsource vector data management to third-party cloud platforms, leveraging their scalable storage and computational capabilities to support ANN queries [12, 13, 14]. Despite the benefits of outsourcing, this paradigm introduces critical trust concerns regarding the execution integrity of the search service. For instance, a rational but dishonest platform might terminate the query process early and return suboptimal results to reduce computational overhead, thereby compromising the accuracy of the results. While authenticated query processing over outsourced data has been extensively investigated for traditional relational databases [15, 16, 17], it remains largely under-explored for high-dimensional vector databases.

papers.title: Runtime Analysis of Cartesian Genetic Programming on Max: A Proven Exponential Speedup
papers.abstract: Genetic Programming (GP) is a search paradigm inspired from natural evolution for the automated discovery of expressions, functions, and computer programs. Cartesian GP (CGP) is a flavor of GP that uses a graph-based model to encode candidate programs, as contrasted to the conventional Tree-based GP (TGP). Since its inception two decades ago, CGP has predominantly been analyzed empirically, thus little is known regarding its theoretical performance guarantees. This paper analyzes CGP for the Max problem, which has been only rigorously studied for TGP with a proven expected runtime superlinear in the optimal program length $n$. We prove that the expected time for the ($1$+$1$)~CGP employing common mutation operators to evolve an equivalent optimal of the same output is polylogarithmic in $n$, specifically at most $O(\log^9{n})$. This is remarkable, as it shows an exponential speedup by switching to CGP. Our results shed light on the benefit and the compactness of the graph-based representation for programs, and on how CGP can navigate its search and fitness spaces efficiently. This is a first proven performance guarantee for CGP on an established benchmark problem. Experiments complement our theoretical findings.

papers.intro:
Genetic Programming (GP) is a search paradigm and a subfield of Evolutionary Computation (EC) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) that evolves computer programs. The goal of applying GP is to automate the process of discovering computer programs based solely on given specifications, such as constraints and input-output examples. Early work by Cramer [7] and Dickmanns et al. [12] applied Genetic Algorithms (GA) to program generation. Koza [42] later introduced tree-based GP (TGP) to evolve LISP S-expressions, and with follow-up work [43] established the research field.

Genetic Programming (GP) is a search paradigm and a subfield of Evolutionary Computation (EC) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) that evolves computer programs. The goal of applying GP is to automate the process of discovering computer programs based solely on given specifications, such as constraints and input-output examples. Early work by Cramer [7] and Dickmanns et al. [12] applied Genetic Algorithms (GA) to program generation. Koza [42] later introduced tree-based GP (TGP) to evolve LISP S-expressions, and with follow-up work [43] established the research field.

In tree-based GP (TGP), or “Koza-style GP”, programs are represented as trees: leaves are input variables or constants from a terminal set TT, internal nodes are compute functions from a set FF, and the root produces the output. Since then, GP has been extended to include different flavors, depending on how programs are encoded, i. e. having different search spaces, for example linear-sequence [66, 62], graph-based [71, 58], rule-based [75] models, or on how they are evolved, i. e. using different search operators, for example semantically driven designs [59]. Recently, AI-related techniques have been used to enhance GP. Components from Neural Architecture Search (NAS), such as transformers [1] and autoencoders [83], have been integrated into GP, while Large Language Models (LLMs) have been used as search operators for evolving program code [73, 32, 61, 46].

papers.title: ScrewSense: Mapping the Invisible - Anomaly Detection and Error Classification in Screwdriving Processes
papers.abstract: The growing volume of process data generated by screwdriving systems, combined with advancements in computing power, data storage, and algorithms, is facilitating the application of artificial intelligence in this field. Accurately detecting and classifying screwdriving errors is crucial for ensuring product quality, avoiding costly rework in manufacturing, and supporting sustainability by facilitating the maintenance, reuse, and recycling of screw-connected products. In this context, machine learning approaches offer a promising alternative to traditional monitoring techniques, such as window-based methods or envelope curves. This study examines the use of deep learning techniques for anomaly detection and error classification in screwdriving processes. The data corpus consists of multivariate time series capturing process parameters, such as torque and rotation angle. For anomaly detection, the embedding space of a vector quantized variational autoencoder was analyzed. In terms of error classification, four different model architectures were evaluated. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of anomaly detection and confirm that deep learning models can distinguish between multiple error categories beyond traditional binary classification. This extends the capabilities of conventional monitoring approaches, achieving accuracies of up to 100%. Additionally, real-world data material was examined in order to further demonstrate model robustness. Overall the results indicate strong generalization capability and highlight the practical potential of the developed models for use in industrial screwdriving processes, eliminating the need for expert knowledge in error identification and significantly reducing manual effort and analysis time.

papers.title: ARTS: An Open-Source, Reproducible Three-Arm Platform for Autonomy Research in Minimally Invasive Surgery
papers.abstract: Research on surgical autonomy needs open platforms that any laboratory can build, yet the most widely shared platform depends on donated clinical hardware, and open alternatives on industrial arms each lack part of the surgical chain. We present the Autonomous Robotic Translational System (ARTS), an open-source three-arm platform for autonomy research in minimally invasive surgery, built entirely from purchasable parts for about USD 137,000. Two UR5e arms hold wristed da Vinci X/Xi instruments, a UR5 arm holds a stereo endoscope with two FLIR cameras, the surgeon console provides haptic handles, footswitches and a stereo viewer, and a hardware stop independent of the software lets a supervisor freeze all three arms in place. The ROS 2 software pins every dependency, installs from the same scripts on bare metal or in containers, and records stereo images with hardware-measured timing. On the real arms, ARTS commands each arm at its controller's full rate (e.g., 500 Hz on the UR5e), the two cameras expose within 12 microseconds of each other, hand motion reaches the arm in 58 ms, and the endoscope image reaches the monitor in 68 ms. The ISO 9283 pose repeatability is 0.14-0.25 mm, comparable to a da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) Classic arm on the same protocol, and an optical tracker measured a mean remote-center-of-motion error of 0.34-0.37 mm. Three expert and three novice operators performed the Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery (FLS) peg transfer through a laparoscopic trainer box, and one of the experts sutured on a suture pad. The hardware designs, firmware and software are available at https://github.com/MRE-Lab-UMD/arts.

papers.title: Where Is Uncertainty Observed? A Mechanistic Understanding of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
papers.abstract: Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. The answer matters because the observation point determines whether an estimator has access to enough information to recover a given target, and how well it can recover it. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, we define four mechanistic observation lenses: the structural lens observes component updates, the representational lens observes hidden states, the distributional lens observes token probabilities, and the semantical lens observes distributions over meanings. We relate these lenses through the residual stream and order them by the information they carry, which gives a principle for selecting UQ methods for different targets. We survey existing methods through the four lenses. Furthermore, we distinguish evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify different UQ evaluation protocols. Finally, we identify open problems and research directions to connect uncertainty estimation to the internal computation and downstream use of LLMs.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on challenging tasks in mathematics, reasoning, and coding (Guo et al., 2025; Lewkowycz et al., 2022; Cobbe et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021). Recently, LLMs have been used to find counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture (Gao, 2026), address the Millennium Prize Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem (OpenAI, 2026; Clay Mathematics Institute, 2000), and improve their own code (Zhang et al., 2026a). However, LLMs may generate hallucinations, plausible content that conflicts with established facts or is unsupported by the provided context (Huang et al., 2025a; Kang et al., 2026). Unreliable responses of LLMs can be particularly harmful when models are used for high-stakes applications such as medical diagnosis (Hager et al., 2024), legal advice (Dahl et al., 2024), or scientific research (Boiko et al., 2023). Knowing when an LLM’s response can be trusted is critical for its safe use (Jiang et al., 2018; European Parliament and of the Council of the European Union, 2026).

The distributional and semantical lenses observe the residual stream readout distribution over vocabulary tokens and over meanings, respectively. The four lenses are ordered by the information they carry, which we examine empirically on correctness prediction.

papers.title: MeerKAT and ASKAP EMU new radio-continuum observations of Wolf-Rayet nebula PCG 11 (Cohen's Ring)
papers.abstract: We present new radio-continuum observations of the well-known Wolf-Rayet (WR) nebula PCG 11 (Cohen's Ring; named after and in honour of the co-author on the discovery paper, Martin Cohen) using observations from the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU), Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) and MeerKAT surveys. We find that the elliptical shell surrounding Cohen's Ring has a flux density of 62$\pm$2\,mJy at 1000 MHz. The angular size of the elliptical emission is measured to be 54\arcsec$\times$45\arcsec\ (at P.A.=69.4\D), which agrees well with observations of the source in H$\alpha$ and at 24\,$\mu$m in the infrared. Using the measured angular size and a distance of 3.94$\pm$0.27\,kpc, we determine that the nebula has a linear size of $1.03(\pm0.07)\times0.86(\pm0.06)$\,pc. Together with our new and previously measured flux density estimates, we determine a spectral index for Cohen's Ring to be $\alpha$=0.06$\pm$0.02, indicating that the emission from the WR nebula is of thermal origin. Based on a typical average expansion velocity of 75~km~s$^{-1}$ for a WR star with a Red Supergiant (RSG) progenitor, we estimate the age of Cohen's Ring to be $\sim$ 13500 years. Our NANTEN telescope CO observations suggest that Cohen's Ring was formed during a relatively recent mass-loss event, while the associated CO-emitting molecular gas reflects the cumulative effects of stellar-wind feedback over a much longer timescale ($\sim$1.5\,Myr). As one of the few WR ring nebulae with linked molecular gas, Cohen's Ring provides a valuable laboratory for studying the long-term impact of massive-star feedback on surrounding molecular clouds.

papers.intro:
WR stars are massive late-type stars with broad emission lines (Crowther 2007) and are easily identifiable through their mass-loss rates (Nugis and Lamers 2000) and visually striking outbursts across the electromagnetic spectrum (Marston 1995). These stars are characterised by the elements that dominate their spectra; the primary elemental emissions being carbon, nitrogen, or oxygen (Crowther 2007). According to the dominant spectral emission, WR spectral classifications are termed WC (carbon-rich), WN (nitrogen-rich), and WO (oxygen-rich). WR stars have unique evolutionary cycles tied to their mass-loss history, with variable and inconsistent outbursts driven by internal pulsations (Langer et al. 1994).

WR stars have been known to emit at radio frequencies for some time (Leitherer et al. 1995), but these detections were often attributed to the stars themselves rather than their ejecta. Recent surveys at radio frequencies have revealed several previously uncharacterised WR shells that are well known at other wavelengths (typically optical and IR). Examples of these are WR16 and WR40 (Bradley et al. 2025b, Bradley et al. 2025a), WN8h stars with prominent emission at 944 MHz as seen with the ASKAP EMU survey (see below). Late WNh stars are preferentially detected in radio (Pennock et al. 2021, Cotton et al. 2026), as these ones also turn out to be. These are among the most massive stars, and actually do not descend from red supergiants. Here, we present new radio detections of the shell surrounding a known WR star, Cohen’s Ring.

Over the last several years, the population of known Galactic radio sources has grown substantially, driven largely by a handful of SKA (SKA) precursor surveys that are conducting surveys at better resolutions and sensitivities than previously possible. These include large-scale surveys undertaken by ASKAP, such as the EMU survey (Norris et al. 2021b, Hopkins et al. 2025), MeerKAT, such as the SMGPS (SMGPS) (Goedhart et al. 2024), as well as by other precursors such as the LOFAR (LOFAR), FAST (FAST) (Jiang et al. 2019), and EVLA (EVLA)** * https://science.nrao.edu/facilities/vla/docs/manuals/oss2013B/intro/project). These instruments have led to the discovery and characterisation of several different astrophysical objects, including SNR (Filipović et al. 2022, Filipović et al. 2023, Filipović et al. 2025b, Mantovanini et al. 2025, Sasaki et al. 2025, Burger-Scheidlin et al. 2026, Lazarević et al. 2026a) and SNR candidates (Smeaton et al. 2024b, Smeaton et al. 2024a, Lazarević et al. 2024b), RN (Bradley et al. 2025c), PWN (Lazarević et al. 2024a, Lazarević et al. 2026b, Ahmad et al. 2025, Ahmad et al. 2026), and others (Velović et al. 2022, Velović et al. 2023, Bordiu et al. 2024, Bordiu et al. 2025, Filipović et al. 2025a, Smeaton et al. 2025b, Koribalski et al. 2026, Zakir et al. 2026). They have also been useful in enabling more detailed analyses of previously known radio objects (Filipović et al. 2024, Asher et al. 2025, Smeaton et al. 2025a, Ghavam et al. 2025, Ingallinera et al. 2026, Castignani et al. 2026, Filipović et al. 2026b) due to their improved sensitivity and resolution. Cohen’s Star and Cohen’s Ring, also known as PCG 11 (Parker et al. 2012), PHR 1633–4928 and WR75ab, is a known WR star with an associated ring nebula. The star (Cohen’s Star) itself and the nebula (Cohen’s Ring) were first discovered and classified by Cohen et al. (2005) using Hα\alpha data from the AAO/UKST Hα\alpha Survey of the Southern Galactic Plane (Parker and Phillipps 1998). They confirmed the star’s WN7h type classification with optical spectroscopy†† † Nitrogen-rich, subtype 7 with characteristic stellar surface temperature ∼\sim50–60 kK, having detectable hydrogen in its winds., determined a distance of 4.1±\pm0.4 kpc, and mapped the radio-continuum properties of the ring nebula using radio-continuum data from SUMSS (SUMSS) and MIR (MIR) data from MSX (MSX). Following this, the central star has been analysed using Gaia DR2 (DR2) and DR3 (DR3) data (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2016, Gaia Collaboration et al. 2018, Rate and Crowther 2020, Gaia Collaboration et al. 2023), and the most recent distance estimate from DR3 is 3.94±\pm0.27 kpc (Arthur 2025), which we adopt for the calculations discussed in Section 3. Cohen’s Ring now appears in the MeerKAT radio surveys as well as in ATCA observations (Buemi et al. 2026), providing a higher-resolution view of the nebula’s radio-continuum morphology.

Among Galactic WR nebulae, Cohen’s Ring stands out for its exceptionally symmetric elliptical morphology, visible across optical, infrared, and radio wavelengths. The availability of new ASKAP EMU and MeerKAT observations now provides the first opportunity to investigate the radio-continuum properties of the nebula with greatly improved sensitivity and angular resolution. Moreover, combining radio-continuum, optical, infrared, and molecular-gas observations allows us to explore massive-star feedback across multiple spatial and temporal scales. While the compact radio shell traces a relatively recent mass-loss episode from the central WR star, the surrounding molecular-gas environment may preserve evidence of the cumulative impact of stellar winds over a much longer evolutionary timescale. As one of the relatively small number of WR ring nebulae with an associated molecular structure, Cohen’s Ring provides an important laboratory for investigating the interaction between massive stars and their surrounding interstellar medium.

papers.title: Improving Algorithmic Trading for BESS on Intraday Electricity Markets through Distributional Price Forecasts
papers.abstract: Grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) are becoming increasingly important in short-term energy markets, where they help balance fluctuations in variable renewable generation. In many countries, the continuous intraday market is the most important wholesale market for BESS to monetize their flexibility. In this paper, we propose an extension to the myopic rolling intrinsic policy that incorporates intraday price forecasts tailored specifically to the BESS trading problem. While a large literature addresses intraday price forecasting, most existing work focuses on volume-weighted prices during the last hours of trading and consequently fails to capture the features most relevant to BESS trading. Our approach addresses this gap by introducing a novel target variable derived from the limit order book and its dynamics. The resulting forecasts are designed to inform the optimization about future profit opportunities while preserving computational efficiency and avoiding the burden of full stochastic optimization. In a realistic high-frequency simulation setting covering 2023 and 2024, our method improves profits by up to 42% over the naive rolling intrinsic formulation. We further analyze the relationship between forecast accuracy, stability, and financial performance, establishing a clear inverse relationship between accuracy and stability. Finally, we find evidence that BESS size and duration jointly influence both overall profitability and the marginal benefit of incorporating forecasts.
papers.intro:
Climate change is the pressing challenge of the 21st century. Widespread electrification and the deployment of renewable energy are seen as crucial parts of the solution. However, electricity is a unique commodity, as supply and demand must be balanced at all times. The inherent uncertainty of variable renewable energy production has increased the importance of short-term electricity markets to react to changes in the fluctuating output of renewable energy sources. Concurrently, grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) have become vital for stabilizing the grid while also shifting supply from hours of abundance to hours of scarcity for financial profit. Historically, BESS have primarily operated in the ancillary services market. However, increased volatility in wholesale electricity prices has expanded opportunities for arbitrage profits through buying (and storing) and selling (and discharging) electricity (Gottfried and Müller, 2026b). Against this background, this paper develops forecast-based trading strategies for BESS on the European continuous intraday electricity markets, which offer the last opportunity to trade. Our strategy matches the millisecond pace of the continuous intraday market, re-optimizing decisions in real time while accurately modeling complex liquidity and market constraints dictated by the full limit order book.

Table 1 surveys the literature on intraday electricity price forecasting, demonstrating two limitations of contemporary approaches: First, there is a strong focus on the last three hours of trading. However, decisions in storage optimization are made throughout the day, and thus forecasts issued with short lead times are insufficient. Notable exemptions are the works by Puć and Janczura (2024), Nickelsen and Müller (2025) and Hirsch and Ziel (2024a). Secondly, there is a strong emphasis on (probabilistic) forecasting of volume-weighted average prices and the intraday indices, which fail to reflect the available options for traders in the limit order book. Forecasting approaches based on data from the limit order book are sparse (Grindel and Graf von Luckner, 2022; Yu et al., 2025a; Yu et al., 2025b, see), and to the best of the authors’ knowledge, no attempts have been made to forecast the order book or its derivative variables directly.

papers.title: Read and Ignore: What Self-Directed LLM Agents Do in Public Service Scenarios
papers.abstract: Underspecified instructions leave LLM agents to decide what to do. In public services, staff write these instructions, but the agent's decisions affect residents, patients, and students. We build four expert-validated public-service scenarios with records and decision levers that can be checked in the files, collect $2{,}400$ trajectories from ten LLMs under four prompt conditions, and compare them with $1{,}000$ runs in a context-free sandbox. Agents read the records in $96.9\%$ of open-ended runs and produce an artifact or a self-chosen task in $18.7\%$; with an explicit task, $86.0\%$ produce. Domain context does not change how many runs produce ($18.7\%$ vs.\ $16.0\%$), and the production ranking of the models largely carries over (Spearman $0.79$), while the ranking by whether a model reads the records does not ($0.19$). Context cuts boundary-probing turns per run by $60\%$, and some artifacts contradict the records. We contribute a test that a public-service institution can run on its own records before procurement; its rule-based taxonomy needs no labeled data, and scenarios, code, and trajectories are released.

papers.intro:
Public services run on recurring operational cycles: a city allocates a participatory budget, a hospital plans the next quarter’s ward coverage, a college assembles a course catalog, a municipality monitors its waterways. Generative AI is already common in these teams, and its use is often not governed: in a survey of UK public-service professionals, 45%45\% report generative AI in use in their area of work, and 32%32\% report clear guidance on its use [6]. An instruction to such a system can be short and open, for example “have a look at the proposals” or “see where we stand,” and leave the agent to decide what to do next. Whether an agent turns this discretion into useful work affects the work a team receives, the records it keeps, and the residents, patients, and students those records concern. In the EU, public bodies that deploy high-risk AI systems, among them systems used in admissions, must assess their impact on fundamental rights before use [17], yet we know of no evaluation that reports how a candidate model behaves under such instructions.

Existing evaluations measure other behavior. Agent benchmarks measure completion of well-specified tasks, from software issues [23] and web navigation [46] to office workflows [14, 42, 41]; by design, they leave the agent no discretion. Studies of self-directed behavior give the agent full discretion and observe it in empty sandboxes [25, 19], where models mostly inspect the environment repeatedly without pursuing a project. An empty sandbox contains nothing the agent could work on, and a task benchmark specifies the work in advance, so neither setting shows what agents do with discretion in a workplace.

Observing agents in a live workplace does not answer the question either, because the cause of an action cannot be attributed there. A working environment produces a continuous stream of external events: a file appears, a colleague replies, a deadline moves. A trace from such an environment cannot separate a model that sets its own direction from a model that responds to its surroundings, and rich environments can produce capabilities on their own [3]. We therefore use static environments. Each scenario is a fixed file tree that changes only through the agent’s own writes; after the first turn, everything the agent reads is a file it chose to open. Behavior can then vary only with the model and the prompt condition, which we control, so a boundary probe or a written artifact can be attributed to the agent. The comparison in Section 5.4 depends on this property: the two environments differ in their content and in nothing else. As a consequence, our results describe behavior in a static environment, and we limit the claims to that scope.

A trace from such an environment cannot separate a model that sets its own direction from a model that responds to its surroundings, and rich environments can produce capabilities on their own [3]. We therefore use static environments. Each scenario is a fixed file tree that changes only through the agent’s own writes; after the first turn, everything the agent reads is a file it chose to open. Behavior can then vary only with the model and the prompt condition, which we control, so a boundary probe or a written artifact can be attributed to the agent. The comparison in Section 5.4 depends on this property: the two environments differ in their content and in nothing else. As a consequence, our results describe behavior in a static environment, and we limit the claims to that scope.

We build four public-service scenarios, one each for governance, healthcare, education, and environmentalism. Each models one recurring operational cycle with its records, stakeholders, procedures, and schedule, and was validated by a domain expert. Each scenario contains decision levers, such as pending reviews, data gaps, and equity shortfalls, whose correct resolution can be checked against the records. An artifact the agent writes can therefore be scored for whether it is useful and whether it agrees with the records it cites. We collect 2,4002{,}400 trajectories from ten LLMs under four prompt conditions, from “Do what you want.” to an explicit summary task, add 600600 runs under a fifth, directed prompt, and compare them with 1,0001{,}000 runs of the same ten models in the context-free environment of prior work [25].

They inspect the domain files in ∼97%{\sim}97\% of open-ended runs, and 84.1%84.1\% of all ∼94{\sim}94k turns are exploration, a third of it re-reading files already read. Fewer than one run in five (18.7%18.7\%) produces an artifact or a self-chosen task. With an explicit task, 86.0%86.0\% of runs produce, and only half of them read the domain files. papers.title: A Code-Level Audit of X
papers.abstract: The transparency regime of recommender systems on Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) is undergoing significant change under the EU Digital Services Act (DSA). The DSA requires platforms to disclose information about their recommendation pipelines and grants vetted researchers access to non-public data, which may extend to recommender code. However, it is not known to what extent such code releases enable substantive and meaningful third-party auditing of a production recommender system. We address this question by proposing a code-level audit methodology for recommender systems and applying it to the X platform, which has voluntarily open-sourced its recommender pipeline. Our methodology is a backwards-walk traversal of the repository, tracing each decision-relevant component from the user-facing timeline back to its upstream producers, checking that it is reachable from the served pipeline, and classifying each under a four-tier inspectability scheme. Applying this procedure, we identify 13 transparency dead-ends on the live serving path: models, services, label lists, and configuration values that the public code depends on but the release does not contain. We find that the components that decide which posts are filtered and how they are ranked fall into the two least inspectable tiers, a pattern that intensifies with the 2025 integration of the proprietary Grok language model into moderation, annotation, and ranking. We further show that the release keeps 2023 code that the 2025 pipeline no longer reaches, with 36 parameter references that would pass for dead-ends without a reachability check. Finally, we discuss which additional artifacts would be required for meaningful auditing.

papers.intro:
Platforms such as X shape public discourse through large-scale recommender systems that determine which posts users see, in what order, and with what prominence. These systems integrate personalization, ranking, and moderation into pipelines that optimize for relevance and for platform-specific economic and political objectives (Leerssen, 2020). Their outputs co-determine exposure to disinformation, discriminatory content, and other systemic risks, making them a central regulatory concern (Meßmer and Degeling, 2023). Despite this scrutiny, recommender systems remain opaque, owing to both technical complexity and deliberate corporate secrecy (cf. (Lipton, 2017)). Most empirical work therefore infers algorithmic behavior from outputs rather than from internal design and relies on so-called black-box methods—sock-puppet audits, scraping, network analyses, and observational studies—which themselves face methodological, ethical, and legal constraints (Urman et al., 2025; Bandy, 2021; Olteanu et al., 2019; Bekavac et al., 2026). For AI audits, researchers have argued more generally that black-box access is insufficient and that auditors also need white-box and “outside-the-box” access, for instance to code, documentation, and deployment details (Casper et al., 2024). In addition to only providing an incomplete view of the external behavior of a system, these methods can merely show that a system behaves in a particular way, but not why. On the other hand, code-level audits—which could address this gap—barely exist as a genre in the domain of recommender systems: a 2025 systematic review of 176 algorithm-auditing studies found only a single study that inspected source code directly, and none targeted a recommender system (Urman et al., 2025; Weber and Kosterich, 2017).
