The EU Digital Services Act (DSA) (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2022) addresses these concerns. It requires very large online platforms (VLOPs), services with more than 45 million monthly users in the EU, to assess and mitigate the systemic risks their services create, such as the spread of illegal content and negative effects on fundamental rights, civic discourse, electoral processes, public health, and minors (Arts. 34 and 35). The design of recommender systems is named explicitly as a factor in these risks. The DSA pairs these duties with transparency obligations that allow users, regulators, and researchers to scrutinize how recommender systems work: Art. 27 requires platforms to disclose their main recommender parameters in plain language; Art. 38 requires VLOPs to offer at least one recommender option not based on profiling; and Art. 40(4) grants vetted researchers access to non-public data necessary to assess systemic risks, under formal access controls (Seiling et al., 2025). While nothing in Art. 40(4) excludes it, the DSA does not name source code, and regulators can already demand that VLOPs explain the design and logic of their recommender systems (Art. 40(3)). Platforms typically satisfy DSA transparency obligations through structured documentation, audit reports, and negotiated researcher access. As data-access requests under the DSA become more common, independent researchers will have increasingly the opportunity to scrutinize source code directly and code-level audit methodologies will matter well beyond the case of voluntary releases. X has voluntarily open-sourced substantial parts of its production recommender pipeline, first in 202311 1 Twitter Engineering, Twitter’s Recommendation Algorithm, 31 March 2023. and again in a major 2025 update. X made this release voluntarily, outside any DSA obligation, and framed it at the time of the 2023 release as enabling independent third parties to “determine, with reasonable accuracy, what will probably be shown to users” (App. B). Within this regulatory landscape, the present study treats X’s release as a test case: because source code is provided, gaps between regulatory transparency requirements and platform disclosures become analytically visible in our study.

The 2025 update is also architecturally distinctive: It extends the pipeline with X’s proprietary large language model (LLM), Grok, into moderation, annotation, and ranking logic. This is a transition to a partially non-deterministic hybrid Code/LLM recommender architecture whose semantic annotations, safety classifications, and contextual embeddings now co-determine what content users see. This shift creates a new form of transparency gap: While the deterministic components remain visible in the open-sourced code, the language model layer---its prompts, weights, and inference logic---remains hidden and/or closed. It is therefore an open question which parts of the 2025 pipeline remain auditable, and how LLM integration reshapes the auditability of production recommender systems across platforms more generally. The broader industry is moving in the same direction, which increases the relevance and urgency of this question. Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg has stated in the company’s Q4 2025 earnings call that Meta is ‘‘working on merging LLMs with the recommendation systems that power Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and our ads system.’’22 2 Meta Platforms Q4 2025 earnings call https://www.facebook.com/zuck/posts/pfbid0XaqxVGXPkGHRnotatVneydxapZsSjHbBXVPuDnJGC9T6P3Z76MeenyiW6H3c69asl. papers.title: Hilbert's 17th problem for symmetric functions: undecidability and a counterexample
papers.abstract: We study inequalities between symmetric functions that hold in every number of variables. First, we prove that it is undecidable whether a symmetric function with rational coefficients is nonnegative in all dimensions, answering a question posed by Acevedo, Blekherman, Debus and Riener. As a consequence, the validity of dimension-free moment criteria for entanglement in quantum information is undecidable. Second, we present a homogeneous symmetric function of degree 8 which is positive definite in every dimension but admits no sum of squares multiplier that is uniform in the number of variables. Consequently, Artin's solution of Hilbert's 17th problem and the Krivine-Stengle Positivstellensatz have no any-dimensional analog and any-dimensional Positivstellens\"atze asked for by Levin and Chandrasekaran cannot hold in general.

papers.title: Gradient-Free Inverse Design of 3D Nanophotonic Devices Using the Level-Set-Method
papers.abstract: Advances in 3D nanophotonic additive manufacturing enable increasingly complex, almost free-form devices for manipulating light at sub-wavelength scales. Extending nanophotonic designs into three dimensions introduces additional degrees of freedom. Exploiting this freedom requires inverse-design methods that can efficiently navigate this large design space while accommodating fabrication constraints. Here, we combine gradient-free optimization with the level-set method (LSM) to provide such an approach for 3D additive manufacturing. Representing the 3D geometry as a level set constructed from Gaussian radial basis functions retains substantial geometric freedom with only a few hundred design variables. This compact representation makes gradient-free optimization practical for fully 3D nanophotonic devices, eliminating the need for adjoint calculations. This unlocks the use of any Maxwell solver or auxiliary algorithms that should express fabrication constraints for which the required derivatives are unavailable or impractical to obtain, and enables embarrassingly parallel workflows. Consequently, binary fabrication requirements, such as structural connectivity, can be rigorously enforced, avoiding the differentiable approximations commonly used in gradient-based optimization. Here, we demonstrate the combination of the gradient-free LSM with a connected-component analysis algorithm to enforce the structural integrity of the design. We demonstrate the applicability of the gradient-free LSM by optimizing a Y-splitter while strictly enforcing the structural integrity of the material and the void in the design.

papers.intro:
Free-form 3D additive manufacturing for nanophotonics allows for the printing of almost any conceivable design in all three spatial dimensions [1, 2, 3, 4]. By exploiting the third dimension, the additional degrees of freedom enable the encoding of complex optical responses in compact devices at the micrometer length scale and below. In turn, the design process of free-form 3D nanophotonic devices requires efficient algorithms to find optimized designs, ideally while also considering constraints that are put on the design given by the fabrication method. Inverse design has emerged as a powerful tool to optimize nanophotonic devices. By encoding the desired functionality into a figure of merit, the material distribution of the nanophotonic device can be optimized, iteratively improving the figure of merit [5, 6, 7]. The material distribution itself is determined by the parametrization of the problem. Popular choices for the parametrization include shape optimization [8, 9, 10, 11, 12], density-based methods [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18], and the level-set method (LSM) [19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27].

In nanophotonics, density-based methods have shown great success and established themselves as one of the most common methods used. Density-based methods assign a continuous material variable to each spatial cell in a discretized computational grid and thereby allow for free-form designs. The resulting problems typically have thousands to millions of degrees of freedom and are commonly optimized using the adjoint method [6]. The continuous distribution must ultimately be converted into a binary, fabricable design. Filters and projections can promote binarization during the optimization, but increasingly sharp projections suppress sensitivities throughout much of the design region and can cause the optimization to stall. Simply thresholding the final distribution, on the other hand, can degrade its optical performance if the design relied too much on non-binarized regions.

For problems with only tens to a few hundred degrees of freedom, gradient-free and global optimization methods provide a useful alternative to adjoint formulations [28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35]. The compact basis-function representation of the LSM makes such approaches feasible, allowing the optimizer to explore changes in topology that are difficult to reach through gradual boundary evolution. Avoiding gradients also enables the direct use of non-differentiable fabrication constraints. This is particularly useful for 3D nanophotonic design, where both the material and, typically, the void must remain connected. 3D laser nanoprinting is a popular fabrication method for printing three-dimensional photonic devices at the micrometer scale. By focusing a laser inside a photoresist, a non-linear absorption process can trigger polymerization precisely at the focal spot of the laser. By controlling the path the laser takes, it is possible to obtain full 3D nanophotonic devices. The non-polymerized photoresist is then removed during development, leaving only the full 3D nanophotonic device [1, 2]. However, an additive 3D printing process naturally also requires connectivity of the design and the void regions. Connectivity of the material guarantees that no disconnected parts appear during development, which would otherwise be washed away during development or simply fall off. Furthermore, void connectivity is also required, as enclosed voids trap the photoresist and can alter the electromagnetic response of the final device. Connectivity is a binary measure and therefore impossible to rigorously impose with a gradient-based optimization scheme. Instead, a differentiable approximation must be used that only promotes connectivity. This makes it challenging to find a connected structure without either overconstraining the design or accepting some amount of free-floating or disconnected parts [36].

papers.title: NORA: Neuro-headstage for Online Recording and Actuation in Freely Behaving Animal Models
papers.abstract: This paper presents NORA, a compact wireless neuro-headstage designed for simultaneous neural recording and stimulation in freely behaving animal models. Separate recording and stimulation interfaces, each managed with a dedicated MCU and wireless module, are integrated into a fully head-mounted device compatible with standard Omnetics connectors; this separation allows for simultaneous recording and stimulation without sample-dropping or stimulation waveform distortion. To minimize stimulation artifacts and cross-domain interference, the recording and stimulation subsystems are electrically isolated with independent power domains and dedicated wireless communication paths. NORA has been validated through in vivo animal experiments, demonstrating acquisition of meaningful neural features with results comparable to a commercial wireless headstage. Together, these features establish a practical platform for artifact-reduced neuromodulation research.

papers.intro:
Bidirectional neural recording and stimulation technologies are essential tools for studying brain function and developing neuromodulation therapies. To capture neural activity under naturalistic behavioral conditions, it is necessary to develop neural interfaces that allow animals to roam freely without restriction by tethers [1, 2]. Recent advances have enabled multichannel wireless neural acquisition and stimulation in rodent models [3, 4, 5] and miniature wireless platforms for closed-loop modulation [6]. More broadly, multimodal wireless sensing systems have enabled home-based monitoring of rehabilitation exercises [7]. Despite this progress, obstacles remain that impede the experimental utility of existing wireless neural interfaces. In miniaturized systems, shared power rails and communication modules can introduce electrical coupling and stimulation artifacts that degrade signal quality [8]; in embedded interfaces, shared processing resources can cause timing conflicts that result in charge-imbalanced stimulation, damaging brain tissue [9]. Integration compatibility further limits adoption, as many wireless platforms require custom probe interfaces or specialized infrastructure [4, 10] that is incompatible with established experimental workflows.

This paper presents NORA, a wireless Neuro-headstage for Online Recording and Actuation in freely behaving animal models. A high-level illustration of NORA is shown in Fig. 1. The system integrates two off-the-shelf neural interface chips (RHD2216 and RHS2116, Intan Technologies), with five channels of each used for recording and stimulation, respectively. Each chip is controlled by a dedicated wireless microcontroller (MCU) (nRF5340, Nordic Semiconductor), eliminating timing conflicts between acquisition and stimulation workloads. The recording and stimulation modules operate from separate power supplies to minimize electrical coupling and stimulation artifacts. To improve experimental integration, the system features a 36-pin Omnetics interface compatible with a wide variety of commercial neural probes.

papers.title: People prefer AI to human advice in multi-turn conversations but neither changes incentivised behaviour
papers.abstract: People increasingly ask AI chatbots for advice, yet large language models (LLMs) are sycophantic, overconfident, and can amplify human cognitive biases. In this article, we investigate how people perceive advice from humans versus LLMs and whether AI advice reshapes incentive-compatible donation decisions. Using Carrier, a new experimental platform, we designed an experiment where participants made a donation decision after discussing it with an AI chatbot advisor, another human, or receiving no advice. Participants judged LLM advisors to be significantly more rational, trustworthy, convincing, and sycophantic than human advisors. Analysis of chatlogs showed that LLMs were more engaged than human advisors: they shared more facts and more often stated their opinion and justified their recommendations. Despite this, donation decisions did not vary across conditions.

papers.title: SteinPnP: Non-Parametric Uncertainty Quantification in the Perspective-N-Point Problem
papers.abstract: We propose SteinPnP, a probabilistic Perspective- N-Point (PnP) solver that models the full 6-DoF camera pose posterior using a non-parametric set of pose particles. By lever- aging Stein Variational Inference (SVI), SteinPnP combines the expressivity of particle-based representations with the efficiency of optimization-based solvers. However, a naive application of SVI struggles in the PnP problem, often missing alternative pose hypotheses or assigning incorrect probability weights to them. To address these limitations, we propose practical remedies that discover new potential poses, identify distinct hypothesis clusters, and balance their relative probability weights to capture the true underlying distribution. Our experiments across synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that SteinPnP accurately captures complex multimodal uncertainties while maintaining competitive accuracy.

Estimating the 6-DoF pose of a camera, i.e., its position and orientation, from visual measurements is a fundamental problem in robotic perception. In robot navigation, pose estimation forms the core of state estimation and mapping, with its applications including visual odometry [1], 3D reconstruction [2], and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) [3]. In robotic manipulation, estimating 6-DoF object poses is likewise essential for capabilities such as object localization [4], rigid object pose tracking [5], and grasp prediction [6]. A central formulation underlying these tasks is the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) problem, which estimates the absolute 6-DoF pose of a calibrated camera from a set of NN known 2D-to-3D point correspondences. Over the past decades, numerous solutions to the PnP problem have been proposed to enhance accuracy and computational efficiency.

In robot navigation, pose estimation forms the core of state estimation and mapping, with its applications including visual odometry [1], 3D reconstruction [2], and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) [3]. In robotic manipulation, estimating 6-DoF object poses is likewise essential for capabilities such as object localization [4], rigid object pose tracking [5], and grasp prediction [6]. A central formulation underlying these tasks is the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) problem, which estimates the absolute 6-DoF pose of a calibrated camera from a set of NN known 2D-to-3D point correspondences. Over the past decades, numerous solutions to the PnP problem have been proposed to enhance accuracy and computational efficiency.

Although existing PnP solvers focus primarily on accuracy and cost, quantifying the uncertainty over the estimated 6-DoF pose is equally relevant in many applications, including robotics. In practice, sensor noise and visual ambiguities, from symmetric objects or distant keypoints, adversely affect the PnP solver’s performance. Characterizing this uncertainty can help robots to prevent failures by avoiding unsafe actions. Moreover, downstream tasks generally depend on uncertainty estimates. In SLAM [3], for instance, visual pose estimates are often fused with IMU or wheel encoder readings according to their covariances. Overconfident PnP estimates may cause the system to overweight noisy visual measurements, potentially leading to inconsistent maps or localization failures.

Existing probabilistic PnP methods can be broadly categorized based on their input noise assumptions: those considering only 2D feature uncertainty (e.g., CEPnP [7], MLPnP [8]), and those modeling both 2D feature and 3D coordinate uncertainties (e.g., EPnP(L)U [9]). Generally, these methods represent pose uncertainty using Gaussian distributions. While efficient, Gaussian assumptions fail when visual data admits multiple plausible poses. For instance, symmetric objects, planar keypoints, or distant feature points often produce multiple distinct pose hypotheses that a Gaussian cannot represent. To address these challenges, we propose SteinPnP, a probabilistic algorithm that models PnP pose uncertainty using a non-parametric representation, i.e., a set of pose particles that capture the underlying probability distribution. While Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods are the gold standard for non-parametric uncertainty quantification, they are inevitably slow to converge, and thus not well suited for robotic applications. SteinPnP leverages SVI [10], which combines the flexible non-parametric representation of MCMC with the computational efficiency of optimization-based variational inference. While SVI has been successfully applied to 3D point cloud registration (e.g., Stein ICP [11, 12]), we extend this probabilistic method to 6-DoF pose uncertainty quantification within the PnP problem.

Specifically, we formulate the PnP problem as an approximate Bayesian inference task and design a new PnP solver using a variant of SVI called Stein Variational Newton (SVN) [13]. In SteinPnP, pose particles initialized from a prior distribution are iteratively driven by SVN toward the target probability distribution. We detail our design choices including the explicit derivations of its score function, Fisher information matrix as a Hessian surrogate, and curvature-scaled kernel design. Importantly, we observe that direct application of SVN suffers from mode collapse and incorrect mass allocation in multimodal PnP settings. To resolve these limitations, we introduce algorithmic remedies featuring randomized initialization, tree-based mode clustering, and importance-sampled mode mass refinement. Finally, we establish a standardized evaluation protocol for PnP uncertainty quantification, demonstrating through extensive synthetic and real-world experiments that non-parametric particles capture visual ambiguities where traditional Gaussian solvers fail.

papers.title: Laser-induced damage threshold of periodic plasmonic metasurfaces
papers.abstract: Plasmonic metasurfaces enable strong nonlinear optical responses due to sub-wavelength field confinement, yet their performance is fundamentally limited by low laser-induced damage thresholds (LIDT). Here, we present a comprehensive experimental and numerical study of the interplay between surface lattice resonances (SLRs), second-harmonic generation (SHG), and LIDT in periodic gold nanobar metasurfaces. Angle-resolved measurements reveal that excitation of SLRs at the fundamental wavelength strongly enhances SHG efficiency while simultaneously reducing the LIDT. In contrast, excitation of an SLR at the second-harmonic wavelength does not affect the damage threshold, allowing the SHG signal to be maximized. Our findings establish a fundamental trade-off between nonlinear efficiency and optical robustness and provide design guidelines for optimizing periodic plasmonic metasurfaces for high-power nonlinear applications.

papers.intro:
Plasmonics has attracted sustained attention due to its ability to enhance light–matter interactions through sub-wavelength confinement of electromagnetic fields. In particular, the excitation of localized surface plasmon resonances (LSPRs) in metallic nanoparticles leads to strongly driven collective electron oscillations, resulting in pronounced near-field enhancement. When nanoparticles are periodically arranged to form a plasmonic metasurface, coherent coupling between the LSPRs of individual particels and the diffraction order of the lattice can give rise to a hybrid plasmonic–photonic mode known as surface lattice resonance (SLR) [2, 28]. The resulting collective resonance has much narrower spectral features than those of the isolated nanoparticles [20]. In suitably designed plasmonic arrays, SLRs can also provide stronger local field enhancements than LSPRs [6].

However, due to the intrinsic optical properties of commonly used metals, the field intensities required to drive significant optical interactions easily surpass the modification threshold of the plasmonic nanostructures, thereby compromising both the performance and durability of plasmonic devices [24, 27]. Consequently, understanding and optimizing the critical fluence above which the optical response is permanently altered, also known as laser induced damage threshold (LIDT), is essential for advancing plasmonic devices.

Resonantly excited plasmonic nanostructures can exhibit a reduced LIDT compared to unstructured metal films [23]. Three major categories of damage mechanisms have been identified [49]: thermal, thermomechanical, and non-thermal. Thermal damage originates from optical absorption, whereby the absorbed energy is initially deposited in the electron system and subsequently transferred to the lattice through electron–phonon coupling, leading to a rapid increase in lattice temperature [18, 31]. Under ultrashort pulse excitation, energy deposition and lattice heating are temporally separated. Laser-induced heating can reshape plasmonic nanoparticles into more spherical structures through partial or complete melting [30, 29, 57], or thermally-activated surface diffusion below the complete melting temperature [22, 52]. At higher excitation fluences, fragmentation into smaller particles can occur [30, 29]. Thermomechanical damage can occur when lattice heating takes place faster than mechanical stress can relax. The resulting pressure buildup and subsequent stress relaxation can cause structural disintegration, including spallation or cavitation [59, 21]. Three major categories of damage mechanisms have been identified [49]: thermal, thermomechanical, and non-thermal. Thermal damage originates from optical absorption, whereby the absorbed energy is initially deposited in the electron system and subsequently transferred to the lattice through electron–phonon coupling, leading to a rapid increase in lattice temperature [18, 31]. papers.title: A Four-Branch Radar Target Simulator with Fractional Delay on a PlutoSDR
papers.abstract: Repeatable test setups support the development and evaluation of integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) hardware and algorithms. Commercial radar target simulators are expensive, while sub-6 GHz ISAC experiments often need only tens of megahertz of bandwidth within their available spectrum allocation. This makes simpler, low-cost test hardware attractive. We present a low-cost, open-source radar target simulator based on an ADALM-Pluto without hardware modification, supporting four independently configurable targets and analog bandwidths up to 56 MHz. The FPGA generates echoes with independent delays, Doppler shifts and gains, using fractional-delay filters for sub-sample adjustment. For motion-consistent echoes, delay and carrier phase are updated together to reproduce both changing range and frequency-dependent Doppler shifts. Over-the-air measurements demonstrate simultaneous echoes, sub-sample delay adjustment, and smooth target motion between sample positions. The FPGA source, firmware and on-device web interface are publicly available.

papers.intro:
Radar target simulators generate virtual radar echoes in hardware by delaying and frequency-shifting a received waveform and adjusting its amplitude. Targets with specified ranges, radial velocities and echo strengths can thus be emulated without moving physical reflectors. Such setups allow integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) algorithms to be evaluated with communication waveforms and actual radio hardware [1]. For example, Bauhofer et al. [2] use a target emulator to evaluate multi-target tracking with 5G-compliant ISAC radios in a factory environment.

Commercial instruments such as the Rohde & Schwarz AREG800A [3] and Keysight ZA0500A [4] control echo delay, Doppler shift and strength for automotive radar testing. Their high carrier frequencies and wide bandwidths serve automotive radar, but are not required for many sub-6 GHz ISAC experiments. Here, the available communication spectrum often constrains the sensing bandwidth anyway [1]. For allocations of a few tens of megahertz, a simulator need not reproduce gigahertz-wide radar signals. The PlutoSDR is therefore well suited to these experiments: its extended tuning range covers sub-6 GHz carriers, and its analog bandwidth reaches 56 MHz. Cost matters especially for antenna array testing: the ZA0500A specifies one simultaneous target at one angle [4], whereas several low-cost simulators could generate echoes from different directions to evaluate the radar’s ability to resolve targets at different angles.

By updating delay and carrier phase on every input sample, we account for both the changing target range and the dependence of the Doppler shift on signal frequency. The processing requires no knowledge of the radar waveform or its repetition period. We evaluate relative delay error, moving-target phase error and self-interference using over-the-air measurements. papers.title: Optimization of Finite Alphabet Message Passing Decoding on Fully Node-Parallel Architectures for 5G LDPC Codes
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel design method for the lookup tables (LUTs) of the minimum reconstruction, computation, and quantization (min-RCQ) LDPC code decoding algorithm. The proposed design method uses Bayesian optimization and samples from a subspace of the design space. The novel design method does not require knowledge about the channel or the modulation format and uses the frame error rate (FER) as loss function. The design method is applicable to irregular low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes with puncturing and shortening. Furthermore, the design method creates a set of iteration-agnostic LUTs that can be used over all iterations, which makes this approach suitable for fully node-parallel decoder architectures. We show that our proposed approach achieves a 38.6 % better energy efficiency than a state-of-the-art normalized min-sum (NMS) decoder without loss in error correction performance.

papers.intro:
Low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes [1] are widely used in modern communication standards, including fifth generation cellular network technology (5G) [2, 3] and wireless LAN (WLAN) [4], due to their excellent error-correction performance under iterative message-passing decoding. While the sum-product algorithm (SPA) can operate close to channel capacity [5], its computational complexity requires simplified algorithms such as the min-sum (MS) [6] and the normalized min-sum (NMS) [7]. Despite their reduced computational complexity, decoder implementations remain challenging because the routing networks between check nodes (CNs) and variable nodes (VNs) must transport high-precision messages across the pseudo-random Tanner graph [8]. Finite alphabet message passing (FA-MP) was proposed to reduce the routing complexity while preserving the error correction performance. FA-MP reduces the quantization-width of the exchanged messages and replaces the node update functions, i.e., in VNs and CNs, by lookup tables (LUTs) [9]. However, conventional FA-MP suffers from exponentially growing multidimensional LUT sizes [10]. To circumvent large LUTs, the reconstruction, computation, and quantization (RCQ) approach maps low-precision messages to a higher-precision domain for computation and back afterward [11]. The min-sum RCQ (min-RCQ) is a flavor of RCQ that uses the MS CN update rule. The min-RCQ achieves frame error rates (FERs) within 0.10.1 dB\mathrm{dB} of floating-point belief propagation (BP), without exponentially growing LUT sizes [11]. Designing the reconstruction and quantization LUTs remains a key challenge. Existing approaches include noisy-critical-number-based optimization [12] and the information-bottleneck method (IBM) [13, 14]. Although the IBM provides excellent decoding performance, it generates node- and iteration-specific LUTs. This approach is efficient for iteration-unrolled architectures for ultra-high throughput communications beyond 100100 Gbit/s\mathrm{Gbit}\text{/}\mathrm{s} [10]. However, the approach is inefficient for non-unrolled fully node-parallel architectures that reuse the same processing units across iterations. In such architectures, iteration-specific LUTs require additional storage, multiplexing, and control logic. To address this limitation, we propose an iteration-agnostic LUT design approach. We use Bayesian optimization [15] with the FER as the loss function to optimize the parameters of min-RCQ decoders. Furthermore, we introduce a search space reduction of the parameter space to enhance sample efficiency. Bayesian optimization only needs access to the decoder parameters and the bit sequences at the transmitter and after decoding. The Bayesian optimization needs no prior knowledge of the channel nor the modulation format. Furthermore, the Bayesian optimization operates directly on the specific code rather than on an asymptotic cycle-free code as the IBM does [13].

papers.title: Spec-Driven PBT: Deriving Semantic Invariants from Code Specifications for Agentic Property-based Testing
papers.abstract: Software is increasingly written by AI agents that produce an implementation from a natural language specification, a practice known as agentic coding. Code is now produced faster than it can be reviewed, and has been shown to exhibit its own characteristic failure patterns. Property-based testing (PBT), a long-standing technique in which invariant properties of a program are checked against many generated inputs, has recently been revisited with LLM agents authoring the properties, thereby removing the high-effort derivation of invariants that has long hindered its adoption. Existing methods, however, derive these properties from the implementation alone (Code-driven PBT). At the same time, a thorough specification such as a product requirements document has become routine within agentic coding, yet its role in testing the resulting code remains underexplored. We study the value of the specification as a source of properties for testing agent-written code. Our key insight is that the specification, unlike the implementation, records what the code was meant to do, and invariants derived from it are not biased by particular implementation choices. We propose Spec-Driven PBT, an agent that first expresses invariants in natural language from the specification and only then inspects the implementation to translate them into concrete tests. Across 25 applications from ViBench, Spec-Driven PBT finds a novel set of bugs that Code-driven PBT misses, while writing 2.4x fewer property tests. Though the two approaches surface a roughly equivalent number of bugs, there is little overlap: nearly 60% of the 169 total bugs are found by only one. Qualitatively, we find that the bugs unique to Spec-Driven PBT tend to violate documented product workflows whereas those to Code-driven PBT instead concentrate on implementation robustness, offering complementary value for bug discovery in agent-written code.

papers.intro:
Software is increasingly developed by AI agents that autonomously generate an implementation from a user’s natural-language description of the intended behaviour, a practice known as agentic coding. As of mid-2026, nine in ten professional developers use coding agents at least weekly (JetBrains Research, 2026), and a growing collection of benchmarks—ViBench (Zhong et al., 2026), Vibe Code Bench (Tran et al., 2026), BaxBench (Vero et al., 2025) and ProjDevBench (Lu et al., 2026)—assesses agents on constructing complete applications from nothing more than a requirements document. The specification has consequently become the main artifact a developer authors, and often the only one they examine in full. Two implications follow. First, human review has become the bottleneck: code is generated at a pace that mandatory human inspection cannot sustain (Monperrus, 2026). Second, correctness has not advanced at the same rate: even frontier models regularly produce applications that are incomplete or incorrect (Zhong et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026), and among the agent-authored patches that pass their tests on SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024), nearly a third behave differently from the developers’ fix (Wang et al., 2026).

Empirical taxonomies of LLM-generated code identify recurring categories of defects particular to generated code (Tambon et al., 2025; Dou et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025); security vulnerabilities are widespread even in functionally correct output (Vero et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2026); and failure analysis for ViBench’s agent builds finds that a substantial proportion of failures in LLM-generated applications arise from omitted or misunderstood requirements rather than from implementation mistakes (Zhong et al., 2026). What these defects share is that they leave behind code that runs, passes the tests created alongside it, and appears plausible when examined in isolation.

What these defects share is that they leave behind code that runs, passes the tests created alongside it, and appears plausible when examined in isolation.

Property-based testing (PBT) is an established technique well suited to defects of this kind (Claessen and Hughes, 2000; Fink and Bishop, 1997): across 40 Python projects, each property-based test kills roughly 50 times as many mutants as the average unit test, even after controlling for coverage (Ravi and Coblenz, 2025). A property is specified once and evaluated against many generated inputs, so an invariant such as “no user can read a record they were not granted access to” is tested across multiple inputs and sequences of operations without listing them manually. Its adoption has historically been constrained by the effort required to derive useful invariants, which practitioners identify as the most difficult part of the practice (Goldstein et al., 2024). LLM agents have recently reduced this barrier by writing the properties themselves: given a codebase, an agent infers candidate invariants, generates tests in a PBT framework such as Hypothesis (MacIver et al., 2019), runs them, and triages the failures, and this approach has uncovered real bugs across widely used open-source packages (Maaz et al., 2025). PBT provides a second advantage in this context; a property is a concise, human-readable description of what the code should do (Goldstein et al., 2024), so a collection of properties gives a reviewer something substantially shorter than the implementation to compare with the specification—a means of verifying agent-written code without reading it all.

This approach works for a mature library whose documentation captures long-established intent. We call this family of approaches Code-driven PBT. Agentic coding creates an opportunity here that Code-driven PBT does not exploit. Prior work has demonstrated that grounding LLM-written unit tests in a specification is what makes them effective (Haeri and Ghelichi, 2026) and has extracted properties from task descriptions to guide code generation (He et al., 2025), but specification-based testing of agent-built applications remains underexplored.

Our central insight is that invariants obtained from the specification are not biased by the behaviour of a particular implementation, and can therefore falsify behaviour about which the implementation is internally consistent. We introduce Spec-Driven PBT, an agent that first formulates invariants in natural language from the specification, and only afterward examines the implementation—using it to identify inputs, boundaries and operation sequences that could falsify those invariants, without regarding it as the oracle. The invariants remain as a standalone natural-language ledger that the agent updates as it works, allowing a reviewer to audit what was tested against the specification without reading either the implementation or the tests. We ask: when an LLM agent writes property-based tests for agent-written code, does deriving the oracle from the specification uncover bugs that code-driven testing misses, and which kinds? The two approaches turn out to generate different kinds of tests. Because a specification describes what users do, spec-derived properties tend to examine workflows: multiple users, a sequence of operations, a state reached through an unusual path. Because code explains how routines operate, code-derived properties test routines with adversarial inputs.

papers.title: Information Thermodynamics in Closed Quantum Many-Body Dynamics
papers.abstract: Although information thermodynamics explains how the second law is modified due to the information acquired by Maxwell's demon, its formulation in many-body systems remains largely open. Here, we develop an information-thermodynamic framework for closed quantum many-body systems initially in microscopic thermal equilibrium (MITE), under physically motivated restrictions: local quantum measurements and finite-time controls generated by local Hamiltonians. By additionally assuming that each local feedback term depends only on nearby measurement outcomes, we rigorously prove that the extractable work coincides in the thermodynamic limit with that extractable from the corresponding canonical ensemble. We further express this extractable work in terms of quantum-information quantities, including the quantum-classical mutual information and the Holevo information for the corresponding canonical ensemble. We also show that feedback based on distant measurement outcomes can exploit long-range correlations hidden in MITE, yielding an extensive increase in extracted work relative to the canonical ensemble.

papers.title: Symmetry-preserving gapped Dirac state revealed by site-selective $^{13}$C NMR in $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$
papers.abstract: We report evidence that the low-temperature insulating phase of $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$ preserves both inversion and time-reversal symmetries using site-selective $^{13}$C nuclear magnetic resonance. $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$ undergoes a metal-insulator transition or sharp crossover at approximately 50 K and has been proposed as a candidate spin-orbit-coupling-induced Dirac insulator, yet the nature of its insulating ground state remains unresolved. The NMR spectra exhibit no additional splitting down to 2 K and remain fully described by one quartet and two doublets associated with the three types of molecular sites, A (=A$^{\prime}$), B and C sites, demonstrating the preservation of inversion symmetry. Furthermore, no anomalous line broadening or critical enhancement of the nuclear spin-lattice relaxation rate is observed, indicating the absence of magnetic ordering and time-reversal-symmetry breaking. Analysis of the Knight shifts yields site-specific spin susceptibilities satisfying $\chi_{\mathrm{C}} > \chi_{\mathrm{A}} > \chi_{\mathrm{B}}$, a characteristic feature of tilted Dirac-cone electronic states as observed in $\alpha$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$I$_3$ under pressure. However, the faint field-induced ferrimagnetic-like spin excitations observed in $\alpha$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$I$_3$, which are ascribed to the gapless tilted Dirac cones, are absent in $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$. These results demonstrate that the insulating ground state of $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$ is a symmetry-preserving gapped Dirac state and provide microscopic constraints on proposed correlated topological phases in this molecular Dirac system.

papers.title: Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.

papers.intro:
Agentic systems operate within socio-technical environments: their behavior depends on, and affects, both people and technical infrastructure. As agents take on extended tasks, make decisions, and act on people’s behalf, successful interaction requires more than interpreting user instructions. It requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating heterogeneous capabilities, accounting for embodied interactions, and maintaining productive relationships over time. In purely multi-agent terms, a human is another agent interacting with another agent. However, humans have a particular set of computational, behavioral, and intentional constraints and capabilities.

It requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating heterogeneous capabilities, accounting for embodied interactions, and maintaining productive relationships over time. In purely multi-agent terms, a human is another agent interacting with another agent. However, humans have a particular set of computational, behavioral, and intentional constraints and capabilities.

Interactions span settings involving one person and one agent, human–agent teams, and larger groups. People may participate as supervisors, operators, peers, or bystanders, with different capabilities, responsibilities, and opportunities to influence the system. These roles help determine what the person is accountable for, what they are positioned to observe, and whether they are a party to the interaction at all. Many taxonomies in this space include an ordinal scale of how much decision authority rests with the system rather than the person. A canonical example is a 10-level scale of automation [131, 105]. Decision authority may also vary across information gathering, analysis, decision selection, and action execution. Moreover, participants’ objectives may coincide, partially overlap, or conflict. Together, these dimensions shape what effective interaction demands, from cooperative planning and shared control to negotiation and resistance to manipulation.

Across these settings, a foundational challenge is reasoning about others whose beliefs, goals, intentions, and capabilities are only partially observable. Theory of Mind (ToM) concerns attributing mental states to others [107], with cognitive neuroscience examining the mechanisms supporting such social reasoning [6]. Computational ToM provides tools to represent and infer these properties, helping agents anticipate behavior, recognize misunderstandings, and communicate in ways that account for a partner’s perspective [152, 52, 104]. For human–agent interaction, this means treating people as partners whose knowledge, objectives, and expectations evolve throughout an interaction.

The Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community and broader multi-agent systems communities have developed complementary, computational approaches to this challenge. Belief–desire–intention architectures provide explicit representations of agents’ mental attitudes and support reasoning about those of others [112, 21, 22, 120, 46, 95]. Plan, intent, and goal recognition address how these latent properties can be inferred from observed behavior [138, 90]. Inverse planning interprets actions through the goals and constraints that could explain them [12], while planning-based recognition uses existing planners to evaluate candidate goals [109, 106]. Goal mirroring similarly reuses an agent’s planning capabilities to generate and compare hypotheses about another’s behavior [149]. Although inspired by accounts of biological mirroring, this computational approach should be distinguished from claims that mirror neurons themselves explain intention understanding, whose functions remain debated [38]. Recursive models, such as interactive POMDPs, further capture how agents reason about others who may, in turn, be reasoning about them [58]. These models connect understanding others to choosing how to interact with them. Observer-aware planning considers how an agent’s behavior will be interpreted [93]; explanation through model reconciliation addresses differences between the agent’s and the human’s understanding of a task [31]; inquiries require balancing interruption costs and the value of potential information [91], and decision-theoretic communication weighs the benefits and costs of exchanging information [154]. In robotics, ToM has also been used to accommodate variability in human teammates’ behavior [65]. Together, these approaches provide foundations for shared autonomy, where assistance and control depend on the human’s intentions and capabilities, and for argumentation, where participants must identify and address differences in beliefs or objectives. Cooperative inverse reinforcement learning adds a complementary perspective: a human and an agent pursue a shared reward that the agent initially does not know, making teaching, learning, and communication part of their joint decision problem.

papers.title: GrAFT-PDX: Growth and Failure-Time Modeling of Patient-Derived Xenograft Experiments
papers.abstract: Cancer drugs are often evaluated for efficacy in mice before proceeding to human clinical trials. To do this, human tumors are engrafted onto immune-incompetent mice to create a patient-derived xenograft (PDX). Engrafted tumors can be propagated to evaluate multiple drugs, but the time and costs involved in PDX studies limit high throughput drug screens in mice. Here we present GrAFT-PDX, a Bayesian model of PDX drug screens that aims to reduce the PDX screening burden by enabling imputation of missing experiments and early stopping of likely unsuccessful drugs. Unlike conventional survival or growth models, GrAFT-PDX jointly predicts tumor growth and survival outcomes using a learned latent function decomposition. In experiments on a large-scale PDX dataset, GrAFT-PDX outperforms Cox proportional hazards models at predicting time of death, outperforms machine learning baselines at predicting tumor growth, and recovers known gene-treatment relationships without genomic input.

papers.intro:
Patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) provide an important method for studying how human tumors may respond to drug treatments in a controlled setting (Tentler et al., 2012). In these experiments, tumor tissue obtained from a cancer patient is implanted into an immunocompromised mouse. This allows researchers to monitor tumor growth over time in vivo. Different drugs or drug combinations can then be administered to individual mice to determine which therapies would more likely be effective in patients with similar tumors. Effective treatments shrink the size of the tumor, or slow its growth, and extend the overall survival of the mouse. When conducted across many mice engrafted with multiple PDXs, these experiments yield datasets consisting of longitudinal tumor measurements coupled with mouse survival outcomes.

Patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) provide an important method for studying how human tumors may respond to drug treatments in a controlled setting (Tentler et al., 2012). In these experiments, tumor tissue obtained from a cancer patient is implanted into an immunocompromised mouse. This allows researchers to monitor tumor growth over time in vivo. Different drugs or drug combinations can then be administered to individual mice to determine which therapies would more likely be effective in patients with similar tumors. Effective treatments shrink the size of the tumor, or slow its growth, and extend the overall survival of the mouse. When conducted across many mice engrafted with multiple PDXs, these experiments yield datasets consisting of longitudinal tumor measurements coupled with mouse survival outcomes.

Because each experiment measures the response of a specific tumor to a particular drug, these datasets let statistical models learn how tumors respond to treatment and identify promising therapies directly from the data. A PDX line can be propagated indefinitely, so the same tumor can be screened against many drugs. PDX biobanks aggregate these screens across many tumors and therapies (Matschos et al., 2021; Meric-Bernstam et al., 2024; Akemi Kido et al., 2025). Even so, exhaustive screening of every PDX-treatment combination remains infeasible due to cost, time, and labor constraints. Computational models that impute and rank the untested combinations can ease this burden by allowing researchers to analyze potential experiments in silico. Such methods support drug repositioning: the identification of new therapeutic uses for existing drugs.

We consider each challenge in turn.

The sparsity of PDXe arises at two levels. First, many combinations are never tested; only 41904190 of a possible 13826​(30.3%)13826\,(30.3\%) PDX-treatment pairs are tested. Second, even within tested combinations, tumor size is recorded on only 29.8%29.8\% of days, on average, over a mouse’s lifespan. Together, these leave the overall dataset 91.7%91.7\% sparse. A model for these data must therefore impute at two levels, predicting both unobserved combinations and unmeasured points along each continuous tumor trajectory.

A model for these data must therefore impute at two levels, predicting both unobserved combinations and unmeasured points along each continuous tumor trajectory.

The coupling between growth and survival arises from the observation process itself. Tumor trajectories are only partially observed because measurements stop when a mouse dies. This missingness is informative. Mice with aggressive tumors tend to die earlier and therefore contribute no later measurements. Modeling tumor growth independently of survival would then bias estimated growth curves downward, since the fastest growing tumors are absent at later times. Capturing the dual nature of effective therapies—shrinking tumors and extending lifespan—requires joint modeling of longitudinal tumor growth and mouse survival.

Finally, treatment response is heterogeneous across PDX lines. The same therapy can shrink tumors in some lines yet appear far less effective in others, producing different trajectories and different lifespans. This variation is hard to predict from observed molecular covariates alone. This is true even in precision oncology, where genomic matching is an imperfect guide to response, with only around 63% of patients responding to targeted therapies selected from tumor genomics (Haslam et al., 2021). Capturing this heterogeneity therefore requires a model that learns PDX line specific response structure directly from the screening data rather than relying on observed covariates.

Motivated by these challenges, we introduce GrAFT-PDX, a Bayesian model that jointly predicts tumor growth and survival in sparse PDX drug screens. GrAFT-PDX represents the sparse, irregular tumor measurements as noisy observations of an underlying smooth continuous-time trajectory and allows tumor growth to inform death risk. This couples the longitudinal and survival outcomes while accounting for the informative termination of tumor measurements at death. GrAFT-PDX uses a low-rank tensor decomposition over PDX lines, treatments, and time to share information across observed experiments, predict untested PDX-treatment combinations, and capture heterogeneous treatment responses across PDX lines. The model represents tumor burden as a continuous trajectory and links its history to the survival process providing a novel description of how tumor burden impacts survival in mouse models. On PDXe, GrAFT-PDX outperforms survival baselines at predicting time of death. For tumor response prediction, it is competitive with strong baselines for held-out experiments and can improve upon static baselines by incorporating partial tumor trajectory information. Although the model uses no genomic covariates, the predictions it generates preserve known associations between genes and drugs, suggesting that it learns biologically meaningful response structure from PDXe. We demonstrate GrAFT-PDX can predict untested PDX-treatment combinations and rationally rank candidates for experimental follow-up.

papers.title: Entire boosted hypersurfaces of vanishing mean curvature in Schwarzschild spacetime
papers.abstract: We prove the existence of entire maximal hypersurfaces, asymptotic to suitable coordinate-dependent boosts in the two asymptotically flat ends of maximally extended Schwarzschild spacetime. As a corollary, this generates a foliation of maximal hypersurfaces in exterior Schwarzschild, which corresponds to a geometric choice of time function associated with any boost parameter. As a crucial step in the proof, we introduce a novel rotationally symmetric time function in maximally extended Schwarzschild, which is Cauchy and has properties of independent interest.

A spacelike hypersurface is called maximal if its mean curvature H\operatorname{H} vanishes identically, that is, it is a solution to the Euler–Lagrange equation of the variational problem of area maximization over (weakly) spacelike hypersurfaces in a Lorentzian manifold.

The existence of foliations by maximal hypersurfaces has been essential in General Relativity, in particular in the study of its dynamic aspects, as well as in the related numerical computation. In fact, setting H=0\operatorname{H}=0 drastically simplifies the Einstein constraint equations, which describes admissible initial data to be evolved into solutions to the Einstein equations; this has been crucial in the conformal method approach initiated in [34, 40]. Moreover, such condition reduces the so-called Dominant Energy condition for admissible initial data to the intrinsic geometric condition of non-negative scalar curvature Rg≥0\R_{g}\geq 0 and was assumed in the first proofs of the Positive Mass Conjecture [13, 18]. Finally, the preservation of H=0\operatorname{H}=0 along the evolution, provides an elliptic PDE for the lapse function, which was essential for the development of numerical methods [45, 46] and in the proof of global nonlinear stability of Minkowski [21]. Motivated by the above physically and numerically relevant problems, the study of the existence of maximal hypersurfaces and the corresponding Dirichlet problem was pioneered by Choquet-Bruhat [19] and Brill–Flaherty [12] (see also [4, 24, 37, 39, 30]), but under the restrictive hypotheses on specific spacetimes admitting compact slices and on the boundary data; preliminary results on asymptotically Minkowskian spacetimes in vacuum were also proposed in [16]. papers.title: Desorption of water from cosmic silicates
papers.abstract: Recent JWST and ALMA observations of protoplanetary disks have identified water reservoirs in the inner regions of the disks. This would provide terrestrial planets forming therein access to a water reservoir. In situ formation of water molecules on grain surfaces was proposed as one possible formation process in the PDS 70 system, but transport by small silicate particles coupled to the gas could be another mechanism. Laboratory experiments on the thermally induced desorption of water molecules from different water-containing silicates at elevated temperatures provide another possibility for the enrichment of water molecules in the inner disk. Physically and chemically bound water in silicates can be released upon annealing processes. Water that is physically bound undergoes desorption at temperatures up to 473 K. In contrast, chemically bound water in form of different silanol or Mg-OH groups in amorphous silicates or phyllosilicates, can be released at higher temperatures, ranging from 773 to 923 K. The relevant temperatures are sufficient to trigger the solid-state recrystallization of amorphous silicates to Mg-rich orthopyroxene and olivine. The existence of these crystalline silicates has been substantiated through Spitzer and JWST-MIRI observations. Based on the experimental results, we postulate that the desorption of bound hydroxyl groups may serve as a mechanism for the formation of the water reservoir at temperatures up to 900 K, much higher than the water sublimation temperature of 100 to 200 K.

papers.intro:
Silicates and carbonaceous grains are two prevalent components of cosmic dust [22, 21]. These particles are regarded as precursors and building blocks of planetesimals and eventually planets in the inner regions of protoplanetary disks. In molecular clouds and protoplanetary disks, dust grains are covered by molecular ice layers composed of various molecules, including water, carbon monoxide (CO), carbon dioxide (CO2), ammonia (NH3), methanol (CH3OH), and methane (CH4). The dust grains provide the surface for interstellar ices and create conditions conducive to a rich chemistry in the ice layers and at the interface between ice and dust [8, for a review].

It is generally assumed that icy pebbles transport the material across the snowline, where water ice is converted in water vapour. ALMA observations of the young star HL Tau show centrally peaked bright emission from transitions of the main water isotopologue indicating the presence of water within 17 au [13].

JWST observations of the inner disk of PDS 70 have recently revealed the presence of water vapour in this region [39]. PDS 70 is a protoplanetary disk in the late stage of accretion characterized by a large gap carved by giant planets which reduce the pebble flux. The observed water molecules were found to have temperatures of up to 600 K. This finding indicates the presence of a water reservoir accessible to potential terrestrial planets forming in this region. The authors suggested that the column densities of water indicate the in-situ formation via a reaction sequence involving O, H2, OH, and survival through water self-shielding. Another possibility could be transport of water bound to small silicate particles well-coupled to the gas. The presence of small silicate particles was already substantiated by Spitzer observations and confirmed with JWST/MIRI spectroscopy. The spectrum exhibits both amorphous and crystalline silicate features [39, 32, 25].

The present study involves desorption experiments of various magnesium silicates, each containing different amounts of physisorbed and chemisorbed water. Laboratory silicate dust analogs, as well as natural minerals, were subjected to thermogravimetric analyses. These analyses were used to illustrate the possible enrichment of warmer inner dust regions with water molecules from silicates.

papers.title: A Convex-Analytic Reformulation for Poisoning Attacks on Logistic Regression
papers.abstract: We study data poisoning attacks on logistic regression with $\ell_2$-regularization, where an attacker chooses the features of a fixed number of injected observations with prescribed labels to maximize the logistic loss on the clean training data. Strong convexity of the defender's problem yields an exact reformulation through its first-order optimality conditions. Using convex conjugacy of the softplus function, we replace the sigmoid relations by a single convex optimality-gap inequality and express the attacker's objective as a concave function. A change of variables makes the stationarity condition affine, leaving bounded bilinear equalities as the only nonconvex constraints. We derive finite bounds on all variables involved in these equalities, including a global bound on the coefficient norm and tighter bounds obtained by preprocessing based on convex optimization. Experiments on eight binary classification datasets evaluate attack effectiveness and compare the two reformulations when solved with \textsf{SCIP}. Attacks obtained by local optimization degrade predictive performance on most datasets, while the convex-analytic formulation produces substantially stronger reported dual bounds within a fixed time limit.

papers.title: AgentTorrent: A Dataset of Context and Harness Engineering Artifacts on GitHub
papers.abstract: Over the past months, developers have moved from formulating detailed prompts to engineering the context that agentic coding tools read and to configuring the underlying harnesses. For example, developers commit context files, skills, hooks, and MCP configurations to their repositories, and these files control which instructions a harness reads and which actions it can take. Developers may also commit the specs, plans, and task files that agentic coding tools and spec-driven development frameworks write for agents to implement. The AgentTorrent dataset records these files for six proprietary and open-source agentic coding tools in 10,944 engineered software projects on GitHub. It contains 62,374 configuration artifacts, the files that these artifacts import, 27,593 agentic planning documents, and more than 1.2 million commits that credit an AI tool. All heuristics used for data collection are grounded in tool documentation or derived from GitHub repositories, and we evaluate their detection accuracy with each collection. We use open-weight models to classify whether GitHub repositories host engineered software projects. Unlike most datasets, AgentTorrent links configuration artifacts, imported files, agentic planning documents, and commits that credit an AI tool within the same repositories. Configuration artifacts, planning documents, and credited commits occur together in 388 repositories. For example, our dataset allows researchers to study whether a tool is credited in commits that add instructions for that same tool and how instruction files import and contradict each other. Our data collection pipeline supports regular updates and automatically checks vendor documentation and reports unknown artifacts and agentic coding tools. The dataset and the pipeline are open-source and are archived on Zenodo.

papers.title: Constructing and Validating Memorisation Audits for EHR Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Autoregressive electronic health record (EHR) foundation models may disclose training information at inference, yet clinical predictability makes patient-specific memorisation difficult to distinguish from generalisation. We evaluate fixed-window token reconstruction, sensitive-attribute disclosure, and random patient-level canaries in GPT-2-style models trained on MIMIC-IV, across early, best-validation, and final checkpoints. Reconstruction improves with additional context, but training--held-out differences remain small. Trajectory-unique prompts containing limited clinical information produce no excess sensitive disclosure for training patients. In a matched model with random binary patient-level canaries, training-patient label-recovery AUROC increases from 0.512 to 0.549 while held-out recovery remains at chance. An overfit 1,000-patient positive control achieves near-perfect recovery, confirming sensitivity to strong memorisation. These results reveal weak cohort-level memorisation but no reliable patient-level disclosure under the evaluated attacks. They motivate clinically grounded inference-time audits that can detect patient-specific memorisation in existing models without retraining with canaries.

papers.title: The Calder\'on Problem with Randomly Distributed Resonant Droplets
papers.abstract: We study the recovery of an acoustic coefficient from boundary measurements made after the injection of a collection of small, highly contrasting droplets. This enters into the framework of quantitative ultrasound imaging using contrast agents. The centers are randomly distributed according to a prescribed strictly positive density $\rho\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$. We choose real incident frequencies near an active Newtonian resonance and prove a point-interaction approximation, followed by a comparison with the effective model $(-\Delta+P^2\rho-\omega^2n^2)u=0$. The constants are uniform as the amplitude $P^2$ increases, provided it is coupled to the size and distribution discrepancy of the droplets. A random rounding and displacement construction verifies the distribution assumption for each such given density. The effective Neumann-to-Dirichlet map is then linearized with a remainder of order $P^{-4}$. We derive reconstruction identities using complex geometrical optics solutions of the known reference operator $-\Delta+P^2\rho$. We also estimate the amplification of the boundary-map error in these identities and give a boundary integral correction for reconstruction from the full (and not the linearized) measured map.

papers.title: Wiener-path-based exact and splitting simulation of linear and semi-linear SDEs with additive noise
papers.abstract:
Strong, or pathwise, simulation of stochastic differential equations (SDEs) requires linking a generated SDE path to the corresponding realization of its driving Wiener process. In this work, we develop Wiener-path-based simulation procedures for multidimensional linear and semi-linear SDEs with additive noise that preserve this connection.
  Building upon a known Wiener-path-based exact simulation approach for linear SDEs, we extend this construction to generate coherent paths simultaneously on different time grids. We further propose an alternative exact simulation procedure that requires fewer random numbers and therefore provides a more efficient construction, while retaining a controlled approximation of the coupling between the SDE path and its associated Wiener path. The proposed methods are illustrated on a stochastic harmonic oscillator, a well-known model from classical mechanics, with the simulation results confirming the theoretical findings.
  We then extend the Wiener-path-based construction to semi-linear SDEs, which arise in many real-world applications. In contrast to linear SDEs, their solutions are generally not available in closed form, making numerical approximation methods necessary. For Euler--Maruyama-type methods, the relation between a given Wiener path and the corresponding approximate SDE path is explicit, whereas constructing Wiener-path-based simulations using structure-preserving splitting methods is less immediate. We address this challenge by incorporating the aforementioned Wiener-path-based constructions into splitting methods. Illustrations on the stochastic FitzHugh--Nagumo model and the stochastic Jansen--Rit neural mass model, two important models from neuroscience, demonstrate the applicability of the proposed procedures to non-linear stochastic systems.

papers.title: Git2KG: Mining socio-technical relationships in GitHub repositories as temporal knowledge graphs
papers.abstract: The widespread use of Git and GitHub in open source software (OSS) projects has produced large volumes of data on collaborative software development. Existing approaches to mine those data often use graph models to (i) capture communication between developers in the issue tracker, or (ii) represent developer-developer co-authorship or developer-file code ownership networks from the editing history of code artifacts. Integrating these data in a single knowledge graph (KG) is complicated by the need to disambiguate authors and match entities from multiple sources. Moreover, most works using network analysis have taken a time-aggregated perspective that neglects temporal dynamics of collaborations. To address these issues, we present Git2KG, an extensible Python library that mines temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) from GitHub repositories. Git2KG extracts fine-grained co-editing relations and code ownership from the Git log. It further disambiguates developer identities to align the resulting graphs with management and communication networks extracted from GitHub issue trackers. Git2KG supports temporal analysis by slicing development events into fixed-size, non-overlapping time windows, yielding a series of knowledge graph snapshots per repository. It further supports computing node features and labels for downstream machine learning tasks. Snapshots can then be exported to PyTorch Geometric, PathPyG, and NetworkX for temporal network analysis, visualization, and graph learning.

papers.title: RipBench: A Unified Benchmark for Multi-Level Rip Current Detection, Classification and Segmentation
papers.abstract: Rip currents are a serious and often under-addressed threat to beach safety and the leading cause of coastal drownings worldwide. They are difficult to detect due to their amorphous structure, similarity to the background, and large variability in viewpoints and environments. Despite their dangers and growing interest in automated detection, existing research remains fragmented across datasets, metrics, models, and approaches, leading to an incomplete understanding of model performance. We introduce RipBench, a unified benchmark that enables controlled evaluation of rip current detection spanning multiple tasks, including classification, axis-aligned and oriented object detection, and instance, semantic, and panoptic segmentation, on the same data with standardized splits. This allows direct comparison of model performance on all levels of visual abstraction. Across $304$ videos ($303{,}491$ frames, $51{,}011$ of them annotated for all six tasks) collected from diverse coastlines, our results expose a clear performance gap between coarse recognition and precise spatial understanding: frame-level classification reaches $F_2 = 0.93$, while the best detector and the best instance segmenter reach $0.72$ and $0.66$, with model rankings that change from task to task. Video-level confidence intervals, a blind inter-annotator study of the spatial labels, stratified analyses by viewpoint and visual signature, and video views with temporal baselines (single-seed, short-schedule reference runs) accompany the benchmark. All tasks are supported with carefully curated annotations and evaluated using standard metrics, with a focus on the $F_2$ score to emphasize recall in this safety-critical setting. RipBench, along with multiple baselines per task, is publicly available at https://RipBench.ai to support progress in real-world, multi-task vision for beach safety.

papers.intro:
Rip currents are powerful, fast-moving surface currents that flow seaward from coastlines, posing a significant threat to beachgoers worldwide [6, 9, 19, 38]. Found in oceans, seas, and large lakes, these hazardous flows vary in size and speed, influenced by nearshore hydrodynamics, underwater morphology, and, at times, human-made coastal structures [7, 12]. With speeds reaching up to 8.78.7 km/h, faster than an Olympic swimmer, rip currents can quickly pull individuals offshore [44]. The danger is often exacerbated by a lack of public awareness: swimmers commonly panic and attempt to fight the current, leading to exhaustion and, tragically, drownings. Recommended responses, such as swimming parallel to the shore, are effective only if the current is correctly identified, preferably before entering the water.

Rip currents pose unique vision challenges due to their amorphous, shifting appearance, often blending into the dynamic water environment through subtle cues such as wave breaks, sediment flows, or water color changes. Addressing these complexities requires a combination of tasks, each offering strengths in different scenarios (see Fig. 1). While segmentation provides fine-grained localization, classification can be more suitable for fast presence alerts, bounding boxes offer interpretable localization cues, oriented bounding boxes help capture flow direction and instance segmentation provides both direction and exact shape, at the cost of increased annotation difficulty. Together with semantic and panoptic segmentation to contextualize the broader scene, these tasks enable more flexible and robust detection systems adaptable to diverse beach monitoring settings.

In summary, our contributions include: • Unified multi-level evaluation framework. We introduce practical annotation guidelines (e.g., tighter boxes than full masks) for signal-to-background ratio and evaluation consistency. The box-protocol ablation (Appendix H) shows that neither box protocol consistently improves F2F_{2}, so the guidelines are only meant to standardize evaluation. • Balanced multi-task dataset enabling controlled comparison. RipBench comprises 304 videos (303,491303,491 frames), evenly balanced between rip and non-rip scenarios, with consistent annotations across tasks, standardized splits, and increased temporal coverage through minimum 55 FPS sampling. papers.title: Zero-Field Optical Readout of Quintet States in Through-Space Coupled Tetracene Oligomers at Room Temperature
papers.abstract: Optically addressable electron spins are promising platforms for quantum technologies, with molecular systems offering chemical control over their spin and optical properties. Achieving optical readout of molecular spin states at room temperature and without an applied magnetic field is an important step towards their practical implementation. Quintet states generated via singlet fission are promising optically addressable multilevel qudits, but their intrinsic spin transitions at zero and weak magnetic fields remain largely unexplored, while substantial room-temperature quintet coherence has predominantly been demonstrated in structurally constrained molecular architectures. Here, we combine zero-field optically detected magnetic resonance (zero-field ODMR) with transient and pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) to investigate the magnetic-field dependence and coherent spin properties of quintet states in conformationally flexible, through-space coupled tetracene oligomers. We demonstrate zero-field optical readout of quintet states at room temperature in both tetracene dimers and hexamers, and map the response of optically detected transitions to weak applied magnetic fields. Complementary EPR measurements support quintet formation through stochastic exchange fluctuations and demonstrate a room-temperature phase-memory time of 446 ns, showing that the conformational dynamics enabling high-spin formation remain compatible with substantial spin coherence. Together, these results integrate field-free optical readout, weak-field response and room-temperature spin coherence within a chemically modular, through-space coupled molecular architecture, expanding the design space for optically addressable molecular qudits and quantum sensors.

papers.title: Mott transitions in Dirac nodal-line semimetals
papers.abstract: Nodal-line semimetals provide a natural setting to investigate how the geometry of a nodal manifold affects interaction-driven quantum phase transitions. Here, we study the Hubbard model on a cubic lattice supporting either nodal-point (cubic $\pi$-flux model) or nodal-line semimetallic states using mean-field theory, determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations, and a weak-coupling renormalization-group (RG) analysis. In both cases, antiferromagnetic order develops only above a finite interaction strength, with the nodal-line system exhibiting a smaller critical coupling due to its enhanced low-energy density of states and markedly stronger finite-size effects. For the nodal-point model, the quantum critical behavior is compatible with $(3+1)$-dimensional Gross--Neveu mean-field scaling. In contrast, the weak-coupling RG reveals that the nodal line itself is unstable against interactions: although the Hubbard interaction is perturbatively irrelevant, its second-order self-energy generates a symmetry-allowed relevant term proportional to $U^2\cos k_z$, reconstructing the nodal line into isolated, strongly anisotropic nodal points. This weak-coupling reconstruction is distinct from the strong-coupling antiferromagnetic transition and highlights the role of nodal-manifold geometry in interacting semimetals.
