papers.intro:
Topological semimetals have attracted considerable attention as systems in which the low-energy electronic structure is governed by symmetry-protected band touchings. In Dirac and Weyl semimetals, the conduction and valence bands touch at isolated points in the Brillouin zone, giving rise to quasiparticles with linear dispersion around the nodal points [4, 39]. In three dimensions, Dirac semimetals may appear either at the transition between topologically distinct insulating phases or as stable semimetallic phases protected by crystalline symmetries [41, 1]. The pointlike character of the Fermi surface leads to a density of states that vanishes as ρ⁡(ω)∼ω2\rho(\omega)\sim\omega^{2}, rendering weak short-range interactions perturbatively irrelevant [21].

In Dirac and Weyl semimetals, the conduction and valence bands touch at isolated points in the Brillouin zone, giving rise to quasiparticles with linear dispersion around the nodal points [4, 39]. In three dimensions, Dirac semimetals may appear either at the transition between topologically distinct insulating phases or as stable semimetallic phases protected by crystalline symmetries [41, 1]. The pointlike character of the Fermi surface leads to a density of states that vanishes as ρ⁡(ω)∼ω2\rho(\omega)\sim\omega^{2}, rendering weak short-range interactions perturbatively irrelevant [21].

Despite this weak-coupling stability, three-dimensional Dirac systems may display nontrivial many-body and disorder-driven phenomena. Long-range Coulomb interactions can renormalize quasiparticle properties and, at sufficiently strong coupling, drive dynamical mass generation or excitonic instabilities [9, 38]. Short-range interactions may also destabilize the semimetal and generate scalar, pseudoscalar, or axionic insulating masses [29]. In addition, disorder can induce transitions from an incompressible Dirac semimetal to a compressible diffusive metal and, at stronger disorder, to an Anderson insulating phase [27, 29, 8, 32]. These results establish three-dimensional Dirac semimetals as a useful toy model for studying the interplay between topology, correlations, and randomness.

These results establish three-dimensional Dirac semimetals as a useful toy model for studying the interplay between topology, correlations, and randomness.

A particularly useful lattice realization of three-dimensional Dirac fermions is the cubic π\pi-flux model [12]. In this system, each plaquette encloses a π\pi flux, and the noninteracting spectrum hosts linearly dispersing Dirac cones. The Hubbard model on this lattice has been investigated using determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations, which showed that the Dirac semimetal remains stable against weak onsite repulsion and undergoes a direct transition to an antiferromagnetic insulating phase only above a finite critical interaction [13]. For three-dimensional Dirac fermions, the corresponding Gross–Neveu–Yukawa theory lies at its upper critical spacetime dimension dc=4d_{c}=4, such that the critical behavior is Gaussian up to logarithmic corrections [25].

Nodal-line semimetals provide a natural extension of this setting. In these systems, the conduction and valence bands touch not at isolated points, but along one-dimensional manifolds in momentum space, which may form loops, chains, or more complex structures [7, 19]. The stability of these nodal lines is generally tied to crystalline or internal symmetries, such as time-reversal, inversion, mirror, or glide symmetry [18]. When the protecting symmetry is broken, the nodal line may become fully gapped or evolve into other topological band structures. Compared with a three-dimensional Dirac cone, a nodal-line semimetal has a larger low-energy phase space. Therefore, interaction effects are expected to be enhanced relative to point-node Dirac systems, although the vanishing density of states at the Fermi level still suggests that a stable weak-coupling semimetallic regime may survive. Indeed, related studies of excitonic quantum criticality in ZrSiS suggest that nodal-line systems may also display strong quasiparticle mass renormalization near a semimetal–excitonic-insulator quantum critical point, even in regimes where a full gap is not observed experimentally [38].

Field-theoretical studies based on renormalization-group and Gross–Neveu–Yukawa approaches have shown that short-range interactions can drive continuous quantum phase transitions from a nodal-line semimetal into fully gapped phases in charge, spin, and superconducting channels [15]. In these approaches, the many-body instability occurs only beyond a finite interaction strength, and the critical exponents depend on the number of order-parameter components. In particular, the dynamical critical exponent is found to be z=1z=1 at one-loop order, while the remaining exponents acquire corrections associated with the anomalous dimension of the bosonic order parameter [15].

papers.title: Work extraction from a single negative-temperature bath: a temperature gradient-driven heat flow
papers.abstract: Work dissipation into a thermal bath is standard, whereas the reverse process -- sole work extraction from a thermal bath without a net state change -- contradicts the Kelvin-Planck formulation of the second law of thermodynamics. However, this prohibition is bypassed for baths at negative absolute temperature, sparking ongoing debate regarding their thermodynamic stability. Here, we reconcile the second law with sole work extraction from a negative-temperature bath by considering a large virtual assembly of weakly coupled working systems rather than an isolated machine. By assigning this assembly a canonical temperature derived from its Shannon/information entropy, the framework naturally extends to molecular-scale machines. We demonstrate paradigmatic examples where the assembly's canonical temperature is cooler than the negative-temperature bath. Consequently, sole work extraction represents standard heat flow from a hot system (the negative-temperature bath) to a cooler system (the working assembly), rendering the process fully consistent with the second law. This informational and statistical-mechanical framework also naturally explains the counter-intuitive phenomenon of "donkey behavior", where increasing the workload in a negative-temperature bath leads to enhanced work extraction.

In summary, one gets for a working machine in contact with some bath: at positive temperatures work can be transformed/dissipated into heat within the bath. This reformulation of the 2nd law sounds awkward because it distinguishes between the sign of the bath’s temperature. Struchtrup avoided this by denying the “real” existence of negative temperatures [6, 7], and instead he considered them as apparent phenomena and as some kind of non-equilibrium parameter. In contrast, our concept accepts negative temperatures of the bath in the same way as positive ones. papers.title: Unconstrained $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory on a triangular lattice: deconfined fermions in a vison crystal and superfluidity
papers.abstract: We investigate an unconstrained $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory coupled to fermions on the triangular lattice at half filling, using auxiliary field quantum Monte Carlo simulations. The triangular geometry gives rise to a global $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry that acts as an Ising symmetry on the plaquette fluxes. At weak transverse field $h$, this symmetry is spontaneously broken, stabilizing a vison crystal. We argue that this phase is deconfined: fermions, charged under an emergent $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge field, propagate in an ordered $\pi$-flux background and form a Dirac semimetal. Increasing the transverse field triggers a first-order quantum phase transition to a confined $s$-wave superfluid, at which confinement and global symmetry breaking occur simultaneously. This contrasts with the square lattice, where the corresponding transition is continuous. We extend our analysis to finite temperature and determine the thermal phase boundaries of both ordered phases. The superfluid melts through a Kosterlitz--Thouless transition, whereas the vison crystal undergoes a thermal Ising transition. Together, our results establish the $T \times h$ phase diagram and demonstrate how the triangular geometry leads to qualitative changes in both the phases and the criticality of the model.

papers.intro:
Gauge theories play an important role in our understanding of phases of matter in the solid state. They very naturally emerge in parton constructions of spin [2, 1, 55], Kondo lattice [11, 12, 41] and tt-JJ models [32]. In this approach the local emergent gauge symmetry stems from the redundancy of the parton representation [56]. The Kitaev spin model is a canonical example since the parton construction in terms of Majorana fermions paves the way to an exact solution [29]. Parton constructions are not the only route to gauge theories. For instance, spin ice with its two-in/two-out constraint – corresponding to the Gauss law – is a classical example of a U(1) gauge theory [10] hosting monopoles and emergent photons. As already hinted, gauge theories provide a framework to understand phases of matter. This includes spin liquids, broadly defined as a deconfined phase of an emergent gauge theory [6], the heavy fermion phase in Kondo lattice models as a Higgs phase of a U(1) gauge theory [11, 12, 43], and Kondo destruction [48].

Usual constructions use the U(1) or SU(2) groups [55, 52, 20, 54]. The decoupling in terms of a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge field can be viewed as a Higgs descendant of the U(1) decoupling [50].

In this work, we study an unconstrained ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} lattice gauge theory coupled to Nf=2N_{f}=2 fermionic matter on the triangular lattice using numerically exact auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AF-QMC) simulations. By unconstrained, we mean that the Gauss operators are locally conserved, but their eigenvalues are not fixed, such that Gauss’s law will be dynamically imposed at low energies [57, 25]. On the square lattice, this model has been studied extensively, and shows a plethora of phases [4, 18] and exotic quantum phase transitions [17]. On bipartite lattices, the model with NfN_{f} fermion flavors has a global O​(2​Nf)\text{O}(2N_{f}) symmetry and no sign problem for all values of NfN_{f}. The model is defined by a single parameter, corresponding to the strength of the transverse field hh. In the hh versus NfN_{f} phase diagram, we observed orthogonal semi-metallic (OSM) [36], antiferromagnetic (AFM), charge density wave (CDW) and valence bond solid (VBS) states. Quantum phase transitions include deconfined quantum critical points at Nf=3N_{f}=3 between VBS and AFM orders [49] as well as continuous and direct quantum phase transitions between the OSM and confined AFM phases with emergent SO(5) symmetry [17]. The model of Ref. [4] is free of the negative sign problem even on frustrated lattices.

It is known that the lattice geometry, in particular whether or not it is bipartite, has a profound impact on the phase diagrams of gauge theories. The canonical example is the quantum dimer model, which on bipartite lattices has a mapping onto height models and emergent U(1) symmetry, but on the triangular lattice provides an instance of a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid [35]. The bipartiteness of the underlying lattice can also influence the type and relevance of low-energy excitations. In Dirac spin liquids, the square lattice formulation is unstable due to relevant monopole excitations, while on the triangular lattice it is stable since these excitations are irrelevant [52]. Therefore, given the aforementioned differences of dimer and spin models on bipartite and frustrated lattices, it is natural to inquire into the nature of the phase diagram of the unconstrained ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge theory on a triangular lattice and whether a spin liquid state is stable.

papers.title: Adaptive carrier signal synthesis for frequency-division multiplexed cryogenic detector readout
papers.abstract: Frequency-domain multiplexing is a fundamental technology for readout of cryogenic detector arrays on a single transmission line. Synthesizing a large number of static carrier tones for resonator stimulation eventually drives the cryogenic low-noise amplifier beyond its P1dB, introducing detector signal distortion. Scaling array sizes to O(10^6) detector pixels therefore demands minimizing the total power on the transmission line by continuous tracking of the resonances, which requires the readout electronics to be capable of updating the carrier tones dynamically. This work presents an scalable FPGA-based implementation for carrier signal synthesis based on a numerically controlled oscillator and a polyphase filter bank, enabling real-time frequency adaptivity as well as frequency resolution of 4 mHz to precisely tune the operating point, while simultaneously reducing resource usage compared to the current memory-based implementation.
papers.intro:
Large-scale cryogenic detector arrays require dedicated readout electronics to benefit from the superior energy resolution of superconducting sensors. Using fdm (fdm) schemes, multiple detectors are operated on a single transmission line by inductively coupling the detector pixels to individual resonator circuits. The high-level readout concept is shown in figure 1, based on an sdr (sdr) for synthesizing a frequency comb with the resonance frequencies and analyzing the carrier signal modulation to reconstruct the detector signals.

Large-scale cryogenic detector arrays require dedicated readout electronics to benefit from the superior energy resolution of superconducting sensors. Using fdm (fdm) schemes, multiple detectors are operated on a single transmission line by inductively coupling the detector pixels to individual resonator circuits. The high-level readout concept is shown in figure 1, based on an sdr (sdr) for synthesizing a frequency comb with the resonance frequencies and analyzing the carrier signal modulation to reconstruct the detector signals.

In our current-generation systems [7, 6], the carrier signals for resonator stimulation are synthesized with an awg (awg)-like module. This module is implemented on the sdr’s FPGA in form of a memory which stores the precomputed, reloadable time-domain samples of the comb. However, the required memory scales linearly with the instantaneous bandwidth and the frequency resolution of the carrier tones, and dynamic frequency changes are not possible. These drawbacks limit further scalability of the readout electronics, both towards wider frequency bands as well as higher channel counts, which requires precise frequency tuning and real-time carrier tone adaptivity for advanced features like tone tracking [13] or active resonator feedback [4]. In this work, adaptive frequency comb generation based on a pps (pps) is presented, eliminating the limitations of the awg and offering a scalable, resource-efficient implementation.

papers.title: What Limits Thermal Infrared Drone Detection? A Cross-Dataset Benchmark Analysis
papers.abstract: Thermal infrared (IR) imaging enables drone detection with reduced dependence on ambient illumination, supporting continuous surveillance beyond the limitations of visible-spectrum sensing. However, substantial and often undocumented variability in camera systems, processing pipelines, and annotation practices across public IR drone datasets complicates the assessment of detector performance and cross-domain generalization. To examine these sources of variability and their implications for drone detection, we systematically characterize existing IR datasets and establish an artifact taxonomy reflecting their origins across the acquisition and processing pipeline, encompassing optical and sensor effects, tone mapping and image enhancement, and recording-related artifacts. Focusing on long-wave IR data, we investigate the impact of training data composition and model characteristics on YOLO-based detection performance, generalization, and condition-dependent failure modes. Our results demonstrate that detection performance is governed more strongly by training data composition than by YOLO generation or model capacity, while cross-dataset generalization exhibits pronounced asymmetries. Even the best-performing configuration fails to detect over 40\% of drones, with elevated miss rates for very small targets, cluttered urban backgrounds, and thermal crossover, highlighting the shortcomings of existing datasets.

papers.intro:
The growing accessibility and operational capabilities of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), commonly known as drones, present increasingly complex challenges for low-altitude airspace surveillance and critical infrastructure protection [21]. Unauthorized or malicious drone operations pose risks to public safety, critical infrastructure, and operational continuity [12], particularly in densely populated urban environments. Early and reliable drone detection is therefore essential for effective surveillance and threat mitigation [12]. Camera-based systems – particularly those operating in the visible (RGB) spectrum – offer a promising and cost-effective approach, combining passive operation and compatibility with existing surveillance infrastructure. Coupled with deep learning (DL) architectures such as You Only Look Once (YOLO) [20], these systems support automated drone detection through real-time image analysis [30, 14]. However, RGB-based detection remains sensitive to adverse illumination and visibility conditions [12]. By capturing emitted thermal radiation rather than reflected visible light, infrared (IR) imaging reduces reliance on ambient illumination [29], providing a complementary modality for continuous, day-and-night drone surveillance.

To address this gap, this work makes three contributions: (i) We systematically characterize publicly available IR drone datasets and establish a taxonomy of artifacts based on their origin along the imaging pipeline. papers.title: Learning Quantum Hamiltonians from the Dynamical Structure Factor
papers.abstract: Identifying the microscopic interactions governing a quantum system is essential for developing predictive theories of materials and validating quantum technologies. Despite considerable progress, learning Hamiltonians from realistic experimental data remains a challenge. Motivated by neutron scattering and quantum simulations, we study the problem of learning a quantum Hamiltonian from the dynamical structure factor (DSF), which captures two-point correlation data in quantum magnets. We show that the DSF encodes sufficient information to efficiently reconstruct broad classes of quantum Hamiltonians. Our approach exploits simple relations between low-order spectral moments of the DSF and microscopic couplings, giving rise to three complementary Hamiltonian tomography protocols based on the high-temperature expansion, strong-field polarization, and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, respectively. The framework we introduce establishes practical and robust Hamiltonian learning from common experimental data, with potentially immediate application to neutron scattering experiments.

papers.intro:
Quantum systems are typically well-described by a local Hamiltonian, specified by a small number of couplings, from which rich collective phenomena such as symmetry breaking, topological order, and quantum criticality can emerge. Constraining and characterizing the Hamiltonian from experimental data presents a recurring challenge across physics, from particle phenomenology to quantum materials. This task of Hamiltonian learning enables one to extract effective models governing the quantum system over energy and length scales of interest, informing theoretical analyses and subsequent experimental refinements. In condensed matter, Hamiltonian learning facilitates the design of quantum materials with targeted properties [48, 1, 23, 31, 53]; in quantum simulation and device engineering, it is essential for benchmarking, calibration, and building scalable platforms with verifiable performance [24, 11, 38, 12, 10, 52, 61, 59].

Hamiltonian learning has prompted many empirical and theoretical approaches, drawing on tools from quantum information and machine learning [60, 27, 13, 3, 2, 29, 6, 35, 67, 30, 65, 56, 69, 4]. A common empirical approach, applied successfully to certain quantum magnets [17, 18, 45], falls into the framework of model fitting, involving iteratively updating a model prediction and classical simulation until convergence to experiment. For generic quantum systems, however, model fitting is computationally prohibitive to scale to large system size, leaving open the existence of a general, scalable approach under realistic experimental measurement constraints. More systematic theoretical approaches often presuppose global digital access to arbitrary measurements. Experimental platforms nevertheless typically operate with far more limited control: Measurements in quantum materials are usually limited to observables characterizing responses to external probe fields, while in quantum simulators, access can be restricted to a few native local observables or correlation functions due to architectural and resource constraints.

It is a priori far from clear that the DSF alone provides sufficient information to recover the entire Hamiltonian. Indeed, while the DSF contains information on magnon dispersions and other spinful excitations, it encodes only a slice of two-point correlation data—a small portion of all observables. Although several machine-learning studies provide empirical evidence of this task’s tractability, at least for specific models with a few free parameters [16, 46], the well-posedness of this inverse problem has not been theoretically established. Indeed, building on known hardness bounds for learning from Gibbs states [29], we rigorously demonstrate that it can be ill-posed: We identify continuous families of few-body Hamiltonians that exhibit identical DSFs. Moreover, even when the inverse problem is in principle well-posed, the DSF potentially depends on Hamiltonian couplings in a highly complex fashion that can in practice stymie finding the inversion needed to learn the Hamiltonian.

In this work, we develop a versatile framework for Hamiltonian tomography from the DSF [Fig. 1a]. Our framework does not require simulation of the Hamiltonian and comes with rigorous guarantees for general classes of Hamiltonians across several broad experimentally relevant regimes, thus providing strong evidence that the aforementioned challenges do not impede practical learnability. Our central insight is that the microscopic Hamiltonian parameters can be extracted from explicit relations, or sum rules, among integrated frequency moments of the DSF [Fig. 1b]. In particular, we provide three scalable Hamiltonian learning algorithms that we dub high-temperature, strong-field, and fluctuation-dissipation protocols—each taming the complex dependence of the DSF on Hamiltonian parameters in complementary regimes [Fig. 1c; see Table 1 for an executive summary]. These protocols respectively rely on a high-temperature expansion, perturbation theory around a strong polarizing Zeeman field, and nontrivial exact identities satisfied by the DSF due to stationarity of thermal states and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Extensive numerical tests across one- and two-dimensional Hamiltonian families demonstrate appreciable robustness of our protocols to measurement noise and experimental imperfections. Together, these results establish a direct, practical, and scalable route to learning Hamiltonians from limited, physically relevant output of quantum experiments.

papers.title: Development of Sapphire-Based Solid-State Neutron Detectors for Fusion Environments
papers.abstract: Single-crystal diamond is the reference solid-state technology for fast neutron detection in fusion devices. Despite this, its complex manufacturing increases their costs and puts limitations on their geometry. Moreover, the limits in their long-term stability and their behaviour in harsh environments further constraint its applications. Synthetic sapphire (Al2O2) is a promising alternative as a solid state detector material: it is available in large, low-cost wafers and features both a wider bandgap and a higher displacement energy compared to diamond. Despite this, it has so far received little-to-no attention as a neutron detector. This work presents the first steps of a development programme for sapphire-based fast neutron detectors. Eight prototypes with 4.5 x 4.5 mm2 and 9 x 9 mm2 active areas and 625 um thickness were fabricated from commercial wafers with Al-Si electrodes and coupled to different electronic configurations. All prototypes detected 5.47 MeV alpha particles from a 241Am source, confirming the viability of both the fabrication process and the use of sapphire as an active material. The small signals (30-40 mV over a peak-to-peak noise of about 8 mV) and the count rate increasing with bias indicate that sapphires will require higher electric fields than the ones experimented in the work (up to about 2.5 kV). Geant4 simulations were also used to estimate the response of a sapphire detector to 14.06 MeV (DT) neutrons, highlighting the perspectives of the detector as a fusion diagnostic.

papers.title: Detection of 2 MeV spectral bump and ~40 MeV emission line from GRB 221009A
papers.abstract: Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are the most energetic transients in the Universe, but prompt MeV--sub-GeV observations remain challenging with current gamma-ray observatories. Here, using unsaturated HEPP-H measurements on board CSES-01 and cross-calibrating with likewise unsaturated GECAM-C data, we reconstruct the continuous spectral evolution of GRB 221009A over 2--255 MeV. We identify an unusual spectral bump at $\sim$2 MeV in the first light-curve peak. We also confirm a narrow emission line whose energy decreases from $\sim$40 MeV following a $t^{-1}$ evolution, and whose flux shows a ``rise-then-fall'' profile, implying weak emission from the central jet. These findings hint that a magnetically dominated, central-empty jet exists in the BOAT.

papers.intro:
Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are the most energetic and violent astrophysical phenomena in the universe. The study of their prompt emission in the MeV–sub-GeV range is crucial to investigate the poorly known physics of the GRB central engines and their released relativistic jets (Zhang, 2019). GRBs mainly emit photons in the MeV domain, with spectral peaks typically lying around a few hundred keV. The prompt emission beyond MeV is expected to bring key information on the central engine and relativistic jets. However, the precise observations of the prompt emission from GRBs are conventionally hindered by a long sought-after MeV–sub-GeV gamma-ray gap (Schönfelder, 2004). This energy range represents the region where Compton and Pair events overlap (Kanbach et al., 2005), resulting in an inherently worse detection sensitivity (Schoenfelder et al., 1993). Bright GRBs are important in this matter, but they are generally rare.

An unprecedented opportunity emerged when GRB 221009A shattered records of GRB brightness. The initial real-time trigger of GRB 221009A was provided by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope’s Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (GBM) (Lesage et al., 2023), but its exceptional brightness caused severe instrumental saturation effects for GBM during the brightest phase. In contrast, the Insight-Hard X-ray Modulation Telescope (Insight-HXMT) recorded high-resolution unsaturated data, thus we adopt its trigger time, Tref=T_{\rm ref}= 13:17:00.050 UT (Zheng et al., 2024), as the reference time for our analysis here. The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory (Swift) provided the first accurate localization of this burst (Williams et al., 2023), which enables a worldwide multi-wavelength observations and the redshift measurement (z=0.151z=0.151) (de Ugarte Postigo et al., 2022; Malesani et al., 2025). Notably, the Gravitational Wave High-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor-C (GECAM-C, also known as HEBS) provided unsaturated measurements, which measures an isotropic equivalent energy of Eiso∼1.5×1055E_{\text{iso}}\sim 1.5\times 10^{55} erg and confirms GRB 221009A as the brightest of all time (BOAT) (An et al., 2023; Burns et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2026). The extreme brightness of this burst leads to several record breaking discoveries. The Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) detected more than 64,000 photons above 0.2 TeV within the first 3,000 seconds (LHAASO Collaboration et al., 2023). Line emission of ∼10\sim 10 MeV is historically discovered in the BOAT using Fermi/GBM data (Ravasio et al., 2024). papers.title: Quasars as a self-sufficient probe of the distance duality relation
papers.abstract: The distance duality relation links luminosity and angular diameter distances under standard photon propagation. It is usually tested by combining distances from different probes, which requires matching their redshifts and assuming sky isotropy. Self-sufficient probes, which measure both distances for the same object, avoid the first requirement and make the second testable. We assess whether quasars can serve as such probes, combining luminosity distances from the UV--X-ray relation with angular diameter distances from spectroastrometry and reverberation mapping (SARM). As a proof-of-concept, we apply the test to the quasar Mrk~509 and find $\eta\equiv d_{\rm L}/[(1+z)^2d_{\rm A}] = 0.50^{+0.61}_{-0.27}$, consistent with no violation at $0.8\sigma$. We then forecast the number of quasars needed to detect a constant and a linearly redshift-dependent violation, motivated by the findings of Teixeira et al. (2025) with potential implications for the Hubble tension and dark energy. A constant violation, $\alpha_0=-0.075$, equivalent to a recalibration of the SNIa distance scale, could be detected at $3\sigma$ with 274--840 quasars. Since SARM distances, unlike BAO, do not rely on early-time physics, this would separate an early-time origin of the Hubble tension from a SNIa miscalibration or a distance duality violation. The redshift dependence is harder to detect: 1000 quasars would exclude $\eta=1$ at $3.4$--$6.6\sigma$, but detecting the dependence itself requires $2.6\times10^4$--$8\times10^4$. GRAVITY+ could bring quasar tests of a constant violation within reach.

Under standard metric photon propagation, its most natural physical interpretation is a test of cosmic transparency, where a measurable violation of this relation would signal the presence of exotic physics such as photon–axion mixing [19, 14, 11], or a non-minimal coupling between electromagnetism and a scalar field, which would result in a varying of the fine-structure constant [30]; or more prosaic phenomena such as scattering by dust in the intergalactic medium. To detect violations of the distance duality relation, measurements of luminosity and angular diameter distances are needed, with the canonical examples in cosmology being SNIa [16] and BAO [23]. Other works have proposed using gravitational waves from standard sirens [31, 20]; HII galaxies [45, 67]; gamma-ray bursts [65, 7, 64]; megamasers [36]; and cosmic chronometers [13]. However, SNIa and BAO measurements are unlikely to cover exactly the same range of redshifts. For example, the angular diameter distances derived from the DESI DR2 BAO lie at seven effective redshifts between z=0.295z=0.295 and z=2.33z=2.33 [1], whereas the Pantheon+ compilation contains 1550 SNIa spread over 0.001<z<2.260.001<z<2.26 [57, 17]. This means that any constraint on the violation of the distance duality relation from these data must be made by interpolating the luminosity distances to the BAO redshifts and extrapolating out to the highest-redshift BAO measurement, which lies beyond the entire supernova sample. This is done either by making assumptions about the underlying cosmology or by employing machine learning [37] or Gaussian process reconstruction [41] methods.

[33]. However, tests of the distance duality relation based on measurements of luminosity and angular diameter distances for different probes inherently rely on assumptions of isotropy. This problem could be addressed by ‘self-sufficient’ probes of the distance duality relation, namely single objects for which both luminosity and angular diameter distances can be measured simultaneously. When the two distances are obtained from different probes, such as SNIa and BAO, isotropy must be assumed in order to compare them; BAO distances in particular, are essentially averages over large areas of the sky. A self-sufficient probe instead tests the distance duality relation along each individual line of sight to the given object. A quasar is a highly luminous active galactic nucleus (AGN), driven by the accretion of gas onto the central supermassive black hole [50]. Their brightness means they are observable at extremely high redshifts, e.g. z=7.5z=7.5 [46] to z=10z=10 [63], and their luminosities can be standardised [48, 46, 56]. Furthermore, angular diameter distances to them can be measured, either from the empirically calibrated sizes of compact radio cores [38, 29, 18], or geometrically, by combining spectroastrometry with reverberation mapping [24, 62, 42, 43], making quasars a powerful probe of cosmology.

papers.title: Development and characterization of monolithic sensors with internal gain in a 110 nm CMOS process
papers.abstract: This paper presents the optimization and characterization of a Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor with internal gain implemented in the 110 nm CMOS process from LFoundry. This work, carried out within the framework of the latest ARCADIA production run, reports on the characterization of sensors with an optimized gain layer. Improvements over earlier prototypes, including substrate current reduction via guard-ring connection, are briefly discussed. Both laboratory and in-beam measurements are presented. Using soft X-rays from a 55Fe source, both the pixel response and the noise performance are analyzed. In addition, laser measurements demonstrate an electronic jitter ranging from 20 to 40 ps for a signal amplitude corresponding to one minimum ionizing particle (MIP). Finally, the results from several test beam campaigns are described, showing the signal amplitude, gain and time resolution of sensors with different doping profiles of the gain layer evaluated with MIPs. A time resolution of about 78 ps was measured in the optimal condition of bias voltage and electronics configuration. The results demonstrate that monolithic CMOS sensors with internal gain can achieve promising timing performance at ambient temperature, highlighting their strong potential for next-generation precision timing applications.

papers.intro:
Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS), implemented using standard CMOS processes, are currently one of the most promising technologies for a wide range of applications, including high-energy physics, medical imaging, and space experiments [3, 2, 5]. MAPS offer several advantages over traditional hybrid pixel detector technologies. In particular, they can be fabricated at relatively low cost even for large-area arrays, while maintaining a low material budget and a reduced power consumption. The upcoming high-energy physics experiments and future particle detectors will demand more stringent requirements, including handling unprecedented pile-up levels [17, 14]. Consequently, detectors will be required to provide enhanced spatial granularity and excellent time resolution in order to efficiently disentangle overlapping interactions and ensure efficient event reconstruction and background discrimination. Moreover, an outstanding time resolution is crucial for Particle IDentification (PID), where precise timing information will significantly improve the separation of particle species over a broad momentum range. In this context, current developments aim at achieving time resolutions of about 30-40 ps for experiments such as ATLAS and CMS [9, 6], and down to approximately 20 ps for next-generation detectors like ALICE 3 [21][11]. Overall, these challenges necessitate significant technological advancements in detector design, and the scientific community is actively working to enhance the timing performance. Currently, monolithic technologies are the primary choice for tracking detector applications, where outstanding efficiency, spatial resolution, low material budget, and high radiation hardness are key requirements. For instance, the ALPIDE sensors employed in the ALICE ITS2 have demonstrated a detection efficiency above 99% after irradiation up to a non-ionizing fluence of 1.7×10131.7~\times~10^{13} 1 MeV neq/cm2n_{\mathrm{eq}}/\mathrm{cm}^{2} [19]. More recently, Analog Pixel Test Structures (APTS) developed in 65 nm CMOS technology for the ALICE ITS3 upgrade have maintained detection efficiencies above 99% up to a fluence of 101410^{14} 1 MeV neq/cm2n_{\mathrm{eq}}/\mathrm{cm}^{2}, one order of magnitude above the ITS3 radiation hardness requirement [2]. However, no large-scale monolithic demonstrator has been produced for HEP applications with sub 50 ps timing resolution requirements, such as the case of the Time-Of-Flight (TOF) detector of the proposed ALICE 3 experiment. Several R&D projects are currently underway to demonstrate the feasibility of achieving timing resolutions of O(10 ps) with monolithic devices [1, 24, 12]. Nevertheless, this timing performance is currently achieved only by prototype implementations, which do not yet fulfill the requirements of large-scale experiments, such as low power consumption and scalability to large areas. Indeed, in some cases, the power consumption remains prohibitively high, or the front-end electronics is integrated outside the pixel to reduce the sensor capacitance. The three main ingredients to achieve good timing performance are: • a fast charge collection, enabled by a full depletion of the sensor; • the optimization of the device geometry and the electric field profile to reduce the distortion term contribution to the time resolution [31]; • a high Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), which can be increased by adding a gain layer below the collection electrode, enabling charge multiplication, as in the case of the Low Gain Avalanche Diode (LGAD).

papers.title: Development of a Cryogenic Anti-Coincidence System Based on Scintillating Crystals Read Out with Kinetic Inductance Detectors for BULLKID-DM
papers.abstract: The BULLKID-DM experiment has been proposed to search for WIMP-like dark matter particles with a mass of 1 GeV or lower and with a WIMP-nucleon interaction cross section down to $10^{-43}$ cm$^2$. To achieve this goal, the experiment utilizes a detector consisting of a stack of 16 silicon wafers instrumented with phonon-mediated superconducting Kinetic Inductance Detectors (KIDs), to be operated at the underground facility of the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS), Italy. To reduce the residual background arising from $\gamma$-rays, neutrons, and muons, a cryogenic active anti-coincidence system (veto) operating at mK temperature, surrounding the main detector, is under development. The veto detector consists of segmented scintillating crystals read out by phonon-mediated KID light detectors. Current status and future developments of the veto system are presented. In particular, we focus on cryogenic tests of both bismuth germanate (BGO) and gadolinium aluminum gallium garnet (GAGG) crystals, which had been previously chosen as veto candidate crystals according to our preliminary studies on the dependence of their optical properties (i.e. light yield and scintillation decay time) on temperature. We finally present the operation and preliminary tests of a two-module veto prototype with multiplexed readout.

papers.intro:
BULLKID-DM [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] aims to search for WIMP-like dark matter particles with masses of 1 GeV or below. The proposed detector consists of a stack of 16 silicon wafers, each instrumented with an array of 145 Kinetic Inductance Detectors (KIDs) to gather phonons produced by particle interactions in a silicon target. Deep grooves machined into the face opposite the KID array divide each silicon wafer into 145 dice, each measuring 4.5×5×5​mm34.5\times 5\times 5~\mathrm{mm}^{3}. Each KID reads out one die. The main advantage of this segmentation is background rejection through anticoincidence between dice and the definition of a fiducial volume, with the outer dice acting as an active veto. The detector has already demonstrated an energy threshold as low as 200​eV200~\mathrm{eV}, suitable for probing dark matter with masses around 1​GeV/c21~\mathrm{GeV}/c^{2}, for which the nuclear recoil endpoint in silicon is of order 500​eV500~\mathrm{eV}. The combination of this threshold, a total target mass of approximately 0.8​kg0.8~\mathrm{kg}, and the large number of multiplexed channels enabling segmentation and background rejection is designed to set new limits on the WIMP–nucleon interaction cross section in the targeted mass range. The experiment will be operated underground at Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS) in Italy, where the muon intensity is reduced by six orders of magnitude with respect to the Earth’s surface and rock radioactivity has been measured to be lower than in other underground laboratories [8, 9, 10]. . An active anticoincidence detector is being developed to complement the passive shielding and bring the background rate in the target detector down to 0.1​counts​kg−1​day−1​keV−10.1~\mathrm{counts\,kg^{-1}\,day^{-1}\,keV^{-1}}. This veto consists of a layer of scintillating crystals read out by KID-based light detectors [11]. In this contribution, we provide an overview of this detector and report the latest developments, focusing on millikelvin tests of selected crystals and the operation of a two-module veto prototype with multiplexed readout.

papers.title: Robustness of the Baryonic Acoustic Oscillation Peak Position against Monopole Fluctuations in Galaxy Surveys
papers.abstract: Precise measurements of the baryonic acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak position are one of the key goals in modern galaxy surveys. We investigate the impact of the monopole fluctuations in galaxy surveys on the BAO peak position in the galaxy two-point redshift-space multipole-correlation functions. The background mean density of a galaxy sample is estimated from the survey itself by averaging the observed galaxy number density, and this averaged number density (monopole) is subtracted to obtain the observed galaxy number density fluctuation, which includes an additional contribution from the monopole fluctuations, propagating to galaxy clustering analysis. We compute the contributions of the monopole fluctuations to the redshift-space multipole-correlation functions. While the monopole contributions in galaxy two-point correlation function are anisotropic and non-negligible in amplitude, the contributions are so smooth around the BAO peak position that they are almost completely absorbed in the BAO broadband model, leaving the BAO peak position unaffected at the sub-percent level. Our results demonstrate the robustness of the BAO analysis against the unknown systematic error.
papers.intro:
Measurements of the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) signals in galaxy clustering are one of the principal methods to map the expansion history of the Universe in modern galaxy surveys (see, e.g., [1, 2, 3] for recent reviews). Originating from the tight coupling of photons and baryons in the early Universe [4, 5], these sound waves in the baryon-photon plasma leave a characteristic imprint in both the cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropies and galaxy clustering. The BAO signature in galaxy clustering manifests itself as a distinct peak in the galaxy two-point correlation function or a series of oscillations in the galaxy power spectrum. Since the comoving scale of the BAO signature is determined by the sound horizon at the end of the baryon drag epoch and is precisely constrained by CMB observations [6, 7], measurements of the BAO signature in the observed redshift and angle provide robust measurements of the Hubble parameter and angular diameter distance to the redshift of the galaxy sample. Using the measurements from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) [8], the first BAO detection was achieved in 2005 [9]. In the following years, observational cosmology has seen a dramatic increase in the development of large-scale galaxy surveys with spectroscopic measurements and increasingly larger redshift ranges, such as the 6-degree Field Galaxy Survey (6dFGS) [10], WiggleZ [11], and the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) [12]. The success of these programs enabled precise measurements of the distance scales [9, 13, 14, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. In the coming years, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) and its extension will achieve the sub-percent level precision measurements of the distance scales.

The level of measurement precision in the current and upcoming surveys demands that our theoretical modeling of galaxy clustering need to be made accurate at the same level of measurement precision to avoid any misinterpretation of the measurements from any systematic errors in the theoretical modeling. In recent work [20], it was shown that there exists a new unknown contribution, called the monopole fluctuations, to the observed galaxy clustering that can affect the BAO measurements. Since the background mean number density of any galaxy samples is unknown, the galaxy survey itself needs to estimate the mean number density for the subsequent clustering analysis, and this estimate obtained by averaging over the angle at a given redshift includes the galaxy monopole fluctuation, which then propagates to the observed galaxy number density fluctuation and its two-point correlation function. In particular, the monopole correction in the observed galaxy two-point correlation function amounts to be a few percent in amplitude of the correlation function at the BAO scale, and it affects the correlation function differently along the line-of-sight and the transverse directions [20].

Following-up the initial investigation in [20], we first compute the observed redshift-space multipole correlation functions and the contributions of the monopole fluctuations to the multipole correlation functions. We then quantify the shift of the BAO peak position due to the monopole fluctuations by using the standard BAO fitting procedure [21] to remove the broadband power and any other systematic effects and by accounting for the proper covariance matrix in a given galaxy survey. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2.1 presents our analytical model for the observed galaxy number density and the covariance matrix in galaxy surveys. In Sec. 2.2, we introduce the monopole fluctuations, following the work in [20]. We then briefly review the standard procedure to estimate the covariance matrix and to measure the BAO peak position in galaxy surveys in the following sections. Section 3 presents our main findings of the impact of the monopole fluctuations on the BAO peak position measurements. We first present the redshift-space multipole correlation functions and the multipole contributions of the monopole correction. Second, we apply the BAO fitting procedure to isolate the BAO peak position from the broadband power by marginalizing over nuisance parameters. Then, we quantify the shift of the BAO peak position due to the monopole fluctuations in the redshift-space galaxy monopole and quadrupole correlation functions. Finally, the implications of our results are summarized and discussed in Sec. 4.

Section 3 presents our main findings of the impact of the monopole fluctuations on the BAO peak position measurements. We first present the redshift-space multipole correlation functions and the multipole contributions of the monopole correction. Second, we apply the BAO fitting procedure to isolate the BAO peak position from the broadband power by marginalizing over nuisance parameters. Then, we quantify the shift of the BAO peak position due to the monopole fluctuations in the redshift-space galaxy monopole and quadrupole correlation functions. Finally, the implications of our results are summarized and discussed in Sec. 4.

papers.title: Revisiting the distance to 4U 1543-475 through X-ray dust-scattering rings
papers.abstract: We derived a geometrical distance of the black-hole X-ray binary 4U 1543-475 based on X-ray dust-scattering rings associated with its 1992 and 2002 outbursts. We analyzed archival ROSAT and XMM-Newton observations and identified an X-ray dust-scattering ring in each observation, produced by two different dust layers along the line of sight. By combining the angular radii of the rings with the independently determined distances of the scattering dust layers and the epochs of the corresponding outbursts, we derive a best-constrained distance to 4U 1543-475 of 4.6 $\pm$ 0.2 kpc. This value is substantially smaller than the distance of 7.5 kpc commonly adopted in the literature and has important implications for the inferred physical properties of the system. In particular, the revised distance favors the presence of a low-mass extended-horizontal-branch donor star over a main-sequence star, calling for a reassessment of the dynamical parameters of the binary and, consequently, of the black-hole mass. The smaller distance also affects the inferred properties of the relativistic jet and the estimate of black-hole spin derived from the spectral continuum-fitting.

papers.intro:
4U 1543−-475 is a Galactic black hole X-ray binary first detected during its 1971 outburst by Uhuru (Matilsky et al., 1972). Since its discovery, the source has undergone several recurrent X-ray outbursts, observed in 1983, 1992, 2002, and 2021, in addition to the discovery outburst in 1971. The parameters most commonly adopted in the literature are iorb=20.7∘±1.5∘i_{\rm orb}=20.7^{\circ}\pm 1.5^{\circ}, derived from the modeling of the ellipsoidal modulation of the companion-star optical light curves (Orosz et al., 1998; Orosz, 2003). The companion, IL Lup, is commonly classified as an A2V main sequence star (Orosz et al., 1998) with a mass M2=2.45±0.15​M⊙M_{2}=2.45\pm 0.15\,M_{\odot} (Orosz et al., 1998). A black-hole mass of MBH=9.4±1.0​M⊙M_{\rm BH}=9.4\pm 1.0\,M_{\odot} is widely adopted in the literature (Ritter, H. and Kolb, U., 2003). The distance to 4U 1543−-475, however, remains comparatively uncertain. A value of 7.5±0.57.5\pm 0.5 kpc, derived from optical observations by combining the spectral classification and photometric properties of the companion star with estimates of the interstellar extinction and the contribution of the accretion disk (Jonker and Nelemans, 2004), has been widely adopted in the literature. More recently, estimates incorporating the Gaia DR3 parallax together with a Galactic spatial prior for black hole low-mass X-ray binaries favour a smaller distance of 5.0−1.2+2.05.0^{+2.0}_{-1.2} kpc (Zhang et al., 2026).

An independent way of measuring distances to Galactic X-ray sources is provided by X-ray scattering from interstellar dust. Dust scattering of X-rays emitted by bright point sources is a well-established and extensively investigated phenomenon. At soft X-ray energies, a fraction of the photons emitted by the source is scattered through small angles by dust grains located along the line of sight. Because the scattered photons travel a longer path than the photons reaching the observer directly, they are detected with a time delay. For persistent sources, the photons scattered by dust distributed along the line of sight produce a diffuse X-ray halo surrounding the source (Predehl and Schmitt, 1995; Smith, 2008). By contrast, when a sufficiently short X-ray flare illuminates relatively thin dust layers, the delayed scattered emission can appear as one or more discrete rings around the source (Vaughan et al., 2004; Tiengo et al., 2010; Heinz et al., 2016; Pintore et al., 2017). As time passes after the illuminating flare, photons scattered at progressively larger angles reach the observer, producing the characteristic apparent expansion of the rings. This geometrical dependence makes dust-scattering rings particularly powerful probes of both the distribution of interstellar material and the distances of transient X-ray sources. If the source distance is known or the source is extragalactic, the angular expansion of the rings can be used to determine the distance of the scattering dust layer (e.g. Tiengo et al. 2023; Vaia et al. 2025; Vaia et al. 2026). Conversely, if the distance of the dust layer can be independently constrained, for example through three-dimensional extinction maps or measurements of interstellar gas, the same geometry can be inverted to determine the distance to the X-ray source. A particularly relevant example for this last case is provided by Lamer et al. (2021), who used eROSITA observations of an expanding dust-scattering ring around the black-hole low-mass X-ray binary MAXI J1348−-630 to derive a geometrical distance to the system.

papers.title: Computational Explanations of Semantic Universals
papers.abstract: Despite their differences, the languages of the world share many deep features when it comes to how they express meaning. These semantic universals are likely to reflect shared aspects of human cognitive, communicative, and social structure. Recent advances in cross-linguistic semantics and computational linguistics allow us to develop explanations of the sources of such properties. This Element presents a body of work doing just that: we explicate a framework for providing computational explanations of semantic universals and then describe several such explanations using principles of ease of learning and efficient communication. Empirical domains include quantifiers, color terms, modals, and indefinites. After providing these explanations, we provide a discussion of future directions for advancing the explanatory power of computational methods in semantic typology.

papers.title: Fewer Expert Transfers Without Changing Routing: Expert Eviction for MoE Offloading
papers.abstract: A mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model uses only a few experts per token, so a server can keep most expert weights in CPU memory and copy an expert to the GPU when the router requests it. Recent methods train the router to keep the same experts for several tokens, and treat fewer routing switches as a proxy for fewer copies. We measure the trade-off directly, in a harness that performs and times real CPU-to-GPU copies for OLMoE-1B-7B. On an L40S GPU, every tested policy that holds an expert set fixed and decodes faster than the least-recently-used (LRU) cache increases next-token loss by at least 0.067 nats. A change that leaves every routing decision intact does better: when the cache must evict an expert, evict the one whose next use lies farthest in the future. This rule copies 2.1x fewer experts than LRU at no loss in quality and is within 3.5% of the fewest copies possible. It needs future requests; the next sixteen tokens of demand recover 96% of its reduction, whereas a rule based on counts of past requests recovers 27%.

papers.intro:
A mixture-of-experts layer activates only a few of its experts for each token. For example, OLMoE-1B-7B uses about 1B of its 7B parameters at a time (Muennighoff et al., 2025). When the expert weights do not all fit on the GPU, the rest can stay in CPU memory while the GPU holds a smaller cache. When the router requests an expert that is not cached, the system copies its weights to the GPU and evicts another expert. The usual rule evicts the least recently used expert (LRU) (Eliseev and Mazur, 2023; Zhong et al., 2024), and an open vLLM pull request implements this design (PR #37190). Because LRU copies whatever the router asks for, the model computes exactly what it would with every expert on the GPU. The price is that each miss stalls decoding until its copy completes.

papers.title: Strict $\mathcal{C}^\infty$-triangulation of subanalytic sets in low dimensions
papers.abstract:
Let $R$ be a real closed field expanded by an o-minimal structure, let $A$ be a definable, closed and bounded subset of $R^n$ and let $p$ be a positive integer. It was recently shown in \cite{pa2} that $A$ admits a strict ${\mathcal C}^p$-triangulation $({\mathcal T},h)$, i.e., there exist a finite simplicial complex ${\mathcal T}$ in $R^n$ and a homeomorphism $h:|{\mathcal T}|\to A$ that is definable and of class ${\mathcal C}^p$.
  The aim of this article is to analyze a generalization of the notion of strict ${\mathcal C}^p$-triangulation of subanalytic sets to the case $p=\infty$. Examples in dimension $n=3$ show that such a generalization is not always possible within subanalytic geometry, where the class ${\mathcal C}^\infty$ is equivalent to the class ${\mathcal C}^\omega$. We formulate the conjecture that strict ${\mathcal C}^\infty$-triangulations of subanalytic sets always exist in the wider o-minimal structure $\mathbb{R}_{{\rm an},\exp}$, generated by subanalytic sets and the exponential function. We check the conjecture for all subanalytic subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ when $n\leq 3$, and prepare tools to address the conjecture for arbitrary $n$.
  We also apply the obtained strict ${\mathcal C}^\infty$-triangulation results to approximate subanalytic continuous mappings $f:X\to Y$ between subanalytic sets $X\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ and $Y\subset\mathbb{R}^m$ by ${\mathcal C}^\infty$-mappings $g:X\to Y$ definable in the o-minimal structure $\mathbb{R}_{{\rm an},\exp}$, with respect to the strong Whitney ${\mathcal C}^0$ topology. If the continuous mapping $f:X\to Y$ is not necessarily subanalytic, we can still approximate it by ${\mathcal C}^\infty$ mappings $g:X\to Y$.

papers.title: Provenance-tracked, experimentally validated neural operator surrogates of three-dimensional laser melting with keyholes and free-form paths
papers.abstract:
A three-dimensional thermo-fluid-dynamic simulation of laser melting resolves the melt pool and vapor depression but costs from one to thousands of core-hours per track. We train FNO, RIGNO and GAOT neural operators that predict the temperature, melt-pool and free-surface fields. Our datasets comprise 3D temperature and melt geometry fields covering lack-of-fusion to keyhole conditions under varied laser power, scan speed, beam radius, beam shape and preheat, and include free-form scan paths with speed changes and up to four beams. We generate them with FLOW-3D WELD, using solver settings validated against published measurements for four materials. We implement an AiiDA framework to store the provenance of every simulation, model and evaluation, so each tabulated metric traces back to the solver and model inputs behind it. On held-out simulations, the best architecture scores below 2 % relative temperature error on quasi-steady straight tracks, below 4 % on single-beam free-form paths and about 5 % with two to four beams. Inference takes under a second per predicted arbitrary time step on our single-GPU setup. We extend a surrogate trained on Ti-6Al-4V to Inconel 718 by growing its training set autonomously, and the extended models reach a relative temperature error of about 3 % or less on both Inconel 718 and Ti-6Al-4V. At 20 Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 conditions held out of training, the two-alloy RIGNO predicts melt-pool and vapor-depression depths within 30 % of published measurements, and its depths differ from FLOW-3D at the same conditions by 2 % on average.
  Furthermore, these results provide a scalable framework which can readily be applied to computationally intensive simulations in fields other than laser melting.

papers.title: Low-Cost Streetlight Shields for Dark-Sky Protection at a Stargazing Camp
papers.abstract: Road lighting at stargazing camps can cause glare and stray light that interfere with observation. We installed directional shields on existing solar-powered streetlights at Bayan Gol Starlight Camp in Inner Mongolia, China, and compared SQM-L measurements before and after installation at the camp center (P1) and a site approximately 500~m away (P2). Measurements were taken at elevations of $0^\circ$, $30^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $90^\circ$. At $0^\circ$, the mean SQM reading across four directions at P1 increased by 1.624~\sqmUnit{}, and the reading toward the camp at P2 increased by 2.312~\sqmUnit{}. These changes correspond to reductions of approximately 77.6\% and 88.1\% in the equivalent SQM signal within the measured fields of view. The largest changes occurred at $0^\circ$; changes at $30^\circ$ and above were smaller. Photographs taken with identical exposure settings showed less visible glare around the shielded lamps. The measurements indicate that the changes were concentrated in low-elevation views. Directional shields provide a relatively low-cost way to reduce unwanted light while retaining the existing road-lighting system.

papers.intro:
Artificial light scattered by the atmosphere creates skyglow and makes faint stars harder to see. A global atlas estimated that more than 80% of people live under skies affected by artificial light (Falchi et al., 2016). Satellite observations showed increases in both the area and radiance of Earth’s artificially lit surface from 2012 to 2016 (Kyba et al., 2017). Based on public star-visibility reports, Kyba et al. (2023) estimated an average annual increase of about 9.6% in sky brightness at participants’ locations from 2011 to 2022. Artificial light at night can also affect animals’ nighttime activity (Longcore and Rich, 2004).

At a stargazing camp, skyglow and direct glare are distinct problems. Skyglow raises the background brightness of the sky, while a visible lamp can cause glare and interfere with dark adaptation. A dark zenith reading does not rule out glare from a lamp near an entrance or road. Site assessments should include low-elevation views as well as the zenith (Hänel et al., 2018).

Possible measures include dimming lamps, shortening operating hours, using warmer light, or replacing fixtures with fully shielded models. We tested a smaller retrofit: shields fitted to existing streetlights to limit sideward and upward light. They fit the original lamp housing, left the underside open, and required no electrical changes. Compared with replacing complete fixtures or modifying the electrical system, this retrofit required fewer new materials and less installation work because the existing lamps, solar panels, poles, and control systems were retained. It therefore provides a relatively low-cost option for improving the nighttime light environment at small stargazing sites. This approach is consistent with guidance to limit obtrusive and spill light (Gaston et al., 2012; Commission Internationale de l’Éclairage, 2017; DarkSky International and Illuminating Engineering Society, 2020).

papers.title: Energy system device sizing under closed-loop operation with imperfect forecasts
papers.abstract: The value of renewable energy devices depends on their operation, which must adapt to weather and demand using limited, imperfect forecasts that update over time. Conventional energy systems planning practices assume unlimited foresight in a single-level formulation, potentially leading to long-term investment in suboptimal device sizes. Accounting for realistic operation corresponds to a bi-level problem: the upper level selects device sizes, while the lower level contains closed-loop operation under evolving forecasts. We solve this problem using backpropagation MPC (BP-MPC), a gradient-based method, with a deterministic MPC as the lower-level controller. Using forecast errors generated by a parameterized martingale model of forecast evolution, we investigate how forecast accuracy affects the benefits of operation-aware energy systems planning and the resulting device sizes. In a case study of an energy system comprising photovoltaics, a battery, a heat pump, and thermal storage with uncertain weather and energy demands, accounting for closed-loop operation yields higher average cost savings as forecast error increases. The resulting designs achieve these savings by progressively shifting investment from battery storage to solar generation and thermal storage, which buffers forecast mismatches.

papers.intro:
The return on renewable energy investments depends on how the installed devices are operated under uncertain weather and energy demands. Standard energy systems planning methods typically co-optimize device sizes with an open-loop operating schedule for a lifetime of future disturbances [1, 2, 3]. This approach assumes that devices are dispatched with foresight that is unlimited in length and fixed in time. In practice, devices are dispatched by rule-based or receding horizon controllers [4] that use forecasts with a limited horizon and errors. As a result, energy systems planning with unlimited foresight can yield suboptimal device sizes, increasingly so as poorer forecasts magnify differences between assumed and actual operation [5, 6].

The return on renewable energy investments depends on how the installed devices are operated under uncertain weather and energy demands. Standard energy systems planning methods typically co-optimize device sizes with an open-loop operating schedule for a lifetime of future disturbances [1, 2, 3]. This approach assumes that devices are dispatched with foresight that is unlimited in length and fixed in time. In practice, devices are dispatched by rule-based or receding horizon controllers [4] that use forecasts with a limited horizon and errors. As a result, energy systems planning with unlimited foresight can yield suboptimal device sizes, increasingly so as poorer forecasts magnify differences between assumed and actual operation [5, 6].

Accounting for realistic operations during planning can be formulated as a bi-level problem: the upper level chooses device sizes to minimize lifetime cost, and the lower level contains a receding-horizon controller that determines power setpoints from the available forecasts at every timestep. This is an instance of control co-design [7, 8], in which the controller is fixed and the plant is sized for its closed-loop performance. Solving this bi-level problem is challenging because the lower level comprises many linked optimization problems that give rise to the system’s closed-loop trajectory. Baker et al. [9] approximate this structure for a wind energy system by summing the objectives of successive MPC horizons in a single storage-sizing problem, which can allow earlier decisions to depend on later information. Fortenbacher et al. [10] instead adapt Benders decomposition for battery sizing and placement in low-voltage grids, using MPC simulations to update Benders cuts. Notably, neither approach establishes optimality for the closed-loop planning objective.

Other studies use zeroth-order optimization methods to solve the bi-level device-sizing problem [1]. For example, Rullo et al. [11] use a genetic algorithm to size devices in a renewable energy system with evaluations of MPC management under perfect forecasts. Sorourifar et al. [12] employ Bayesian optimization to size a PV–battery system under only two levels of forecast error. Nonetheless, derivative-free search becomes expensive as the number of design variables grows. Moreover, prior works have not characterized how the level of forecast error impacts the added value of operation-aware design.

By treating device capacities as parameters of the MPC optimization problem, these approaches can be extended to energy systems design.

This paper makes two contributions. First, we extend BP-MPC to plant design by differentiating the closed-loop cost with respect to device capacities through both the MPC and a low-level controller that adjusts its inputs to the realized disturbances. Second, we use this method to quantify how forecast error affects optimal designs and annualized costs, comparing operation-aware and single-level sizing under the same MPC across forecast error levels. The system in this study comprises photovoltaics (PV), a battery (BESS), a heat pump (HP), and short-term thermal energy storage (TES). Forecast errors are varied using a parameterized martingale model of forecast evolution (MMFE) [17]. Our results show that the average cost advantage of BP-MPC sizing grows with the standard deviation of the one-step forecast error, while increasing forecast error shifts investment from the BESS toward PV and TES.

papers.title: A convergent Lagrangian scheme for the Navier Stokes equations on the normed Wasserstein space
papers.abstract: We extend the differential structure on Wasserstein spaces of Schichl (arXiv:2508.15140) to the normed Wasserstein space $\mathbb{W}_1$ of finite signed measures, the natural setting for measure differential equations with source terms. We generalize the averaged flow dispersion and expectational flow operators to $\mathbb{W}_1$ and show that along divergence--free tangent vectors they act by measure--preserving flows, and further define source operators. As an application, we construct a purely Lagrangian splitting scheme for the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^N$, inspired by the Averaged Flow Approximation Series (AFAS) in \cite{Schichl2025}. We recover, with explicit constants, the classical lifespan bound, a blow--up rate and the inviscid limit with rate $O(\eta^2)$, and a linearised scheme yields $L^{\infty}$, H\"older, $L^1$ and moment estimates for classical solutions.

In Section 3, we illustrate the scope of the theory of Schichl [25] on normed Wasserstein spaces by building a convergent approximation scheme for solutions of a system of particularly prominent non–linear parabolic PDEs: the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations. We then focus on divergence–free tangent vectors, for which the expectational flow operators act on densities by composition with a measure–preserving flow. This leads to particularly strong estimates on the operators and allows us to build Euler–type schemes—the Incompressible Flow Approximation Series (IFAS) and their linearised version (LIFAS)—for the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, which we write in the form (3.58) below. Two connections should be pointed out. First, the intended scope of the framework is the class of measure differential equations with source terms studied in [23, 22, 24], such as transport–diffusion equations with birth and death terms. Second, the non–linear scheme we build for the Navier–Stokes equations is a purely Lagrangian splitting scheme, in which the diffusion is realised by a symmetric average of translations—the expectation over one step of a random walk—the transport by composition with the flow of the current velocity, and the pressure by a Leray projection. It is thus the Euler–step analogue of the stochastic Lagrangian representation of the Navier–Stokes equations of Constantin & Iyer [10], and from the numerical point of view, a projection method of Chorin type with semi–Lagrangian advection and random–walk diffusion [7, 8]. Our convergence result is accordingly uniform in the viscosity and includes the Euler equations.

papers.title: Permutation codes via spectral graph theory
papers.abstract: We use the Eigenvalue Method to obtain upper spectral bounds on the size of permutation codes in the Hamming, Ulam, Cayley and Kendall metrics. For the Kendall metric, we improve the double-ball upper bound of Buzaglo and Etzion [IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2015] at minimum distance four and lengths seven and eight. For the Cayley metric, we improve the sphere packing bound, and determine when these spectral improvements occur. We derive theoretical spectral criteria for improvements from the ratio-type bounds of low degree, and show that the quadratic ratio-type bound for the Kendall metric always equals sphere packing. Furthermore, we prove sharp spectral bounds and recover known optimal code sizes for the Hamming and Ulam metrics.

Permutation codes are subsets of the symmetric group SnS_{n} whose distinct elements are separated by a prescribed minimum distance. They model coding with ordered symbols and arise in rank-based representations, communication channels and data storage [19, 22, 32, 30, 13, 20]. Rank modulation for flash memories particularly motivates metrics based on adjacent transpositions and translocations [41, 8, 24]. The choice of metric determines the permitted errors and the combinatorial structure of the code problem.

papers.title: Sharp partition function bound for the attractive logarithmic gas
papers.abstract: For the attractive logarithmic potential, we prove that the partition function is bounded uniformly in the number of particles on every compact inverse-temperature interval $[0,\be_0]$ with $\be_0<B$, where $B\in(0,2\d]$ is the sharp constant in the logarithmic Hardy--Littlewood--Sobolev inequality. The proof separates a smooth bulk, which inherits the entropy inequality, from a short-range singular interaction. The singular contribution is controlled on the event that each box of a fixed grid contains few particles. The complementary overcrowding event has exponentially small probability, which compensates a crude linear-in-$N$ bound on the log partition function. The resulting estimate supplies the partition bound that can be used recycled in a few different results. A separate Lean formalization verifies the conditional partition-bound theorem under the log-HLS assumption.

papers.title: The Neighbour's Label: Opposite Subgroup Effects of Same-Dialogue Exposure in Next-Act Evaluation
papers.abstract: Window-based next-act evaluation often aims to measure generalisation across dialogues, yet overlapping windows and similarity retrieval can expose labelled examples from the test dialogue. The nearest such example is the target's labelled predecessor, whose act is correct when the target continues it and wrong when the target changes act; a model that copies it can gain and lose in two subgroups that one aggregate averages. We induce this exposure under controlled designs on SGD, STAR and AMI, whose official splits are clean. Randomly including the predecessor's row in training raises a lexical classifier's continuation scores and lowers its transition scores in all three corpora, and purging the adjacent rows removes most of the gain. With TF-IDF-retrieved demonstrations, two 7B instruction-tuned models show the same opposite pattern in all eight model-corpus-sample arms (some single-cell intervals include zero; one replication is partial), while natural-weight accuracy changes by only -0.05 to +0.04. Exposure frequency depends on the retrieval pipeline. We evaluate two diagnostic comparisons without model retraining and find that excluding the test dialogue does not detectably reduce accuracy on SGD. All exposure is induced; no published system was re-evaluated.

papers.intro:
Models that predict the next dialogue act, intent, or strategy are trained and evaluated on examples that pair a window of preceding turns with the act of the turn that follows. Consecutive windows of one dialogue share most of their text, and the label of one window’s target is the previous act of the next window’s target. When an evaluation aims to measure generalisation to unseen dialogues (Setting A, Section 2), no gold label of a test dialogue may reach the training set or the labelled demonstration pool; yet a row-level split places the window preceding a test target in training with probability equal to the training share, and similarity retrieval over a pool of windows often returns it. A prospective evaluation within a dialogue (Setting B) may use earlier acts only if they are observed at run time. Among the 78 accessible context-window dialogue studies we reviewed (2019–2026), 4 reported a window-level split and 22 did not clearly state their split unit (Appendix B).

Each ingredient of this mechanism is documented. Language models copy the label of a demonstration that is near-identical to the test input, even when it is wrong (Lyu et al., 2023), and their accuracy rises with the share of demonstrations that carry the query’s label (Chen et al., 2026). The closest analogue to our task is next-activity prediction in process mining, where most test prefixes duplicate training prefixes under standard splits, a source of overestimated performance (Pfeiffer et al., 2025); there the duplicated item is the test input itself, here a neighbouring example whose label is right for one subgroup and wrong for the other. papers.title: A General Concept-based Decomposition for Vision-Language Embeddings
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models are designed to capture the compositional structure of the world through multi-modal alignment; however, it remains unclear whether their representations truly align with the way a human would naturally describe the same visual input. Prior works attempt to decompose visual embeddings into their concept-level contributions, but their instance-level optimization is inherently local and does not capture the model's global semantic structure, which is essential for compositional generalization across different inputs, tasks, and domains. We introduce GRACE, a method that learns this concept-based structure at the feature space level, producing semantic and general concept decompositions. To achieve this, we propose a novel training objective that preserves the geometric relations of different samples in the concept space, enabling a better understanding of how concepts compose and relate to each other. We validate GRACE on several image and video benchmarks, showing that its concept decomposition is aligned with human perception and achieves faithful decompositions across different tasks and domains. With minimal overhead, GRACE makes existing Vision-Language Models more interpretable, while preserving most of their original performance.
papers.intro:
Humans have the remarkable ability to perceive and understand reality by decomposing it into atomic semantic abstractions [1]. In vision, few volumetric primitives are enough for our visual system to recognize familiar objects, even under occlusion or visual degradation [2]. This mechanism, known as recognition-by-components, forms the basis of human generalization. Natural language provides a powerful mechanism to express visual abstractions in a human-interpretable form and to enable their composition into rich descriptions of the world. Thus, we expect interpretable models to expose a reasoning structure that is well aligned with these abstractions, which is essential for compositional generalization [3], i.e., the ability to recognize novel compositions of known concepts.
