Natural language provides a powerful mechanism to express visual abstractions in a human-interpretable form and to enable their composition into rich descriptions of the world. Thus, we expect interpretable models to expose a reasoning structure that is well aligned with these abstractions, which is essential for compositional generalization [3], i.e., the ability to recognize novel compositions of known concepts.

Vision–Language Models [4] align their visual representations with this language-based compositional structure, achieving strong generalization [5, 6]. However, visual data are inherently complex and often encode multiple, tightly entangled, semantic concepts. This challenge is particularly severe in videos, where objects, actions, and human motion co-occur and evolve over time [7, 8, 9]. As a result, it remains unclear whether their internal representations truly align with human-understandable concepts, which leads to a crucial question: can we explicitly expose the interpretable concept-based structure of visual information in VLMs? In this regard, the linear hypothesis suggests that high-level concepts are already represented linearly in feature space [10, 11], even across modalities [12]. Several works build on this intuition to decompose the visual embeddings of a VLM into text-based human-interpretable concepts. SpLiCE [13] learns a per-sample reconstruction of the embeddings from these concepts, while EXPLAIN-R [14] builds a concept-based surrogate representation that mimics the multi-modal alignment of the original model. Yet, many challenges remain unsolved. Instance-level decomposition may encourage shortcut learning and does not explicitly consider the different geometries of the visual and text modalities [15], while the surrogate representations in EXPLAIN-R are obtained by collecting concept evidence from external captioning models [16], rather than leveraging the intrinsic concept-based structure of the underlying VLM. These models encode concept-level interpretability but lack a general mechanism to expose it. Indeed, concept-based interpretability should capture not only the concept-level contributions within individual inputs, but also how concepts combine and relate across inputs, tasks, and domains, which is an essential property for generalization [5].

We leverage cross-modal matching over a large concept vocabulary to capture concept evidence directly from visual inputs, and propose a geometry-based reconstruction pipeline to ensure that the matched concepts are semantically relevant. papers.title: AFTER: A World Model with Adaptive Fast--Slow Timescales for Error-Driven Retention
papers.abstract: In robotics and embodied AI, a core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics during interaction. For instance, when a robotic arm grasps an object with an unknown payload, the robot dynamics change suddenly. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to simultaneously satisfy three critical requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, reacting promptly to sudden changes to curb prediction error accumulation; stability, distinguishing persistent changes from transient disturbances to prevent incorrect updates; and persistence, retaining the adapted dynamics without new observations so that later predictions do not revert to the old dynamics. Inspired by predictive coding in the human brain with multi-timescale adaptation, we propose AFTER-WM, a world model with Adaptive Fast-slow Timescales for Error-driven Retention, whose prediction errors drive a fast correction that fades and a slow correction that persists, while dynamically adjusting the combination weights of pre-trained experts without altering them, to overcome the trade-offs among responsiveness, stability and persistence. On five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, AFTER-WM has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task. In simulation, its multistep mean error is 16%-34% below the strongest compared model's and is also the lowest 1-4 steps after a change and under transient disturbances alone, and its step-40 error is the lowest as well, reflecting responsiveness, stability and persistence. All code (method, baselines, experiments) and datasets will be released online.

(1) Responsiveness is needed because the change is sudden and, in the open-loop rollout, each prediction is fed back as input, so prediction errors accumulate [38, 18]. (2) Stability is needed because a transient disturbance is equally sudden and initially hard to distinguish from a persistent change [39, 7]. (3) Persistence is needed because the change persists, yet no new observations arrive during the open-loop rollout, so if adaptation fades, later predictions revert to the old dynamics. Satisfying all three at once is hard. The faster adaptation reacts, the more easily a transient disturbance misleads it [40, 14], and adaptation that fades quickly enough to drop a transient disturbance cannot persist.

papers.title: MOON-RL: Multi-Objective Optimization via Objective Space Navigation with Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Many engineering design problems involve multiple conflicting objectives and strict feasibility constraints. They are typically solved with population-based optimizers that require many evaluations and offer limited online control over where the search is focused. We present MOON-RL, a reinforcement-learning-based optimization framework that formulates constrained multi-objective search as preference-directed navigation in the objective space. In MOON-RL, a lightweight PPO policy receives objective-space and constraint-related observations and acts as an instance-specific adaptive search process. It learns how to update the design so that the current solution advances along a user-specified trade-off direction, while a simple meta-algorithm periodically resets the policy, resamples starting designs from a continuously updated archive of non-dominated solutions, and adjusts step-size and penalty schedules. We evaluate MOON-RL on real-world actuator-design problems and additional convergence-hard constrained benchmarks, comparing against established evolutionary algorithms under matched evaluation budgets. In focused search scenarios, MOON-RL achieves competitive performance in the region of interest, and ablation studies show that both the RL-driven adaptive sampling process and the meta-algorithm contribute to this behaviour, suggesting that repurposing RL training as objective-space navigation is a viable building block for interactive, preference-guided design tools. Additional experiments show that the framework also accommodates adaptive non-RL samplers, while PPO remains a strong choice for fixed-target, preference-directed objective-space navigation.

papers.intro:
Many real-world design problems involve multiple, often conflicting objectives and strict feasibility constraints. Unlike single-objective optimization, the outcome of multi-objective optimization (MOO) is a set of trade-off solutions known as the Pareto front. Population-based methods like NSGA-II (Deb et al., 2002) and MOEA/D (Zhang and Li, 2007b) are robust and parallelizable, but in their standard formulations they commonly distribute evaluations across broad regions of the objective space to approximate the Pareto front. From a practical engineering perspective, however, it can be more beneficial to guide the search toward a user-specified region of interest instead of spreading computational resources over the whole front, as the designer might be interested only in a specific region of the objective space. That region may not be known in advance: as feasible solutions reveal which trade-offs are attainable, the designer may wish to redirect the search toward newly identified areas of interest. The policy’s continual updates serve to bias exploration toward the desired direction, effectively turning the RL agent into a self-adjusting sampler for the current navigation task. This avoids spending evaluations on preference-generalization whose cost is not amortized in static design tasks, where each optimization instance and preference direction is solved only once. papers.title: Fundamental Limits of Data-Driven Predictive Control
papers.abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) has attracted substantial interest, and many variants have been proposed; however, comparatively less is known about the statistical closed-loop performance of these methods and the fundamental limits they are subject to. In this contribution, we apply the statistical decision framework developed in our earlier work to study fundamental limits of DDPC. The performance of a data-driven controller is measured by its risk, the expected deterioration in control performance relative to an oracle model-based controller at a given system, and by its total risk that measures the overall performance across all systems of interest. Lower bounds on these risks are derived using the bias-variance decomposition and the Cramer-Rao inequality. In particular, a lower bound on the total risk is obtained by a calculus-of-variations method. This bound applies to any DDPC design, thereby quantifying unavoidable performance limitations and providing a benchmark for assessing existing DDPC methods. In an illustrative example, we compare the risks of certainty-equivalence model predictive control, subspace predictive control, and data-enabled predictive control with the derived lower bounds, providing a quantitative performance assessment of these methods and some guidance on tuning regularization parameters in DDPC.

Data-driven control (DDC), the task of designing controllers directly from process data, has been studied for more than half a century (Gevers, 1993; Hjalmarsson, 2005) and has recently witnessed a renewed surge of interest, driven by advances at the intersection of control, machine learning, optimization and related fields. In particular, two canonical benchmark problems have attracted considerable attention: the linear quadratic regulator (LQR) (Fazel et al., 2018; Recht, 2019; Dean et al., 2020; Mania et al., 2019; De Persis and Tesi, 2019; Van Waarde et al., 2020; Dörfler et al., 2023b; Zhao et al., 2025a; Zhao et al., 2025b; Zeng et al., 2025), and data-driven predictive control (DDPC) (Coulson et al., 2019; Berberich et al., 2020; Dörfler et al., 2023a; Breschi et al., 2023; Smith et al., 2024; Chiuso et al., 2025; Sasfi et al., 2026). We refer to Dörfler (2023a); Dörfler (2023b) for many more contributions.

We refer to Dörfler (2023a); Dörfler (2023b) for many more contributions.

Most of these works focus on the design and analysis of particular controllers, and comparisons of performance of these controllers often lead to the answer “it depends” (Dörfler, 2023b). Since the advantage of one method over another is typically demonstrated by showing that its performance is closer to that of the optimal model-based controller, a more foundational question arises: is there a limit to how close any data-driven controller can get to this oracle model-based controller? Answering this question is important, because such a limit points directly to the inescapable hardness of the problem, thereby clarifying what is achievable, and conversely what is not achievable, in DDC. In system identification, such a limit typically serves as a benchmark for assessing the efficiency of algorithms, such as the prediction error method (Ljung, 1999), subspace identification (He et al., 2024) and identification with quantized observations (Wang et al., 2024). In DDC, fundamental limits of this kind exist for the regret of online LQR (Simchowitz and Foster, 2020; Ziemann and Sandberg, 2024; Bartos et al., 2026) and, in a local minimax sense, for offline LQR (Lee et al., 2023) and LQG (Lee et al., 2026). In our earlier work He et al. (2026), we formulated explicit DDC as a statistical decision problem, treating a controller as a decision rule whose risk measures the expected performance degradation relative to the oracle model-based controller. We then derived risk lower bounds and illustrated the approach through case studies, including the benchmark problem of infinite-horizon LQR.

In this paper, we turn to another benchmark problem, finite-horizon DDPC. Whereas the infinite-horizon LQR has an explicit time-invariant optimal feedback policy, the optimal policy considered in DDPC is time-varying, depending on the initial condition, and often simply an implicit time series. These features make DDPC policies harder to learn in general and introduce additional challenges in characterizing their fundamental limits. The main contributions of this paper are: • We formulate the finite-horizon DDPC within the statistical decision framework of He et al. (2026) and derive a risk lower bound for any DDPC design. This bound reveals quantitative limitations that no controller design can avoid. • We derive explicit gain sequences for some representative DDPC methods under a shrinking-horizon implementation and evaluate their performance against the derived lower bounds. This comparison quantifies how far these methods are from the fundamental limits. • In an illustrative example we show that there is no uniformly best DDPC over the prescribed domain. Moreover, the total risk lower bound implies a “waterbed” effect: any pointwise risk below the lower bound in one parameter region must be compensated by excess risk elsewhere, analogous to the fundamental tradeoff in classical sensitivity shaping.

papers.title: An Analytical Model for Fast Design Optimization and Performance Studies of nuSTORM
papers.abstract: The concept of generating neutrino beams from stored muons (nuSTORM) has been explored for several decades. A few nuSTORM facilities have been designed for GeV muons, and a design of a sub-GeV nuSTORM, proposed for the European Spallation Source, is now underway. At low energy, the much larger beam divergence can significantly reduce the neutrino flux reaching the detector. Therefore, optimization of facility parameters is essential to avoid additional flux losses. This optimization, however, is not trivial due to the interdependency of the parameters. In this paper, we derive an analytical expression for the absolute neutrino flux incident on the detector front face and show how it can guide the optimization of a nuSTORM facility. The analytical expression is furthermore validated with published data and Monte Carlo simulations from five separate cases. In addition, we show how it can be extended to also predict the neutrino energy distribution at the detector, thus offering a convenient method to estimate the facility performance without time-consuming Monte Carlo simulations of particle transport and decay.

Conventional neutrino beams, for example those for long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments, are produced by directing a high-intensity hadron beam onto a target, focusing the secondary pions produced in the process with a magnetic horn. The pions are then allowed to decay in an evacuated tunnel to produce neutrinos. Uncertainties in pion production and focusing, however, translate into sizable neutrino beam systematic errors, making such a scheme unsuitable for neutrino cross-section measurements [9].

A nuSTORM facility is a short-baseline neutrino experiment that consists of a proton driver and a target, a magnetic horn, a pion-transfer beamline, a muon storage ring, and a neutrino detector, as illustrated in Fig. 1. It starts with an intense proton beam that strikes a target embedded inside the horn to produce pions. The pions are then focused by the horn and directed into the pion transfer line. Pions will be injected into the racetrack storage ring at the start of one of the straight sections. As they propagate through the straight section, the pions decay and yield muons that span a broad momentum range, of which only the fraction within the transverse and momentum acceptance is captured and stored in the ring. Muons that fall outside of the acceptance, as well as any remaining pions, will be dumped at the end of the straight section or lost in the arc.

At a certain distance away from the end of one of the straight sections, called the production straight, is the neutrino detector. The stored muons circulate until they decay or are lost on the aperture. A neutrino created in the production straight section can reach the downstream detector only if its emission angle at the creation point is smaller than the acceptance angle of the detector. These must all be tuned to balance the neutrino yield and the facility cost, while considering other design constraints such as the energy of the proton driver. In this paper, we will focus on the geometry of nuSTORM, with particular emphasis on the length of the production straight section, ss.

papers.title: HARE: Fast Read Disturbance Threshold Profiling in Modern DRAM Chips via Reduced Timing Constraints
papers.abstract:
Modern DRAM chips are vulnerable to read disturbance, which manifests as bitflips in a victim row physically near an aggressor row that is repeatedly activated. State-of-the-art mitigations rely on accurate and exhaustive profiling of the read disturbance threshold (RDT), i.e., the minimum number of aggressor row activations needed to induce the first bitflip. However, RDT changes significantly and unpredictably over time, motivating online profilers that dynamically adjust a mitigation's RDT configuration. RDT profiling is costly for online profilers (e.g., hundreds of seconds for a 16-bank DDR4 module) because 1) measuring a single DRAM row's RDT requires many activations and 2) each DRAM row can have a different RDT, requiring many rows to be profiled.
  We introduce HARE, an online RDT profiling technique that intentionally exacerbates read disturbance to quickly profile a DRAM module. HARE's key idea is to reduce the timing constraints between consecutive DRAM commands during profiling. Doing so significantly reduces profiling time by 1) directly reducing the execution time of the profiling command sequence and 2) exacerbating read disturbance such that the first bitflip occurs at a smaller activation count than with the conventional RowHammer sequence.
  From our characterization of 180 real DDR4 DRAM chips from four major DRAM manufacturers, we make three observations. First, HARE measures a DRAM row's RDT 31.2% faster than the RowHammer profiler and a DRAM module's minimum RDT with an average reduction of 21.7%. Second, HARE flips more than 95% of the cells that the RowHammer pattern flips. Third, HARE preserves the RDT ranking of rows well enough such that it can exhaustively reprofile a small set of rows to improve its minimum RDT estimation. Our end-to-end evaluations show that HARE enables significant system performance improvements and outperforms the RowHammer profiler.

papers.title: Chaos without Local Spectral Instability in a Kicked Oscillator
papers.abstract: A damped harmonic oscillator kicked by a pulsed periodic potential can be chaotic although every local Jacobian has eigenvalues inside the unit circle. Damped rotation between kicks lets non-normal shears of opposite curvature compound, so ordered products of contracting Jacobians amplify perturbations. We derive the exact joint spectral radius of the Jacobian family and an exact Lyapunov-exponent decomposition showing how this geometric pumping overcomes dissipation. The proposed mechanism can be realized with laser-cooled trapped ions in a pulsed optical lattice.

papers.title: Equidistribution of Hecke neighbours and continued fraction patterns
papers.abstract:
We prove uniform tightness of Hecke neighbours of any probability measure of positive entropy that is invariant and ergodic under the diagonal flow. As an application, we confirm a conjecture of Einsiedler concerning a homogeneous dynamics analogue of an equidistribution theorem of Johnson and Rudolph on the torus. We also obtain applications to continued-fraction patterns in arithmetic sequences and to the \(p\)-adic Littlewood conjecture.
  Our proof studies escape of mass using dynamics on the boundary of the Chabauty compactification of the space of lattices, together with averaging operators defined by leafwise measures along horospherical subgroups.

papers.title: Contrastive Bootstrap Representation Learning for Label-Efficient Agricultural Image Classification
papers.abstract: Expert annotation remains a major bottleneck in agricultural image classification, where collecting images is often easier than obtaining reliable labels from domain specialists. Self-supervised learning can reduce this dependence by pretraining transferable representations on unlabelled imagery. Contrastive and bootstrap methods provide two established but distinct training signals, motivating an empirical study of a formulation that applies both signals within one representation path under severe downstream label scarcity. We present Contrastive Bootstrap Representation Learning (CBRL), which jointly optimises SimCLR-style NT-Xent contrastive learning and bidirectional BYOL-style exponential-moving-average target prediction within a shared online projection space. Using a ViT-L/16 backbone and 10% of the downstream labels, we report single-seed point estimates on four primary agricultural test benchmarks plus an exploratory 33-image New Plant Diseases evaluation. CBRL records the highest macro-F1 point estimate on the four primary benchmarks. On DeepWeeds, its 79.77% test macro-F1 is 32.29 points above the random-initialisation, label-only baseline and 15.78 points above the next-highest comparison point estimate; on PlantVillage, its 98.14% macro-F1 is 10.43 and 0.43 points higher, respectively. On PlantDoc, however, all methods fail to reach practically useful performance. These results identify the evaluated joint formulation as a promising candidate for label-limited transfer, but they do not establish objective synergy, statistical superiority, or robustness across stochastic runs.

Agricultural image classification is an important application of computer vision in which the annotation bottleneck is particularly pronounced. Images can be collected at scale from field surveys, mobile diagnostic tools, phenotyping systems, and online agricultural platforms, yet obtaining reliable labels often requires domain expertise. This challenge is especially evident in plant disease recognition, where annotations may vary across crops, disease categories, growth stages, and acquisition conditions. PlantVillage Hughes and Salathé (2015) was released as an open image collection to support mobile plant disease diagnostics and contains more than 50,000 curated crop-leaf images. Deep neural classifiers have demonstrated that such datasets can support automated disease recognition Mohanty et al. (2016). However, supervised learning assumes access to sufficient labelled data and therefore does not address a broader challenge faced by agricultural vision systems: how effectively can large amounts of unlabelled agricultural imagery be exploited when downstream annotations are scarce?

Self-supervised learning (SSL) provides a natural approach to this problem by learning transferable visual representations without requiring task-specific labels during pretraining. In general computer vision, methods such as SimCLR Chen et al. (2020), BYOL Grill et al. (2020), Barlow Twins Zbontar et al. (2021), DINO Caron et al. (2021), DINOv2 Oquab et al. (2023), and MAE He et al. (2022) have demonstrated that carefully designed self-supervised objectives can produce representations that transfer effectively to downstream tasks. These methods, however, optimise substantially different learning signals. Contrastive approaches such as SimCLR Chen et al. (2020) encourage inter-instance discrimination by attracting representations of augmented views of the same image while separating different images in a batch. Bootstrap approaches such as BYOL Grill et al. (2020) instead promote cross-view consistency by predicting representations generated by a slowly updated target network, without explicitly relying on negative samples. Other approaches rely on redundancy reduction, self-distillation, or masked reconstruction. Although these objectives have been extensively studied on large-scale natural-image benchmarks, their joint use for label-limited agricultural representation learning remains insufficiently characterised.

This question is particularly relevant because agricultural imagery can differ substantially from the natural-image benchmarks on which many SSL methods have been developed. Agricultural classification may depend on subtle texture variations, localised lesions, colour changes, plant morphology, and spatial patterns that distinguish visually similar categories. Consequently, representations that perform well for generic object recognition may not necessarily capture the features most useful for agricultural transfer. Vision Transformers (ViTs) Dosovitskiy et al. (2021) provide a suitable backbone for investigating this problem because their patch-token representation supports contrastive, bootstrap, redundancy-reduction, masked-reconstruction, and dense-feature objectives within a common architecture family. However, the effectiveness of jointly exploiting contrastive discrimination and bootstrap-based cross-view consistency within a controlled ViT architecture and under a limited-label downstream protocol remains insufficiently characterised.

papers.title: Ultrasound Elastography: Excitation Methods and Low-Cost Alternative
papers.abstract: Ultrasound elastography (or elasticity imaging) is a method that characterizes the tissue mechanical properties with the purpose of aiding the diagnosis of certain pathologies. Many novel clinical applications use the assumption that these tissue properties are changed in the presence of pathological processes. Characterization of tissue mechanical properties is achieved by imaging the response of the tissue to an induced stress or excitation. A plethora of approaches have been used in the scientific community to induce excitation in tissue, which usually require additional tools or devices than are costly. Furthermore these are usually integrated in the imaging pipeline using additional software or hardware for control. An alternative that is simpler, faster to integrate (and low-cost) is proposed in this work, by using readily available smartphones as a source of mechanical excitation. The induced displacements are used to solve the elasticity inverse problem (IP) using a finite element method (FEM) approach. Preliminary elasticity reconstructions of a phantom that mimics tissue are similar to when using a dedicated actuator as means of inducing harmonic displacements, illustrating the feasibility of our low-cost ultrasound elasography approach.

papers.title: GraSLA: A Lightweight Spatial-Language-Action Model with Grasp Hypotheses as Geometric Priors
papers.abstract: This paper focuses on improving the behavioral diversity and effectiveness of language-conditioned manipulation policies trained through imitation learning. Recently, continuous-action policies have become mainstream in robotic manipulation, but the lack of diverse demonstrations tends to restrict their behavioral diversity. For grasping, a fundamental subtask of manipulation, 6-DoF grasp detection provides diverse grasp hypotheses, but open-loop execution constrains responsiveness in dynamic environments. This motivates us to combine the diversity of grasp hypotheses with the adaptability of continuous-action policies. To this end, we propose GraSLA, a lightweight and effective spatial-language-action model with grasp hypotheses as geometric priors. In particular, we employ spatial and language foundation models to encode scene geometry and task semantics, and integrate them with grasp hypotheses through bidirectional cross-attention for continuous action prediction. On LIBERO, GraSLA achieves an average success rate of 99.30%.

papers.title: Sliced Inverse Regression Revisited: When the Number of Predictors Grows Proportionally With the Sample Size
papers.abstract: Li (1991) introduced sliced inverse regression (SIR) as a dimension reduction method and established its theoretical properties under the assumption that the number of predictors $p$ remains fixed as the sample size $n$ tends to infinity. In this paper, we revisit the theoretical properties of SIR in the high-dimensional regime where $p/n \to \gamma \in [0,1)$, assuming normally distributed predictors and a fixed number of slices. We show that the sample SIR eigenvalues exhibit an upward bias when $\gamma>0$, that their fluctuations are governed by the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble, and that the signal eigenvalues are asymptotically normal after an appropriate bias correction. We demonstrate that Li's chi-squared test requires a scaling adjustment to achieve the nominal asymptotic size when $\gamma>0$. We further propose two additional tests that achieve the nominal asymptotic size: an exact test based on Li's test statistic and a largest-eigenvalue test. In addition, we derive closed-form limits for the accuracy of the estimated SIR directions and show that their first-order expansions in $\gamma$ agree with Li's approximation. Finally, we establish the limiting distribution of the estimated sufficient predictors for a new observation and show that, when $\gamma>0$, they contain an additional independent Gaussian noise component. Simulation studies corroborate our theoretical findings.

papers.title: Search for gravitational wave coincident neutrinos in DEAP-3600
papers.abstract: We searched DEAP-3600 data for neutrino signals coincident with gravitational waves from compact object mergers observed by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA collaborations (LVK). While mergers involving neutron stars are expected to produce neutrinos, these have never been detected. The DEAP-3600 experiment is sensitive to electron neutrinos as recently observed through charged current neutrino absorption on its $^{40}$Ar target. Between 2016 and 2020, the detector recorded data during seven compact merger events involving neutron stars that were observed gravitationally by LVK. Upon examination, there is no statistically significant evidence of neutrinos from any of the mergers analyzed. Exclusion limits are set on the electron neutrino fluence, e.g. from GW170817 in the mono-energetic model at $6.8\times10^{12}~\text{cm$^{-2}$}$ ($1.8\times10^{10}~\text{cm$^{-2}$}$) for 10 MeV (100 MeV) neutrinos.

papers.intro:
Since the first detection of gravitational waves (GWs) in 2015 by the LIGO and Virgo collaborations [3], a precise record of many compact binary coalescences (CBCs) has been available to physicists. The third GW data catalog (GWTC-3.0 [6]) included two binary neutron star (NSNS) mergers, five neutron star-black hole (NSBH) mergers, and 83 binary black hole (BHBH) mergers. This presents an opportunity to search for other signals from these mergers, as the GW information can be used to establish a limited time window in which to expect them. For example, in 2017 the Swope Supernova Survey used a GW signal to help identify light from a kilonova that followed after a NSNS merger [28].

A vast body of nuclear astrophysics literature concurs that neutrinos will be produced in and ejected from CBCs involving neutron stars (NSs) or black holes (BHs) [26, 38, 33, 19]. As far back as 1989, and encouraged by the detection of neutrinos from a supernova in 1987 [36], proposals have been made for what kind of equipment would be needed to accomplish this [30]. As such, many detector experiments have carried out searches for neutrinos from CBCs (including ANTARES [16], Borexino [21], IceCube [2], KM3NeT [14], Super-Kamiokande [9], and XENON1T [18]) with no successful detections so far. This study continues that work in DEAP-3600, looking only at mergers involving neutron stars.

The DEAP-3600 experiment has collected data since 2016 with the goal of detecting dark matter and other exotic particles in the universe using a single-phase liquid argon (LAr) scintillation detector [17]. The detector was principally designed to search for the dark matter candidates Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) with minimal backgrounds. Owing to the low backgrounds and dense target, it was recently found to also be able to observe interactions with solar neutrinos through charged current neutrino absorption on 40Ar nuclei [13]. According to LVK data [6, 4, 5, 7], nine mergers likely involving a NS occurred while DEAP-3600 was taking data over the course of its “second fill” from November 2016 to March 2020. In this work, the data taken during seven of these mergers are analyzed in comparison with empirical background models to search for GW-coincident neutrino interactions.

papers.title: Lang-SVG: Hierarchical Image Vectorization with Language Priors
papers.abstract: Image vectorization reconstructs raster images as compact scalable vector graph- ics (SVG), providing a structured and editable code representation of images. However, most existing vectorization methods optimize for pixel-level render- ing fidelity, often producing SVGs that lack alignment with human-perceived object-part hierarchies, making them difficult to manipulate. To address this, we propose Lang-SVG, which introduces an explicit tree structure to organize SVG primitives with semantic labels and parent-child relationships. Lang-SVG incorporates granularity-controllable and open-vocabulary segmentation priors to initialize object-part hierarchies and leverages multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with SVG tree context to assign semantic labels to unlabeled nodes. To reduce redundancy, we introduce depth-adaptive simplification to reduce shape complexity and Tree-Guided Pruning and Merging to eliminate redundant SVG nodes. L1-SAM-Prompting further recovers missing regions to improve recon- struction fidelity and structural completeness. Beyond reconstruction fidelity, we introduce a new evaluation protocol that measures structural quality and semantic part alignment. Experiments demonstrate that Lang-SVG achieves state-of-the-art performance in both rendering fidelity and structural quality. Project website: https://xiliu8006.github.io/Lang-SVG/.

papers.intro:
Image vectorization transforms raster images into compact scalable vector graphics (SVG), providing a structured, renderable, and editable code representation of visual content. As a text-based representation, SVG is increasingly becoming an interface between images and language models. Recent MLLMs learn to generate SVG code [1, 2, 3, 4], benchmarks evaluate visual understanding through image-to-SVG generation [5, 6], and code-based approaches [7, 8, 9, 10, 11] explore structured visual code for generation, manipulation, and reasoning. However, existing SVG datasets [1, 2, 12, 13] largely focus on icons and illustrations, offering limited coverage of complex natural images. Vectorizing natural images offers a much larger and more diverse source of SVG code beyond simple icons and illustrations, but representing their complex visual content as structured code remains challenging.

Vectorizing natural images offers a much larger and more diverse source of SVG code beyond simple icons and illustrations, but representing their complex visual content as structured code remains challenging.

Recent differentiable SVG methods [14, 15, 16, 17] have substantially advanced image vectorization in terms of rendering fidelity, efficiency, and compactness, with recent approaches [18, 19, 20, 4] further exploring layered and semantic representations to improve editability. However, these methods typically organize SVG primitives as flat layers without explicitly encoding object-part hierarchies. As a result, primitives belonging to the same object may be distributed across different layers, making it difficult to select and edit individual objects or their parts. Moreover, without hierarchical guidance, SVG optimization may allocate excessive primitives to redundant shapes or high-frequency textures rather than meaningful semantic regions. These limitations highlight the need for image vectorization that preserves semantic structure while maintaining high rendering fidelity.

We argue that this limitation partly stems from the lack of explicit semantic and structural constraints in existing image vectorization objectives. While pixel-level reconstruction losses effectively optimize SVG geometry, opacity, and color, they do not explicitly encourage primitives to form meaningful semantic structures. SGLIVE [19] incorporates SAM [21] to improve structural alignment, but SAM masks do not explicitly capture fine-grained semantic object-part hierarchies. papers.title: Imitating the Imperfect: Offline-to-Online Robust Imitation Learning from Heterogeneous Demonstrators
papers.abstract: Imitation learning (IL) typically relies on large-scale offline demonstrations collected from multiple human or algorithmic demonstrators. However, most existing approaches assume these demonstrators are homogeneous or near-optimal experts, a convenient but unrealistic assumption in real-world applications. In practice, demonstrations are often collected from heterogeneous demonstrators with unknown and varying levels of expertise, resulting in highly mixed-quality data. In this work, we study a challenging yet practical setting of imitation learning from such heterogeneous imperfect demonstrators. We propose Latent Expertise and Optimality Scoring based Imitation Learning (LEOS-IL), a principled framework that jointly learns (i) a state-action optimality scoring model and (ii) latent expertise levels for each demonstrator from unlabeled suboptimal offline demonstrations. The learned scoring model is then integrated into an online policy optimization procedure, where the agent is trained to maximize estimated optimality scores while its online rollouts are iteratively leveraged to refine the scoring model, thereby mitigating distributional shift during online adaptation. We further provide theoretical guarantees for optimality score identification and conditional optimal occupancy and policy recovery under explicit sufficient conditions. Experiments on continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms existing baselines across highly heterogeneous and low-quality demonstration regimes.

papers.title: Strategically Robust Multi-Agent Control
papers.abstract: A key source of uncertainty in multi-agent systems is the behavior of other agents. Game-theoretic control approaches ignore this uncertainty, while robust control approaches treat others as fully adversarial. In this paper, we introduce strategically robust multi-agent control to populate the spectrum between these two paradigms. Specifically, in dynamic games, we propose that players are strategically robust and seek protection against misspecified control policies of the other players. This formulation induces a novel equilibrium concept, strategically robust dynamic equilibrium, that interpolates between game-theoretic control and robust control. We study this concept across canonical open- and closed-loop settings and show that accounting for strategic robustness also has computational benefits over classic approaches in game-theoretic control. Numerical experiments on vehicle platooning, inventory management, and network control illustrate resilience to misspecification, and also exhibit a "free-lunch" phenomenon in which strategic robustness can improve performance or social welfare.

papers.intro:
In multi-agent systems like autonomous driving [1], electricity markets [2], and real-world robotics tasks [3], one of the largest sources of uncertainty is the behavior of others. This strategic uncertainty can arise from various sources such as misspecified models of others’ intent, irrational behavior, or limited computation. Unlike standard exogenous disturbances commonly studied in control, strategic uncertainty is endogenous to the problem: by changing their behavior, an agent affects the uncertainty they are trying to address.

Two common approaches in multi-agent control are to ignore strategic uncertainty and compute game-theoretic controllers under the implicit assumption that other agents’ objectives are well-modeled, or to account for strategic uncertainty through adversarial or worst-case modeling, i.e., robust control.

In game-theoretic control, agents are modeled as rational decision-makers minimizing their own control cost. The natural solution concept is that of Nash equilibrium, a configuration at which no agent can lower their cost by unilaterally changing their control policy. While natural in theory, the practical deployment of Nash equilibrium control policies suffers from a fundamental limitation: policies are brittle, i.e., sensitive to misspecification of the other agents’ control policies. For instance, [4] demonstrates that adhering to a standard Nash equilibrium when opponents are non-rational can lead to significantly suboptimal outcomes.

In addition to their poor robustness, Nash equilibria also pose significant computational challenges, and can generally be computed efficiently only under structural assumptions, such as monotonicity of the pseudo-gradient or the invertibility conditions arising in linear-quadratic games [5], which restrict the class of problems that can be solved in practice.

In robust control, instead, the other agents are modeled as adversarial disturbances, whose goal is to maximize the control cost. The classical ℋ∞\mathcal{H}_{\infty} control problem can be cast as a zero-sum game between the control engineer, who minimizes control cost, and a fictitious agent, who instead maximizes control cost and whose influence is attenuated only through a penalty on its magnitude. A natural way to inject robustness to strategic uncertainty is thus to treat the control policies of the others as exogenous disturbances, as in, e.g., [6, 7, 8]. Doing so, however, completely disregards the underlying game-theoretic interactions: the other agents are not arbitrary disturbances, but decision-makers with their own objectives, whose behavior should be expected to remain close to the policies prescribed by the game. Thus, while computationally tractable, it inevitably leads to overly conservative behavior and sacrifices nominal performance. In other words, game-theoretic control trusts the other agents entirely, while robust control treats their control inputs as arbitrary disturbances.

In this paper, we populate the spectrum between these two solution concepts; see Figure 1. We take inspiration from recent work on strategic risk aversion in multi-agent reinforcement learning [9] and strategically robust game theory in one-shot games [10], from which we also inherit the name “strategic robustness.” Specifically, we propose that agents choose their strategy not by playing against the policies of the other agents (as in game-theoretic control) but instead against a fictitious adversary who seeks to inflict maximum damage (as in robust control), but pays a penalty for deviating from the policies of the other agents. This deviation penalty controls how tightly the adversary is anchored to the other players’ policies. When it is prohibitively large, deviations are too expensive and the adversary is forced toward the policies of the other agents, recovering standard game-theoretic control. As the penalty weakens, the adversary gains power and the player’s policy becomes increasingly robust. When an explicit disturbance penalty keeps the adversarial problem well posed, the zero-deviation-penalty limit is a classical worst-case ℋ∞\mathcal{H}_{\infty} control problem—a connection we make precise in this paper. Together with the direct disturbance penalty, the deviation penalty defines a two-parameter family containing the standard Nash and ℋ∞\mathcal{H}_{\infty} problems as distinct limiting cases.

We instantiate these ideas in the setting of discrete-time dynamic games. Dynamic games are used in a wide variety of control applications, including robotics [11], aerospace [12], and economics [13], to name a few. In these games, the state of a dynamical system is controlled by a set of agents that select policies to minimize their personal control cost, which depends on the state of the system and on the agents’ inputs. Specifically, we study two classes of dynamic games: the finite-horizon open-loop setting, with linear dynamics, convex costs, and convex constraints, and the finite-horizon closed-loop linear-quadratic setting, which we further extend to the infinite horizon.

papers.title: I See What You Want: Decoding Hierarchical Operator Intent from Visual Teleoperation History
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a powerful foundation for robotic scene understanding, task planning, and language-conditioned control. A natural question follows: can these models also decode what a human operator intends while teleoperating a robot, without any explicit instruction? We formulate this as hierarchical intent prediction, jointly inferring the ongoing atomic action and the broader mission it serves from a short visual teleoperation history. To study this, we introduce VI AMO (Vision Intention Action and Mission Ongoing), a dataset of 6,600 episodes from eleven robot sources with 13,653 temporally aligned action annotations and 9,702 mission annotations. Large proprietary models struggle with this problem: on held-out episodes, GPT-4o reaches Sentence-BERT similarities of only 0.563 and 0.470 for action and mission, and GPT-5.6 Luna achieves only 0.581 and 0.554. Fine-tuning a VLM on VI AMO yields our Vision-Intention Model (VIM), which raises these scores to 0.825 and 0.821 and still reaches 0.726 and 0.717 on the 35.4% of test actions with both labels absent from training. Finally, as a downstream application, VIM's predicted mission enables a vision-language-action (VLA) policy to take over from the operator mid-task in a real-world environment unseen during VIM fine-tuning, reducing human teleoperation time by 34.6% relative to GPT-4o and 39.8% relative to GPT-5.6 Luna, while cutting intent-prediction latency by roughly 70% on average.

SayCan [1] grounds language plans in learned affordances, Code as Policies [2] generates executable robot programs from language, and Inner Monologue [3] closes the loop with textual feedback. PragmaBot [4] uses visual feedback and lessons from real-world experience to refine robot task plans. On the execution side, vision-language-action (VLA) policies map a language instruction and visual observations directly to motor commands [5, 6, 7, 8]. All of these translate human language into robot behavior. We ask the inverse question: given only the partial visual history of a teleoperated robot, can a VLM decode what the human operator intends, without an instruction ever being provided?

Recent work has begun to explore this direction. VOSA [9] identifies candidate target objects through detection and segmentation, and CASPER [10] uses VLM reasoning over teleoperation history to select a skill–object pair from a predefined library and then executes that skill. Both represent intent at the level of the current step, as a target object or position, or as a skill drawn from a predefined library. However, these methods do not explicitly infer the broader mission behind the current action, yet it is what a robot needs in order to continue: grasping an apple does not by itself reveal whether the apple should go on a plate, to a person, or into a basket. Progress is further limited by data: existing demonstration corpora [11, 12, 13] mainly provide episode-level instructions, while existing intermediate supervision is either synthetically generated from task instructions [14], or annotated at the primitive-skill level [15], rather than providing temporally aligned action–mission supervision for instruction-free intent inference.

papers.title: Dissecting and diagnosing the LISA Galactic binary population
papers.abstract: LISA will individually resolve thousands of Galactic double white dwarf (DWD) binaries, while the majority stays buried in an unresolved gravitational wave (GW) confusion foreground. Which systems get resolved depends on the binary's parameters, on the global population and on instrumental sensitivity, so the resolved population is not a representative sample of the underlying Galactic population. Interpreting LISA's future catalog therefore requires understanding these selection effects. Here we characterize the resolved and unresolved subpopulations of a simulated Milky Way DWD catalog, using an iterative subtraction pipeline applied over different observation times. Resolvability is driven primarily by chirp mass: higher chirp mass, inspiraling systems are strongly favored over lower mass, outspiraling or monochromatic ones, and this reflects on the rate with which different composition subtypes are resolved. Spatially, resolved sources trace the Galactic bulge, because it is intrinsically the densest region of the Galaxy. The confusion background shows an internal bimodal chirp-mass structure, and is not generated uniformly by the same subpopulation in different frequency bands. We introduce a diagnostic for the minimum number of sources needed to reproduce a given fraction of the confusion power in a frequency band, and show that a residual confusion floor persists even after 100 years of integration. These biases are significant and need to be accounted for when using LISA's resolved DWD catalog and the confusion background to constrain the Galactic DWD population.

papers.title: Natural Gradient Learning in Predictive Coding through Lateral Circuits
papers.abstract: Predictive coding (PC) trains neural networks through local energy-minimization dynamics without depending on a global error signal that backpropagation (BP) requires. Although PC is a promising alternative algorithm for efficient learning, the computational cost of inference dynamics currently outweighs the resulting learning benefits in practice. In this work, we take inspiration from optimization theory to extract more learning benefit from each inference phase. We introduce Natural PC, which augments standard PC with a lateral circuit, enabling exact and efficient natural gradient learning locally in space and time. Our lateral circuit learns the activity correlations that determine the Fisher information matrix and implicitly computes its inverse, avoiding expensive matrix inversion. Across all tested image reconstruction benchmarks, Natural PC achieves state of the art in terms of sample and compute efficiency compared to existing PC approaches. Most notably, Natural PC scales to ImageNet and matches the performance of BP trained with AdamW and various second-order optimizers at an order of magnitude lower computational cost while also using two orders of magnitude fewer training samples. Our results demonstrate that local natural gradient learning makes PC competitive with BP in both sample efficiency and computational cost in reconstruction tasks.

papers.intro:
Predictive coding (PC) is a prominent theory of cortical computation, where higher cortical areas predict lower-level sensory inputs, unifying perception and learning as the local minimization of prediction errors (Rao & Ballard, 1999; Friston, 2005; Friston, 2008; Friston, 2010; Spratling, 2010; Bastos et al., 2012; Shipp, 2016). The local computation of prediction errors in PC provides a mechanism to solve the credit assignment problem in the brain (Rumelhart et al., 1986; Lillicrap et al., 2020) and has therefore motivated the development of algorithms for training artificial neural networks. Although PC can approximate or exactly implement backpropagation (BP) under specific conditions (Whittington & Bogacz, 2017; Song et al., 2020; Salvatori et al., 2021; Rosenbaum, 2022; Millidge et al., 2023; Innocenti et al., 2026; Seely & Gould, 2026), recent work suggests that PC can also provide computational advantages over BP, including fewer weight updates (Alonso et al., 2022; Alonso et al., 2024), improved online and continual learning (Song et al., 2024), faster escape from saddle points (Innocenti et al., 2024), and greater sample efficiency (Oliviers et al., 2026; Pokel & Grewe, 2026). Together, these properties make PC a promising foundation for efficient learning in neural networks.

Together, these properties make PC a promising foundation for efficient learning in neural networks.

Despite this promise, standard PC remains difficult to apply in practice, since even relatively simple problems can require substantial computational resources (Pinchetti et al., 2025). Unlike BP, which straightforwardly computes synaptic updates by differentiating a global loss function, PC treats the network as a dynamical system and requires an inference process to solve the dynamics before synaptic weights are updated (Song et al., 2024; Aceituno et al., 2025). Once inference has minimized prediction errors and the dynamics have reached equilibrium, the synaptic weights are updated to reduce the residual prediction errors at that equilibrium (Whittington & Bogacz, 2017). However, reaching equilibrium often requires hundreds or thousands of inference iterations per sample, and PC becomes practical only when the trade-off between inference costs and learning benefits is favorable.

Recent work has sought to improve this trade-off by reducing inference costs or increasing the learning benefit from inference. To reduce inference costs, some approaches learn activity estimates from the input or initialize activities from progress on earlier samples to provide inference with a more informative starting point (Song et al., 2019; Tschantz et al., 2023; Pinchetti et al., 2026). Other approaches improve the learning benefit from inference by mitigating ill-conditioned inference (Innocenti et al., 2025), balancing prediction errors across layers (Qi et al., 2025), preventing prediction errors from vanishing or exploding (Ha et al., 2026), or improving credit assignment through local constraints (Seely & Gould, 2026). Although these existing approaches improve inference and learning, their synaptic updates do not follow the local geometry of the model distribution (Amari, 1987; Amari, 1998), leaving open an information-geometric route to more efficient learning.

In this work, we introduce Natural PC, an extension of standard PC with a lateral interneuron circuit enabling natural gradient learning. We first derive an exact layerwise form of the natural gradient for PC, identifying the activity correlations required for geometry-aware synaptic updates. We then show that lateral weights learn these activity correlations and that the dynamics of the interneuron circuit implicitly invert the correlations during inference, removing the need for explicit and expensive matrix inversion. We theoretically show that the natural gradient of the PC learning objective coincides with Newton and Gauss–Newton updates, explaining how Natural PC can obtain more learning benefit from each costly inference phase. As the lateral circuit controls both the geometry and learning rate of the network, we remove both the learning rate hyperparameter and the weight optimizer. Across multiple image reconstruction datasets, Natural PC achieves state of the art in terms of reconstruction error, sample efficiency, and computational cost compared to existing PC methods. Most notably, Natural PC scales to ImageNet-1k and matches the performance of BP trained with AdamW and various second-order optimizers at an order of magnitude lower computational cost while also using two orders of magnitude fewer training samples.

papers.title: The coercivity conjecture for nonlocal energies
papers.abstract: The coercivity conjecture for nonlocal energies asks whether uniform ellipticity implies $H^s$-coercivity for symmetric nonlocal kernels of order $2s$, with $0<s<1$. We show that the conjecture fails whenever $n>2s$ for every $s \in (0,1)$ and $n \geq 1$, even for smooth compactly supported test functions; for $n=1$ and $s>1/2$, we show that it holds. The construction also gives bounded discontinuous weak solutions in $H^s_{\rm loc}$ to nonlocal equations in divergence form with kernels in this class. Despite the failure, we show that the conjecture holds for several important classes of kernels. We establish a general local coercivity criterion based on annular cancellation, which applies in particular to kernels satisfying both divergence- and nondivergence-form symmetry. The criterion also allows us to treat kernels comparable to stable kernels with bounded measurable coefficients, as well as non-cutoff Boltzmann kernels under a geometric nonconcentration assumption. As an application, we obtain a short and self-contained proof of the Gressman--Strain anisotropic coercivity estimate. Furthermore, by combining our new criterion with existing regularity results, we obtain H\"older estimates under ellipticity and cancellation assumptions.

papers.title: Detection Is Not Early Warning: Evaluating Token-Level Alarms on Language Model Failures
papers.abstract: Many failures of language models begin at a specific token, the onset. A monitor that reads the model during generation can classify the finished response, detect the failure once it is under way, or warn before it begins, and only a warning leaves time to stop or steer the generation. Monitors are usually evaluated with response-level metrics such as AUROC, which ignore when the monitor fires. We introduce PREWARN, an evaluation protocol for any failure with an annotated onset. It calibrates each monitor's threshold on validation data to an error rate chosen for the application, runs the monitor, and scores its alarms relative to the onset on all three tasks. As a case study we apply it to repetitive degeneration in three open language models, with early warning as the main task, using linear probes on activations and six untrained baselines. Response-level metrics saturate on this failure, and a rule that reads only the response length scores almost perfectly, while probes that AUROC ranks as equal warn very differently under PREWARN. Probes warn before the onset on most degenerate responses of two of the three models, low-rank adapters below the probe more than double the share of tokens just before the onset that it flags, largely by flagging degenerate responses long before the onset, and no untrained baseline warns much more often than random alarms. We release the probes with calibrated thresholds at https://huggingface.co/collections/marcodene/prewarn-degeneration-probes

papers.intro:
Many failures of language models begin at a specific token, the onset. From that token on, a response may, for example, turn harmful (Li et al., 2025), make unsupported claims (Niu et al., 2024), or fall into a repetition loop that runs until the token budget is exhausted (Holtzman et al., 2020; Welleck et al., 2020; Pipis et al., 2026). A monitor that reads the model during generation can serve three tasks: response classification gives one verdict on the finished response, failure detection raises an alarm once the failure is under way, and early warning raises one before it begins. Only an early warning leaves time to stop, steer or resample the generation before any of the failure is produced (Li et al., 2025; Hedström et al., 2025; Zhang and others, 2025). We ask how such monitors should be evaluated, focusing on early warning, with repetitive degeneration as the case study.

Because every unit after the onset counts as a positive, these metrics reward flagging the failure, not flagging it early. A probe that fires only once the failure is visible in the text scores as well as one that fires before it begins (Figure 1, left).

papers.title: Kosmo-GFM: A Production-Ready Geometry Foundation Model
papers.abstract: We present Kosmo-GFM, a scene reconstruction system that integrates a geometry foundation model (GFM), a pose optimization engine (PoseEngine), and reconstruction-derived supervision from KosmoWorld. GFM predicts camera parameters, depth, cross-view correspondences, and dynamic 3D points from images and videos. PoseEngine combines these predictions with geometric optimization to recover scene-level camera poses and geometry for downstream 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting. KosmoWorld generates images and geometric supervision from reconstructed real-world scenes to improve GFM's geometric predictions. On the Sparse and Medium subsets of SpatialBench, GFM achieves the lowest absolute relative depth error and the highest relative-pose AUC at 5 degrees among the compared methods. It also achieves the lowest mean endpoint errors for dynamic points and scene flow across the five evaluated datasets. Across 34 scenes completed by all compared reconstruction systems, PoseEngine achieves the highest scene-averaged pose AUC at thresholds of 1, 3, and 5 degrees, with a cumulative runtime of 14.07 hours, approximately 20% of GLUEMAP's 69.67 hours. PoseEngine Flash provides a further accuracy-efficiency trade-off, with a measured mixed-precision runtime of 2.62 hours, approximately 4% of GLUEMAP's runtime. Separate scaling experiments show generally favorable trends with increased data, model computation, and training budgets. These results support the use of learned geometric priors within a scene-level reconstruction pipeline.

papers.intro:
Recovering real-world geometry and motion from images and videos is a central problem in computer vision. Traditional reconstruction systems recover scenes through feature matching, camera pose estimation, and geometric optimization. While these methods benefit from explicit geometric constraints, they depend on reliable visual correspondences and sufficient overlap between views. Textureless regions, repetitive structures, wide baselines, and scene dynamics introduce uncertainty that can compromise both camera estimation and geometry recovery. As the number of input views increases, maintaining scene consistency can also incur substantial computational cost. Balancing reconstruction quality, efficiency, and robustness to complex scenes therefore remains an important challenge.

Recovering real-world geometry and motion from images and videos is a central problem in computer vision. Traditional reconstruction systems recover scenes through feature matching, camera pose estimation, and geometric optimization. While these methods benefit from explicit geometric constraints, they depend on reliable visual correspondences and sufficient overlap between views. Textureless regions, repetitive structures, wide baselines, and scene dynamics introduce uncertainty that can compromise both camera estimation and geometry recovery. As the number of input views increases, maintaining scene consistency can also incur substantial computational cost. Balancing reconstruction quality, efficiency, and robustness to complex scenes therefore remains an important challenge.

Geometry foundation models offer a new approach to these challenges. Through large-scale pretraining, they learn transferable spatial priors and directly predict cameras, depth, cross-view correspondences, and dynamic geometry from visual observations. These predictions provide information where conventional geometric constraints are insufficient. However, model predictions do not inherently satisfy cross-view and temporal consistency across an entire scene, particularly for long sequences, large environments, and dynamic observations. Spatial priors and geometric optimization are therefore complementary: the former provide useful predictions and initialization, while the latter integrate them into coherent scene structure. The objective is not to eliminate optimization altogether, but to exploit model capabilities to reduce the optimization required for reliable reconstruction.

Following this principle, we build Kosmo-GFM, a scene reconstruction system that combines a geometry foundation model, GFM, with a pose optimization engine, PoseEngine. GFM estimates camera parameters, depth, cross-view correspondences, and dynamic 3D points from images and videos, providing spatial priors for both static geometry recovery and dynamic scene understanding. The system thus connects geometric predictions from visual observations to scene-level reconstruction and renderable 3D and 4D representations.

papers.title: Off-diagonal decay of capacitance matrices via Brownian motion
papers.abstract: We establish upper and lower bounds for the off-diagonal entries of the capacitance matrix of infinite systems of spherical resonators in chain, screen and crystal geometries. Let $d$ denote the distance between two resonator centres. For chains contained in a cylinder of bounded radius and with bounded axial gaps, the decay is of order $d^{-1}\log^{-2}(2+d)$. For screens contained in a slab and relatively dense in the tangential directions, it is of order $d^{-3}$. For relatively dense three-dimensional configurations, we obtain exponential upper and lower bounds. No periodicity is assumed. Our proofs are based on the classical connection between the Dirichlet problem and Brownian motion, which enables us to relate the decay estimates to hitting probabilities of Brownian motion.

papers.title: Reasoning Supervision and Capability Retention in LoRA Domain Adaptation
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning foundation models on financial data has a wide range of applications, including identifying event types from news, monitoring risk and compliance language, and answering questions over filings and earnings calls. In this setting, the main challenge is to improve task performance without degrading the generalization capabilities of the model. In this paper, we present an extensive set of ablations for fine-tuning Qwen3-8B with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We compare three training regimes: (1) response-only LoRA, where the supervised response is the label alone; (2) single-adapter reasoning, where reasoning traces from a teacher model are included alongside the labels in the training loss; and (3) dual-adapter composite training, where separate LoRA adapters are trained on traces and labels. Response-only LoRA improves in-domain performance and leaves general capabilities near those of the frozen model. The in-domain change is largest for calibration and argmax accuracy. Under single-adapter reasoning, the in-domain metrics remain behind those of the response-only regime, while MMLU-Pro can rise slightly and the other retention benchmarks stay within ordinary variation. Dual-adapter composite training remains on the same side of this comparison and yields no further gain. Finally, we compress the teacher traces by summarizing them before training, and show that shorter summaries move calibration toward the response-only regime without reaching it.

papers.title: Nearly Optimal Dilation for Non-Uniform k-Center with Constant-Factor Budget Violation
papers.abstract:
In Non-Uniform $k$-Center, we are given a metric space $(V,d)$ and $L$ levels of balls with prescribed radii $r_1 \ge \ldots \ge r_L$ and nonnegative integer budgets $k_1,\ldots,k_L$. The goal is to place at most $k_\ell$ centers of each level $\ell \in [L]$ in $V$ and minimize the dilation $\lambda$ such that the corresponding balls of radii $\lambda r_1,\dots,\lambda r_L$ cover $V$. While this problem admits no subexponential approximation factor unless P=NP, the picture changes drastically when additional centers are allowed. An $(\alpha,\beta)$-bicriteria approximation to Smooth Non-Uniform $k$-Center covers $V$ with dilation $\beta \lambda_{\text{opt}}$ such that, for each $\ell \in [L]$, the number of centers of the first $\ell$ levels is at most $\alpha$ times their total budget.
  For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, we give a randomized $(1+\varepsilon,8+\varepsilon)$-approximation and a deterministic $(O_{\varepsilon}(1),2+\varepsilon)$-approximation, both running in polynomial time. Even for classical $k$-Center, obtaining an $(O(1),2-\delta)$-approximation is NP-hard for every fixed $\delta \in (0,1]$. Thus, our second result almost settles the optimal dilation when a constant-factor violation of the budget is allowed, unless P=NP. We combine a new primal-dual enumeration procedure with a simple bucketing argument that yields a new trade-off between the two approximation factors. It remains open whether there is a polynomial-time $(1+\varepsilon,2+\varepsilon)$-bicriteria approximation, which would almost match the classical $2$-approximation for $k$-Center.

papers.title: Universal sampling rules for the signed friendship paradox
papers.abstract: The friendship paradox describes a bias in mean degree induced by neighbour sampling. We study signed weighted networks, with transitions proportional to edge magnitudes and signed strength as the vertex score. We characterize all positive initial weights, depending on total strength and score, that guarantee a nonnegative one-step mean change on every connected graph. Without regularity assumptions, the same condition yields stochastic dominance at every fixed time. Continuous admissible rules are precisely total strength multiplied by a positive continuous nonincreasing function of the score. It is enough to test connected graphs with at most five vertices and two vertex types. The bound of five is optimal even for continuous rules; the proof uses a sharp four-vertex energy inequality. The complete score vector alone cannot determine a universally valid initial law with full support. Under marked local convergence and suitable integrability assumptions, we also obtain joint limits for local conditional mean score increments and compute an explicit limiting law and mean for independently signed random regular graphs. Under joint cut-norm convergence of the magnitude and signed kernels and uniformly bounded normalized strengths, we also obtain Wasserstein convergence of the sampling-weighted distributions of normalized local biases and convergence of their means.

papers.title: Neural Render Proxies for Interactive and Differentiable Lighting
papers.abstract: Within the CG animation production pipeline, the challenges artists tackle in Lighting can be immense. Even minor adjustments require re-rendering massive scenes with slow offline renderers; global illumination has to be sampled and complex shaders have to be evaluated, leading to iteration times of minutes to hours per frame. To accelerate this process, we introduce a novel neural render proxy (NRP) that enables differentiable relighting of static scenes with fixed camera and materials at interactive rates. Our main insight is the decoupling of traditional rendering into path sampling and emission computation. From a single, light-agnostic render pass, we collect light transport data in the form of path samples. This enables rapidly sampling lighting conditions on the fly, and training a scene-specific lightweight neural network that learns how light is transported from any scene location to any image pixel. This approach is compatible with non-differentiable production renderers, induces minimal memory requirements during inference, and scales only with resolution and the number of light sources and parameters, but independently of scene and appearance complexity. Our evaluation demonstrates interactive frame rates for relighting (~30-60 Hz) while closely approximating the visual fidelity of ground-truth path tracing. In addition, the differentiable NRP enables fast, gradient-based inverse workflows, allowing artists to efficiently solve for lighting parameters from intuitive image-space edits or generative targets.

papers.title: The Gator low-background spectrometer: readout upgrade and photomultiplier tube radioassay for XLZD
papers.abstract: We report on a readout upgrade of Gator, a low-background high-purity germanium spectrometer operated at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso for material radioassay. The upgraded data acquisition records digitised waveforms, enabling noise rejection on an event-level basis, and offline energy reconstruction. Measurements before and after the upgrade show an improved energy resolution of 17% at the 2614.5 keV line of 208-Tl, with (2.14 +- 0.22) keV at FWHM, and suppression of electronic noise in the low-energy region. We assess the resulting sensitivity for a specified sample geometry, and present a new background measurement. The background rate in the (100-2700) keV range is (86.6 +- 0.5) counts/(kg day). We also show the radioassay results of sixteen Hamamatsu R17317 3-inch photomultiplier tubes with an improved stem design, which reduces the activities from the primordial 238-U and 232-Th chains by a factor of three, making them suitable candidate photosensors for the XLZD experiment.

papers.title: PACER: GPU Excursion Management for ML Workloads
papers.abstract:
Variability is an inherent characteristic of modern GPU systems, arising from a combination of process variation, dynamic environmental conditions, and power management decisions. Prior work has characterized inter-GPU variability and found consistent performance differences across GPUs. However, we observe that modern workloads, particularly large language models (LLMs), exhibit significant intra-GPU variability. Their short-running kernels interact poorly with the coarse granularity of dynamic power management mechanisms, leading to unpredictable performance.
  A key source of this intra-GPU transient variability is power excursions, also referred to as electrical design power peaks (EDP$_{p}$), where power temporarily exceeds the GPU's rated power limits. While power management mechanisms are designed to ensure reliable operation despite the presence of EDP$_{p}$ sustained power peaks cause throttling that detrimentally impacts overall application performance. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to characterize the magnitude and frequency of EDP$_{p}$, showing that frequent, significant power overshoots are especially common in ML workloads, which combine high power draw, short kernels, and rapidly changing compute demands. To address this, we design and leverage hardware and firmware mechanisms to provide consistent power management behavior that reduces intra-GPU variability due to EDP$_{p}$ and improves overall performance. We evaluate our techniques across a range of popular workloads. Our approach improves performance by 3-12% over state-of-the-art GPU power management and comes within 3% of an oracular solution.

papers.title: Stable $s$-minimal hypersurfaces in dimensions seven and eight
papers.abstract:
We establish optimal sheet separation estimates for stable $s$-minimal hypersurfaces in dimensions up to seven, using an iteration argument in the nonlocal approximation theory of Chan-Dipierro-Serra-Valdinoci. These estimates imply that every stable $s$-minimal hypersurface in $\mathbb{R}^7$ is a hyperplane when $s$ is close to $1$. More generally, every finite Morse index $s$-minimal set in $\mathbb{R}^7$ is a half-space.
  We also establish a compactness theorem for stable $s$-minimal cones in $\mathbb{R}^8$. We prove uniform curvature and area estimates for their links and show that, as $s \uparrow 1$, they subconverge graphically in $C^{2,\alpha}$, either with multiplicity one to a classical stable minimal cone, or with multiplicity two to a hyperplane. The stability of Lawson and axisymmetric $s$-minimal cones in $\mathbb{R}^8$ shows that these results are optimal.

papers.title: Separations Between Submodular-Like Graph Widths
papers.abstract:
Many algorithmic frameworks exist for evaluating join queries. They range from simple ones, such as dynamic programming over a single tree decomposition, high-degree-low-degree splitting from graph algorithms, and the degree uniformization of Joglekar and R\'e, to sophisticated ones based on information-theoretic inequalities, such as the PANDA framework for submodular width. Each of these frameworks except high-degree-low-degree splitting comes with a width notion of the query that determines its running-time exponent. We fill this gap by formalizing high-degree-low-degree splitting with $\ell$ degree classes, which gives rise to the degree-splitting width $\mathrm{ds}_\ell$-width. These width notions form a hierarchy, but it was not known whether the more complicated frameworks achieve better worst-case exponents than the simpler ones on any graph query.
  We study this question for full self-join-free join queries with binary relations, which amounts to colored subgraph isomorphism for a pattern graph $H$. We show that every inequality in the hierarchy $\mathrm{subw} \le \#\mathrm{subw} \le \text{m-width} \le \mathrm{ds}_\ell\text{-width}$ can be strict. For instance, $\text{m-width}(K_{3,3}) = 2 < \mathrm{ds}_\ell\text{-width}(K_{3,3})$ for every constant $\ell$, so no constant number of degree classes reaches the exponent of degree uniformization. We find the smallest separating patterns, with 8, 9, and 6 nodes, respectively, by an exhaustive search with a software tool that computes these widths via mixed integer linear programming. Along the way, we give a degree-based algorithm that removes the polylogarithmic overhead of degree uniformization when evaluating full join queries. Furthermore, we show that with logarithmically many degree classes, the degree-splitting width coincides with the m-width of Joglekar and R\'e. Finally, we discuss several open problems.

papers.title: A superconducting quantum point contact in Ge
papers.abstract: Hybrid superconducting-semiconducting circuits provide a versatile platform for investigating coherent transport in mesoscopic weak links. Superconducting quantum point contacts (SQPCs) are particularly interesting in this context, as their supercurrent is carried by a discrete number of ballistic transport modes. Here, we investigate a gate-tunable superconducting quantum point contact realized in Ge/SiGe. By incorporating the QPC into a highly asymmetric superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID), we gain access to its current-phase relation (CPR) and switching current, enabling phase-sensitive studies of few-mode superconducting transport. We observe a direct correspondence between conductance quantization and switching-current quantization, linking the normal-state transport modes to the superconducting response. In addition, we demonstrate strong gate tunability of the effective transmission near the onset of the first conductance plateau. Under microwave irradiation, the QPC exhibits photon-assisted multiple Andreev reflections at lower transparencies and Shapiro replicas in the high-transparency, few-mode regime.

authors.name: Stephen W. Bedell
authors.institution: University at Albany, State University of New York

papers.title: Beyond Row-Level Prediction: Evaluating and Learning Composition for Reusable Table Representations
papers.abstract: Tables are compositional, with content spread across a schema, cell values, rows, and columns.
