papers.title: SPEC CPU2026 Under the Microscope: Programs, Phases, and Samples
papers.abstract: SPEC CPU2026, the latest generation of the SPEC CPU benchmarks, is set to become the standard benchmark suite in computer architecture research, where new designs are often evaluated through sampled simulation with tools such as SimPoint. Existing characterizations of the suite focus on whole-run averages, which reveal neither how behavior changes within a run nor how well sampling captures it. We characterize CPU2026 on real hardware at three levels: programs, phases, and samples. At the program level, we report whole-run metrics and top-down bottleneck classes for all four suites and examine how they change with workload size, compiler version, and platform, across machines with three different instruction set architectures: x86, Arm, and RISC-V. Notably, changing only the compiler version can halve or nearly double the IPC of individual benchmarks. At the phase level, we track hardware counters every 10 ms over all 90 SPECrate inputs, identify recurring patterns of time-varying behavior, and divide the inputs into three groups: steady, multi-phase, and bursty. More than half of the inputs show time-varying behavior, and IPC within a single input can vary by more than an order of magnitude. At the sample level, we validate SimPoint against hardware measurements of every interval it can select. SimPoint is accurate on steady inputs, but its error reaches 43% on the others, and changing only the random seed spreads the error of one input over a range of 58 percentage points. Keeping SimPoint's clusters but choosing each representative by measured CPI brings every input within 2.6%, so the error comes from the choice of representatives, not from the clustering. We conclude with practical recommendations on sampling strategy for CPU2026, which give researchers a deeper understanding of the suite and show where additional simulation effort is needed to keep sampled results accurate.

papers.title: Protocol-Aware Auditing of Domain-Blind Feature Attribution in Network Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: Feature-attribution methods can query rule-violating network states through perturbations, coalitions, references, paths, and ablations, making explanations and their evaluation sensitive to model behavior outside the operational domain. We formalize this failure mode as domain blindness and prove valid-query invariance: when models agree on the required oracle information within a declared rule-valid set, a procedure confined to that set returns the same attribution. We instantiate one protocol-aware query-control principle in LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, and DeepLIFT and audit paired configurations across four NIDS datasets and three classifier families. In six settings where standard LIME reports perfect top-feature repeatability, PA-LIME reveals substantial variability, with a mean of 0.575. Under FGSM followed by protocol repair, PA-DeepLIFT and PA-IG achieve the largest attribution-similarity curve areas, 0.452 and 0.413, while mean within-PA rank agreement rises to 0.366 from 0.217. PA-XAI therefore turns structured domain assumptions into explicit, testable controls for explanation auditing; support modeling, raw-flow reconstruction, and adaptive explanation attacks provide complementary validation layers.

papers.title: Robustness Within a Fairness Budget: Parity Frontiers and Equal-Opportunity Reversal
papers.abstract: Adversarial training protects predictive performance under attack but does not determine how decisions are distributed across protected groups. We formulate binary classification as projected gradient descent (PGD) adversarial-risk minimization under a squared soft demographic-parity (DP) budget, optimized with projected multiplier and one-sided penalty updates. On Adult Income, using the binary sex field supplied by the benchmark for group auditing but excluding it from prediction, we test logistic regression and a one-hidden-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) across three paired seeds, four PGD strengths, and five budgets. At $\varepsilon=0.3$, PGD training improves balanced accuracy over empirical-risk minimization (ERM) by $7.77$ and $11.45$ percentage points and removes $85.7\%$ and $89.5\%$ of attack-induced growth in hard demographic-parity difference (DPD). At the representative interior value $\tau=0.015$, constrained training cuts DPD relative to PGD training by $52.2\%$ and $49.2\%$, while remaining $3.18$ and $8.34$ balanced-accuracy points above ERM. Across all eight seed-averaged model-attack paths, the sampled budget path strictly orders DPD and accuracy and reverses mean signed equal-opportunity difference (EOpp). A rate theorem gives the exact true-positive-rate shift required for reversal, and the measured group rates satisfy it. Within this controlled feature-space study, robustness and parity admit useful joint operating points, but one fairness metric cannot replace a full group-rate audit.

papers.title: Adapting Monocular Depth Estimation in Novel Scenes through Disparity Refinement and Robot Ego-Motion
papers.abstract: The geometric understanding of a scene is a crucial component for safe and efficient robotic operations in novel and unstructured environments. The recent emergence of foundation models for Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) has provided an opportunity to enrich robotic perception capabilities with dense long-range depth predictions, replacing expensive onboard hardware (e.g., LiDARs and stereo cameras). However, these offline models are primarily trained on affine-invariant depth representations, and their generalization to novel scenes remains unclear. In this work we present EM-ViT, a monocular depth estimation model that learns to adapt online relative depth inputs from a foundation model prior to the metric scale with observations collected during robotic operations. Motivated by the stereo camera parameterization, our method decomposes depth prediction via dense disparity refinement to recover the scene's relative structure and an effective baseline scalar prediction to determine the missing metric scale. The learning process leverages sparse LiDAR points and, optionally, the robot's Ego-Motion (EM) to rapidly train a lightweight Vision Transformer (ViT), while an internal gradient matching loss preserves the fine-grained semantic structure of the input disparity in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on publicly available sequences, such as KITTI, and show that our online learning pipeline can adapt to novel scenes faster and with higher accuracy than existing MDE foundation models. The code and supplementary materials will be publicly available at https://emvit-mde.github.io.

papers.title: Toward Cross-Rubric Surgical Skill Assessment via Joint Embedding Prediction
papers.abstract: Expert review of surgical videos is essential for surgical training but labor-intensive, motivating AI-assisted skill assessment to provide feedback at scale. Although surgical assessment rubrics may use different language to describe similar skills, existing automated methods commonly predict predefined skill levels or numerical scores tied to fixed rubrics, limiting their ability to transfer across semantically equivalent assessment criteria. We propose Predictive Rubric Alignment (PRA), a joint embedding prediction approach that scores surgical videos using natural-language descriptions of skill levels. Rather than matching level probabilities, PRA predicts a rater-weighted combination of skill-level description embeddings. Adjacent description features define a score-parameterized path, and the predicted embedding is projected onto this path to read the score. We introduce two variants: \textit{PRA-item}, which uses learned queries for predefined assessment items, and \textit{PRA-cond}, which generates queries from textual item names to enable assessment of unseen items without retraining. On AIxSuture, a dataset of expert-rated suturing videos, PRA outperforms published baselines in skill classification. We further evaluate zero-shot transfer to the smaller surgical skill assessment benchmark JIGSAWS. Trained on only two AIxSuture rubric items, PRA-cond assesses unseen JIGSAWS items without further training, yielding positive score correlations and greater Grad-CAM overlap with instruments and suture than a description-matching baseline. These results support predictive rubric alignment as a promising direction for flexible and explainable automated surgical skill assessment.

papers.title: Starscream: Reimagining LLM Sharding on AMD Instinct GPUs with GPU Partitioning
papers.abstract: As GPU accelerators grow larger to meet rising compute demands, they exhibit increasingly pronounced non-uniform memory access (NUMA) characteristics that challenge existing LLM frameworks. Chiplet-based architectures provide a practical path to larger GPUs while mitigating manufacturing yield constraints. Modern GPUs such as AMD Instinct MI300X employs such a multi-die design, and further offer GPU partitioning capabilities, partitioning a single physical GPU into multiple logical devices with NUMA-aware memory domains, promising faster kernel launches, and reduced memory access latencies with improved locality. However, current parallelization strategies, designed for homogeneous GPU topologies, when applied under partitioning, extend its unidimensional sharding causing significant performance degradation. Three bottlenecks emerge: (1) memory redundancy; (2) arithmetic intensity collapse; (3) communication overhead from flat collectives. We present Starscream, a rethinking of LLM sharding for the chiplet era. Rather than stretching inter-GPU sharding thinner, Starscream adds intra-GPU sharding along an orthogonal dimension, grounded in three foundational principles: kernel shape preservation, memory redundancy elimination, and communication overhead minimization. These principles form the basis for extending any sharding strategy into the partitioning regime. We demonstrate their effectiveness using tensor parallelism as a case study. On AMD MI300X and MI355X, exploiting partitioning capabilities yields up to 4x speedup for attention and 1.43x for fused GEMMs compared to chiplet-oblivious baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of chiplet-aware designs. Starscream's principles generalize across sharding strategies and future architectures.

papers.title: LoCoJAX: Host-Local Coordination for Small-Model RL on TPUs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly targets small language models, and executing these workloads efficiently across multiple accelerators requires effective coordination. On TPUs, Pathways-based RL uses a single controller to coordinate computation across hosts. This execution model is effective for large models, but its coordination computational costs are harder to amortize when small models repeatedly invoke short computations. To characterize these computational costs, we sweep dense models from 0.6B to 405B parameters on TPU v7x under a decode-heavy workload and measure how host and network computational overhead vary with model size. At 0.6B, host orchestration occupies 36% of step time and network communication 2%, whereas for large models, estimated network computational costs dominate the non-compute time. Motivated by these findings, we present Local Coordination JAX (LoCoJAX), which implements local rollout and reward processing on each TPU host with synchronous global training. In controlled comparisons against a tuned and optimized Pathways baseline on Qwen3-0.6B across three workloads and 8-64 TPU v7x chips, its colocated mode (LoCoJAX-CO) is 1.3-3.6x faster per step; on GSM8K, it completes a step faster on 8 chips than Pathways does on 64. Finally, a Ray-managed disaggregated mode (LoCoJAX-DA) overlaps rollout and training on separate hosts, and placement experiments establish when this overlap compensates for dividing devices and transferring weights: only when rollout dominates the step and receives most of the hosts. On NuminaMath-CoT at 256 chips, giving rollout 75% of hosts cuts step time by about 15% compared with LoCoJAX-CO.

papers.title: Feature-Aware Edge Sampling for Approximate One-Step Laplacian Propagation
papers.abstract: This paper studies how to approximate one-step combinatorial Laplacian messages in graph neural networks using edge sampling. We propose a spanning tree based hybrid sampler that combines feature-conditioned message scores and effective-resistance leverage scores, derive the expected one-step message error and obtain the optimal sampling probabilities and error frontier for a given expected edge budget. Preliminary experiments on synthetic community graphs show that message error decreases, while classification accuracy increases slightly, as the edge budget grows, and performance of the hybrid sampler is in between of optimal selection uniform random sampling. We leave multi-step propagation and evaluation on larger and real graphs for future work.

papers.title: FlinkEval: A Synthetic Corpus for Evaluating Natural Language Interfaces to Streaming SQL
papers.abstract: Existing natural-language-to-SQL benchmarks primarily evaluate queries over bounded relational data, leaving streaming semantics underexplored. We introduce FlinkEval, an execution-grounded synthetic benchmark comprising 3,903 question--SQL pairs across 45 industry domains and 45 semantic labels. We create diverse schemas and domain-plausible, temporally consistent data through iterative generation and validation. SQL patterns collected from the human-written NL2SQL pairs and vendor documentation drive quota-balanced generation, and execution with a repair loop on Confluent Cloud Apache Flink produces reference queries covering windowing, temporal joins, pattern matching, nested types, and data manipulation. The corpus includes paired schema-explicit and business-language requests, with annotations for analysis by query pattern, complexity, and execution mode. A seven-level Question Specification Ladder examines semantics-preserving reformulation and underspecified requests augmented with oracle-derived clues. Baseline evaluations combine execution outcomes with adjudicated LLM judgments, revealing challenges in pattern composition and request specification.

papers.title: Riordan Arrays as Structured Operators for Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract:
Riordan arrays have traditionally been studied as infinite lower-triangular matrices that encode generating-function transformations and combinatorial relationships. This note proposes a complementary direction: using Riordan arrays as structured operators in artificial intelligence and data analysis. For a data sequence with generating function $A(z)$, a Riordan array $(g(z),f(z))$ produces the transformation \[
  A(z)\longmapsto g(z)A(f(z)). \] This yields a parameterized family of causal linear operators that combine convolution, substitution, and multiscale mixing. The resulting structure may support parameter-efficient neural-network layers, variable-length sequence models, interpretable recurrent systems, invertible architectures, and models for hierarchical or recursively generated data. We explain what the infinite-dimensional viewpoint does and does not provide, outline several possible architectures, identify theoretical and numerical challenges, and propose an initial experimental program. The aim is not to claim that Riordan arrays are appropriate for all data, but to identify settings in which their algebraic structure supplies a useful inductive bias.

papers.title: Sprint3D: Accelerating End-to-End 3D Asset Generation through Pipeline Optimization
papers.abstract: Image-to-3D generative models now produce asset-quality textured meshes, but at minutes per asset they remain slow to iterate with and costly to deploy. Prior work has mostly accelerated the sampling of the networks, and where it also optimizes the mesh processing, it trains its own generators. We instead start from a publicly released pipeline and ask how much of its end-to-end time can be saved. Profiling the public Pixal3D pipeline shows that its latency is dominated by what happens after the networks: the four rectified flows take 14% of the wall-clock time and mesh post-processing takes 85%, most of it in CPU-based UV unwrapping. We therefore first rebuild the mesh post-processing on the GPU and take it off the critical path, then cut the per-evaluation overhead of the flows and distill them from 76 to 8 network evaluations. The resulting pipeline, Sprint3D, reduces the median time per asset from 133 s to 4.05 s on one H200 GPU at the same export settings (33$\times$). At the same time, on 2,653 held-out Toys4K objects it improves every input-view normal metric of the Pixal3D protocol, with a slightly lower mean silhouette IoU, lower point-cloud alignment scores and less fine texture detail. The rebuilt post-processing alone also speeds up TRELLIS.2, which uses the same export code, by 6.7$\times$ without a detectable change in the evaluated metrics.

papers.title: Exceptional parameters in the Erd\H{o}s similarity problem
papers.abstract: The Erd\H os similarity conjecture says that for every infinite set $A \subset \mathbb{R}$, there exists a set $E$ of positive Lebesgue measure which does not contain any affine copy of $x + tA$ of $A$ (with $t \neq 0$). Kolountzakis proved that for every infinite $A$, there exists $E$ of positive Lebesgue measure so that the exceptional sets $D_E(A)$ of scales $t$, and $\mathcal E_E(A)$ of affine maps $(x,t)$, for which $x+tA\subseteq E$, are both Lebesgue null. We show that these exceptional parameter sets are small in two finer senses. First, given any countable family of Fourier decay rates, a single $E$ can be constructed so that $D_E(A)$ is null with respect to every measure whose Fourier transform decays at one of these rates. Consequently, there are compact sets $K$ of measure arbitrarily close to $1$ for which $D_K(A)$ and $\mathcal E_K(A)$ have modified Fourier dimension zero. Second, we give a criterion, depending both on the growth of a gauge function $h$ and on the gaps between elements of lacunary sequences in $A$, which guarantees that $\mathcal H^h(D_E(A))=0$ for gauges with $h(u)/u\to\infty$, as well as a similar result for $\mathcal E_K(A)$. For sets such as $A = \{1/n!\}$ and $A = \{e^{-n^q}\}$, this yields explicit gauges of the form $h(u) = u\exp((\log 1/u)^\theta)$ with $0 < \theta < 1$.

papers.title: Central limit theorems for Frobenius, Hecke and Kloosterman angles
papers.abstract: The Frobenius angles of non-CM elliptic curves and the Hecke angles of non-CM newforms are equidistributed with respect to the Sato--Tate measure, while for Kloosterman angles, this is known on average over natural families. We study the fluctuations around these laws in large families, for smooth test functions. We prove an unconditional central limit theorem for Frobenius angles of elliptic curves for a much larger class of test functions than previously considered; earlier results assumed the Riemann hypothesis for $L$-functions of Hecke eigenforms of full level. This result follows from a general framework, developed here, which yields Gaussian moments for statistics of sequences in $[0,1]$ varying over families. In this framework, independence is replaced by two quantitative conditions: approximate independence at distinct indices, and convergence of the family averages to the Weyl limits at a suitable rate. As further applications, we extend central limit theorems for Kloosterman angles and for Hecke angles of newforms to larger classes of test functions, the latter with the weight and the level varying simultaneously. We also treat the dilated angles $\alpha\theta$ for integers $\alpha\geq2$, whose limiting distribution is uniform. Finally, we discuss sharp statistics, obtaining a central limit theorem for Hecke angles and explaining the obstruction for the other two families.

authors.name: Kaneenika Sinha
authors.institution: Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Pune

papers.title: Peak Performance in Matched Filtering: Fused Correlation and Statistically Controlled Screening on CPUs and GPUs
papers.abstract: Batched matched filtering and cross-correlation over large template banks are a primary computational cost in gravitational-wave astronomy, seismology, and radio transient searches. Standard pipelines pair a general-purpose inverse Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) with separate multiplication and peak-finding kernels, writing intermediate spectra and full correlation series to memory for every template. We fuse the conjugate product into the first inverse-transform butterflies and the peak reduction into the last so only candidate peaks leave processor registers, and tile batches in 2D so $K^2$ correlations reuse $2K$ cached spectra. This shifts filtering from a DRAM-bandwidth-bound to an on-chip cache-bandwidth-bound regime. In some situations, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is concentrated toward lower frequencies while higher frequencies dominate the transform length. We develop a hierarchical screening method that exploits this via a sequence of short low-frequency transforms before evaluating the full band, deriving stage thresholds from the spectral power profile and matched-filter noise autocovariance to target a specified false-dismissal probability. We demonstrate these methods in the open-source matchedfilter library across eight CPU architectures and two integrated GPUs (AMD Radeon 8060S via Vulkan and Apple M2 via Metal). On an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 at $N=4096$, fused peak-only filtering is $1.4\times$ faster than a standalone AOCL-FFTW inverse transform on one CPU core and $6.2\times$ faster than rocFFT on its Radeon 8060S GPU ($3.1\times$ over MLX FFT on the M2 GPU). For a fiducial gravitational-wave search ($\rho_\mathrm{th}=5.5$, $10^{-2}$ false-dismissal target), hierarchical screening yields a $26\times$ speedup over AOCL-FFTW on CPU, $21\times$ over rocFFT on the 8060S GPU, and $19\times$ over MLX FFT on the M2 GPU.

papers.title: DiSKO: Distribution Steering for Nonlinear Systems using the Koopman Operator
papers.abstract: This paper studies the problem of data-driven covariance steering for stochastic, nonlinear dynamical systems. We utilize Koopman operator theory to learn, directly from data, an approximate linear representation of the nonlinear dynamics in a lifted space of observable functions of the state. By exploiting this linear model, we design controllers for the mean and covariance of the underlying nonlinear system by utilizing linear distribution steering algorithms. To account for approximation errors in the learned dynamics and the ambiguity in the disturbance distribution induced in the lifted space, we formulate the problem as a distributionally robust covariance steering problem. Furthermore, we leverage a deep neural network (DNN) to simultaneously learn the Koopman observables and the linear model parameters, thus eliminating the need for manual observables basis selection while also reducing the dimensionality of the lifted representation. Additionally, we can promote desirable model properties, such as stability, during DNN training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework via numerical simulations.

papers.title: An Extensive Evaluation of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Approaches for Sentiment Analysis: Insights from Amazon Customer Reviews
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of user-generated text on online platforms creates opportunities for understanding customer opinion and supporting data-driven decisions. This study compares five traditional machine learning classifiers (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Bernoulli Naive Bayes, Linear Support Vector Classifier, and Multinomial Naive Bayes) and six deep learning architectures (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, GRU, RNN, Attention, and FastText) for three-class sentiment classification of 568,454 Amazon Fine Food Reviews. Machine learning models used Bag-of-Words (BoW) and TF-IDF features limited to 5,000 terms; deep learning models used learned embeddings over a 20,000-word vocabulary. Models were evaluated on the original imbalanced data and on a random-oversampled balanced set of 1,070,469 reviews, using accuracy, macro and per-class precision, recall, and F1-score, and training time. On the balanced set, Random Forest with BoW achieved 99\% accuracy and the Attention model achieved 98.7\%. Linear SVC reached 89\% accuracy in 1 min 15 s, and Logistic Regression reached 90\% in 3 min 37 s. On the imbalanced set, the Attention model achieved 97.8\% accuracy, and FastText achieved 95.3\% in 3 min 26 s, while the RNN reached 91.9\% with a neutral-class F1-score of 0.08. Deep learning models were more stable across class distributions, whereas the best classical model depended on balancing. We also report a user-facing application that applies the trained Random Forest and Attention models to new review text. Because the labels are derived from star ratings, the results measure agreement with rating-derived sentiment classes rather than annotated sentiment; the dataset is a single source, and the findings should be read with that limitation in mind.

papers.title: Code as Explanations: Executable and Verifiable LLM Explanations
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly make consequential decisions and solve problems alongside humans, we must understand how models arrive at their conclusions. Understanding how an LLM behaves requires observing it across multiple inputs, yet free-text explanations such as chain-of-thought (CoT) are generated per instance and cannot be easily verified on new inputs. We propose {code explanations to address the mismatch in how LLM explanations are generated versus how they are evaluated: a program explains LLM behavior across a dataset of inputs, and its execution enables automatic verification. We define Consistency metric that measures the fraction of inputs on which the program reproduces the LLM's outputs, and use it to evaluate and select candidate programs. Across three open-source code-capable LLMs and eight tasks, we find that LLMs can produce highly consistent code explanations in several settings. Code explanations are also 6$\times$ to 100$\times$ shorter than CoT, and better align with model behavior in 9 out of 24 settings. However, consistency is significantly lower on tasks with more complex linguistic components, where generated programs reproduce model outputs no more frequently than an uninformative explanation baseline, and these programs often rely on longer hard-coded patterns. In experiments with Claude Opus 5.5, providing the model with consistency feedback and code execution improves explanation consistency across tasks, but consistency remains significantly lower on more complex tasks. Our findings establish executable code as a novel, verifiable, and compact approach to explaining LLM behavior and highlight verification feedback as a promising direction for improving explanation consistency. The code for this paper is at https://github.com/rajesh-lab/code-as-explanations.

papers.title: Sharp Lower Bounds for Parallel Log-Concave Sampling
papers.abstract:
How many rounds of parallel queries are needed to sample from a smooth, strongly log-concave distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$? For every fixed condition number $\kappa \in (1, \infty)$, we prove that any sampler making polynomially many queries per round requires $\Omega_\kappa(\log d)$ rounds to achieve constant total variation error in the worst case. The lower bound holds even if queries return derivatives of all orders. Together with the first-order parallel Picard algorithm of \cite{zhou2025parallel}, this establishes a depth complexity of $\Theta_\kappa(\log d)$ for parallel log-concave sampling with $\operatorname{poly}(d)$ width.
  We then study centered Gaussian targets to understand how much width is needed at a given depth. From \cite{chewi2023query,zhou2026complexitygaussiansampling}, it is known that either one round of width $d$ or $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\kappa} \log d)$ rounds of constant width suffice for first-order Gaussian sampling. At fixed $\kappa$ we characterize the depth-width tradeoff interpolating between these regimes: when using $ \lceil c \log d\rceil$ rounds, if $0 < c < c_\star(\kappa)$ then the optimal width at constant TV error is $\widetilde{\Theta}(d^{1-c/c_\star(\kappa)})$, while if $c \geq c_\star(\kappa)$ then it is $\Theta_\kappa(1)$. Here, $c_\star(\kappa)$ is an explicit constant with $c_\star(\kappa) \sim \sqrt{\kappa} / 8$ as $\kappa \to \infty$.

papers.title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
papers.abstract: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.

authors.name: Shang-Wen Li
authors.institution: The University of Texas at Austin

papers.title: Improving Nonequilibrium Thermal Conduction in CaF2 by Breaking the Phonon Bottleneck Effect
papers.abstract: Heat dissipation in laser optical materials depends not only on their thermal conductivity but also on how absorbed energy is redistributed among various phonon modes. In calcium fluoride (CaF2), rapid energy transfer from hot electrons to weakly propagating longitudinal optical (LO) phonons can create a nonequilibrium phonon bottleneck effect that limits efficient heat removal. Here, we propose selective phonon excitation as an effective strategy to break this bottleneck. Combining electron-phonon scattering calculations, phonon Boltzmann transport analysis, and nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations, we identify LO phonons as the primary modes that preferentially receive energy from hot carriers, leading to energy accumulation due to their inefficient transport and relaxation. Guided by three-phonon scattering phase-space analysis, selective excitation of transverse acoustic (TA) modes can accelerate LO relaxation and promote energy transfer toward heat-carrying acoustic modes. While sustained LO-phonon excitation reduces the thermal conductivity by approximately 12%, additional TA-mode excitation improves heat conduction by approximately 21% compared to the state limited by the LO-phonon bottleneck, surpassing the unexcited value. These findings demonstrate that controlling interbranch energy redistribution can counteract phonon-bottleneck-induced heat accumulation and reveal a working route for active thermal management in laser optical materials through selective control of phonon populations.

authors.name: Chenbo Zhang
authors.institution: Xi'an University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Scaling VLA Serving Under Robotic Execution Constraints
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation. In our production setting, hundreds of VLA-powered robots are already operating in real-world environments, creating an immediate need for efficient fleet serving. We present XInfer, a production-deployed VLA serving system designed to reduce the inference infrastructure cost of large-scale robotic deployments. XInfer jointly coordinates heterogeneous VLA computation with the evolving response requirements of robotic execution. By exploiting computational parallelism while managing interference, XInfer improves GPU efficiency while protecting time-critical robotic feedback. We evaluate XInfer across three VLA models using production-derived workloads, achieving 1.26-3.75 times the effective robot capacity (ERC) of state-of-the-art systems under physical-execution constraints. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/X-Square-Robot/xinfer.

papers.title: Bridging Update Coordination and Flatness in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning combines complementary knowledge across clients to alleviate local data limitations without sharing raw samples. However, data heterogeneity can cause conflicting updates and hinder generalization. Update coordination reduces interference among client updates, while flatness optimization reduces sensitivity to parameter perturbations to improve generalization. Existing joint designs largely target specific algorithms, limiting flexible combinations of these approaches. To address this problem, we propose a unified federated learning framework that bridges update coordination and flatness optimization. Clients separately accumulate descent signals and flatness corrections along the same local trajectory. The server coordinates both groups with independent states before fusing their outputs into a global update. Explicit conversion between trajectory signals and model updates enables different coordination strategies to work with compatible local or globally guided flatness mechanisms without changing the inference architecture. Experiments show that the evaluated combinations generally improve average and worst-client accuracy over update coordination alone, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework in combining these complementary optimization mechanisms.

papers.title: Recover, Don't Just Continue: Learning from Feedback for Physical Failure Understanding and Correction
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models are regarded as the cognitive foundation of embodied intelligence, but planning from instructions alone cannot make them reliable. During execution, actions deviate from intended effects, constrained by the embodiment and environment. An embodied brain must understand why execution deviates, identify what can be reliably realized, and revise decisions using interaction experience. These correspond to causal failure localization, capability-constrained adaptation, and experience-driven revision. Current embodied foundation models largely lack these capabilities. To address this, we introduce Embodied-Corrector. We construct failure-recovery data by injecting perturbations at subtask boundaries of successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and keeping failures that are observable from public evidence and recoverable from the current state. We align actions, consequences, failure causes, and recoveries into Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision. Training uses evaluation-first SFT: the model learns Judge and Cause first, then Sub and Fine conditioned on accurate prefixes. Since deployment uses self-generated prefixes, evaluation errors propagate into recovery planning, and response-level rewards are too coarse to locate affected planning tokens. We therefore use OPD to internalize the planning distribution under accurate prefixes into that under self-generated ones: the model generates plans from self-generated prefixes, while a contrastive forward pass with accurate prefixes compares token probabilities to reinforce or suppress planning tokens. At deployment, this branch is removed. Experiments show stronger failure analysis and corrective planning: with a frozen VLA, composite task success improves by 6.1 percentage points; with fixed GPT-5.5 execution, manipulation and navigation tasks improve by 13.9 percentage points.

authors.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Single-spike superradiant free-electron lasers
papers.abstract: Free-electron lasers (FELs) deliver high-brilliance radiation from the infrared to X-rays, enabling atomic-scale studies on femtosecond-to-attosecond timescales. Yet conventional facilities rely on large, costly radio-frequency accelerators. Laser wakefield accelerators (LWFAs), combining high accelerating gradients with ultra-high peak currents, offer a compact alternative and open up new prospects for advanced FEL operation. Here, we demonstrate a tabletop superradiant FEL driven by single-spike, pre-bunched electron beams from a LWFA. By manipulating the energy chirp during acceleration and compressing the bunch to sub-wavelength duration, we obtain coherent radiation extending into the vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) regime within a remarkably compact 3-metre beamline--from gas target to radiator. Under optimized conditions, the measured photon yield reaches 2.8x10^10 per pulse after transmission through a 500-um slit, with a reproducibility of approximately 70%. This approach uniquely exploits the energy chirp and high-current characteristics inherent to LWFA beams without recourse to exponential gain, substantially minimizing device length while obviating the need for external synchronization and offering enhanced tolerance to jitter--thereby establishing a practical route toward efficient, compact FELs suitable for applications in academic, industrial, and clinical settings.

papers.title: A neural quantum state variational Monte Carlo study of Aharonov-Casher bands
papers.abstract: We use neural-network-based variational Monte Carlo to investigate the competition between fractional Chern insulators and generalized Wigner crystals in the Aharonov-Casher Hamiltonian, a continuum model for moir\'e materials. We introduce a variational wave function inspired by flux attachment that captures fractionalized phases and, by comparing its energy with that of a Slater--Jastrow ansatz that captures crystalline phases, we determine the phase diagram at fractional fillings in regimes of strong band mixing and for system sizes beyond the reach of other methods. We find that discrete translation symmetry, encoded in a nonuniform quantum geometry, affects fractionalized states at filling fractions $\nu=1/3$ and $\nu=2/3$ differently, and that band mixing can stabilize incommensurate crystalline ground states. Our results further reveal the delicate competition between topological and non-topological crystalline phases.

authors.name: Miguel A. Morales
authors.institution: Instituto de Investigaciones Biomédicas, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México

papers.title: Active-space construction in single-fragment coupled-cluster embedding for chemical reactions
papers.abstract: We benchmark single-fragment quantum embedding, in which electron correlation---at the level of coupled-cluster theory with single, double, and perturbative triple excitations [CCSD(T)]---is restricted to orbitals associated with a chosen molecular fragment, and the remaining orbitals are frozen at the Hartree-Fock level. We compare several methods for constructing fragment active spaces, and we test their performance on 60 organic reaction energies and three reaction profiles. A common fragment projection operator is used to relate several of the tested orbital constructions. Regional embedding, based on density matrix embedding theory, is shown to give accurate and robust performance when used for both the occupied and virtual active orbitals. For virtual orbitals, fragment-centered projected atomic orbitals and fragment natural orbitals (defined by eigenvectors of a fragment MP2 density matrix) also perform well, but the latter typically retains larger virtual spaces. Composite MP2 corrections yield the largest improvement: combined with fragment natural orbitals, they give average reaction energy errors below 0.3 kcal/mol relative to full-system CCSD(T), with all individual errors below 1 kcal/mol. Reaction profiles show that accurate endpoint energies can conceal substantial barrier errors, emphasizing the importance of approximating omitted correlation.

papers.title: Mach2: Scientific Discovery Platform with Deterministic Execution Constraints
papers.abstract: Language-model agents can formulate workflows and invoke specialized tools, yet compliance with natural-language operating rules is not guaranteed by prompting alone. Mach2 addresses this limitation by coupling Eigen orchestration to deterministic, lint-like checks of tool requests, source changes, acceptance tests, and artifact contracts. Domain requirements are represented as executable predicates: mandatory failures prevent advancement of the checked operation, while diagnostic findings are retained for correction or review. User-specified test-driven development (TDD), CodeGrapher's abstract-syntax-tree analysis, and history-guided evolutionary search provide complementary verification and optimization mechanisms. Mach2 also generates task-specific agent packages for execution through independently selected endpoints. The originating harness validates returned artifacts against declared interfaces and evidence requirements without assuming continuous supervision of the remote run. Model-internal-knowledge (MIK) dependencies are recorded separately from source-grounded and test-supported findings. This paper formalizes the rule-gated execution model and the agent-package lifecycle, and proposes measurable criteria for evaluating rule compliance, engineering validity, and cross-endpoint task continuity.

authors.name: Vansh Sharma
authors.institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

papers.title: Learning Low-Latency Action Verification for Frozen Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made significant progress in general-purpose robotic manipulation. However, sampled action sequences can be ineffective, while evaluating alternatives with computationally expensive verifiers adds latency at each policy query. In this work, we propose HDH, a lightweight framework that uses hindsight from a frozen VLA's own deployments to improve action verification. The framework has three stages. First, we deploy the policy and collect its autonomous rollouts. We then train a compact action verifier to assign each action chunk a predicted task-success score. Finally, the frozen VLA generates action candidates, and the verifier selects the candidate with the highest score for execution. Across four LIBERO-10 tasks, HDH achieves an average success rate of 82.3\% and on three real-world manipulation tasks, HDH improves average success over the baseline policy by 22.6\%.

papers.title: The Price of Anarchy in Markets for Lemons
papers.abstract: We study the worst-case equilibrium gains from trade in simple bilateral trade mechanisms with interdependent valuations. Equilibria in such settings are typically complex, as proposed prices can convey private information held by the proposer. Such equilibria suffer lost gains from trade both due to the inefficiency introduced by screening (as in independent private value settings) and due to adverse selection. We identify broad conditions under which, nevertheless, sequential equilibria are guaranteed to achieve a constant fraction of the first-best gains from trade. Our bounds quantify the central role of rare pessimistic seller signals and rare optimistic buyer signals. The results apply to seller-proposer, buyer-proposer, and random-proposer mechanisms. The key idea in our analysis is to relate equilibrium gains from trade to proposer profits in an auxiliary market with independent private values.

papers.title: Synthetic Data Augmentation for Fairness under Data Imbalance: Theory and Adaptive Allocation
papers.abstract: Data imbalance across sensitive groups and class labels is common in classification problems and can contribute to substantial fairness disparities. We study how such imbalance affects Equal Opportunity and how synthetic data augmentation can mitigate the resulting unfairness. We first identify two mechanisms, prevalence imbalance and group-size imbalance, through which changes in the training distribution shift the learned decision boundary and induce disparities in group true positive rates. Motivated by this analysis, we study exact full-balance augmentation, which equalizes all group-label cells. We establish conditions under which full balancing strictly improves Equal Opportunity together with a prediction-error comparison under the oracle balanced distribution, and show that the Equal Opportunity gap of the synthetic-data classifier converges to that of the oracle balanced classifier as the sample size grows and the generator error vanishes. The finite-sample convergence rate agrees, up to logarithmic factors and generator-approximation error, with the information-theoretic lower-bound rate under the corresponding regularity regimes. Since exact balancing need not provide the best fairness-accuracy trade-off in practice, we further propose Accuracy-Constrained Adaptive Synthetic Augmentation (ACASA), which learns both where and how much to augment by minimizing estimated fairness disparity subject to a constraint on predictive accuracy. We provide a finite-sample guarantee comparing the selected augmentation allocation with the population-optimal accuracy-feasible allocation. Simulation studies and real data application support the theoretical findings and demonstrate that synthetic augmentation can substantially reduce fairness disparities while achieving favorable empirical fairness-accuracy trade-offs.

papers.title: When Does a Recommendation Spark Curiosity? Theory, Measurement, and Field Evidence
papers.abstract: Curiosity, the drive to close the gap between what one knows and what one wants to know, pulls consumers beyond their familiar content, sustains engagement, and breaks them out of the filter bubbles of repetitive, relevance-only recommendations. Despite its importance, curiosity is hardly incorporated into modern recommender systems for lack of a formal measure. The information-gap theory of curiosity provides no formal quantitative model that a recommender system can operate on, and existing proxy metrics do not accurately measure the curiosity that a recommended item evokes. To fill this research gap, we formalize the information-gap theory into five axioms of curiosity and construct the canonical formulation of a computational measure of the curiosity that a recommended item evokes in a consumer. We validate our curiosity measure through a survey-based study, in which it matches consumers' self-reported curiosity and outperforms alternative proxy metrics. We subsequently build a curiosity-aware recommender system that incorporates this measure into the utility function design, and we show through offline experiments on three real-world datasets that it significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we conduct a large-scale online controlled experiment at a major video-streaming platform in Asia, where we show that our method significantly increases click-through rate, video views, and time spent over the latest production system, leading to tangible economic impact for the company. Our method has since been deployed on the platform and remains in operation. Our findings establish consumer curiosity as a measurable and actionable objective for recommender systems, with important managerial implications for digital platforms to recommend what consumers wonder about.

papers.title: Reality Perception Gap: Are AI-Manipulated Video Detectors Ready for the Real World?
papers.abstract: AI-manipulated video detectors are typically evaluated on clean, curated datasets. In deployment, however, videos have usually passed through repost compression on social-media platforms and sometimes were captured by imperfect hardware. To measure detection under these conditions, we introduce Reality Perception Gap (RPG), a benchmark of 10,000 videos from frontier generators and partially synthetic edits, processed with cross-platform repost compression and paired with real footage that carries camera-side optical artifacts. RPG also includes socially fragile content, such as crime and wartime footage, where fabricated videos can cause severe social harm. Across 18 detectors, none catches more than 15% of fakes at a 1% false-positive rate. A positive control and a re-encoding sweep separate two sources of failure: generator and content shift degrades detectors before any compression, and repost compression erases the low-level traces that the artifact-based detectors relies on. Existing detectors therefore struggle when deployment conditions strip away the generation artifacts they rely on. These complementary failures suggest that robust detection requires training under deployment conditions and combining low-level, temporal, and semantic evidence, where passive detection may have reached its limits.

authors.name: Xiangrui Liu
authors.institution: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

authors.name: Xinyuan Wang
authors.institution: Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine

papers.title: VecDBLens: An Evaluatology-Based Framework for Vector Database Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Vector databases are increasingly deployed as retrieval pipelines in which representation, indexing, and query-time execution jointly determine accuracy, throughput, and cost. Existing vector database evaluations primarily focus on indexing while treating embeddings as fixed inputs and ignoring the role of query-time execution, making it difficult to decide whether a bottleneck should be addressed by changing the embedding model, the index, or the query-processing functions. To address the above limitation, we introduce VecDBLens, an Evaluatology-based framework that treats the function under diagnosis as an evaluated object and all remaining dataset, workload, parameter, and runtime factors as matched evaluation conditions. VecDBLens attributes performance differences to individual evaluated objects through comparisons under matched evaluation conditions, summarizing their performance and stability across multiple datasets and workloads. It further analyzes interactions among objects using analysis of variance (ANOVA), thereby turning vector database benchmarking from leaderboard ranking into a reproducible diagnostic procedure. VecDBLens reveals two key insights. First, retrieval performance is fundamentally upper-bounded by embedding quality, revealing that many apparent indexing failures are therefore representation-side limitations. Second, stronger index parameterization is not always beneficial: overly aggressive configurations can reshape neighborhood topology and cause recall regression. These results challenge the common practice of evaluating vector databases primarily through indexing and show that real-world limitations arise from constraints across retrieval functions rather than any single function alone. VecDBLens provides a principled basis for identifying the true performance drivers of vector databases and for guiding their design in practical applications.

papers.title: PolyMorphWBC: Whole-Body Control from End-Effector Trajectories for Quadrupedal Mobile Manipulation across Arm Morphologies with Extended Reach
papers.abstract: Quadrupedal mobile manipulators can extend their manipulation workspace by coordinating the mounted arm with the mobile base. At the task level, short-horizon end-effector (EE) trajectories provide an interface for specifying the desired manipulation motion without prescribing how it should be realized by the arm and base. However, executing such trajectories remains challenging because the controller must determine when and how the base should move, and this decision depends on the mounted-arm morphology. We therefore present PolyMorphWBC, a hierarchical controller that takes an EE trajectory as the sole task-level motion command and generates coordinated arm--base motions across four families of 6-DoF mounted arms, with extended-reach trajectories beyond the initial fixed-base reach. Within PolyMorphWBC, a trajectory-conditioned coordinator determines the base motion from previewed EE targets, while arm-specific Inverse Kinematics (IK) tracks the current target, and a frozen locomotion backend executes the resulting motion. Cross-arm reuse is enabled by a Unified Robot Description Format (URDF)-derived morphology conditioning, together with online residual-wrench feedback. We train PolyMorphWBC on procedurally generated arms and structured trajectories within and beyond fixed-base reach. In IsaacLab, it achieves 93.95% completion with 2.30cm position error and 4.81{\deg} orientation error on held-out trajectories and arm morphologies. In MuJoCo evaluation against UMI-on-Legs, PolyMorphWBC reduces EE position error by 69--72% and orientation error by 91--97% across four within- and extended-reach trajectories. On a physical Go2--ARX5 system, we demonstrate language-conditioned extended-reach pick-and-place using EE trajectories from pi_0 without vision-language-action (VLA)-generated base commands.

authors.name: Yifan Duan
authors.institution: Henan University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Wenhao Yu
