Queue layouts were introduced by Heath and Rosenberg [16] and have been studied extensively over the years [15, 7, 18, 8, 12, 10, 23, 20, 2, 14, 17, 3, 21, 4]. Several basic graph classes have bounded queue number. Every tree has queue number one [16], outerplanar graphs have queue number at most two [15], and series-parallel graphs have queue number at most three [23]. Alam, Bekos, Gronemann, Kaufmann, and Pupyrev [2] showed that the queue number of planar 33-trees is at most five; they also gave a lower bound of four. The central problem in the field for many years was whether planar graphs have bounded queue number. Heath, Leighton, and Rosenberg [15] conjectured that this is the case. Di Battista, Frati, and Pach [7] and Dujmović [13] obtained logarithmic upper bounds. Subsequently, Bekos, Förster, Gronemann, Mchedlidze, Montecchiani, Raftopoulou, and Ueckerdt showed that planar graphs of bounded maximum degree have constant queue number [6]. Finally in 2020, Dujmović, Joret, Micek, Morin, Ueckerdt, and Wood settled the conjecture by showing that the queue number of every planar graph is bounded [9]. Their proof uses the planar product structure theorem: every planar graph is a subgraph of the strong product of a graph of simple treewidth at most 33, a clique K3K_{3}, and a path. Combining this theorem with Wood’s bounds for queue layouts of graph products [24] gives the constant 4949.

papers.title: A counterexample on the main flatness conjecture for $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$-Fock bundles
papers.abstract: The main flatness conjecture for $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$-Fock bundles predicts the existence of a unique strongly positive flat compatible Hermitian metric for every $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$-Fock bundle. We use cyclic Higgs bundles to disprove this conjecture for every rank $n \geq 3.$

papers.title: Relative divisors and intersections of noncommutative rational localizations
papers.abstract:
The simple constituents of monic pencils determine singularity support in a free skew field. For a pencil inverse algebra that is a free ideal ring, the multiplicities of the nonbase constituents compute the scalar-regular part of Cohn's matrix divisor theory. For independent generic invertible matrices of size at least two, every entry of a nonidentity free-group word is an atom with one relative singularity component. In rank two, opposite pivots give the exact identifications among these components. Intersections of word-entry localizations are then given by intersections of their label sets. An irreducible pencil of dimension six represents a commutator entry.
  For an algebra finitely generated over the free polynomial algebra at a common regular scalar point, the residual closure is a finite pencil inverse algebra determined by the generators' common domain. Every nonzero inverse-adjoining defect is infinite-dimensional. We compute how free-group quotients change intersections and give additive formulas for general quotient and tensor intersections. We prove Berenstein--Retakh's polygon conjecture using $n-2$ charts for $n\geq4$. For an unpunctured M\"obius strip with $n\geq2$ boundary marks, the upper-algebra equality follows from $n+1$ charts. For the once-marked strip, the allowed algebra is strictly smaller than its residual hull, which equals the full chart.

papers.title: Abelian covers and the index of the centre in a group
papers.abstract: Let $h(n)$ be the largest number of abelian subgroups needed to cover a group in which every set of more than $n$ elements contains two distinct elements that commute, and let $\zeta(n)$ be the largest index of the centre under the same constraint. Erd\H{o}s asked for the growth of $h$, Neumann proved that both quantities are finite, and Pyber bounded both $\zeta$ and $h$ exponentially. We determine $h(n)$ for every positive integer $n$ and prove that $h(n)=1+\sqrt{\zeta(n)}$ whenever the constraint admits a nonabelian group. The covers are built directly from the commutator geometry of a scalar quotient, and the comparison with $\zeta$ is made afterwards. Beyond finitely many small cases, both maxima are attained by the same groups, those isoclinic to an extraspecial $2$-group of order $2^{1+2\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor}$, confirming Pyber's prediction for the central index in this range.

The proof compares cliques and covers in the fibres of a quotient map. Call the largest clique size in a fibre its width. If the kernel is abelian, a fibre can be covered by exactly that many abelian subgroups. More generally, an abelian subgroup of index II in the kernel gives a cover of size at most II times the width. A clique in the quotient allows us to combine cliques in its fibres, so the sum of their widths is at most ω⁡(G)\omega(G). Averaging over quotient cliques then bounds the total number of subgroups in the cover (Section 2).

The former provides large cliques; the latter provides common isotropic subspaces and hence covers. papers.title: Prediction or Persistence? What Future-Prediction Scores Miss About World Models
papers.abstract: Pretrained video world models are compared and chosen as components for robot learning largely by future-prediction scores. On its own, such a score cannot be read as evidence of prediction, because it mixes encoder quality, the near future's resemblance to the recent past, and the predictor's own contribution. We separate the three with a matched control. On 27,000 future-retrieval trials from household egocentric video, a model must pick the true continuation of a clip among eleven candidates from the same video (chance 0.091), ranked zero-shot by its own training criterion. Each model is paired with a persistence control, an identical copy whose predictor is never invoked, so the paired difference isolates the predictor. Score and contribution dissociate within the native-video V-JEPA family alone: the predictor adds +0.291 top-1 for V-JEPA 2.1 but +0.03 to +0.04 for V-JEPA 2 on the identical trials. Across five models the contribution ranges from +0.291 to negative, and it is negative only for the two action-conditioned models, which we evaluate outside their training regime. Persistence alone recovers the encoder ordering expected from pretraining, a sign that the probe tracks real signal. We suggest reporting each future-prediction score together with its persistence baseline. The gap between them, not the score, is what makes the number interpretable: a necessary check costing one forward pass. Establishing downstream usefulness is a separate matter, for a planning or control evaluation.
papers.intro:
Robot learning increasingly builds on pretrained video world models, such as V-JEPA 2, DINO-WM and the wider latent-predictive line, as components a policy is initialised from, plans against, or is evaluated with [7, 10, 1, 18]. Which one to trust is decided largely by future-prediction score. If that score misleads, the decisions built on it (which model to pretrain from, plan against, or evaluate with) inherit the error. Our probe uses passive video with no robot in the loop: it concerns what the score measures, not control. That is still a question for robot learning, because the model under test and the decision the score informs are the same ones.

A future-prediction score reflects three things at once: an encoder that represents the scene well, a near future that resembles the recent past, and a predictor that anticipates what comes next. Only the last is prediction in the intended sense, yet the score sums all three. A predictor that contributes nothing still scores well on the first two, and a harmful one can still beat chance. The score alone therefore cannot show what the predictive machinery adds.

We separate the three with a matched control. A model must identify a clip’s true continuation among eleven candidates from the same video. It is paired with a persistence control, an identical copy whose predictor is never invoked, isolating the predictor for one extra forward pass. Score and contribution diverge (Fig. 1). Within the native-video V-JEPA family, V-JEPA 2’s predictors add +0.028+0.028 to +0.041+0.041 top-1 to scores above 0.420.42, while V-JEPA 2.1’s adds +0.291+0.291 on the identical trials. DINO-WM, measured off-distribution, scores 0.1360.136 against 0.0910.091 chance, yet its persistence baseline reaches 0.3150.315. We therefore offer a diagnostic for reading the score: without the persistence gap, a future-prediction number cannot be interpreted. We do not try to settle whether world models are needed; we show that the score alone cannot settle it, and we measure the predictor’s share directly. papers.title: Cyclic fibers and exponential lower bounds for Erd\H{o}s--Ginzburg--Ziv constants
papers.abstract: We show that for every integer $n\ge2$ that is not a power of two there are constants $c_n>0$ and $B_n>2$ such that $s(C_n^r)\ge c_nB_n^r$ for all $r\ge1$. For powers of two, Harborth's formula gives growth rate exactly $2$. For the remaining even exponents, the previous lower bounds were of order $r2^r$. When $n=2m$ with $m\ge3$ odd, we prove the transfer inequality \[ A_n(H\oplus C_n^5)\ \ge\ 12\,A_n(H\oplus C_n)+8\,A_n(H\oplus C_m), \] where $A_n(G)$ is the maximal length of a sequence over $G$ without an $n$-term zero-sum subsequence and $H$ is any finite abelian group whose exponent divides $n$. The transfer extends a configuration of Elsholtz to twenty full cyclic fibers. Combined with a nine-point binary construction for $2m$-term zero-sums over $C_m^r$, it gives bases at least $2.0341$ that tend to $2.0394\ldots$; combined with a finite-field construction, it gives $s(C_6^r)\ge c\cdot 2.0491^r$. For exponents divisible by $4$ that are not powers of two, we obtain a base above two from a weighted random construction on the eighteen-point configuration of Wang and Zeng.

papers.abstract:
We study the areas of the cells determined by an arrangement $\mathcal{A}$ of $n$ distinct great circles on the unit sphere, with no three concurrent. Let $m(\mathcal{A})$ and $M(\mathcal{A})$ denote the smallest and largest cell areas, respectively. Our first result is the bound \[
  m(\mathcal{A})\le \frac{C_*+O(n^{-3/4})}{n^2},
  \qquad C_*=7.0666071493\ldots , \] where the implied constant is absolute. This improves the coefficient $\pi^2$ obtained from classical polygonal perimeter estimates. We also prove that $M(\mathcal{A})/m(\mathcal{A})>13$ for all sufficiently large $n$, improving the bound $7.43$ of L.~Fejes T\'oth. The main tool is a perimeter inequality for planar polygons which takes account of their exterior angles. We combine this with a positive semidefinite kernel on the sphere and use gnomonic projection to obtain bounds for spherical cells.

papers.title: Tracking What Works: Social Engineering Lures as Signatures for Victim-Centric Infostealer Campaign Discovery
papers.abstract: Despite advances in antivirus technology, infostealer infections persist at scale, driven primarily by social engineering rather than exploits. Yet, existing campaign detection efforts have focused on technical artifacts, overlooking the social-engineering lures exploiting human behavior and driving successful infections. To address this gap, we introduce a dual-framework system that discovers and tracks infostealer campaigns using victim-side artifacts from stealer logs. By treating social engineering lures as campaign signatures, the framework automatically aggregates individual infections into high-fidelity campaigns in near real-time. Recognizing distinct patterns between software and gaming ecosystems, we developed ecosystem-specific pipelines detecting all large and medium campaigns in both ecosystems (one medium gaming campaign was only recovered merged with another), though performance decreased for small campaigns. Analysis of 177 real-world campaigns identified by our framework reveals distinct temporal and infrastructure patterns with direct remediation implications. Software campaigns accumulate over 60% of infections within the first ten days, demanding rapid intervention following detection, while gaming campaigns grow more intense the longer they last, requiring continuous monitoring. Using social engineering lures as campaign signatures provides robustness to infrastructure fragmentation where traditional IoC-based detection fails. This work shifts campaign tracking from infrastructure correlation to victim-centric analysis, capturing why campaigns succeed rather than only how they operate, enabling awareness-driven prevention that addresses the human decision-making dimension absent from existing research.
papers.intro:
Infostealers have emerged as one of the most pervasive and impactful forms of malware in today’s threat landscape. By covertly harvesting credentials, session cookies, cryptocurrency wallets, and other sensitive data from infected devices, infostealers enable large-scale account compromise, financial fraud, and ransomware attacks.

Infostealers have emerged as one of the most pervasive and impactful forms of malware in today’s threat landscape. By covertly harvesting credentials, session cookies, cryptocurrency wallets, and other sensitive data from infected devices, infostealers enable large-scale account compromise, financial fraud, and ransomware attacks.

Despite advances in antivirus technologies and malware detection systems, infostealer infections continue to occur at scale, with tens of millions of compromised devices observed globally in recent years. A key reason for this persistence lies in how infostealers spread. Unlike exploit-driven malware, infostealers predominantly rely on social engineering. Users are persuaded to download and run malware disguised as cracked software, gaming tools, productivity applications, or other seemingly legitimate applications, often while being instructed to disable security protections for ’successful’ installation.

Malware detection research has traditionally focused on identifying malicious activity through static file characteristics, dynamic behavior, network traffic, and infrastructure-level indicators. Parallel efforts in campaign detection have successfully grouped malicious activity by correlating technical artifacts such as domains, IP addresses, URLs, and communication patterns. While these approaches are effective at identifying coordinated activity, they provide limited insight into why campaigns succeed, and very few specifically address infostealers or the social engineering mechanisms that drive their infections.

Malware detection research has traditionally focused on identifying malicious activity through static file characteristics, dynamic behavior, network traffic, and infrastructure-level indicators. Parallel efforts in campaign detection have successfully grouped malicious activity by correlating technical artifacts such as domains, IP addresses, URLs, and communication patterns. While these approaches are effective at identifying coordinated activity, they provide limited insight into why campaigns succeed, and very few specifically address infostealers or the social engineering mechanisms that drive their infections.

At the same time, successful infostealer campaigns generate massive amounts of post-infection data. Stealer logs circulate in the millions across underground platforms, implicitly capturing the infection vectors, lures, and deceptive techniques that successfully led to infection (i.e. they worked in real-life scenarios). These artifacts represent a uniquely valuable but largely untapped data source for understanding malware campaigns from the victim’s perspective. Their volume, however, makes manual analysis unrealistic, which has limited their use in both academic and industry research.

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have opened new opportunities for processing these artifacts at scale. Prior work has shown that LLMs can extract structured information from infostealer logs, enabling automated analysis of individual infections. What remains missing is a way to move beyond isolated cases and derive campaign-level intelligence from this data.

In this paper, we address this gap by introducing a framework for discovering and tracking infostealer campaigns using victim-side infection artifacts. By leveraging infection themes extracted with an LLM-based pipeline and treating social engineering lures as campaign signatures, our approach enables near real-time campaign identification and analysis. This work shifts the focus of campaign detection toward successful infections, providing new insights into campaign structure, evolution, and the social engineering strategies that drive infostealer success.

papers.title: Semigroups with periodic complex-time boundedness and holomorphy regions
papers.abstract: We study the periodicity of complex-time boundedness and holomorphy domains of operator semigroups. We show that an imaginary-time covariance identity involving an isometry yields periodicity of these domains. The method is applied to the Ornstein--Uhlenbeck operator and the hypoelliptic Laplacian on the circle, providing a spectral explanation of periodicity independent of the explicit geometry of their boundedness regions. We also discuss the distinction between boundedness and contractivity, using the classical heat semigroup as an example.

We shall use the terminology analytic semigroup and analyticity in the standard sectorial sense. A C0C_{0}-semigroup on a Banach space is called analytic if it admits a holomorphic extension to a sector with vertex at the origin, bounded on every smaller closed subsector. When the complex-time parameter ranges in a more general domain, not necessarily a sector, we shall instead speak of a holomorphic extension, a bounded holomorphic continuation, and its bounded-holomorphy region.

There is a classical reason why sectors play a privileged role in the theory of holomorphic semigroups. A C0C_{0}-semigroup is initially defined for nonnegative real time, and if one seeks a complex-time extension that itself retains the semigroup structure, it is natural to let the complex parameter range over an additive subsemigroup of ℂ\mathbb{C} containing the positive real half-axis. Open sectors with vertex at the origin provide the canonical domains of this kind. This point of view is standard and emphasized, for example, in [5, Section 1.4].

papers.title: Analysis choices decide whether untrained networks beat trained ones at V1: a multiverse analysis of model-brain RSA
papers.abstract: Untrained convolutional networks have been reported to rival trained networks as models of visual cortex, and we had reported an untrained-network advantage over backpropagation at V1 in THINGS fMRI, together with a dependence on evaluation resolution. Under a pre-specified ridge readout, the untrained network scored below the trained one at every pooling grid (median r difference -0.043 at g = 4, 0 of 5 seeds positive), and also in MSE skill and per-fold r. In exploratory analyses, across 36 combinations of unit normalisation, distance measure and voxel normalisation (28 distinct analyses), the sign of the V1 contrast depended on the analysis (intervals above 0 in 5 and below 0 in 9 distinct analyses), and in our networks the resolution dependence of the original convention appeared in only one cell. Raw correlation-distance representational similarity analysis (RSA) covaried with the alignment of model and voxel patterns with the unit-mean profile (Spearman 0.97 across our networks, 0.79 across six ImageNet architectures); the advantage was absent from the component orthogonal to the mean profile, and the parallel component alone did not resolve it. On the unweighted angular component of centred patterns, trained networks were ahead at V1 (our network and 5 of 6 ImageNet models) and at LOC (all seven); the norm-weighted angular term was not resolved. A luminance-and-contrast bank scored above every network under ridge (point estimates), and adding network features under a shared penalty did not improve prediction. Intervals are stimulus-bootstrap intervals for three subjects, and 6 pre-stated predictions were not met. We recommend reporting sensitivity to centring over the evaluated stimuli on both sides, reporting components separately, and including a small multiverse and simple baselines.

Comparisons between artificial networks and neural data have become a standard way to ask which models capture the computations of visual cortex. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) is one of the most widely used tools for this purpose: it summarises each system by the dissimilarities between its responses to a set of stimuli and compares these summaries directly, without fitting a mapping (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008). A recurring and surprising result is that networks with random, untrained weights can rival trained networks as models of visual cortex, in some reports exceeding them (Truzzi and Cusack, 2020; Kazemian et al., 2025). If true, such results bear on how much of early visual representation follows from architecture alone and how much from learning.

We reported a result of this kind ourselves. In THINGS fMRI (Hebart et al., 2023), an untrained network with uncalibrated batch-normalisation statistics exceeded a backpropagation-trained network at V1 when images were evaluated at 224 px, but not at 32 px, the resolution at which the networks had been trained (Leutenegger, 2026a); a related claim appears in Leutenegger (2026b). Both analyses used a single convention: globally pooled features, correlation distance between units, and voxel responses normalised over all trials of the experiment.

Both analyses used a single convention: globally pooled features, correlation distance between units, and voxel responses normalised over all trials of the experiment.

That convention has a property that is easy to overlook. Correlation distance across units is not invariant to constant offsets of individual units over the stimulus set: when units have different mean responses, the dissimilarity between two stimuli depends in part on how strongly each stimulus pattern is aligned with the shared profile of unit means. Euclidean distance is invariant to such offsets but not to the norm of each stimulus’s response vector. Different distance measures and normalisations therefore weight a gain-like quantity and the direction of the response pattern differently. The role of centring is explicit in related similarity measures (Kornblith et al., 2019), and the choice of dissimilarity measure is known to affect the reliability of RSA (Walther et al., 2016; Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte, 2017), but its effect on the ranking of candidate models has rarely been examined.

papers.title: A note on equivariant twisted holomorphic analytic torsion
papers.abstract: In this note, we introduce an equivariant version of twisted holomorphic analytic torsion for the twisted Dolbeault complex on a complex manifold equipped with an action of a compact Lie group. Our construction is motivated by Ray and Singer's holomorphic analytic torsion, by the equivariant analytic torsion developed for elliptic complexes with group actions, notably in the work of Donnelly and later in the holomorphic setting by Bismut, and by Mathai and Wu's twisted analytic torsion for the twisted de Rham complex. Using pseudodifferential operators and the equivariant noncommutative residue, we define the equivariant twisted holomorphic analytic torsion. We also state its variation formulas under changes of the metric and of the twisting element, and present its functorial properties.

papers.title: Small Heads, Strong Decisions: A Controlled Study of Typed-Decision Models
papers.abstract: In September 2026, TypeSafe announced Jev as the first model in its System One category: unstructured state goes in, and typed, calibrated decisions that software can use directly come out. Jev's architecture and training data are unpublished, but many open typed-decision models have followed, including Nimble, the Decision 1.0--3.0 family and Clef. They answer structured questions about a piece of text, such as a yes/no check, a choice among labelled options or a graded score, by reading the text with a language model and scoring the options with a small readout. Each pairs a different readout with a different backbone, training mix and recipe, so it is unclear which design choices matter. We re-implement five readouts and train all of them under one protocol: the same backbone, the same 15 public English training sources, the same recipe with a per-head learning-rate sweep, and the same seed. Our experiments demonstrate that: The complexity of the head does not affect accuracy: on Qwen3-0.6B every readout reaches 81.3--82.0\% in-domain accuracy, and a 0.5M-parameter cosine head, which scores each option by its cosine similarity to the question, matches the 27M-parameter joint schema head adapted from Clef in-domain at half its inference time. Reading all of a text's questions from one prompt also matches one prompt per question in accuracy, with 1.6 times faster inference and 2.1--2.5 times faster training on one H100. The backbone's size matters more than either choice: moving from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-4B adds 4 points in-domain and 11 points on held-out sources, while the base, instruct and thinking checkpoints of the same model tie. We recommend spending effort on the backbone and keeping the head minimal.
papers.intro:
Many systems built around large language models need fast, structured judgements about text rather than free-form generation: does the answer follow the policy, is the question answerable from the passage, how helpful is the response on a 1–5 scale. Typed-decision models serve this need. They read a piece of text (the state) together with one or more typed questions, each with a closed set of options, and return a probability distribution over each question’s options without generating any text. TypeSafe announced Jev in September 2026 as the first model in its System One category [1]. Questions come in three types [32]: a noul asks a yes/no question, a choice picks one option from a list, and a score rates the state on a rubric.

Jev’s architecture, weights and training data are unpublished; it is available only through an API. Many open Jev-like models have followed; one public leaderboard lists about 150 [25]. We focus on those whose architectures are documented [4, 22, 7]. They differ along two axes. The prompt regime: Nimble and Decision 1.0–3.0 build one prompt per question, while Clef encodes the state and all its questions in one prompt. The readout: an LM letter readout that uses the LM-head rows of the answer letters (Nimble), a learned letter readout that learns a copy of those rows (Decision 3.0), a bilinear-MLP head over option endpoints (Decision 1.0/2.0), or a 27M-parameter joint schema head (Clef). Each release also uses its own backbone, training data and recipe, so published numbers do not show which design choice matters.

The prompt regime: Nimble and Decision 1.0–3.0 build one prompt per question, while Clef encodes the state and all its questions in one prompt. The readout: an LM letter readout that uses the LM-head rows of the answer letters (Nimble), a learned letter readout that learns a copy of those rows (Decision 3.0), a bilinear-MLP head over option endpoints (Decision 1.0/2.0), or a 27M-parameter joint schema head (Clef). Each release also uses its own backbone, training data and recipe, so published numbers do not show which design choice matters.

We run a controlled comparison. We re-implement the four published readouts, verify our implementations against the original code, and add a minimal one, the cosine head: the cosine similarity between the pooled question and each pooled option, scaled by a learned temperature. All five train on the same backbone, the same 15 public English sources and the same recipe, with each head’s learning rate chosen by the same sweep. We evaluate on the 15 training sources and on five held-out sources, with paired, row-clustered statistics and a one-point non-inferiority margin. We then fix the head and vary the backbone: scale (Qwen3 0.6B to 14B, three Gemma 4 models), base vs. post-trained checkpoints, and instruct vs. thinking post-training. Our contributions are: 1. A taxonomy of open typed-decision architectures by prompt regime and readout (section 2, table 1); 2. A controlled comparison of their readouts and prompt regimes under one backbone, data mix and recipe (section 5); 3. The cosine head, a minimal readout that matches the largest head at 2% of its parameters (section 3.3); 4. A backbone study across scale, base vs. post-trained checkpoints, and instruct vs. thinking variants (section 6). Our main findings are: • The complexity of the head does not affect accuracy. On Qwen3-0.6B, every readout reaches 81.3–82.0% in-domain accuracy, and the 0.5M-parameter cosine head matches the 27M-parameter joint schema head in-domain at half its inference time (sections 5.1 and 5.2). • One prompt per row is enough. Reading all of a row’s questions from one prompt matches one prompt per question in accuracy, with 1.6 times faster inference and 2.1–2.5 times faster training on one H100 (sections 5.1 and 5.2). • The backbone dominates. Moving from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-4B adds 4 points in-domain and 11 points on held-out sources, while the base, instruct and thinking checkpoints of the same model tie (section 6).

papers.title: When Agents Need to Consolidate Memories: What RRR Consolidation Explains, and What It Does Not Explain, in Conversation ESAA
papers.abstract: Language-model agents can share conversational history across sessions, but persistence does not guarantee retrieval of current decisions and their provenance. This engineering study presents Memory-TCG, a Conversation ESAA extension inspired by ringing, resonance and renormalization (RRR), and an exploratory synthetic evaluation comparing chronological retrieval, two simplified baselines (B, recency-aware, and B', authority-aware), full RRR, and variants under three output budgets. With 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, full RRR recalled 0.44 of current decisions, versus 0.06 for chronological retrieval and 0.58 for the oracle ceiling; with 4,096 tokens it recalled all of them. B' and the no-resonance variant matched full RRR in decision recall across all nine scale-budget combinations, as expected when the active decision set and the adapter ordering are the same. The isolated contribution of ringing to decisions was not measured: comparator D1 cuts facts before the graph is built, and the product retains active decisions by rule. Before the output limit, full-RRR conflict F1 was 0.615 at all three scales; after it, at 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, it was 0.000. Reserving 20% of the budget for conflicts raised that F1 to 0.431 in that scenario, at the cost of lowering decision recall from 0.44 to 0.34, and to 0.930 at 4,096 tokens without decision loss. Fixtures are repetitive, comparators are simplified, and the evaluation was not independently replicated; the results support an engineering analysis, not a claim of selectionist superiority.
papers.intro:
Using heterogeneous agents on a shared task requires continuity across sessions and tools. A decision made in one conversation may be absent from the next context window; an old summary may survive after a decision changes; and a repetition made by another agent may be mistaken for new evidence. Text persistence is necessary to recover history, but selecting what to present remains a distinct problem.

ESAA establishes the separation between agent intentions and state mutations performed by an orchestrator [3]. ESAA-Conversational addresses continuity through a local event log and handoff projections [1]. Its focus is recording and exposing conversational state across agents. Haber and Tononi [2], in turn, discuss the cost of plasticity in continually learning systems and propose an analogy with memory consolidation during sleep. The authors present as a testable hypothesis that a selectionist approach to consolidation can outperform instructionist alternatives as memory grows and becomes interconnected.

This paper investigates the following question: how can RRR-inspired consolidation be integrated into a shared conversational memory while preserving provenance and exposing the limits of automated decisions, and which components explain the gains? The answer is presented as an engineering study of Memory-TCG, a component of Conversation ESAA. The contributions are: (i) a mapping between the phases proposed in [2] and operations implemented over the history of [1]; (ii) an architecture with inspectable proposals, explicit promotion, and reconstruction from events; and (iii) an exploratory evaluation with ablations and an authority-aware baseline, delimiting what the results allow and do not allow attributing to each component.

papers.title: What World Model Does Active Object Search Need? A Study under Imperfect Detection
papers.abstract: In active object search, a robot must decide where to look and when to stop. Imperfect detection complicates both decisions: a non-detection may indicate occlusion, an out-of-view target, or a false negative, while a detection may be a false positive. This raises the question of which representations a world model needs to support reliable search under imperfect detection. We introduce Bayesian Active Miss-aware Object Search (BAMOS) to investigate how target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors affect search decisions. Through comprehensive ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses, we examine the roles of these representations and their update mechanisms across different detector configurations. Notably, target belief and its update mechanisms are critical to search performance, with their contribution generally increasing as detection errors become more prevalent. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining and updating target beliefs to support reliable active search under uncertain detector observations, providing insights into the design of world models for embodied agents. Code is available in https://github.com/gokyeongryeol/BAMOS.
papers.intro:
In active object search, a robot chooses where to point its camera until it can state where a target object is [2, 32]. Consider a mobile manipulator instructed to “bring me the mug” while the mug is behind a box on a shelf. Before grasping, it must decide where to look next and when it has gathered enough evidence. When a view yields no detection, the target may be occluded, outside the frame, or visible but missed by the detector (a false negative). Open-vocabulary detectors miss targets often enough that a non-detection alone cannot distinguish these cases. They also report objects that are absent (false positives), so a single detection does not settle the target’s location either.

Open-vocabulary detectors miss targets often enough that a non-detection alone cannot distinguish these cases. They also report objects that are absent (false positives), so a single detection does not settle the target’s location either.

Interpreting such observations calls for a world model. Most robot world models reconstruct the scene or predict future observations [4, 23, 26]. Active object search, however, depends on a narrower quantity: the probability that a view detects the target, given the detector’s error rates. Previous methods already maintain beliefs over the target and model visibility [32, 11], but few predict detection from probabilistic occlusion and fitted detector error rates together [31, 34, 33]. To our knowledge, no controlled study has isolated which of these components the decisions use [29, 22, 35]. We therefore ask which world-model representations active object search requires when the detector is imperfect.

We make two contributions. First, we present Bayesian Active Miss-aware Object Search (BAMOS), a belief-based world model that predicts detection rather than the scene (Section 2). It maintains a target belief over the target’s location and size and an occupancy belief used only to predict visibility, and it trains no network. Second, the separable components enable a controlled study with an oracle and two open-vocabulary detectors in Isaac Sim [27] and in Habitat Synthetic Scenes Dataset (HSSD) houses [21] in Habitat-Sim [28]. The study replaces the occupancy belief with the true geometry, ablates each component, crosses view and stop rules, and injects detector errors.

Probabilistic object search updates a belief after non-detections, with a hand-set detection probability and binary occlusion [32, 31], or with a point target [11, 34]. BAMOS instead fits the detector’s error rates and treats the target’s size as uncertain. Open-vocabulary object navigation uses real detectors [29, 6] and lowers map values where nothing was detected, with heuristic weights [35, 22]. BAMOS replaces these weights with a likelihood. World models reconstruct the scene [17, 25, 24, 20] or predict observations [14, 15, 1], although a model need only be accurate in the quantities a decision depends on [13, 30]. BAMOS is a case study of this principle (Appendix E).

papers.title: $q$-$\gamma$-positivity of two $q$-Narayana polynomials
papers.abstract: We address the question of $q$-$\gamma$-positivity of $q$-Narayana polynomials for $q$-super Catalan numbers $A_{n,m}(q)$ and their duals, $B_{n,m}(q)$. We offer three main results. First, both the $q$-$m$-Narayana polynomials, whose coefficients refine the q-super Catalan numbers, and the dual q-Narayana polynomials are $q$-$\gamma$-positive of index one. Second, the dual $q$-Narayana polynomials are also $q$-$\gamma$-positive of index two. Third, both the $q$- Narayana numbers and their duals are coefficient-wise $q$-unimodal.

papers.title: Second homology of some quandles
papers.abstract: We derive formulas from Eisemann's formula for the second quandle homology of quandles. We prove that for a finite injective quandle $Q$, the second quandle homology $H_2(Q)$ can be computed in a representation group of $Q$, which is a finite quotient of the enveloping group of $Q$, by giving a formula for that. We use this to compute $H_2(Q)$ for $Q$ the subquandle of $k$-cycles of $S_n$ and $Q$ the quandle corresponding to the conjugacy class of a diagonalizable element of $SL(n,q)$, with some exceptions. For $G$ a finite group with trivial Bogomolov multiplier, as many classical groups, simple groups and (with exceptions) quasi-simple groups, we derive a formula for $H_2(Conj(G))$ that can be computed in $G$ alone. The formula relies on conjugacy classes of $G$, centralizers in $G$ of representative of such classes and the derived group of $G$. If $G$ is moreover perfect this formula can be related to the first Hochschild homology of the group ring $\mathbb{Z}[G]$. As an application, we compute $H_2(Q)$ for $Q$ the conjugacy quandle of $GL(2,q)$ for $q\neq 2,3$.

papers.title: Formal completions and decompositions of matrix factorization categories of Fano mirrors
papers.abstract: We study the derived categories of matrix factorizations for certain toric Landau--Ginzburg models that are mirror dual to del Pezzo surfaces and Fano threefolds. Some of these models have non-isolated singularities: their critical loci may contain curves and surfaces, possibly with intersecting irreducible components. We handle these cases by studying the potential in the formal neighborhood of each irreducible component of the critical locus. Away from $\operatorname{Sing}(\operatorname{CritLoc}(W)_{\mathrm{red}})$, we construct global formal coordinates and determine the local normal form of the singularity. Near the singular or intersection strata, we analyze how the pieces of the whole connected formal neighborhood are related by localization. This gives explicit decompositions of the derived categories of matrix factorizations after idempotent completion. For the five rank-one pairs $(B_d,V_{4d+2})$, we also compare projective compactifications. The isolated sectors and central-component counts agree for $d=2,3,4,5$ and differ for $d=1$. Equivalence of the distinguished compactified contributions for the remaining matched pairs requires compatible global gluing data or compactified Homological Mirror Symmetry.

papers.title: A Bright L4 Neptune Trojan Found by Stacking Archival ZTF Images
papers.abstract: We report a Neptune Trojan found by a shift-and-stack search of archival Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) difference images of 2019 October, and recovered in public images of seven other telescopes back to 2008. The orbit uses 88 positions on 54 nights from 2008 to 2025, a 17.22-year arc, all measured on our own Gaia DR3 plate solutions. Its heliocentric osculating elements at JD 2460000.5 are a = 30.2158 +/- 0.0004 au, e = 0.0661 and i = 20.32 deg; a fit of the same positions with the independent orbit code Find_Orb agrees within 0.4 sigma in every element. The nominal orbit librates about Neptune's leading Lagrange point L4 with a period of 9.25 kyr and an amplitude of 8.7 deg over the next Myr, and 84 +/- 2% of 500 clones of the orbit remain L4 Trojans for 4.5 Gyr. Its absolute magnitude is H_V = 6.96 +/- 0.10 (linear phase law), or 6.81 +/- 0.06 on the H, G convention of the Minor Planet Center's list of Neptune Trojans, whose brightest L4 member has H = 7.26, so the object is possibly the brightest known L4 Neptune Trojan. Its color, g-r = 0.52 +/- 0.05, lies in the g-r range of the red Neptune Trojans, and for albedos of 0.05-0.15 its diameter is about 140-240 km.
papers.intro:
Neptune Trojans share Neptune’s orbit and librate about its L4 or L5 Lagrange point, 60° ahead of or behind the planet. The first was found in 2001 [15]; the population is mostly dynamically hot (inclinations to tens of degrees) [62, 42], is found at L4 [23] and L5 [63], and is thought to have been captured during Neptune’s migration [55, 44, 25]. It appears several times larger than the Jupiter Trojan population [62]. Its long-term stability has been mapped with integrations of up to 1 Gyr [17] and 34 Myr, checked to 4.5 Gyr along two lines [71]; unstable members are a possible source of Centaurs [32]. Their colors resemble those of the Jupiter Trojans [36]; a few ultra-red members have since been found [40, 49]. The Minor Planet Center’s list of Neptune Trojans [53], last updated 2026 May 30, holds 28 objects at L4 and 7 at L5. The known Neptune Trojans were found in deep surveys of the outer solar system [15, 62, 42], in wide-field surveys [41] and in the Dark Energy Survey [23, 8]; the two brightest listed L4 objects are (530930) 2011 WG157, found by Pan-STARRS1 (PS1) in 2011 [41], and 2015 VU207, found in Dark Energy Survey images of 2015 [52].

Here we report an L4 Trojan found in archival ZTF data and recovered in the archives of seven other telescopes, with its orbit, the evidence that all its positions belong to one object, its long-term dynamics and its physical properties. The object has no Minor Planet Center designation yet; we use our internal identifier A108661. Our first positions were reported to the Minor Planet Center on 2026 November 9. We find no earlier report of it in the Minor Planet Center’s records, apart from one unlinked tracklet of 2025 November 21 in its Isolated Tracklet File (Section IV). The frames are listed in Appendix A, the measurement details, frame criteria and linkage tests in Appendices B–D, and the positions are released with the paper (Section IX).

papers.title: Evolution of Internal Waves on Surfaces of Revolution with Flat Ends
papers.abstract: We generalize the 2D linear internal wave equation to non-compact surfaces of revolution with flat ends. We show that the leading profile of this equation with oscillatory forcing is the unique incoming solution to the corresponding stationary equation. This is done by proving a limiting absorption principle via propagation of semiclassical defect measure.

papers.title: A thermodynamically consistent, fully compressible, fluctuating hydrodynamics model of a Cahn Hilliard binary fluid mixture
papers.abstract: We derive, from first principles, a thermodynamically consistent set of fully compressible fluctuating hydrodynamic equations for a Cahn-Hilliard binary fluid mixture, in isothermal and non-isothermal form and for symmetric and non-symmetric mixtures. The derivation uses the GENERIC formalism, with the friction operator constructed from flux fluctuations following Jelic and Ottinger, so that deterministic and stochastic fluxes derive from the same operator and correlation matrix and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem holds by construction. We show that the momentum equation must use the total mass density, that the Cahn-Hilliard variable is the mass fraction, and that the diffusion flux must be driven by the specific, not the volumetric, exchange potential. We derive a generalized Korteweg tensor for square-gradient energies in density and composition, and show that the reversible pressure tensor of the non-isothermal model is fixed by the degeneracy condition, producing a thermal capillary stress when the interfacial free energy has an entropic part. Thermodynamic consistency is proved in full: Jacobi identity, positivity and degeneracy, local energy conservation with interstitial-working fluxes, a local entropy balance, Soret-Dufour reciprocity, and Einstein statistics of the linearized equations. The final equations are written in conservative form for finite-volume discretization, and closed-form static and dynamic structure factors are given for all models as analytic benchmarks. An appendix shows that the same models follow from classical irreversible thermodynamics with the Helmholtz or Gibbs free energy; this route is unique for isothermal flows and has a gauge freedom in the non-isothermal case that GENERIC removes.

papers.title: A Probabilistic Characterization of the Ideals of Resolvent Algebras
papers.abstract: We give a probabilistic characterization of the ideals of resolvent algebras. Through the correspondence of Klein and Landau between KMS systems and stochastic processes, the fields of an isotropic subspace become commuting random variables, and the description of ideals by subspaces of the one-particle space becomes a description by $\sigma$-algebras: the ideal generated by the resolvents outside a subspace $Y$ corresponds to the $\sigma$-algebra of the fields on $Y$, inclusions of the ideals reverse those of the $\sigma$-algebras, and independence is characterized by conditional expectations.
papers.intro:
Unlike the Weyl algebra, which is simple, the resolvent algebra of Buchholz and Grundling has a rich structure of closed two-sided ideals [6, Theorem 3.8], and the ideals carry physical information: they are the kernels of the representations in which some fields take infinite values [6, Section 9], a unital C∗C^{\ast}-algebra admitting a sufficiently diverse variety of dynamics cannot be simple, and the nesting of the primitive ideals encodes the dimension of the symplectic space [8, Section 1]. Buchholz classifies the ideals through the subspaces of the symplectic space, the one-particle space of a Bose field: the primitive ideals of a finite-dimensional resolvent algebra correspond to the subspaces with a character of the commutative algebra of the radical of σ\mathsf{\sigma} on the subspace [8, Definition 3.2 and Propositions 3.3 and 3.5], the maximal ideals to the isotropic subspaces with a character [8, Theorem 4.6], and all ideals are built from principal ideals generated by resolvents [8, Section 4]. On the other hand, Klein and Landau showed that stochastically positive Kubo–Martin–Schwinger (KMS) systems are equivalent to periodic stochastic processes with a positivity of Osterwalder–Schrader type [13, Theorem 6.1 and Sections 7 and 8], and Dereziński and Gérard construct KMS states from β\beta-Markov path spaces [9, Section 21.4, Theorems 21.43 and 21.47].

We ask what corresponds on the side of the stochastic processes when the resolvent algebra is the basic algebra of a KMS system. Since the classification of Buchholz is given through the one-particle space, it should have a definite probabilistic counterpart; and since σ\sigma-algebras carry the information of a system in probability theory, as filtrations show [3, Sections 4 and 35], a basic question is whether the information carried by the ideals is carried by σ\sigma-algebras in the same way. Moreover, probabilistic techniques often solve problems that are hard for operator theory and operator algebras alone, as in constructive quantum field theory [12, 23, 14, 15] and in the uses of path and function space methods recalled in [9, Introduction to Chapter 21] and [13, Introduction], so that a probabilistic interpretation may be useful also for the purely operator-algebraic formulation of the ideals. These two points are the subject of this paper.

The concrete motivation is Bose–Einstein condensation (BEC) of quasiparticles whose number is not conserved, which according to Yukalov occurs only in nonequilibrium systems with external pumping, self-consistently defined collective excitations such as phonons not condensing [25, Abstract and Conclusion]. A series of preprints examines this statement mathematically for Bose fields coupled linearly to a source or to particles, the free Bose gas [17], the van Hove model [22, 18], the spin–boson model [21], and the Nelson and Pauli–Fierz models [20], both on the resolvent algebra and on the singular Gaussian β\beta-Markov path spaces [19], which extend those of [9, Section 21.4] to one-particle Hamiltonians without a spectral gap and realize the Araki–Woods representations [19, Theorem 5.4]. Above the critical density the condensate is carried by the test functions on which the zero-mode form does not vanish, and the infrared singularity of a linear coupling restricts the test functions to a subspace. On the resolvent algebra, this gives the ideals generated by the resolvents of the condensate directions and of the infrared-singular directions: the passage to the admissible test functions is the quotient by the second, and the condensate is removed when the first is contained in the second. On the path space, the fields of the condensate directions are correlated with the order coordinate of the condensate, and those of the infrared-singular directions escape to infinity as the infrared cutoff is removed. The revisions of [17, 22] and the other models thus need a general theory of these ideals and of their probabilistic counterparts on an abstract symplectic space.

papers.title: When can an interpretability claim be trusted? Stability and certification of feature dimensionality, ridge leverage and the feature recovery rate
papers.abstract: Interpretability tools increasingly support safety claims, such as that a sparse dictionary has recovered most of a model's features. Such claims rest on measurements with arbitrary thresholds, and small changes to the model weights, a different training seed or a different threshold can reverse them. We study two widely used measurements in toy models and synthetic dictionaries with known ground truth: the feature dimensionality of Elhage et al. and the feature recovery rate (FRR) with a cosine threshold. We characterize exactly where feature dimensionality is discontinuous and replace it with a regularized (ridge) version with sharp stability bounds: the ridge leverage score changes by at most $3\sqrt{3}/(8\sqrt{\lambda})$ times the operator-norm change of the weights, and this constant cannot be improved; for the regularized dimensionality the stability constant grows like $\rho/4$ in the scale $\rho=R/\sqrt{\lambda}$, with explicit upper and lower bounds. We also prove certificates stating when a claim "feature $i$ is recovered" must survive a given change of the dictionary. The certificates held in every test and are informative for small perturbations, but certify no feature non-trivially across independently trained dictionaries; at the standard threshold, whether a feature counts as recovered changed with the training seed for 55 percent of features. Experiments use toy models only. The proofs, code and text were drafted by AI agents directed by the authors and checked by an independent blind AI reviewer and by numerical tests; the authors take full responsibility for the content.

papers.title: Testing Density Discontinuity Using Spacings
papers.abstract: In the regression discontinuity design, researchers assess the credibility of assumptions by testing the running variable's density for a discontinuity at the cutoff. This paper proposes a novel such test. The test uses q spacings on each side of the cutoff, where spacings are the widths between ordered observations. Spacings yield a continuous statistic that behaves well under weak assumptions. I study its properties in two asymptotic frameworks: one where q is fixed as the sample size increases and one where q slowly diverges to infinity. With q fixed, the test achieves exact asymptotic size control without user randomization. When q increases slowly, the test becomes consistent without sacrificing exact asymptotic size. Compared to the preferred version of Bugni and Canay's (2021) test, the only other test with comparably weak assumptions, this test reduces sensitivity to the tuning parameter and performs similarly when theirs is well-chosen.
papers.intro:
The regression discontinuity design (RDD) has only increased in popularity as a method for identifying causal treatment effects. The sharp design is characterized by a deterministic treatment rule: individuals are treated if an observed score crosses a known threshold. RDD nonparametrically identifies the average treatment effect for individuals at the cutoff under an arguably weak assumption: the potential outcomes must have continuous conditional expectations at the cutoff (Hahn et al., 2001).

The regression discontinuity design (RDD) has only increased in popularity as a method for identifying causal treatment effects. The sharp design is characterized by a deterministic treatment rule: individuals are treated if an observed score crosses a known threshold. RDD nonparametrically identifies the average treatment effect for individuals at the cutoff under an arguably weak assumption: the potential outcomes must have continuous conditional expectations at the cutoff (Hahn et al., 2001).

The widespread adoption of RDD reflects the attractive credibility of its assumption, but there are situations where it fails. For example, suppose individuals can freely choose their running variable based on knowledge of their potential outcomes. The consequent sorting can create jumps in the conditional expectations. Despite this, the continuity assumption is fundamentally untestable, so researchers tend to assess the credibility of RDD using a set of stronger assumptions proposed by Lee (2008). Sacrificing a little generality buys interpretable conditions and two testable implications: (i) a continuous distribution of the covariates at the cutoff and (ii) a continuous density of the running variable (score) at the cutoff. Bugni and Canay (2021) find tests of the implications in two thirds of empirical RDD papers across four major journals. Rejecting the implications rejects the stronger assumptions.

This paper proposes a new test for the second implication, continuity of the running variable’s density. The test offers several advantages over competitors, including applicability, robustness, and simplicity. First, the test is asymptotically valid under two asymptotic frameworks, both of which require similarly weak assumptions. The test is asymptotically unbiased under one and becomes consistent under the other. The second framework also accommodates random, data-dependent choices of the tuning parameter. Second, the test is more robust to choices of the tuning parameter than the preferred version of Bugni and Canay’s (2021) test, the only other test with comparably weak assumptions. It achieves this through a continuous test statistic, which avoids the need for user randomization and simplifies methods for choosing the tuning parameter. Finally, the test statistic is a ratio of two differences requiring only two order statistics and the cutoff point. The test requires only one tuning parameter and does not require consistent estimators of the density.

The test builds on the intuition that spacings, the distances between ordered observations, reflect the density where they occur. After all, a higher density implies that the observations should be more dense. To formalize this, I show under weak assumptions that the spacings, defined using order statistics as Di:=X(i)−X(i−1)D_{i}:=X_{(i)}-X_{(i-1)}, are approximately independent exponential random variables near the cutoff. When scaled by nn, the limiting rate parameter equals the limiting density on that side of the cutoff. We exploit this fully with the optimal two-sample test of parameter equality for exponential distributions. I show that this translates into asymptotic optimality among all tests that use a fixed number of observations on each side of the cutoff.

For a chosen value of qq, the test takes the qq closest observations to the cutoff on each side. This gives an effective total sample size of Q=2​qQ=2q. To better understand the advantages of the spacings test, consider the existing alternatives. McCrary (2008) requires three bounded and continuous derivatives of the density on each side of the cutoff. Otsu et al. (2013) require two derivatives. Cattaneo et al. (2020) require one continuous derivative. Such smoothness assumptions effectively require the density to be approximately cubic, quadratic, or linear near the cutoff. Importantly, higher assumed orders require the density to more tightly conform to that polynomial shape. These methods perform poorly in the presence of spikes, kinks, and discontinuities near the cutoff point. Assuming only one-sided continuity imposes the weakest requirements on the density. Besides the present test, only Bugni and Canay (2021) make such weak assumptions.

Bugni and Canay (2021) use the Q=2​qQ=2q closest observations to the cutoff and count how many are above. Each local observation occurs above or below the cutoff with probability near 1/2 under a continuous density, so they approximate the count by a Binomial(Q,1/2)(Q,1/2) distribution. Statistics with discrete limiting distributions cannot provide exact asymptotic size control without randomization. The problem is largest for smaller QQ. The number of observations nn dwarfs the number used by the test (e.g., QQ proportional to n\sqrt{n}), so nn must be very large for QQ to be large. The preferred version of their test is nonrandomized and is asymptotically conservative with a fixed QQ. The spacings test overcomes this challenge through a continuous statistic, providing exact asymptotic size control without user randomization or restrictions on QQ that can have adverse effects in smaller samples. When the density is twice as high on one side of the cutoff, this results in 5.6 more percentage points of limiting power, averaged across 2≤Q≤1002\leq Q\leq 100. For 97% of these QQ, the spacings test provides at least as much limiting power, uniformly across alternatives. Bugni and Canay’s (2021) test is competitive when requiring a heavily restricted choice of the tuning parameter. The restrictions can harm performance and account for most differences between the tests in simulations.

papers.title: BWM-Forge: Agentic World Programming for Embodied Intelligence
papers.abstract: Generating diverse robot videos requires control over scene geometry, robot motion, and viewpoints. End-to-end video generation offers limited direct access to these variables, making targeted edits and reuse across tasks difficult. We present BWM-Forge, a code-driven framework for controllable video generation in robotics. Given robot assets and a task description, the framework accepts an initial image, an image with motion data, or a human demonstration video. A coding agent constructs editable Blender scene programs that specify objects, robot motion, and cameras. The resulting proxy videos provide structural and motion references for a video generation model, which adds visual detail. A multi-agent harness coordinates input processing, scene construction, review, and rendering. Automated evaluation and user feedback support iterative refinement, while an experience repository stores and retrieves reusable modeling and rendering rules. This design supports multiple robot embodiments, synchronized viewpoints, and appearance variation from a shared scene program. We evaluate the framework on 15 tasks covering five robot types. Compared with LingBot-World Base Cam on these tasks, BWM-Forge achieves higher aesthetic quality, imaging quality, subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, and RoboJudge-9B physical adherence and instruction alignment scores. The baseline scores higher in dynamic degree. Qualitative cases illustrate viewpoint control, scene variation, feedback-driven edits, and experience reuse across scenes. These results demonstrate a practical approach to generating controllable robot videos through editable, executable scene representations.

papers.intro:
Video provides a natural representation of physical-world dynamics, motivating video world models that predict future visual observations. When world state is represented implicitly in generated frames, however, users have limited direct access to scene objects, robot configurations, and camera trajectories for editing and reuse. For embodied data generation, these limitations concern changing a task object while preserving the surrounding scene, observing the same interaction from another camera, and adapting an existing scene to a different robot. Recent code world models offer a complementary approach. WorldCoder and subsequent work represent world dynamics as executable programs for prediction and decision making [1, 2]. Code World Model and Code2Worlds extend this direction toward code-mediated visual generation and the construction of 3D scenes and motion [3, 4]. These approaches motivate an explicit, executable representation through which scene structure and motion can be inspected, modified, and rendered.

The agentic workflow is implemented by a Harness that coordinates four specialized agents. The Preprocessing Agent parses requests, validates robot assets and motion data, and extracts visual evidence. The Building Agent constructs and animates scenes through code. The Rendering Agent uses the resulting proxy videos, reference images, and prompts to generate and evaluate high-fidelity outputs. Automated checks and optional user feedback guide revisions to both proxy and rendered videos. papers.title: Decisions at the end of the world
papers.abstract: International treaties are often described as tigers without teeth, failing to secure compliance or change outcomes. Cooperation also depends on how states maintain the rules they have already made -- especially where no sovereign stands above the states. Here we map more than six decades of decision-making under the Antarctic Treaty, linking submitted proposals to recorded responses and tracing how instruments act on earlier ones. Shared references tie decisions together across the agenda. Recurring revision concentrates in specialised histories, above all the management of protected areas, beyond what activity, popularity and reference age predict. Periodic administrative reviews retire outdated instruments in bulk, joining otherwise separate histories without coordinating policy across subjects. Binding Measures build overwhelmingly on earlier Measures, with little direct succession from non-binding Resolutions. Distinguishing these layers shows how a shared rule system is sustained by consensus, and provides a basis for comparing cooperation across global commons.

papers.title: Evidence-Governed Adoption of Self-Generated Updates in Autonomous AI Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. Yet a plausible modification is not necessarily suitable for persistent adoption: candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect, and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline. We introduce Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a framework for governing adoption of self-generated agent modifications. EGE separates candidate generation from confirmatory adoption, evaluates frozen candidates on fresh paired audits, requires meaningful improvement on a prespecified primary objective, protects declared capabilities through reference-relative non-inferiority tests, and applies governance constraints before bounded canary deployment. We establish an evaluator-calibrated simultaneous lower-bound construction for a countable sequence of adaptively generated candidates. It combines candidate-wise Hoeffding bounds with independent calibration samples comparing the operational evaluator with a prespecified reference procedure. We also formalise reference replacement through bridge tests, derive a cumulative degradation bound along a versioned reference lineage, and provide an audit-planning condition relating effect-size margin, sample sizes, and acceptance probability. A Monte Carlo stress test illustrates calibration under candidate-dependent evaluator optimism; it is a stylised statistical experiment, not an evaluation of a deployed agent. The guarantees are conditional on bounded paired scores, fresh sampling, a valid reference-evaluation construct, and declared evaluation distributions; they do not establish universal agent safety or robustness to arbitrary distribution shift.

An agent can therefore change its behaviour without modifying its underlying model. Candidate changes may be generated from execution traces, user feedback, self-reflection, search, or optimisation.

The adoption problem has several properties that make it different from ordinary offline model selection. First, candidate proposals are often adaptive: the next proposal may depend on previous successes, failures, evaluator feedback, or deployment traces. Second, the candidate can modify the mechanism that will later produce evidence, for example by changing a prompt, retrieval policy, tool-selection rule, or evaluator-facing output format. Third, the system may optimise a narrow objective while being expected to preserve a much broader capability profile. Fourth, deployment is not a purely statistical event. A candidate can pass a benchmark and still fail under production load, interact unexpectedly with tools, or create external side effects that cannot be undone by restoring an earlier configuration.

These properties motivate a layered adoption design. The proposal mechanism is permitted to explore the design space, but it does not control the confirmatory audit process. The audit process measures a frozen candidate against prespecified comparators and margins. A governance layer enforces requirements that must not be traded against average task performance. Finally, an operational deployment layer limits exposure while collecting evidence about behaviour in the target environment. The layers are related but not interchangeable: a confidence bound cannot replace a permission boundary, and a canary cannot repair an invalid statistical comparison.

papers.title: Small Language Models for Inference-Capability Routing: Effects of Model Capacity and Prompt Optimization on Downstream Quality and Efficiency
papers.abstract: Optional reasoning, retrieval, web search, and tool use can improve large language model responses but incur unnecessary computation when activated indiscriminately. This study investigates whether prompt optimization can compensate for limited router capacity and whether classification gains translate into downstream efficiency. The proposed framework uses prompt-driven small language models to make four independent capability decisions, allowing multiple capabilities to be selected per query. Qwen2.5 routers ranging from 1.5B to 14B parameters are compared across five prompting strategies, followed by an evaluation of capability-specific optimized configurations using a fixed GPT-OSS-120B downstream model on 127 questions. Under minimal prompting, increasing router capacity does not consistently improve classification performance. Prompt optimization narrows the capacity gap for reasoning and calculator routing, whereas RAG and web search retain larger benefits from higher capacity. Similar classification F1 scores do not necessarily imply equivalent downstream behavior: false-positive activations increase unnecessary computation, while missed capabilities can reduce answer quality. The 14B router achieves a mean BERTScore F1 of 0.8408, compared with 0.8418 when all capabilities are enabled, while reducing average downstream token consumption by 68.7\% (8,837 to 2,764 tokens) and median downstream latency by 80.5\% (9.79 to 1.91 seconds). These savings exclude router overhead, which is measured separately in a different inference environment and increases with router capacity. The findings demonstrate that the relationship between router capacity, prompt design, and downstream efficiency is capability-dependent. Consequently, router selection must consider error profiles and routing overhead alongside classification performance.
papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate within inference pipelines that combine generation with retrieval, reasoning, and external actions. These mechanisms address different information and computational requirements. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies external evidence, web search provides access to online information, and calculator tools support arithmetic execution. Additional reasoning effort can help with difficult tasks, although its benefits depend on the input and downstream model. Studies on adaptive retrieval and selective reasoning therefore motivate allocating inference resources according to query requirements rather than enabling every mechanism uniformly (Jeong et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2026a).

Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate within inference pipelines that combine generation with retrieval, reasoning, and external actions. These mechanisms address different information and computational requirements. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies external evidence, web search provides access to online information, and calculator tools support arithmetic execution. Additional reasoning effort can help with difficult tasks, although its benefits depend on the input and downstream model. Studies on adaptive retrieval and selective reasoning therefore motivate allocating inference resources according to query requirements rather than enabling every mechanism uniformly (Jeong et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2026a).

This allocation creates a capability-routing problem: which inference capabilities should be enabled for a given query before downstream answer generation? Activating an unnecessary capability can introduce additional context, execution steps, and token consumption. Conversely, omitting a useful capability can deprive the downstream model of relevant evidence or computational support (Jeong et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2026a). Routing must therefore be evaluated in terms of both decision quality and downstream execution consequences. Existing research addresses several forms of adaptive inference. Adaptive-RAG selects among retrieval strategies according to question complexity (Jeong et al., 2024). Think When Needed selects between reasoning and direct inference for ranking tasks (Guo et al., 2026a), while HRBench compares thinking-mode switching strategies across models and reasoning domains (Ning et al., 2026). Select-then-Solve examines selection among complete inference paradigms (Zhou et al., 2026). These studies establish the importance of adaptive inference, but their routing targets differ from the independent selection of multiple capabilities for the same query.
