papers.title: Accuracy Is Not Welfare: Evaluating AI Buyers under Strategic Price Complexity in a Synthetic Duopoly
papers.abstract: AI buying agents may alter sellers' incentives as well as consumers' decisions. In a synthetic duopoly, we evaluate price-comparison pipelines on a fixed menu and in empirical correlated-equilibrium games. Calculator assistance selects an optimal offer 84.00% of the time, versus 68.57% under verified-total disclosure, yet disclosure has a 20.14-unit higher consumer-worst equilibrium surplus. A frozen-strategy holdout comparison favors disclosure, while re-solving equilibria under scenario resampling produces a range spanning zero. These model-based results show why accuracy, loss severity, seller incentives, and welfare incidence require separate measurement.

papers.title: How many LLM-labelled rows does a decision encoder need, and how wrong can the labels be?
papers.abstract: A decision encoder such as Laya reads a question with named options (for example, which department should handle a ticket) and a text, and picks an option. It reads both in one forward pass and returns a probability for every option, without writing any text. We ask how many LLM-written training rows such an encoder needs and how wrong those labels may be. We ran 19 fine-tunes of Laya (ModernBERT-large) on nested subsets of a 2,818-row pool and scored them on 1,065 held-out items from the same generator, so every test item is in-distribution and no out-of-family test was run. Accuracy rises from 69.4% before fine-tuning to 74.3% with 5% of the rows, 84.8% with 50% and 86.9% with all rows. The curve flattens, and a saturating fit with bootstrap intervals cannot pin down its plateau. Seed spread at 20% of the rows (s.d. 1.6 points) exceeds some of the steps between sizes. Giving small subsets as many updates as the full pool gains 1.9 points at 5% and 1.9 points at 20% of the rows (one seed; p=0.14 and 0.13), and at 20% that is below the 2.3-point difference between two ordinary seeds. A single run with 10% symmetric label noise shows no detectable change (-0.2 points, 95% interval -1.7 to +1.4); 20% costs 3.4 points and 40% costs 8.7 points. Confusable-pair noise at 20% costs 7.4 points, and under noise the model moves from over-confident to under-confident. An independent labeller disagrees with the gold labels on 3.5% of held-out items, and about half of its choice disagreements (16 of 33, leaving each item out of the partner map) name the partner option that the confusable-pair noise uses. Laya is +0.9 points ahead of a TF-IDF classifier trained on the same rows at full size (the interval includes zero) and +21.1 points ahead at 5% of the rows. Everything is synthetic, LLM-labelled and from one backbone, one trainer and mostly one seed.

papers.title: Recalibrating a Typed-Decision Model in an Afternoon: A Hands-On Recipe for Laya's Confidence Scores
papers.abstract: A typed-decision model such as Laya reads a text and a list of options that the caller defines, for example ticket categories, and returns a probability for each option. Code around it compares the top probability with a threshold to answer, abstain or escalate to a person. Earlier work reports, for a Turkish model, that temperature scaling can raise held-out calibration error (ECE). This tutorial gives a five-step recipe (measure, diagnose, fit, validate, deploy) in 130 lines of numpy with standard methods, none new. On 1,065 synthetic, LLM-labelled items the released Laya checkpoint has a pooled ECE of 0.073 but a bucket-macro ECE of 0.143 (0.127-0.184), the mean over buckets (questions grouped by type and option count): the 12-option bucket is over-confident by +0.22, the three-to-five-option bucket under-confident by 0.05, and they cancel. One global temperature makes pooled ECE worse (0.173); a cross-fitted temperature per bucket brings macro-ECE to 0.073 (0.078 over 10 fold assignments) and reaches 0.089 with 10 labelled items per bucket, but holding out one of seven evaluation sets gives 0.099. After the refit, a gate aimed at 10% error answers 46.3% of items (10.5% wrong) against 6.9% on the published confidences, but one cut-off per bucket on the published confidences answers 45.4%, so most of the gain comes from separating buckets. Confidence-only maps (Platt, histogram, isotonic) need 20 or more labelled items per bucket to approach the temperature; with 320 per bucket the lowest macro-ECE belongs to Platt. In these files the retrained checkpoints store no per-bucket table and the stored 12-option value 0.1006 is clamped to 0.5 at runtime; the refit helps 31 of 33 checkpoints on random folds and 21 with a set held out. Fit and test share one generator and LLM labels, so these are findings about these checkpoints and this data.

papers.title: Inverse Confounding Analysis: Part 2. Applications to Real- World Observational Data
papers.abstract: Unmeasured confounding factors in observational data may lead to biased estimates of the effect of an exposure on an outcome. Consequently, a central problem in causal inference based on observational data is sensitivity analysis with respect to unmeasured confounding. Existing sensitivity-analysis methods generally focus on worst-case bounds. We propose an exact method for quantifying the significance of confounding, defined here in terms of the complete range of analytical values of the stratification-based Risk Ratio over the set of all joint distributions compatible with the observed characteristics. We refer to the proposed method as Inverse Confounding Analysis (ICA) - it is described in [1]. This paper presents examples of applying ICA to several real-world statistical datasets and examines an important issue that has attracted criticism of the method: the practical feasibility of obtaining the input data required for its application. The results are compared with those of two other methods for confounding analysis, the E-value and the method proposed by Pena.

papers.title: Kobayashi distance to submanifolds in a Riemannian manifold
papers.abstract: We prove that totally geodesic hypersurfaces are at infinite Kobayashi distance in a Kobayashi hyperbolic Riemannian manifold. To do this, we prove a Schwarz lemma on minimal maps with a uniform control on their Laplacians. Finally we give a full characterisation of submanifolds at infinite distance on spaces of constant sectional curvature in dimension at least 4.

papers.title: Asymmetric Multimodal Learning with Decomposed JEPAs
papers.abstract:
Cross-modal alignment is the standard objective for building multimodal representations. We show that alignment as a \emph{sole} objective is lossy wherever modalities are informationally asymmetric---where neither can express what the other carries. Visual question answering is an obvious case: a question is a selective relational operator probing a dense visual field whose fine-grained features no query recovers, so what alignment preserves is not what the task requires. We prove an \textbf{Alignment Redundancy Bound}: alignment-only Dirichlet energy minimization retains at most the redundant information atom $\Red(Z; X_1, X_2)$, annihilating private modality-specific structure $\Unq(Z; X_m)$ and cross-modal synergy $\Syn(Z; X_1, X_2)$.
  We introduce \textbf{Decomposed JEPA (D-JEPA)}, which factorizes latents into an aligned shared core and private modality-specific fibers. The shared core retains most of the structure alignment targets; the private fibers recover what alignment discards, via contextual masked prediction and asymmetric cross-subspace independence. Under information asymmetry, alignment-only training undergoes catastrophic semantic collapse on compositional reasoning benchmarks, surviving only on binary queries. D-JEPA averts this collapse, substantially improving downstream accuracy over both alignment-only and alignment-with-reconstruction baselines, and restoring a positive multimodal synergy gap in place of the baseline's inverted gap. Information-theoretic audits confirm that D-JEPA recovers most of the mutual information available from a frozen backbone, and causal fiber-swap interventions demonstrate that the recovered information is causally localized in the private fibers.

Cross-modal alignment is the default objective for building multimodal representations. Its appeal is not merely practical: it rests on a specific and usually implicit claim about the data. When two observations X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} are equally informative views of the same underlying state ZZ—two simultaneous camera angles of one scene, or a dense image paired with an exhaustive caption—the task-relevant content of each view is content the other also carries, and forcing their latents to agree is the right thing to do. We call this the redundancy premise: that what matters about ZZ is shared across the modalities that observe it. Under the redundancy premise, alignment is not merely a convenient proxy for shared structure; it is the objective that recovers it, and anything alignment discards is, by construction, not worth keeping.

The premise is rarely true, and it is rarely checked. Real multimodal pairs satisfy it only when the pairing is dense and descriptive. Consider visual question answering: the image X1X_{1} encodes a dense field of objects, textures, and spatial relations, while the question X2X_{2} encodes a selective relational operator (e.g., “how many blue cubes are behind the cylinder?”). The two modalities are informationally asymmetric: neither can express what the other carries, and the information the task requires is not the information the pair shares.

papers.title: On the size of the defect set of an analytic matrix field
papers.abstract: In this note, we study the defect set of a symmetric analytic matrix field $M$ defined on an open set $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^d$ with $d\ge2$. A defect point $x \in \Omega$ of $M$ is defined as a point for which no eigenframe can be chosen continuously in any neighborhood of $x$. We show that the defect set $S(M)$ is contained in a locally finite union of analytic submanifolds of codimension at least $2$. The proof follows fairly directly from results by Parusinski and Rond (Trans. Am. Math. Soc., 2020) and by Kurdyka and Paunescu (Duke Math. J., 2008). This result can be applied in the context of the Landau-de Gennes Theory to estimate the physical defects of a nematic liquid crystal.

papers.title: On the randomized lattice-point count problem
papers.abstract: Counting (integer) lattice points in a convex body $K$ has a rich history, beginning with the famous circle problem imposed by Gauss in 1834. Clearly, the number of covered lattice points depends on the position, orientation, size, and shape of $K$ in a delicate way. In 1947, Kendall was the first to consider a randomized version of this problem by allowing random translations of $K$. In this survey, we aim to provide an overview of the current state of research on the \emph{randomized lattice-point count problem}, i.e.\ on the distribution of the lattice-point count under random rotations and translations of $K$. As it turns out, even the variance is far from being well-understood, leaving multiple open questions for future research. The motivation for the present work grew out of the author's research interest in a related combinatorial problem, dealing with the convex hull of all covered lattice points.

papers.title: Kezek: Splitting Mono Two-Person Conversations into Per-Speaker Tracks for Full-Duplex Dialogue Data
papers.abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models learn turn-taking, overlaps and backchannels from conversations recorded with one channel per speaker, but most available conversational audio is a single mono mix. We present Kezek, a model that turns a mono recording of exactly two people into one track per person with the original length and timing; overlaps and short replies ("yeah", "mm-hm") stay on the track of the person who said them. Kezek decides who speaks when and who is who once for the whole recording (stage 1: a two-voice activity model guided by a speaker fingerprint trained to be insensitive to phase), and a conditioned time-domain separator only carries out that decision (stage 2), with outputs that always sum to the input. Standard separation metrics miss the failures that matter for dialogue data, so we report short-reply retention, leakage onto the other person's solo, channel swaps and coverage. Against the open pipeline pyannote -> DialogueSidon on the same recordings, Kezek keeps more short replies (0.83 vs. 0.69 on Open Yap test; 0.80 vs. 0.71 over the other's speech on unseen telephone speech from CallHome English), mostly because it returns the whole recording while the external pipeline drops part of it (on the audio both return, reply retention is about the same: 0.859 vs. 0.865 on Open Yap); it also leaks less, swaps channels less often, and runs 4-5 times faster (about 230 hours of audio per GPU-hour). We also report negative results and an ideal-mask ceiling that locate the remaining gap: quiet replies under a louder voice. Code and weights are released under permissive licences.
papers.intro:
Full-duplex spoken dialogue models listen and speak at the same time [14, 3]. To learn when to interrupt, when to back off and when to say “mm-hm” without taking the turn, they are trained on conversations where each participant has a separate channel. Such recordings are scarce. Most conversational audio (podcasts, interviews, call recordings) exists only as a single mono mix.

Such recordings are scarce. Most conversational audio (podcasts, interviews, call recordings) exists only as a single mono mix.

Turning a mono mix into per-speaker tracks is usually done with a cascade: a diarization system decides who speaks when, and a separation or restoration model produces the tracks [12]. For dialogue data, three failure modes of such cascades matter more than average separation quality: 1. A channel swap puts a stretch of one person’s speech on the other person’s track, and the dialogue model learns the wrong turn-taking. 2. Short replies get lost. Backchannels are short, quiet and often overlap the other speaker; they are exactly what a full-duplex model needs to learn, and exactly what diarization tends to drop. 3. Leakage, the other person’s voice audible on a track, teaches the model to treat its own channel as containing both speakers. A data-preparation tool must also return the whole recording with the original timing, and it must be fast enough to process tens of thousands of hours.

papers.title: AnalogLayoutWorld: An Open Benchmark for Agentic Analog Layout Design
papers.abstract: Coding agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in software development, yet their ability to tackle long-horizon engineering tasks governed by physical constraints remains less understood. We study this question through analog circuit layout, which demands domain knowledge, geometric reasoning, and iterative interaction with design and verification tools. We introduce \textbf{AnalogLayoutWorld}, an open-source agent benchmark with 40 expert-reviewed tasks for end-to-end layout generation from fixed transistor-level netlists. It combines an integrated design environment with independent physical and post-layout electrical verification, as well as objective layout quality metrics co-designed with analog layout experts. Across 13 model--harness configurations, 91.1\% of attempts produce GDS layouts, but only 23.0\% satisfy the benchmark's acceptance criteria. We also evaluate Novara, an internally developed agent system, which achieves the highest reported aggregate score. Our analysis links performance differences to test-time scaling under fixed budgets, suggesting that reasoning efficiency and effective use of verification feedback help sustain design quality as task complexity grows.

papers.title: Spin-Boson Hamiltonians as Generators of Spin-Dressed Bogoliubov Dynamics
papers.abstract: Following Bach, Lieb and Solovej, quadratic Hamiltonians can be defined as generators of unitary groups implementing one-parameter groups of Bogoliubov transformations. We develop an analogous dynamical definition of generalized spin--boson Hamiltonians. For a single spin level, we review results of Guichardet and Derezi\'nski: the van Hove Hamiltonians, including the renormalized ones, are exactly the generators of affine Bogoliubov dynamics that do not mix creation and annihilation operators. For several spin levels, there is no analogue of this group, and we introduce spin-dressed implementations, that is to say the free flow of the fields is implemented up to bounded operator-valued displacements, which vanish at a rate measured by a so-called regularity scale and have a spin observable, the coupling map, as derivative at time zero. The one-particle Hamiltonian $\Upsilon$ and the coupling map are determined by the Hamiltonian, and the field obeys a quantum Langevin equation. Spin-dressed implementations in Fock space, at the finest scale and for form factors in $D(\Upsilon^{-1/2})$, are exactly the generalized spin--boson Hamiltonians, unique up to the spin Hamiltonian. At the roughest scale, the renormalized spin--boson Hamiltonian of a two-level system with ultraviolet-singular form factor and arbitrary tunnelling is a spin-dressed implementation, and the definition alone yields asymptotic Weyl operators on the test functions along which the coupling map is integrable, a dense set under standard assumptions.

papers.title: GraphInfer: Statistical Inference for Decomposable Graphical Models in R
papers.abstract: Decomposable graphical models combine closed-form maximum likelihood estimation with local model comparison, which makes structure inference practical with many variables. The R package GraphInfer provides one likelihood framework for decomposable models of continuous, discrete and mixed data, the last as conditional Gaussian models. Structure inference ranges from exact minimum forests and stepwise search to stochastic global search. Nested models are compared by likelihood-ratio tests whose null distributions are exact in finite samples: conditionally on the discrete data for edges with a continuous endpoint, and conditionally on the discrete margins of the smaller model for edges between discrete variables. Missing values are handled by EM, by structural EM, which reuses complete-data searches through a weighted pseudo-sample of expected sufficient statistics, and by multiple imputation; selected models are fit to the observed-data likelihood. The package also treats the graphical models induced by irreversible event accumulation on trees: a search over the compatible graphs whose tree moves overcome an obstruction to single-edge moves, fitting of the full accumulation model with measurement noise and bootstrap tests of the accumulation hypothesis. GraphInfer is an independent, pure R successor to the archived package gRapHD. The implementation is validated against independent references, and simulation studies inform its defaults.

papers.intro:
Undirected graphical models describe the conditional independences among a set of variables through a graph (Lauritzen, 1996; Edwards, 2000; Whittaker, 1990). Among them, decomposable models have a special computational position: their likelihood factorises over the cliques and separators of the graph, their maximum-likelihood estimates are available in closed form, and the effect of adding or removing one edge can be obtained from a few low-dimensional marginal models. These properties extend to mixed data through conditional Gaussian distributions, under the stronger requirement of strong decomposability (Lauritzen and Wermuth, 1989; Frydenberg and Lauritzen, 1989). They are what make a search over graphs feasible when the number of variables is large.

The R package GraphInfer supports the whole of an analysis with such models: a first overview of the dependence structure, the search for a graph, the fitting and testing of selected models, and the treatment of incomplete observations, for continuous, discrete and mixed variables. Its contribution can be organised around four themes. 1. A common inferential framework. Decomposable Gaussian, discrete and conditional Gaussian models are handled by one likelihood calculation, with one convention for model dimension, shared by all fitting, testing and search procedures (Sections 3 and 5). This includes likelihood-ratio tests that are exact in finite samples, for edges with a continuous endpoint and, conditionally on the discrete margins, for edges between discrete variables. 2. Structure inference at several levels of effort, from minimum forests, where the optimum is obtained exactly, through local stepwise procedures to non-greedy global searches (Section 4). 3. Inference with missing values, by EM for a given graph, by structural EM for an unknown graph, and by imputation (Section 6). 4. Models with a substantive origin. The graphical models induced by irreversible event accumulation on trees (Labouriau, 2026) show how the framework extends to a restricted, scientifically motivated class of graphs (Section 7).

We distinguish three levels throughout: the statistical model, decomposable Gaussian, discrete or conditional Gaussian distributions (Section 3); the inferential procedures, maximum likelihood, model comparison, structure selection, EM and exact tests (Sections 4 to 7); and their computational implementation, whose details are collected in Appendix A. Much of the package rests on classical results: the closed-form estimates and the clique–separator decomposition of decomposable models, the minimum-forest construction (Chow and Liu, 1968), the exact Beta distributions of Gaussian likelihood-ratio tests (Lauritzen, 1996), EM for graphical models (Lauritzen, 1995), structural EM (Friedman, 1998) and multiple imputation (Rubin, 1987). Other parts are new implementations of established methods: an accelerated stepwise engine, iterated local search over (strongly) decomposable graphs, a row-wise EM for large discrete tables, the extended BIC for conditional Gaussian models, and likelihood-ratio tests whose degrees of freedom compare both models on one support. Exact likelihood-ratio tests of a single edge in mixed models are classical (Frydenberg and Lauritzen, 1989; Lauritzen, 1996; Edwards, 2000; Tur and Castelo, 2011; Tur et al., 2014), and Lauritzen (1996, Proposition 6.27) states, with an outline of the proof, that along a sequence of single-edge removals the likelihood-ratio factors of edges with a continuous endpoint are independent conditionally on the counts. We give a complete proof, with the parameters in terms of occupied cells, and implement the resulting exact tests for nested mixed models differing by several edges, homogeneous or heterogeneous (Section 5.3, Appendix C). To our knowledge, three results are new: the weighted pseudo-sample by which structural EM reuses the complete-data searches for conditional Gaussian models (Section 6.2); an obstruction that prevents single-edge moves from reaching some accumulation-tree compatible graphs, and the connectivity of the tree moves that overcome it (Section 7.2); and, for accumulation on a tree, a likelihood in which each unit follows a single lineage that stops at a node, with event-specific measurement noise, fitted by EM and compared at two levels with decomposable graphical models (Section 7.3). Accumulation under observation error has a long history in models of tumour progression (Szabo and Boucher, 2002; Gerstung et al., 2009); Section 7.3 sets out how the formulation here is different.

The minimum-forest construction and its extension to penalised criteria and mixed data (Edwards et al., 2010) were made available, together with stepwise search, in the R package gRapHD (Abreu et al., 2010), since archived on CRAN. GraphInfer is its independent successor: it was written from the published statistical theory, contains no code from gRapHD, and retains the calling conventions of minForest() and stepw() so that existing analyses can be migrated. It is a readable reference implementation in pure R: it contains no compiled code, depends only on the base packages stats and utils, and uses igraph only optionally, for plotting. Its speed comes from the local structure of decomposable models rather than from a compiled language. A planned companion package, GraphInferComplex, is intended to speed up the identified computational kernels for the larger problems.

papers.title: Equidistribution of curves in hypersurfaces of low degree
papers.abstract: We prove that over $\mathbb{C}$, for any smooth projective curve $\mathscr{C}$ and any smooth hypersurface $V \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ of degree $d$ such that $n \geq 2^d(d-1)$, Faisant's equidistribution principle holds for $(\mathscr{C},V)$. In other words, for any reasonable set of jet conditions $W$, the moduli space $\mathrm{Hom}^e(\mathscr{C},V|W)$ of degree $e$ maps $\mathscr{C} \to V$ satisfying conditions $W$ converges in the Grothendieck ring of complex varieties, after renormalisation, as $e \to \infty$. This provides the dimension and decomposition into irreducible components of $\mathrm{Hom}^e(\mathscr{C},V|W)$ for $e$ large enough. The strategy follows Bilu and Browning's motivic version of the circle method, and Hase-Liu's framework for genus $\geq 1$.

papers.title: Quantum Boltzmann Equation for Static Correlation with Cumulant Kernel Closure
papers.abstract: We present a Quantum Boltzmann Equation for static correlation by mapping the Bogoliubov-Born-Green-Kirkwood-Yvon hierarchy to discrete atomic-orbital matrix mechanics via the Wigner-Weyl isomorphism to evaluate scattering of the correlated two-body cumulant. This Quantum Boltzmann Equation converges to the active-space static correlation limit and preserves pure $N$-representability constraints during the kinetic relaxation. To resolve scaling bottlenecks of explicit two-body cumulant methods, we project the two-body cumulant onto its lowest unitary invariant and evaluate a susceptibility-windowed orbital scattering scale via a single Coulomb-exchange contraction. Relaxing onto a hyperbolic-tangent cumulant attractor through Markovian collisional relaxation yields a parameter-free Quantum Boltzmann Equation Cumulant-Kernel that regularizes derivative cusps without thermal smearing. Using the collinear $\mathrm{H}_3$ exchange reaction, the symmetric $D_{4h}$ square $\mathrm{H}_4$ dissociation, the non-adiabatic avoided crossing in $\mathrm{BeH}_2$, the symmetric bond cleavage of $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$, the triple-bond dissociation of $\mathrm{N}_2$, the 11-molecule MR-MGN-BE17 dissociation test set, and the singlet diradical isomers of benzyne as case studies, we show that this kinetic relaxation resolves strong static correlation at zero electronic temperature.
papers.intro:
Conventional electronic structure theory isolates the molecular ground state by solving a static matrix eigenvalue problem Szabo and Ostlund (2012). In contrast, phase-space formulations treat the electron cloud as a fluid governed by kinetic transport equations, allowing the evolution of probability density to be tracked in position and momentum space. Wigner (1932); Weyl (1927) Early investigations by Dahl, Springborg, and others utilized the Wigner quasi-probability distribution to provide a phase-space view of density functional theory and atomic shell structures Dahl and Springborg (1982); Dahl (2009), while recent advances by Subotnik and coworkers have established phase-space electronic Hamiltonians and Wigner-transformed many-body electronic friction for coupled nuclear–electronic dynamics Subotnik et al. (2016); Dou et al. (2017); Dou and Subotnik (2018); Tao et al. (2024); Tao et al. (2025); Bian et al. (2025). In our previous work, we introduced the Quantum Boltzmann Equation Self-Consistent-Field (QBE-SCF) framework Chakraborty (2026). We demonstrated that relaxing the one-electron reduced density matrix via a Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) collision operator Bhatnagar et al. (1954) can entropically regularize mean-field singularities. By escaping the idempotency constraints of traditional solvers, QBE-SCF resolved the derivative discontinuities of the H3\mathrm{H}_{3} dissociation and the BeH2\mathrm{BeH}_{2} avoided crossing without invoking explicit multireference wavefunctions. To regularize diabatic traps, the single-particle system required the introduction of a finite electronic temperature to utilize macroscopic configurational entropy. To capture multi-reference electronic correlation at the zero-temperature limit without thermal broadening, we now extend phase-space collisional relaxation beyond the mean-field approximation.

In this work, we present a kinetic theory of multireference correlation and its cumulant-kernel closure. By coupling the one-particle distribution to the two-particle Wigner distribution via the first equation of the Bogoliubov-Born-Green-Kirkwood-Yvon (BBGKY) hierarchy Bogoliubov (1946); Born and Green (1946); Kirkwood (1946), we derive the Quantum Boltzmann Equation for Static Correlation (Q-BESC) which captures both the single-particle mean-field energetics and the kinetics of multi-body momentum scattering under the Born-Oppenheimer approximation. By mapping the BBGKY hierarchy to discrete matrix mechanics, we replace thermal smearing with zero-temperature collisional relaxation governed by the correlated two-body cumulant (𝚫2{}^{2}\bm{\Delta}) Kutzelnigg and Mukherjee (1999); Mazziotti (1998); Mazziotti (2006); Mazziotti (2007); Mazziotti (2012); Mazziotti (2016); Smart and Mazziotti (2021); Liebert and Mazziotti (2025). We demonstrate that this two-body collision operator resolves strong zero-temperature static correlation, and converges to the Complete Active Space (CASCI\mathrm{CASCI}/CASSCF\mathrm{CASSCF}) and Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) White (1992); Chan and Head-Gordon (2002) static correlation limits which coincide with Full Configuration Interaction, FCI, in few-electron systems. To overcome the combinatorial cost of explicit two-body tensors, we project this collision operator onto the lowest unitary invariant of the cumulant, closing the hierarchy within the one-electron density matrix to formulate the Quantum Boltzmann Equation Cumulant-Kernel (Q-BECK). Through case studies in static correlation spanning the H3\mathrm{H}_{3} collinear exchange reaction, the square H4\mathrm{H}_{4} (D4​hD_{4h}) dissociation, the BeH2\mathrm{BeH}_{2} avoided crossing, the symmetric double dissociation of H2​O\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}, the N2\mathrm{N}_{2} triple-bond cleavage, the ortho-, meta-, and para-benzyne biradical isomers, and the 11-molecule MR-MGN-BE17 dissociation test set at 5.0​Å5.0\,\text{\AA}, we show that Q-BECK delivers smooth, cusp-free potential energy surfaces and accurate biradical splittings. Finally, we analyze the scaling and memory requirements of Q-BECK to find quadratic one-body storage costs and near-cubic empirical time scaling in dense regimes, which reduces toward near-quadratic scaling in spatially extended systems via Schwarz screening of localized atomic orbitals.

papers.title: Stability for the Bray-Brendle-Neves Scalar Sphere Rigidity Theorem
papers.abstract: Let $(M^3,g)$ be a closed and oriented 3-dimensional Riemannian manifold with $\pi_2(M)\neq 0$ and let $A_{\pi_2}(M,g)$ denote the least area among homotopically nontrivial two-spheres in $M$. By a theorem of Bray-Brendle-Neves, $A_{\pi_2}(M,g)\inf_M R_g \leq 8\pi$ with equality characterizing the cylindrical geometry $S^2\times\mathbb{R}$. Motivated by Sormani's questions on volume preserving intrinsic flat stability for scalar curvature rigidity problems, we study the almost equality regime of this theorem. We build, using Sweeney's tunnel construction, a sequence satisfying $A_{\pi_2}(M_j,g_j)\inf_{M_j} R_{g_j} \rightarrow 8\pi$ with uniformly bounded volume and diameter whose volume preserving intrinsic flat limit is not the Bray-Brendle-Neves rigidity space, showing that stability fails in general. We then prove stability in two special cases: for sequences of rotationally symmetric metrics (with non-collapsing assumptions) and for sequences of manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature.

papers.intro:
Rigidity theorems are among the most interesting results in Riemannian Geometry. A typical rigidity theorem asserts that equality in a sharp geometric inequality forces the underlying manifold to be isometric, or closely related, to a distinguished model space. Once such a theorem is understood, a natural subsequent problem is to understand whether such a conclusion persists under almost equality. More precisely, one asks whether a sequence of manifolds for which the relevant geometric quantity approaches its extremal value must converge, in a suitable sense, to one of the corresponding rigidity models.

Rigidity theorems are among the most interesting results in Riemannian Geometry. A typical rigidity theorem asserts that equality in a sharp geometric inequality forces the underlying manifold to be isometric, or closely related, to a distinguished model space. Once such a theorem is understood, a natural subsequent problem is to understand whether such a conclusion persists under almost equality. More precisely, one asks whether a sequence of manifolds for which the relevant geometric quantity approaches its extremal value must converge, in a suitable sense, to one of the corresponding rigidity models.

In the context of scalar curvature, stability questions are particularly delicate. The scalar curvature of a Riemannian manifold is a pointwise trace quantity and places much weaker restrictions on the global geometry than, for example, sectional or Ricci curvature. In particular, positive scalar curvature is compatible with thin tunnels, wells, bubbles and other local modifications which can have dramatic effects on metric convergence while occupying arbitrarily small volume. For this reason, one cannot in general expect Gromov-Hausdorff compactness under scalar curvature bounds alone, and other notions of convergence, such as the intrinsic flat introduced by Sormani and Wenger [12], have become important tools in the study of these problems.

papers.title: $C^{1,\alpha}$ Regularity of $W^{2,2}$ $Q$-Valued Maps with Small Laplacian
papers.abstract:
We establish a regularity criterion for $Q$-valued maps $u\in W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega,\mathcal A_Q(\mathbb R^k))$, where $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ is open. If $|\Delta u|\leq\delta_*|D^2u|$ almost everywhere, with $\delta_*=\delta_*(n,k,Q)>0$ sufficiently small, then $u\in C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for some $\alpha=\alpha(n,k,Q)>0$, with quantitative estimates. The result holds for arbitrary $n\geq2$, $k\geq1$, and $Q\geq1$.
  The proof establishes uniform energy decay using a rigidity principle for positive-semidefinite matrix-valued measures with an aperture bound and approximately atomic divergence, extending the target-stress argument for the homogeneity gap in \cite{Luc26}. The argument relies only on first variation identities.
  As consequences, we obtain $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity for Dirichlet-stationary $W^{2,2}$ maps and for locally Lipschitz $W^{2,2}$ maps whose graph varifolds are stationary and have sufficiently small slope. Combining the latter result with Bellettini's Lipschitz sheeting theorem \cite{Bel25}, we establish $C^{1,\alpha}$ sheeting in the multiple-valued sense for two-sided stable minimal immersions whose singular set has vanishing $2$-capacity relative to the immersion, under suitable flatness and mass bounds. Our results allow us to reduce the proof of compactness within this class, under locally uniform mass bounds, to the conjecture that branch sets of stationary $C^{1,\alpha}$ multiple-valued graphs in codimension one have vanishing $2$-capacity.

Almgren’s theory of Dirichlet-minimizing QQ-valued functions [Alm00], developed as part of the regularity theory for area-minimizing currents and revisited by De Lellis and Spadaro [DLS11], establishes local Hölder continuity and a bound of n−2n-2 for the Hausdorff dimension of the singular set. Branching is compatible with energy minimization, and these conclusions do not in general extend to continuity of the first derivative: the 22-valued square root already provides an example. For maps which are just stationary with respect to the Dirichlet energy, much less is known. On 22-dimensional domains, Lin [Lin14] proved continuity, and Hirsch and Spolaor [HS24] subsequently established Hölder continuity and a sharp lower bound of 11 for the codimension of the singular set. These results concern maps in the natural energy space W1,2W^{1,2}.

The connection with [Luc26] also concerns the method of proof. We use a generalisation of the variational identities established there for the differential of W2,2W^{2,2} QQ-valued maps. The basic idea behind the energy-decay argument is already present in the target-stress argument used there to establish the homogeneity gap, although in that setting it is formulated for maps already known to be homogeneous. That argument relies on a rigidity lemma for positive-semidefinite matrix-valued measures with an aperture bound and atomic divergence, showing that the divergence must vanish. Here we extend this rigidity lemma to approximately atomic divergence, allowing the atomic loads to move and come together, and use it to establish uniform energy decay. The argument relies only on first variation identities and does not use minimisation properties, either directly or through previous regularity results.
